profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2026-01-27T13:41:47.011+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Composed by Xiāo Jí (蕭吉), Grand Master of Court Discussion with Special Ceremonies (Shàng Yítóng Sānsī 上儀同三司) and Founding Duke of Chéngyáng Commandery (Chéngyáng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng 城陽郡開國公).
All things naturally possess a body and substance.
The Sages modeled them after categories
and then established their names.
Thus it is said, "Names establish substance."
Without a name, it is the beginning of Heaven and Earth;
with a name, it is the origin of all things.
Because they are based on function and involved in use,
appellations are established.
The Lǐ Yún (禮云) states:
"When a child is three months old,
it is named with a cry."
Before its birth,
it originally had no name.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng 五行) precede all things,
their forms and functions relying on creation and transformation.
How could their names not be established first,
and then their forms and functions clarified?
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo (春秋元命苞) says:
"Wood (Mù 木) means 'to touch' (chù 觸)."
It touches the earth and grows.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Wood (Mù 木) means 'to sprout' (mào 冒)."
It means it sprouts from the earth.
The character follows 'cǎo' (屮, grass)
and the bottom part resembles its roots.
Its season is spring.
The Lǐ Jì (禮記) says:
"The meaning of 'spring' (chūn 春) is 'to stir' (chǔn 蠢)."
It is what produces all things.
Its position is in the east.
Shī Zǐ (尸子) says:
"'East' (dōng 東) means 'to move' (dòng 動)."
It is due to the activating qi (zhèn qì 震氣) that there is movement.
The Báihǔ Tōng (白虎通) says:
"The meaning of 'fire' (huǒ 火) is 'to transform' (huà 化)."
When the Yang qi (yáng qì 陽氣) is active,
all things undergo transformation.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Fire (huǒ 火) means 'to blaze upwards' (yán shàng 炎上)."
Its character shows blazing upwards,
being a pictograph.
Its season is summer.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn (尚書大傳) says:
"Why is it called 'summer' (xià 夏)?
Summer (xià 夏) is 'to nurture' (jiǎ 假)."
Nurture (jiǎ 假) means to summon all things
and raise them.
The Shìmíng (釋名) says:
"Summer (xià 夏) is to nurture (jiǎ 假),
meaning to broadly nurture all things
and allow them to grow."
Its position is the south.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn (尚書大傳) says:
"South (nán 南) is 'to bear' (rèn 任)."
It is when things are bearing.
The Yuánmìng Bāo (元命苞) says:
"The meaning of 'earth' (tǔ 土) is 'to emit' (tǔ 吐)."
It contains and emits qi (qì 氣) and essence (jīng 精),
thereby giving birth to things.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Earth (tǔ 土) is that which emits life."
Wáng Sù (王肅) says:
"Earth (tǔ 土) is a separate name for 'dì' (地, ground),
used as one of the Five Phases."
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Its character has two horizontal strokes symbolizing the space beneath the earth and the interior of the earth.
With a single vertical stroke,
it symbolizes things first emerging from the earth."
Its season is late summer.
Late (jì 季) means old (lǎo 老).
All things achieve completion at this time.
It is likened to the elderly king (lǎo wáng 老王) at the end of the four seasons.
Hence it is called 'old'.
Its position is the center,
center (nèi 內) means 'to connect' (tōng 通).
The Lǐ Dǒu Wēiyí (禮斗威儀) says:
"It obtains the upright qi (zhèng qì 正氣) of the imperial ultimate (huángjí 皇極),
contains the virtue of the yellow center (huángzhōng 黃中),
and is able to embrace all things."
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Metal (jīn 金) means 'to prohibit' (jìn 禁)."
The Yin qi (yīn qì 陰氣) begins to rise,
and all things are prohibited.
Earth gives birth to metal;
the character follows 'tǔ' (土, earth),
with strokes on the left and right,
symbolizing the form of metal within the earth.
Its season is autumn.
The Lǐ Jì (禮記) says:
"The meaning of 'autumn' (qiū 秋) is 'to sorrow' (chóu 愁)."
It is to observe and uphold righteousness according to the season.
Shī Zǐ (尸子) says:
"Autumn (qiū 秋) is 'sternness' (sù 肅)."
All things are reverent, respectful, and solemn;
it is the master of propriety.
The Shuōwén (說文) says:
"The earth reversing things is autumn."
Its position is the west.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn (尚書大傳) says:
"West (xī 西) is 'fresh' (xiān 鮮)."
Fresh (xiān 鮮) is 'to announce' (xùn 訊).
Announce (xùn 訊) means the appearance of things beginning to enter.
The Shìmíng (釋名), Guǎngyǎ (廣雅), and Báihǔ Tōng (白虎通) all say:
"Water (shuǐ 水) is 'level' (zhǔn 準)."
It levels all things.
The Yuánmìng Bāo (元命苞) says:
"The meaning of 'water' (shuǐ 水) is 'to flow' (yǎn 演)."
Yin (yīn 陰) transforms into fluidity and moistness,
spreading and moving stealthily.
Therefore, the character is formed
by two people (rén 人) crossing, with one (yī 一) emerging from the center, which is water.
One (yī 一) is the beginning of numbers.
Two people (liǎng rén 兩人) symbolize male and female.
Yin and Yang (yīnyáng 陰陽) interact to give rise to one.
Water (shuǐ 水) is the beginning of the Five Phases,
the converging fluid of primordial qi (yuánqì 元氣).
Guǎnzǐ (管子) says:
"Water (shuǐ 水) is the blood and qi (xuèqì 血氣) of the earth,
the flowing channels of sinews and vessels."
Therefore, it is called water.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) says:
"Its character symbolizes springs flowing side by side,
with a subtle Yang qi (yáng qì 陽氣) in the middle."
Its season is winter.
Shī Zǐ (尸子) says:
"Winter (dōng 冬) is 'to end' (zhōng 終)."
All things reach their final storage here.
The Lǐ Jì (禮記) says:
"The meaning of 'winter' (dōng 冬) is 'to store' (zhōng 中)."
To store (zhōng 中) means to conceal.
Its position is the north.
Shī Zǐ (尸子) says:
"North (běi 北) is 'to hide' (fú 伏)."
All things hide in winter.
Noble and humble are alike.
These are the seasons and positions of the Five Phases,
thus they are separated and explained.
The Heavenly Stems (Gān 干) and Earthly Branches (Zhī 支)
were established based on the Five Phases.
In the time of Xuānyuán (軒轅),
they were created by Dànào (大撓).
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) Yuèlìng Zhāngjù (月令章句) says:
"Dànào (大撓) observed the essence of the Five Phases
and divined by the positions of the Dipper's pivot."
He first created Jiǎ (甲) and Yǐ (乙)
to name the days,
calling them 'Gān' (幹, stems).
He created Zǐ (子) and Chǒu (丑)
to name the months,
calling them 'Zhī' (支, branches).
When there were matters concerning heaven,
days were used;
when there were matters concerning earth,
chén (辰, branches) were used.
Due to the distinction between Yin and Yang,
there are the names 'Zhī Gān' (支幹).
Each has general and specific meanings.
First, we discuss the general names,
then the specific appellations.
The general name 'Zhī Gān' (支幹):
The character 'Gān' (幹) has three different forms:
one is 'gàn' (幹),
the second is 'gǎn' (簳),
and the third is 'gān' (干).
Now, explaining the character 'gǎn' (簳):
These branches (zhī 支) and stems (gǎn 簳),
since they are paired and used together,
are like the branches, twigs, stems, and stalks of a tree
which together form the body of the tree.
Therefore, it is called 'gǎn' (簳).
Also, 'gàn' (幹) means 'to manage and assist' (gàn jì 幹濟).
'Zhī' (支) means 'to support and bear' (zhī rèn 支任).
With these days and branches (rì chén 日辰),
all matters are supported and assisted.
Thus, it is called 'Zhī Gān' (支幹).
And the character 'gān' (干)
also carries the meaning of 'gǎn' (簳),
like an object on a pole (gān 竿)
that can stand upright and be clearly visible.
Thus, it is also called 'gān' (竿).
Scholarly writings follow ease,
hence 'gān' (干) is more common.
These are the alternative names
for the cyclical characters. The *Shī Wěi Tuī Dù Zāi* (詩緯推度災) states:
Jiǎ (甲) means "to suppress" (押).
In spring, things open;
in winter, they close.
Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the *Lǐ Jì Yuè Lìng* (禮記月令) says:
Jiǎ (甲) means "to suppress" (押).
Yǐ (乙) means "to rub" (軋).
In spring, all things break open their shells
and emerge, rubbing their way out.
Bǐng (丙) means "handle" (柄).
As things grow,
each holds its own handle.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) says:
Bǐng (丙) means "bright" (炳).
In summer, all things are strong and large,
appearing brightly and distinctly.
Dīng (丁) means "pavilion" (亭).
"Pavilion" (亭) is similar to "to stop" (止).
The growth of things
is about to stop.
Wù (戊) means "trade" (貿).
Growth has reached its peak.
At its peak, it should become the pre-form for trade.
Jǐ (己) means "discipline" (紀).
Once things begin to form,
they have order and discipline.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) says:
Wù (戊) means "lush" (茂).
Jǐ (己) means "to rise" (起).
It means all things are lush with branches and leaves,
and those containing flowers
bend down and then rise.
Gēng (庚) means "to change" (更).
Xīn (辛) means "new" (新).
It means all things regenerate,
changing and becoming new again.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) says:
It means all things solemnly change,
and the fruits of their bloom are newly formed.
Rén (壬) means "to bear" (任).
Guǐ (癸) means "to measure" (揆).
Yīn (陰) bears in Yáng (陽),
and sprouts emerge from things in a measured way.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) says:
This is when all things are closed and stored,
bearing within below,
and sprouts emerge in a measured way.
Zǐ (子) means "to multiply" (孳).
The Yáng (陽) energy has moved,
and all things multiply and sprout.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
The Yáng (陽) energy arrives,
fostering growth.
Chǒu (丑) means "knot" (紐).
"Knot" (紐) means "to tie" (繫).
Continuous sprouting and tying into growth.
Therefore, it is said:
"Multiplying sprouts in Zǐ (子),
knotting shoots in Chǒu (丑)."
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
It refers to being at the juncture of beginning and end.
Therefore, it is named after "knotting and tying."
Yín (寅) means "to move" (移).
It also means "to draw" (引).
Shoots gradually emerge,
drawing and extending themselves,
moving out from the earth.
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Yín (寅) means "earthworms moving and life stirring" (螾動生).
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Yín (寅) means "to draw" (引).
It is the meaning of "to set forth."
Mǎo (卯) means "to cover" (冒).
Things grow large,
covering the earth.
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Mǎo (卯) means "lush" (茂).
It is the state of lushness.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Mǎo (卯) means "lush" (茂).
When the Yáng (陽) energy reaches this point,
things grow luxuriantly.
Chén (辰) means "to shake" (震).
Shaking, moving, and stirring quickly,
shedding their old form.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
At this month's time,
all things shake and grow.
Sì (巳) means "to stop" (已).
The old form is washed away.
At this point, it is finished.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Sì (巳) means "to rise" (起).
When things reach this time,
they are all completed and rise.
Wǔ (午) means "to oppose" (仵).
It also means "calyx" (萼).
In the middle month of summer,
all things are flourishing and grand,
their branches and calyxes spread out in Wǔ (午).
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Wǔ (午) means "to go against" (忤).
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Wǔ (仵) means "to grow long" (長),
"to be big" (大).
It means all things are growing long and large.
Wèi (未) means "dim" (昧).
The Yīn (陰) energy has grown,
all things gradually decline,
and their forms become dim.
Therefore, it is called "dim in Wèi (未)."
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Wèi (未) means "taste" (味).
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
At this time, things are nearing completion,
and all have flavors.
Shēn (申) means "to extend" (伸).
"To extend" (伸) is similar to "to draw" (引),
"to grow" (長).
Old age extends.
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Shēn (申) means "to groan" (呻).
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Shēn (申) means "body" (身).
All things achieve their physical form.
Yǒu (酉) means "old" (老).
It also means "ripe" (熟).
All things reach extreme old age and ripen.
The *Huái Nán Zǐ* (淮南子) says:
Yǒu (酉) means "full" (飽).
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Yǒu (酉) is like "to be like" (猶),
the meaning of "likeness."
At this time, all things shrink and form.
Xū (戌) means "to extinguish" (滅).
"To kill" (殺).
In the ninth month, killing is extreme,
and all things are extinguished.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
At this time, things decline and are extinguished.
Hài (亥) means "core" (核).
"Barrier" (閡).
In the tenth month, all things are closed and stored,
entering their core and becoming obstructed.
The *Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng* (三禮義宗) says:
Hài (亥) means "to prosecute" (劾).
It means the Yīn (陰) energy prosecutes and kills all things.
The Ěryǎ says about the twelve-year cycle:
When Tàisuì is in Yín, its name is Shè tí gé.
The Huáinánzǐ commentary says:
Gé means "to rise."
All things rise, receiving the yang.
Mǎo is named Dān è.
Dān means "to exhaust."
È means "to stop."
This means the yang qi pushes all things to rise,
while the yin qi exhausts and stops.
Chén is named Zhí xú.
Zhí means "to hibernate."
Xú means "to spread out."
This means hibernating creatures
all spread out and emerge.
Sì is named Dà huāng luò.
Huāng means "great."
This means all things are flourishing and great,
scattering and spreading out in abundance.
Wǔ is named Dūn zāng.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Chán qiāng
Dūn means "flourishing,"
Zāng means "strong."
This means all things are flourishing and strong.
Wèi is named Xié qià.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Xié means "harmony."
Qià means "union."
This means the yin wishes to transform,
and all things are in harmony and union.
Shēn is named Tūn tān.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Tūn tān means "great cultivation."
This means all things cultivate their vital essence.
Yǒu is named Zuò è.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
It is named Zuò è.
Zuò è means "to wither and fall."
This means all things are declining and falling.
Xū is named Yān mào.
Yān means "to cover."
Mào means "to envelop."
This means all things are covered and enveloped.
Hài is named Dà yuān xiàn.
Yuān means "to hide."
Xiàn means "to greet."
This means all things end in Hài,
big and small hiding deeply,
burrowing and lurking to greet the yang.
Zǐ is named Kùn dūn.
Kùn means "chaos."
Dūn means "primordial chaos."
This means the yang qi is in primordial chaos,
and all things sprout and bud.
Chǒu is named Chì fèn ruò.
Fèn means "to rise vigorously."
Ruò means "to follow."
This means the yang qi vigorously raises all things to rise,
and there is nothing that does not follow its nature.
Chì is the color of yang.
The Chūnqiū Wěi says:
Names for where the great yin is located
differ from the Huáinánzǐ and Ěryǎ.
These are all alternative names for the earthly branches and heavenly stems.
The general meaning is ultimately explained by the qi.
Therefore, they are all explained here.
The "body" refers to names based on form and substance,
while "nature" refers to meanings based on function and utility.
The bodies and natures of the Five Phases
benefit all things.
Therefore, they are combined and differentiated.
Wood occupies the position of lesser yang.
The spring qi is harmonious,
warm, gentle, and weak.
Fire is hidden within it.
Therefore, wood takes warmth and gentleness as its body,
and bending and straightening as its nature.
Fire occupies the position of greater yang,
blazing, scorching, and intense.
Therefore, fire takes brightness and heat as its body,
and ascending flames as its nature.
Earth is in the midst of the four seasons,
at the end of late summer,
when yang declines and yin grows.
It occupies the central position,
encompassing the four phases,
accumulating dust to become solid.
When accumulated, there is space.
Having space,
it is thus inclusive.
Becoming solid,
it is thus able to sustain.
Therefore, earth takes inclusion, dispersion, sustenance, and solidity as its body,
and sowing and reaping as its nature.
Metal occupies the position of lesser yin.
The west is the place where things are formed;
when things are formed, they become congealed and strong.
Lesser yin is clear and cold.
Therefore, metal takes strength and coldness as its body,
and transformation and alteration as its nature.
Water takes coldness and emptiness as its body,
and moistening and descending as its nature.
The Hóngfàn says:
Wood is called bending and straightening,
Fire is called ascending flames,
Earth is called sowing and reaping,
Metal is called transformation and alteration,
Water is called moistening and descending.
These are their natures.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The accumulated essence of Heaven and Earth becomes yin and yang;
the concentrated essence of yin and yang becomes the four seasons;
the scattered essence of the four seasons becomes all things.
The cold qi of accumulated yin,
when reversed, becomes water;
the hot qi of accumulated yang,
when reversed, becomes fire.
Although water is a yin substance,
yang is within it.
Therefore, the body of water is bright internally.
Although fire is a yang substance,
yin is within it.
Therefore, the body of fire is dark internally.
Wood is lesser yang.
Its body also contains yin qi.
Therefore, it is empty internally,
with flowers and leaves externally,
flourishing and delightful to behold.
Metal is lesser yin.
Its body is hard and sharp,
its destructive nature is external,
and internally it is also bright and illuminating.
Earth encompasses the four virtues.
Therefore, its body can combine emptiness and solidity.
The Hóngfàn Zhuàn says:
Wood is called bending and straightening, referring to the East.
The Yì Jīng says:
Wood on the ground is Guān (Contemplation).
This means that the wood emerging from the ground in springtime
is all bending and straightening,
with flowers and leaves delightful to behold.
Like a person's dignified demeanor and appearance.
Xǔ Shèn says:
Among things on the ground that are delightful to behold,
none surpass wood.
Therefore, the character "相" (xiàng, to observe) has "木" (mù, wood) next to "目" (mù, eye).
The ancient kings,
when ascending their chariots, had the rhythm of the luán hé bells;
when descending from their chariots, they had the measure of jade pendants;
during hunting, they had the three-drive system;
during drinking feasts, they had the rites of offering and returning toasts.
They did not conduct inspection tours without reason,
nor did they usurp the people's time.
This was because spring is the beginning of farming.
They had no greedy desires or insidious plots,
thereby following the qi of wood.
When the qi of wood is harmonious,
it follows its nature,
flourishing and bearing fruit,
to be used by the people.
The straight ones conform to the string,
the curved ones conform to the hook.
If a monarch loses dignity,
indulges in wine and debauchery,
imposes heavy corvée and taxes,
and hunts without restraint,
then wood loses its nature,
fails to grow in spring,
and is not used by the people.
Bridges and rafters will not conform to the ruler and compass.
Therefore, it is said that wood does not bend and straighten.
Fire is said to "flame upward."
That which "flames upward" is the south,
radiating brilliant light,
in the height of summer,
its *qì* reaching its peak.
Hence, it is called "flaming upward."
A king governs by facing the light.
This is derived from its symbolism.
In ancient times, enlightened kings faced south to attend to government,
gathering outstanding talents from within the seas,
accumulating them at court,
to assist in enlightenment.
They dismissed corrupt and sycophantic officials,
casting them into the wilderness,
to clear obstructions.
When the right people are appointed,
the world achieves great order,
and the ruler can "hang down his robes and do nothing."
The *Yì* takes *Lí* to be fire and light.
Double *Lí* means double brightness,
signifying that both ruler and ministers are enlightened.
When enlightened, one accords with the *qì* of fire.
When the *qì* of fire is harmonious,
it is true to its nature.
When true to its nature,
it can ripen and mature,
and people’s uses are accommodated.
When employed, they rise;
when abandoned, they cease.
If the ruler is not enlightened,
keeping worthy and good people at a distance and advancing sycophants,
abandoning laws and alienating kin,
executing loyal admonishers and pardoning criminals,
deposing the legitimate heir and establishing a secondary son,
and treating concubines as wives,
then fire loses its nature.
It rises even when not employed,
traveling diagonally with the wind,
burning ancestral temples and palaces,
and spreading to people's dwellings.
Thus, it is said fire does not "flame upward."
Earth is said to "sow and reap."
As for "sowing and reaping,"
planting is called *jià*,
and harvesting is called *sè*.
Earth is the Way of the earth,
through which all things penetrate and grow.
Hence, it is called "sowing and reaping."
Earth is in the center,
presiding over the four quarters,
and completing the four seasons.
The center represents internal affairs.
It is symbolized by palaces, marriage, and relatives.
In ancient times, from the Son of Heaven to the scholar-officials,
their palaces, residences, and sleeping quarters
all had proper distinctions of rank and measure.
Better to be frugal than extravagant.
Yǔ's humble palace
was praised by Kǒngzǐ.
Queens, consorts, and concubines on either side had their distinctions,
the nine clans had their order,
and kin had their benevolence.
This is how one should be
to serve as a model for the common people.
When the *qì* of central harmony is followed,
earth obtains its nature.
When it obtains its nature,
then the hundred grains become full,
and sowing and reaping are successful.
If the ruler indulges his desires,
enlarges palaces and terraces,
carves and engraves in five colors,
exhausts human labor,
makes no distinction between close and distant relations,
and has excessive wives and concubines,
then earth loses its nature.
When earth loses its nature,
then the *qì* is disordered,
and sowing and reaping fail.
Thus, the five grains do not grow abundantly,
and wind and fog cause harm.
Thus, it is said earth does not "sow and reap."
Metal is said to "obey transformation."
As for "obeying transformation,"
it means change and reform.
It changes according to a mold,
and its form is transformed into an implement.
In the west, things are already formed,
and the *qì* of killing is abundant.
Hence, when autumn *qì* arises,
hawks and falcons strike;
when spring *qì* stirs,
hawks and falcons transform.
These are the two extremes of killing and giving life.
Therefore, white dew becomes frost.
Frost is a manifestation of killing and striking.
A king trains troops,
assembles military affairs,
to punish injustice,
suppress violence and chaos,
to bring peace to the common people.
The rulers of ancient times
did not forget danger in times of peace,
to guard against unforeseen circumstances.
Therefore, it is said,
"Though the world be at peace,
those who forget war are in peril;
though the state and cities be strong,
those who love war will perish."
Killing and striking must accord with righteousness.
When it accords with righteousness, the *qì* of metal is harmonious.
When the *qì* of metal is harmonious,
it is true to its nature.
When it is true to its nature,
artisans smelt and cast,
transforming forms into implements.
If the ruler delights in aggression,
loves warfare,
covets wealth and bribes,
and disregards the lives of the common people,
and the people are agitated,
then metal loses its nature.
Smelting and casting will not transform,
remaining congealed, stagnant, and hard,
and many things will not be completed.
In autumn, all things mature,
and the hundred grains are ripe.
If one goes against the *qì* of metal,
then all things will not be completed.
Thus, it is said metal does not "obey transformation."
Water is said to "moisten downward."
As for "moistening downward,"
it means water flows to damp and low places.
The north is the ultimate *yīn*,
symbolizing ancestral temples and sacrifices.
It is where winter *yáng* begins,
and *yīn* ends.
Ending and beginning
regulate the seasons.
The *hún* *qì* of the dead ascends to heaven to become a spirit (*shén*),
and the *pò* *qì* descends to become a ghost (*guǐ*).
The essence *qì* scatters externally and does not return.
Therefore, ancestral temples are established
to gather what has scattered.
The *Yì* says,
"Dispersion succeeds.
The king approaches his temple."
This is what it refers to.
How can the virtue of a sage
be surpassed by filial piety?
Therefore, the Son of Heaven personally plows
to provide grain for offerings,
and the queen personally raises silkworms
to provide sacrificial robes.
This is the utmost reverence.
When reverence is utmost,
the spirits and ghosts repay it
with great blessings.
This accords with the *qì* of water.
When the *qì* of water is harmonious,
it is true to its nature.
When it is true to its nature,
then springs and fountains flow freely,
benefiting people's uses.
If the ruler neglects sacrifices,
disregards spirits and ghosts,
and goes against the seasons,
then water loses its nature.
Water bursts forth violently,
drifting, overflowing, and submerging,
destroying cities and towns,
and causing harm to people.
Thus, it is said water does not "moisten downward."
All things, in their beginning,
always begin from nothing and then come into being.
Therefore, the *Yì* has the Great Ultimate (*tàijí*),
which gives rise to the Two Forms (*liǎngyí*),
the Two Forms give rise to the Four Seasons (*sìxù*),
and what the Four Seasons give rise to.
Only when all things flourish and multiply
do all things then come into being and grow.
All are due to the two *qì* of *yīn* and *yáng*,
which dance, sculpt, and cast,
interacting with each other.
Thus, solitary *yáng* cannot generate alone,
and solitary *yīn* cannot complete alone;
they must combine
as in a furnace and forge.
Then all things transform and circulate.
Thus, Heaven has its phenomena,
its essence *qì* flows downward,
and the Way of Earth contains and transforms,
to provide for the beginning of forms.
*Yīn* and *yáng* wax and wane,
giving rise to life and death, achieving their functions.
To make clear that its Way is difficult to comprehend,
it cannot be fully understood without numerology.
Therefore, it is explained through numerology.
The manifest principles of numbers
are like snares and traps for catching fish and rabbits.
When yang leads and initiates,
yin assists its completion.
Those who exhaust the numbers of odd and even,
complete the way of mutual accomplishment,
and reach the source of transformation,
are detailed in the numbers of milfoil stalks and divination.
Seven and eight are still;
nine and six are moving.
Yang moves and advances,
transforming seven to nine.
This symbolizes the breath and spirit.
It clarifies the expansion of the yang way,
symbolizing the virtue of a sovereign.
Initiating without cease,
without yielding or holding back,
it is one step removed from the extreme,
yet still advances.
Therefore, nine is moving.
Yin moves and retreats,
transforming eight to six.
This symbolizes the dissipation of qi.
It clarifies the method of a minister.
There is yielding and holding back;
it merely initiates and responds.
When matters are close to the sovereign,
one rests in quietude to await orders,
and must retreat and yield to clarify one's duty.
Therefore, eight is still.
The *Yì* says,
“Divide into two to symbolize the two primary forces (liǎng);
hang one to symbolize the three primary powers (sān);
lay them down by four
to symbolize the four seasons.”
The remainder in hand is four sevens,
hence it is named seven.
There are four eights,
hence it is named eight.
These are the numbers of the still lines (jìng yáo).
The Xià and Yīn dynasties valued simplicity (zhì),
thus they used still lines for divination.
The remainder is four nines,
hence it is named nine.
There are four sixes,
hence it is named six.
These are the numbers of the moving lines (dòng yáo).
The Zhōu dynasty encompassed both simplicity and refinement (zhì wén).
Therefore, both moving lines and still lines were used.
The great expansion (dà yǎn) numbers of heaven and earth total fifty-five.
Jīng Fáng (京房) associated the ten heavenly stems (shí rì), twelve earthly branches (shí'èr chén), and twenty-eight lunar mansions (èrshíbā xiù)
to correspond to fifty.
The one not used
is the vital energy (shēng qì) of heaven,
which seeks to find the real from the void.
Therefore, forty-nine are used.
Mǎ Róng (馬融) considered the Great Ultimate (Tài Jí) of the *Yì*
to be the North Star (Běi Chén).
It gives birth to the two primary forces (liǎng yí);
the two primary forces give birth to the sun and moon (rì yuè);
the sun and moon give birth to the four seasons (sì shí);
the four seasons give birth to the five phases (wǔ xíng);
the five phases give birth to the twelve months (shí'èr yuè);
the twelve months give birth to the twenty-four solar terms (èrshísì qì).
The North Star remains in its position, unmoving;
the remaining forty-nine
rotate and are put into use.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said,
“The sixty-four hexagrams (zhēn huǐ liù yáo) originally had fifty;
those designated for use
are forty-nine.
The numbers of heaven and earth
are originally fifty-five.
Heaven's five and Earth's ten communicate;
Heaven's one and Earth's six communicate.
When counting them,
the qì can be combined,
and when combined, it should be reduced.
The great expansion reduces by five,
thus there are fifty.
For its use, one is reduced,
thus there are forty-nine.
What is not combined
cannot be reduced.
Now, summing the numbers,
fifty
is from Heaven's one to Earth's ten,
making a total of fifty-five.
This combines the numbers of generation and completion (shēng chéng).
If we only speak of the generative numbers (shēng shù),
there are only fifteen,
from one to five.
What the *Yì* symbolizes,
the lines exhaust with profundity.
Therefore, from heaven and earth downwards,
the numbers of the sun, moon, and so on,
are all encompassed by milfoil divination.
They circulate and transform,
endlessly through ten thousand generations,
and there are fifty-five.
The five is originally a combined number.
A combined number means that heaven and earth
each have a body.
Each body has one,
precisely corresponding as opposites.
Now, exceeding five,
this is the combined number of qì;
what is combined is not used again;
this is its associative meaning.
When associated, it becomes empty,
not corresponding to the real.
When it does not correspond to the real,
then events have no master,
which is why the laying out of milfoil does not use it.
Moreover, emptying one
means that hanging one symbolizes nothingness,
and nothingness cannot be symbolized.
Therefore, when the utility of being reaches its extreme,
the function of non-being becomes apparent.
Thus it is said,
“Seek the great undertaking (tài yè) to find good and ill fortune;
seek good and ill fortune to find the eight trigrams (bā guà);
seek the eight trigrams to find the four seasons;
seek the four seasons to reach the two primary forces;
seek the two primary forces to reach the Great Ultimate.”
The Great Ultimate
is the great cessation at its extreme,
the ultimate attainment of nothingness.
To abandon being to reach profundity,
to reduce the many to achieve the few—
this is what is meant.
Therefore it is said,
“The Great Ultimate has nothing further to symbolize,”
clarifying its emptiness and stillness,
which cannot be elucidated by words or symbols.
The mention of five
clarifies that although the myriad things are many,
their numbers do not exceed five.
Thus, in heaven, they are the five planets (wǔ xīng);
their spirits are the five cosmic emperors (wǔ dì).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
“In the past, Qiū (丘) heard from Lǎo Dān (老聃) that
Heaven has five phases:
wood, metal, water, fire, and earth.
Their spirits are called the five cosmic emperors.
On Earth, they are the five directions (wǔ fāng);
their guardians are the five sacred mountains (wǔ yuè).”
The *Wùlǐ Lùn* (物理論) says,
“Guarded by the five sacred mountains.”
In humans, they are the five viscera (wǔ zàng);
their manifestations are the five sense organs (wǔ guān).
The *Huángdì Sùwèn* (黃帝素問) says,
“The five viscera manifest in the five sense organs:
the eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and tongue.”
The five phases (wǔ xíng) alternately support and carry each other,
resting and flourishing, generating each other,
producing myriad things,
and operating without cease.
Therefore, it is called "movement" (xíng).
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* (春秋繁露) says,
“The qì of heaven and earth
is arranged into the five phases.
Indeed, the five phases are movement.”
The Xi Ci (上繫) of the Yi (易) says:
The numbers of Heaven are five.
Wáng (王) says:
This refers to one, three, five, seven, and nine.
Hán (韓) says:
The five odd numbers.
The numbers of Earth are five.
Wáng (王) says:
This refers to two, four, six, eight, and ten.
Hán (韓) says:
The five even numbers.
The five positions obtain each other,
Wáng (王) says:
The five positions are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
And each has a union.
Wáng (王) says:
This means water in Heaven is one,
On Earth is six;
Six and one unite in the north.
Fire in Heaven is seven,
On Earth is two;
Two and seven unite in the south.
Metal in Heaven is nine,
On Earth is four;
Four and nine unite in the west.
Wood in Heaven is three,
On Earth is eight;
Three and eight unite in the east.
Earth in Heaven is five,
On Earth is ten;
Five and ten unite in the center.
Therefore it says,
The five positions obtain each other,
And each has a union.
Xiè (謝) says:
Yīn (陰) and yáng (陽) respond to each other,
Odd and even numbers match,
Each having a union.
Hán (韓) says:
The numbers of Heaven and Earth,
Each have five.
The five numbers match,
To form metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
The Hóngfàn (洪範) chapter of the Shàngshū (尚書) says:
The five phases:
The first is water,
The second is fire,
The third is wood,
The fourth is metal,
The fifth is earth.
These are all their generating numbers.
The Yuèlìng (月令) chapter of the Lǐjì (禮記) says:
The number of wood is eight,
The number of fire is seven,
The number of metal is nine,
The number of water is six,
The number of earth is five.
These are all their completing numbers.
Only for earth is the generating number mentioned.
Heaven, by one, generates water in the north,
The position of a jūnzi (君子).
Yáng (陽) energy subtly moves beneath the Yellow Springs.
The initial movement has no second;
The number of Heaven combines with yáng (陽) to be one.
Although water is a yīn (陰) substance,
Yáng (陽) is within it.
Following the beginning of yáng (陽),
Therefore the number of water is one.
Extreme yáng (陽) generates yīn (陰);
Yīn (陰) begins at Wǔ (午).
The beginning also has no second.
The two energies of yīn (陰) and yáng (陽),
Each has its beginning.
It should rightly be one,
But it says two;
This is because yáng (陽) is revered.
Reverence already encompasses the beginning.
Yīn (陰) is humble, assists, harmonizes, and matches,
Therefore it can generate while the yáng (陽) number,
Even yīn (陰) is in fire.
Although fire is a yáng (陽) substance,
Its meaning follows yīn (陰) for matching with the beginning of yīn (陰),
Therefore it establishes its meaning from the beginning.
Thus the number of fire is two.
Lǎozǐ (老子) says:
Heaven obtains one to be clear,
Earth obtains one to be tranquil.
From this, we know that all have the meaning of one,
Singing and harmonizing from the same beginning.
Therefore it says,
Wood matches yáng (陽) movement,
And grows on the left in the east.
Growth means proliferation,
Proliferation means an increase in number.
Therefore the number of wood is three.
Yīn (陰) assists yáng (陽) in diminishing;
The yīn (陰) path turns to the right and resides in the west.
Being after yáng (陽),
Logically there is no equal meaning.
Therefore the number of metal is four.
The numbers of yīn (陰) and yáng (陽),
Begin a full cycle,
Then yáng (陽) reaches the center,
Encompassing the four phases.
The contained becomes ever more.
Therefore the number of earth is five.
These are all generating numbers.
All say they are based on the beginning,
but the numbers of completion are not yet clear.
Since the numbers are not yet complete,
they also cannot be used.
Yǐng Róng,
in *Chūnqiū Shìlì*, says:
The generative numbers of the Five Phases
are unable to transform and each accomplish their functions.
Water congeals but is unable to flow;
Fire has form but does not produce flame and light;
Wood's essence is brittle and its body is rigid;
Metal is strong but can be hewn;
Earth is barren and fragments easily.
Thereupon,
Heaven oversees the people with the number five,
and the ruler brings about their transformation.
A tradition states:
When paired with five, they are completed.
The reason for using five is that
it is Heaven's central number.
Thereupon,
Water, obtaining from five,
its number becomes six,
and thus it can moisten downwards.
Fire, obtaining from five,
its number becomes seven,
and thus it can flare upwards.
Wood, obtaining from five,
its number becomes eight,
and thus it can bend and straighten.
Metal, obtaining from five,
its number becomes nine,
and thus it can yield to transformation.
Earth, obtaining from five,
its number becomes ten,
and thus it can sow and reap.
Zhèng Xuán says:
If the numbers were to stop at five,
then Yang would have no match,
and Yin would have no paired principle.
Therefore, they are combined to form the numbers of completion.
The odd numbers, being Yang, initiate at the beginning,
serving as the standard and the measure.
The even numbers are the foundation of Yin;
only by obtaining Yang are they completed.
Therefore, Heaven begins with one,
generating Water in the North;
Earth completes it with its six,
making it flow and moisten.
Earth generates Fire in the South with two;
Heaven completes it with seven,
making it shine brightly.
Heaven generates Wood in the East with three;
Earth completes it with its eight,
making it spread out, grow long, flourish, and become great.
Earth generates Metal in the West with four;
Heaven completes it with nine,
making it hard, sharp, and refined.
Heaven combines energies in the Center with five to generate Earth;
Earth completes it with ten,
thereby completing all things existing between Heaven and Earth.
When combined, Earth's six is a pair to Heaven's one,
Heaven's seven is a pair to Earth's two,
Earth's eight is a pair to Heaven's three,
Heaven's nine is a pair to Earth's four,
and Earth's ten is a pair to Heaven's five.
When Yin and Yang each have their pairings,
only then
can their qi and natures mutually align,
and their transformations proceed.
Therefore, the movements of the four seasons
are completed by the Five Phases,
with Earth encompassing the four phases,
residing at the end of the seasons,
thereby completing them.
*Wǔxíng Zhuàn* and *Báihǔ Tōng* both state:
Without Earth, Wood cannot grow,
for its roots and core flourish and thrive.
Without Earth, Fire cannot thrive,
as it obtains Earth to establish its form.
Without Earth, Metal cannot be completed,
for it enters the mold to achieve its form.
Without Earth, Water cannot be contained,
as dikes and dams prevent it from overflowing.
Earth supports the subtle and helps the declining,
thus completing its way.
Therefore, the Five Phases all mutually require Earth.
Earth reigns in the four seasons,
and resides in the center,
not completing the seasons by its own named period.
Thus we know they all arise at the same time,
but rely on the principle of mutual generation.
A tradition states:
The Five Phases arise concurrently,
each distinguished by name.
Cháng Cóng, in his numerical principles, says:
The North's Hài Zǐ are Water;
its generative number is one.
Chǒu is Earth;
its generative number is five.
One and five combine to become six,
thus Water's number of completion is six.
The East's Yín Mǎo are Wood;
its generative number is three.
Chén is Earth;
its generative number is five.
Three and five combine to become eight,
thus Wood's number of completion is eight.
The South's Sì Wǔ are Fire;
its generative number is two.
Wèi is Earth;
its generative number is five.
Two and five combine to become seven,
thus Fire's number of completion is seven.
The West's Shēn Yǒu are Metal;
its generative number is four.
Xū is Earth;
its generative number is five.
Four and five combine to become nine,
thus Metal's number of completion is nine.
The Center's Wù Jǐ are Earth;
its generative number is five.
Moreover, Earth's position is in the center,
its inherent number is five.
The two fives combine to become ten,
thus Earth's number of completion is ten.
These two qi of Yin and Yang,
each complete one cycle.
Completing one cycle together results in the generative numbers.
Each completing one cycle results in the numbers of completion.
Yang, with its lightness and purity, rises to become Heaven;
Yin, with its heaviness and turbidity, descends to become Earth.
However, Yang, upon reaching the fifth,
enters the center,
for its nature is restless and swift.
Therefore, it completes one cycle together and enters the center.
Yin, upon reaching the tenth, only then enters the center,
for its nature is slow and dilatory.
Therefore, it is only after each completes one cycle that it begins to enter.
However, all Five Phases obtain the central qi before they are completed.
Earth resides in the center and reigns in the four seasons,
and all require Earth to complete them.
The Hóngfàn,
is a book of ancient creations.
Thus, it speaks of generating numbers.
The Lǐjì Yuèlìng,
is a book of seasons.
What it values is the completion of undertakings.
Thus, it speaks of completing numbers.
Only earth speaks of generating numbers,
because earth is valued for its ability to generate,
and also for completing the four elements,
which suffices to briefly explain it.
This is its meaning of being able to generate
and to complete.
Zhèng Xuán said:
"By matching heaven and earth,
one takes the principle of Yīn and Yáng."
Cháng Cóng said:
"By combining the numbers of the cyclical stems and branches,
one takes the day-hour for use."
Although the two explanations differ,
their general meaning is still similar,
ultimately converging with the meaning of the Yìjīng's 'Heaven One to Earth Ten'.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
"With one, establish;
with two, deliberate;
with three, emerge;
with four, multiply;
with five, combine;
with six, delight;
with seven, transform;
with eight, spread;
with nine, intense;
with ten, balance."
The five phases, with one establishing water,
one is a generating number.
By matching five with one,
it is the completing number of water.
Therefore, it says 'one establishes and six delights'.
Delight (xī) is the meaning of flourishing (xīng).
Two is the generating number of fire,
seven is the completing number of fire,
therefore it says 'two deliberate'.
Fire's ability lies in transformation,
therefore it says 'seven transform'.
Deliberation (móu) is because it is the beginning of change.
Three is the generating number of wood,
eight is the completing number of wood.
The five phases begin in the east,
therefore it says 'three emerge'.
Eight signifies growth and completion,
therefore it says 'eight spread'.
Four is the generating number of metal,
nine is the completing number of metal,
the west signifies achievement,
therefore it says 'four multiply'.
Due to the diversity of categories,
it is called 'nine intense'.
Five is the generating number of earth,
ten is the completing number of earth.
By taking the five of heaven,
and combining it with the ten of earth.
The meaning of the numbers is thus complete.
Therefore, five speaks of its combination,
and ten speaks of its balance.
Balance (jūn) is the meaning of completeness and preparation.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"The embryo (tāi) is mistaken (cuò) for dancing (wǔ) and continuous (lián),
to balance as one.
Movement combines in two, hence Yīn and Yáng.
Reception completes in three, hence sun, moon, and stars.
Order is arranged in four, hence seasons.
Establishment begins in five, hence the elements (phases).
Movement spreads in six, hence pitches.
Emergence divides in seven, hence constellations.
Transformation sprouts in eight, hence wind.
Pervasiveness reaches its extreme in nine, hence provinces.
Emission completes in ten, hence merit is accomplished and numbers cease."
These, combining warp and weft,
collectively illustrate that the numbers of generation and completion of the five phases do not exceed ten.
As for the cyclical stem and branch numbers,
there are two types.
First, general numbers;
second, specific numbers.
Now, we first discuss general numbers,
then specific numbers.
General numbers refer to
the ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches.
Why there are ten stems
corresponds to the great numbers of heaven and earth.
The Yìjīng Xìcí states:
"Heaven's numbers are five,
Earth's numbers are five."
The numbers of heaven and earth
do not exceed ten.
Therefore, the stems culminate at ten.
Ten governs the day,
and ten days make one xún (period of ten days).
Why there are twelve branches:
The Lǐjì Jīmìngzhǐ states:
"The government is arranged in twelve,
with an order of hierarchy."
The Yuánshénqì states:
"Three threes participate in action,
four fours mutually support."
Heaven has the qi of four seasons,
with three months forming one season.
Therefore, it says 'three threes participate in action,
four fours mutually support'.
Heaven, Earth, and humanity are called the Sāncái.
These three
are the constant numbers for the generation of things.
Consequently, each generates three,
originating from three and ending in nine,
thus making twelve.
The Yuánmìngbāo states:
"Numbers complete in three,
therefore they combine in three."
Three months.
Yáng culminates in nine,
therefore one season is ninety days.
The branches symbolize the months,
and twelve months make one year.
This concludes the discussion of general numbers.
Regarding the separate numbers:
For the earthly branches' numbers,
Zǐ is nine,
Chǒu is eight,
Yín is seven,
Mǎo is six,
Chén is five,
Sì is four,
Wǔ is nine,
Wèi is eight,
Shēn is seven,
Yǒu is six,
Xū is five,
Hài is four.
The Tàixuán Jīng says that Zǐ and Wǔ are nine
because yang arises at Zǐ
and ends at Wǔ;
yin arises at Wǔ
and ends at Zǐ.
Therefore, Zǐ and Wǔ are in opposition,
and they are where the two qì of yin and yang arise.
Yín is the beginning of yang,
and Shēn is the beginning of yin.
Counting leftward from where it arises,
the number is fixed at where it begins.
Therefore, counting from Zǐ to Shēn gives nine,
and counting from Wǔ to Yín also gives nine,
which is why Zǐ and Wǔ are nine.
Chǒu and Wèi are in opposition.
Counting from Chǒu to Shēn gives eight,
and counting from Wèi to Yín also gives eight,
which is why Chǒu and Wèi are eight.
Yín and Shēn are in opposition.
Counting from Yín to Shēn gives seven,
and counting from Shēn to Yín also gives seven,
which is why Yín and Shēn are seven.
Mǎo and Yǒu are in opposition.
Counting from Mǎo to Shēn gives six,
and counting from Yǒu to Yín also gives six,
which is why Mǎo and Yǒu are six.
Chén and Xū are in opposition.
Counting from Chén to Shēn gives five,
and counting from Xū to Yín also gives five,
which is why Chén and Xū are five.
Sì and Hài are in opposition.
Counting from Sì to Shēn gives four,
and counting from Hài to Yín also gives four,
which is why Sì and Hài are four.
It also says,
the number of yang culminates at nine,
and Zǐ and Wǔ are the warp of heaven and earth,
hence the extreme number of yang is taken.
From Chǒu and Wèi downwards,
each number is reduced by one,
from eight to four,
the principle is self-evident.
For the celestial stems' numbers:
Jiǎ is nine,
Yǐ is eight,
Bǐng is seven,
Dīng is six,
Wù is five,
Jǐ is nine,
Gēng is eight,
Xīn is seven,
Rén is six,
Guǐ is five.
The Tàixuán Jīng says that Jiǎ and Jǐ are nine
because Jiǎ begins with Jiǎzǐ,
and since it begins with Zǐ, it is nine.
Jǐ pairs with Jiǎ,
hence it is also nine with Jiǎ.
Yǐ begins with Yǐchǒu,
and since it begins with Chǒu, it is eight.
Yǐ pairs with Gēng,
and is also eight with Gēng.
Bǐng begins with Bǐngyín,
and since it begins with Yín, it is seven.
Xīn pairs with Bǐng,
and is also seven with Bǐng.
Dīng begins with Dīngmǎo,
and since it begins with Mǎo, it is six.
Dīng pairs with Rén,
and is also six with Rén.
Wù begins with Wùchén,
and since it begins with Chén, it is five.
Guǐ pairs with Wù,
and is also five with Wù.
There are twelve branches,
and those in opposition share the same number,
hence from nine to four.
There are only ten stems,
and those that pair share the same number,
hence from nine to five.
It also says,
the branches follow the earth,
hence their numbers end in yin,
with four being even.
The stems follow heaven,
hence their numbers end in yang,
with five being odd.
Five then stops at the five phases (qì).
Four then culminates at the four seasons.
Not exceeding nine
is the extreme number of yang.
For the numbers of the five phases and the stems and branches:
in the *xiāng* (auxiliary) state, multiply by two;
in the *wáng* (prosperous) state, multiply by ten and then by two;
in the *xiū* (leisure) state, it is as per the original;
in the *qiú* (imprisoned) or *sǐ* (dead) state, halve it.
By multiplying in these four ways,
the numbers become inexhaustible.
This is all according to the increase and decrease of qì.
When qì is strong, the number is greater;
when qì declines, the number is smaller.
Nàyīn shù zhě,
refers to the sound associated with a person's birth year.
The sounds are Gōng, Shāng, Jué, Zhǐ, Yǔ.
Nà means to take these sounds,
to determine the inherent nature.
The Yuè Wěi states,
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Qiū sets the nature by blowing the pitch pipes."
One word yields earth, called Gōng.
Three words yield fire, called Zhǐ.
Five words yield water, called Yǔ.
Seven words yield metal, called Shāng.
Nine words yield wood, called Jué.
These are all yang numbers.
Generally, the Five Phases have three types of numbers: birth numbers, strong numbers, and old numbers.
Wood's birth number is three,
strong number eight,
old number nine.
Fire's birth number is two,
strong number seven,
old number three.
Earth's birth number is five,
strong number ten,
old number one.
Metal's birth number is four,
strong number nine,
old number seven.
Water's birth number is one,
strong number six,
old number five.
Guǎn Lù said,
"Earth's old number is one because
earth is the master of all things,
everything returns to it,
hence it is one."
"The Three Powers interact and human principles are complete.
The virtue of fire
takes its meaning from the Three Powers.
Therefore, its old number is three."
"Water corresponds to the Five Planets above,
and the Five Zàng organs below.
Therefore, water's old number is five."
"Metal corresponds to the Seven Luminaries,
therefore metal's old number is seven."
"Wood is the Nine Stars in heaven,
the Nine Provinces on earth,
and the nine orifices in humans.
Therefore, wood's old number is nine."
First are the birth numbers,
next the strong numbers,
then the old numbers.
Nàyīn discusses one's intrinsic nature,
therefore it uses the final numbers.
This explanation is still incomplete.
All things are endowed with the Qi of the Five Constants,
which transform and combine to create living beings.
After birth,
they must reach maturity.
After maturity,
there must be decline and old age.
Hence, there are these three meanings.
The way of being human,
from maturity to old age,
is invariably based on ritual and righteousness to establish oneself.
However, among those who uphold ritual and righteousness,
none do not have a beginning,
but few see it through to the end.
Now we discuss the Nàyīn affiliation of a person.
Without people, ritual and righteousness cannot be practiced.
Therefore, the numbers for old age, ritual, and righteousness clarify it.
"One word yields earth" means
earth, with its encompassing and profound virtue, high position, acts as ruler.
The ruler is the lord of the people;
the lord is unrivaled,
the initiator of speech,
hence its number is one.
"Three words yields fire" means
fire represents ritual,
with filial piety and reverence as primary,
not daring to abandon the virtue of birth,
therefore its number is three,
following the wood number.
Water occupies a yin position,
the way of a minister.
Earth can control water,
like a ruler controls a minister.
If allowed, it flows;
if obstructed, it stops.
Water is not self-reliant,
therefore it follows the earth number five.
Metal represents righteousness,
righteousness is the way of husband and wife.
The wife is not self-reliant;
she has the righteousness of following her husband.
Fire is the husband of metal,
therefore the fire number seven is used.
Wood represents benevolence and filial piety.
Metal can overcome wood,
symbolizing ancestral temples.
The Shì Jīng says,
"Metal is the bones,
wood is the coffin."
This illustrates metal and wood for matters of spirits and gods,
to be served with reverence.
Therefore, wood follows the metal number,
hence its number is nine.
One shows the virtue of the ruler,
two obedience to parents,
three the integrity of a minister,
four reverence and following one's husband,
five serving spirits and gods.
This completes ritual and righteousness,
and human affairs are concluded.
Therefore, Nàyīn uses these numbers.
As for Nàyīn,
Zǐ and Wǔ belong to Gēng,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Zhèn hexagram.
Chǒu and Wèi belong to Xīn,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Xùn hexagram.
Yín and Shēn belong to Wù,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Kǎn hexagram.
Mǎo and Yǒu belong to Jǐ,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Lí hexagram.
Chén and Xū belong to Bǐng,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Gèn hexagram.
Sì and Hài belong to Dīng,
corresponding to the Dìzhī of the Duì hexagram.
"One word yields earth" means
the Běnmìng is Gēngzǐ.
Zǐ belongs to Gēng,
and counting one word
yields this.
"Three words yields fire" means
the Běnmìng is Bǐngyín.
Yín belongs to Wù.
Counting from Bǐng to Wù,
there are three.
"Five words yields water" means
the Běnmìng is Rénxū.
Xū belongs to Bǐng,
counting from Rén to Bǐng,
there are five.
"Seven words yields metal" means
the Běnmìng is Rénshēn.
Shēn belongs to Wù,
counting from Rén to Wù,
there are seven.
"Nine words yields wood" means
the Běnmìng is Jǐsì.
Sì belongs to Dīng,
counting from Jǐ to Dīng,
there are nine.
The sixty Jiǎzǐ cycles
all follow this pattern.
The earthly branches belong to the eight trigrams,
and for Nàyīn,
they are all taken in sequence and opposing pairs,
like Zǐ and Wǔ belong to Gēng,
Zǐ and Wǔ are opposing pairs.
The rest follow the same rule.
Indeed, the Yang emits and the Yin transforms.
Therefore, the reception of *qì* and the shaping of forms
all depend on Yin and Yang
for their development.
This is why all that pertains to humans
is expressed in Yang numbers.
The reason why *zǐ* and *wǔ* belong to *Gēng*, for example, is this:
Qián is the father,
Kūn is the mother,
and they have six children in total.
Thus it is said,
Qián has three sons:
Zhèn, Kǎn, and Gèn.
Kūn has three daughters:
Xùn, Lí, and Duì.
Yin and Yang generate each other,
so one seeks daughters from Qián
and sons from Kūn.
Therefore, Qián's first search yields Xùn, called the eldest daughter;
a second search yields Lí,
called the middle daughter;
and a third search yields Duì,
called the youngest daughter.
Kūn's first search yields Zhèn,
called the eldest son;
a second search yields Kǎn,
called the middle son;
and a third search yields Gèn,
called the youngest son.
Jiǎ is the beginning of the Yang *gān*;
it is taken from the three lower lines of Qián.
Rén is the end of the Yang *gān*;
it is taken from the three upper lines of Qián.
Yǐ is the beginning of the Yin *gān*;
it is taken from the three lower lines of Kūn.
Guǐ is the end of the Yin *gān*;
it is taken from the three upper lines of Kūn.
There remain six *gān*.
The Yang *gān* are assigned to the sons,
and the Yin *gān* to the daughters.
After Jiǎ and Yǐ,
comes Bǐng and Dīng.
Therefore, Bǐng is assigned to the youngest son, Gèn,
and Dīng is assigned to the youngest daughter, Duì.
After Bǐng and Dīng,
comes Wù and Jǐ.
Therefore, Wù is assigned to the middle son, Kǎn,
and Jǐ is assigned to the middle daughter, Lí.
After Wù and Jǐ,
comes Gēng and Xīn.
Therefore, Gēng is assigned to the eldest son, Zhèn,
and Xīn is assigned to the eldest daughter, Xùn.
Thus, assignments proceed from younger to elder,
from small to great,
and from subtle to manifest.
After assigning the *gān*,
the *zhī* are assigned.
Zhèn is the eldest son.
Therefore, its first line, *chūjiǔ*, obtains the *zǐ* of Qián;
the fourth line, *jiǔsì*, obtains the *wǔ* of Qián.
Zhèn corresponds to the *gān* Gēng,
thus *zǐ* and *wǔ* belong to Gēng.
Xùn is the eldest daughter.
After *zǐ* comes *chǒu*;
thus its first line, *chūliù*, obtains the *chǒu* of Kūn.
After *wǔ* comes *wèi*;
the fourth line, *liùsì*, obtains the *wèi* of Kūn.
Xùn corresponds to the *gān* Xīn,
thus *chǒu* and *wèi* belong to Xīn.
Kǎn is the middle son.
After *chǒu* comes *yín*;
its first line, *chūliù*, obtains the *yín* of Qián.
After *wèi* comes *shēn*;
the fourth line, *liùsì*, obtains the *shēn* of Qián.
Kǎn corresponds to the *gān* Wù,
thus *yín* and *shēn* belong to Wù.
Lí is the middle daughter.
After *yín* comes *mǎo*;
thus its first line, *chūjiǔ*, obtains the *mǎo* of Kūn.
After *shēn* comes *yǒu*;
the fourth line, *jiǔsì*, obtains the *yǒu* of Kūn.
Lí corresponds to the *gān* Jǐ,
thus *mǎo* and *yǒu* belong to Jǐ.
Gèn is the youngest son.
After *mǎo* comes *chén*;
thus its first line, *chūliù*, obtains the *chén* of Qián.
After *yǒu* comes *xū*;
the fourth line, *liùsì*, obtains the *xū* of Qián.
Gèn corresponds to the *gān* Bǐng,
thus *chén* and *xū* belong to Bǐng.
Duì is the youngest daughter.
After *chén* comes *sì*;
thus its first line, *chūjiǔ*, obtains the *sì* of Kūn.
After *xū* comes *hài*;
the fourth line, *jiǔsì*, obtains the *hài* of Kūn.
Duì corresponds to the *gān* Dīng,
thus *sì* and *hài* belong to Dīng.
The six children take *gān*,
while Qián and Kūn have the remainder.
They take *zhī*,
all obtained from Qián and Kūn.
Yang is taken from Qián,
Yin is taken from Kūn.
All are received from the parents,
thus the six children conjointly govern the twelve *chén*.
Human *nàyīn*
are all inherited from this.
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Rén, and Guǐ
are not considered *nàyīn*
because they belong to Qián and Kūn.
Someone asked:
When the six children use *gān*, they take those not used by the parents;
when they use *zhī*, why are they all the same as the parents?
The answer is:
*Gān* are Yang,
and Yang is odd in nature,
so it is directly obtained and used once.
*Zhī* are Yin,
and Yin is even in nature,
so they are used by going twice.
Moreover, divination by tortoise shell uses days,
thus it directly seeks from the *gān*.
Therefore, the omens are divided into ten parts.
Divination by yarrow stalks uses *chén*,
directly seeking from the *zhī*.
Therefore, the "flying and hidden" six lines
all discuss the twelve *zhī*.
Although the forms are not combined,
they must be matched to clarify their meaning.
*Gān* are considered superior.
Therefore, they must be established first, and only then are the *zhī* sought.
Although divination by yarrow stalks does not directly use *gān*,
it still requires the assistance of *gān*
to manifest its significance.
This is like tortoise shell divination determining the twelve *zhī*;
although the omen itself has no *zhī* image,
it must be discussed by approximation.
Although divination by yarrow stalks omits three Jiǎ, three Rén, three Yǐ, and three Guǐ,
it also approximates the virtual to seek the real.
Let us set the *gān* in motion:
First, beginning with the parents,
then reaching the six children.
Jiǎ is assigned to Qián,
Yǐ to Kūn,
Bǐng to Gèn,
Dīng to Duì,
Wù to Kǎn,
Jǐ to Lí,
Gēng to Zhèn,
and Xīn to Xùn.
After traversing the eight *guà*,
Rén returns to Qián,
and then Guǐ returns to Kūn.
The ten *gān* are located in the six lines;
Qián and Kūn hold the honored positions,
taking their beginning and end, which is logical.
Each entity receives two *gān*.
Since the *zhī* are directly used in the lines,
each *guà* is fully equipped.
Yang *guà* take their Yang *zhī*,
Yin *guà* take their Yin *zhī*.
Four *guà* are entirely Yang,
and four *guà* are entirely Yin,
not precisely the same as the parents.
When Fúxī drew the eight *guà* as three lines,
they encompassed Heaven, Earth, and Man.
Therefore, when dividing the *gān*,
each *guà* takes three.
Qián and Kūn occupy the beginning,
thus they take Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Later, Shénnóng reiterated this,
considering them the eight pure *zǐ*.
There is a principle of recurrence.
Thus, the six *gān* of the *guà* are all the same as the parents,
without any distinction.
Therefore, later *guà* take Rén and Guǐ.
As for Jiǎ, Yǐ, Rén, and Guǐ,
each lacking three,
they are all arranged within the realm of virtual use.
They are not entirely absent,
because Yin has the meaning of following Yang.
The Nine Palaces
are divided above among the heavens,
and separated below among the earth,
each with nine positions.
The heavens have the twenty-eight lunar mansions [èrshíbā xiù]
and the Nine Stars of the Northern Dipper [Běidǒu jiǔxīng].
The earth has the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the center.
They are distributed among the Nine Domains [Jiǔyǒu].
They are called palaces [gōng]
because they are all places where spirits [shén] reside and roam.
Therefore, they are named palaces.
Zhèng Sīnóng [鄭司農] said:
The Grand Unity [Tàiyī] traverses the palaces of the Eight Trigrams [Bāguà],
and every four times it enters the center.
The center
is where the earth spirits reside,
hence it is called the Nine Palaces.
The Yìwěi Gān Záo Dù [易緯乾鑿度] says:
The Yì [易] speaks of the Way [dào] as one yīin [陰] and one yáng [陽].
Therefore, the Grand Unity takes these numbers
to traverse the Nine Palaces.
The Yì [易] says:
Heaven is one, Earth is two;
Heaven is three, Earth is four;
Heaven is five, Earth is six;
Heaven is seven, Earth is eight;
Heaven is nine, Earth is ten.
The numbers of Heaven and Earth
sum to fifty-five.
For the application of the Nine Palaces,
one is subtracted for Heaven,
two for Earth,
and three for humanity.
The remainder is forty-nine,
which corresponds to the number of yarrow stalks [shīcè].
Further, four is subtracted for the four seasons,
leaving forty-five.
The five [wǔ] refers to the Five Phases [Wǔxíng],
the forty refers to the completion number of the Five Phases.
Combined, it is the number for one season.
They are distributed among the five directions.
Each direction having nine
is the number of days in one season, ninety days;
the four directions complete the four seasons.
The three palaces facing each other,
with fifteen as a stop,
is the number for one qì [氣],
making twenty-four qì [二十四氣].
The Shàngshū Gōngfàn [尚書供範] says:
First is one, called
the Five Phases [Wǔxíng].
Its position is in the north,
the beginning of yáng [陽] energy,
where all things are about to sprout.
Next is two, called
Reverently Use the Five Matters [Jìngyòng Wǔshì].
Its position is in the southwest,
humble and approaching virtue,
with court audiences and auspicious celebrations.
Next is three, called
Agriculturally Use the Eight Policies [Nóngyòng Bāzhèng].
Its position is in the east,
sowing and planting all grains,
hemp, ramie, silkworms, and mulberry.
Next is four, called
Harmoniously Use the Five Records [Xiéyòng Wǔjì].
Its position is in the southeast,
with sun, moon, stars,
clouds and rain arising together.
Next is five, called
Establish and Use the August Ultimate [Jiànyòng Huángjí].
Its position is in the Central Palace [Zhōnggōng],
where all officials establish their standards,
and governance transforms dukes and ministers.
Next is six, called
Order and Use the Three Virtues [Àiyòng Sāndé].
Its position is in the northwest,
suppressing and subduing the violent and oppressive,
deciding and regulating legal cases.
Next is seven, called
Clearly Use Scrutiny and Doubt [Míngyòng Jīyí].
Its position is in the west,
determining good and ill fortune,
distinguishing what is doubtful.
Next is eight, called
Mindfully Use the Various Portents [Niànyòng Shùzhēng].
Its position is in the northeast,
reverent and respectful in the virtuous regions,
mad and presumptuous in chaotic conduct.
Next is nine, called
Receive and Use the Five Blessings [Xiàngyòng Wǔfú],
Wield and Use the Six Extremities [Wēiyòng Liùjí]. Its position is in the south,
where all things are full and solid,
yīn [陰] energy is proclaimed,
the seasonal and yearly virtues are accomplished,
yīn [陰] and yáng [陽] are harmonized,
and the Five Phases [Wǔxíng] are without error.
Therefore, the *Jiǔgōng Jīng*
of Huángdì states:
Wearing nine, treading one;
three on the left, seven on the right;
two and four form the corners;
six and eight form the feet;
five resides in the central palace,
collectively governing gains and losses.
The numbers are Kǎn one,
Kūn two,
Zhèn three,
Xùn four,
Central Palace five,
Qián six,
Duì seven,
Gèn eight,
Lí nine.
Tàiyī travels through the Nine Palaces,
starting from one,
from the lesser to the greater,
following the sequence of numbers.
Calculation states:
The center and the four cardinal directions
each distribute nine tallies.
It is named:
Wood returns to its root,
six parts reach hài.
Therefore, take six tallies from Zhèn
and place them in Qián.
Water flows to its end,
eight parts reach chǒu.
Therefore, take eight tallies from Kǎn
and place them in Gèn.
Metal is righteous and firm,
two parts return to wèi.
Therefore, take two tallies from Duì
and place them in Kūn.
Fire is originally fierce and prosperous,
it naturally resides in its own region.
Therefore, the Lí tallies remain untouched.
Earth reigns in the four seasons,
originally born in sì.
Therefore, distribute four tallies from the Central Palace
and place them in Xùn.
Thus, the position of wearing nine and treading one is formed.
Next, the method for initially forming the Eight Trigrams
assigns the tallies for the cardinal directions.
First, take nine tallies from the North.
It is named:
Water generates wood.
One tally is placed on yín,
one tally on mǎo,
one tally on chén.
Also, one horizontal tally is placed on jiǎ,
one tally on yǐ.
Next, take nine tallies from the East.
It is named:
Wood generates fire in the South,
arranging five positions.
Next, take tallies from the South.
It is named:
Fire generates earth in the Center.
One tally is in the northwest for wù,
one tally in the southwest for jǐ.
Next, take tallies from the Center.
It is named:
Earth generates metal in the West,
arranging five positions.
Next, take tallies from the West.
It is named:
Metal generates water in the North,
arranging five positions.
Once the five directions have the ten Heavenly Stems and twelve Earthly Branches arranged,
then add one for each Yin Stem.
It is named:
Yin numbers are even.
Next, add one for each Yang Branch.
It is named:
The Branches inherently add to their beginning.
The remaining tallies are the numbers of the twelve months.
One tally is placed in the northwest.
It is named:
The beginning of Qián.
Two tallies are placed in the southwest.
It is named:
The beginning of Kūn.
The remaining nine tallies are placed in the center,
representing the image of the Yì.
It is named:
Qián governs jiǎ and rén.
Immediately take the tallies from jiǎ and rén
to form the Qián trigram.
It is also named:
Kūn governs yǐ and guǐ.
Next, take the tallies from yǐ and guǐ
to form the Kūn trigram.
Once the trigrams of the Father and Mother
and their line images are settled,
next come the six children.
First, begin with the eldest son.
It is named:
Zhèn governs gēng, zǐ, and wǔ.
Immediately take the tallies from gēng, zǐ, and wǔ
to form the Zhèn trigram.
Next, the eldest daughter.
It is named:
Xùn governs xīn, chǒu, and wèi.
Next, take the tallies from xīn, chǒu, and wèi
to form the Xùn trigram.
Next, the middle son.
It is named:
Kǎn governs wù, yín, and shēn.
Next, take the tallies from wù, yín, and shēn
to form the Kǎn trigram.
Next, the middle daughter.
It is named:
Lí governs jǐ, mǎo, and yǒu.
Next, take the tallies from jǐ, mǎo, and yǒu
to form the Lí trigram.
Next, the youngest son.
It is named:
Gèn governs bǐng, chén, and xū.
Next, take the tallies from bǐng, chén, and xū
to form the Gèn trigram.
Next, the youngest daughter.
It is named:
Duì governs dīng, sì, and hài.
Next, take the tallies from dīng, sì, and hài
to form the Duì trigram.
The Eight Trigrams are now formed.
Question:
From where do the Eight Trigrams originate?
Answer:
They originate from the Five Phases.
Again question:
From where do the Five Phases originate?
Answer:
They originate from Heaven and Earth.
From where do Heaven and Earth originate?
Answer:
They originate from Tàiyī.
From where does Tàiyī originate?
Answer:
It originates from the Yì.
Therefore, it is said:
"The Yì has the Great Ultimate (Tàijí),
which generates the Two Principles (Liǎngyí)."
Therefore, the character for Yì is changed to Tàiyī.
The character for Tàiyī is changed to Heaven.
Heaven generates one,
Earth generates two.
The character for Heaven is changed to Water.
Heaven generates Water.
The character for Water is changed to Wood.
Water generates Wood.
The character for Wood is changed to Fire.
Wood generates Fire.
The character for Fire is changed to Earth.
Fire generates Earth.
The character for Earth is changed to Metal.
Earth generates Metal.
The character for Metal is changed to the Eight Trigrams.
The Eight Trigrams originate from the Five Phases.
The character for the Eight Trigrams is changed to the Twelve Months.
The months governed by the Eight Trigrams.
The character for the Twelve Months is changed to Earth.
All things emerge and ultimately return to Earth.
The nine divisions of the palace, number one,
begin from the north.
Kǎn (坎) one is due north,
corresponding to the beginning of Heaven.
As the beginning is one and has no second, it is one.
The north is the beginning of the Wǔxíng (五行),
hence the Wǔxíng (五行) are in the north.
Therefore it is said,
"The beginning of Yáng (陽) energy,
when all things are about to sprout."
The five affairs, number two,
are in the southwest.
The five affairs are appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thought.
They will be explained in a later chapter.
Since the five affairs arise from the Wǔxíng (五行),
they come second, hence two.
It is also said,
Kūn (坤) two is in the southwest.
It corresponds to the number of Earth.
The southwest is the Línzhōng (林鐘) pipe,
the second in the order of vital energy.
The five affairs are foremost among human affairs.
Therefore it is said,
"Humility leads to virtue,
morning audiences bring good fortune."
These are governed by the five affairs.
The eight policies, number three,
are in the east.

The eight policies are food, wealth, sacrifices, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空), the Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒), the Minister of Justice (Sīkòu 司寇), diplomatic guests, and the military instructor.
Once the five affairs are established,
the eight policies are then cultivated,
hence three.
It is also said,
Zhèn (震) three is due east,
corresponding to the number of humanity,
thus completing the meaning of the Three Powers (Sāncái 三才).
The east is spring,
the beginning of agriculture.
Food refers to plowing, sowing, cooking, and preparing.
Wealth refers to accumulating and storing treasures,
money, cloth, gold, and weapons.
Sacrifices refer to offerings and serving spirits.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空) oversees land and acreage.
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) manages the number of households, population, and demographics.
The Minister of Justice (Sīkòu 司寇) prohibits and prevents theft and banditry,
and investigates unusual occurrences.
Diplomatic guests register comings and goings,
and receive joyful receptions.
The military instructor teaches and controls farmers,
establishing methods for plows and hoes.
Therefore it is said,
"Cultivating all grains,
hemp, ramie, silkworms, and mulberries."
The five regulators, number four,
are in the southeast.
The five regulators are the year, month, day, rituals of transformation, and calendrical computations.
Once the eight policies are cultivated,
without the seasons, months, and days,
there is no way to sow and plant.
They come next, hence four.
It is also said,
Xùn (巽) four is in the southeast,
where the wind moves through the four seasons,
corresponding to the number of the four seasons.
The southeast is SÌ (巳),
where pure Qián (乾) is in operation;
Qián (乾) governs Heaven,
and Xùn (巽) governs decrees.
Therefore it resides in the southeast.
The year
implies an ordered sequence of flourishing, decline, beginning, and end through the four seasons.
The sun and moon
illuminate all things and indicate the climate's proximity and distance.
Rituals of transformation
mean reverently accepting the king's transforming influence,
and therefore needing to establish achievements and offer treasures.
Day and hour
order Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽),
and determine the production of things.
Calendrical computations
record and connect measurements,
allowing farmers to observe and anticipate,
and taxes to be levied according to the seasons.
Therefore it is said,
"The king attends to the year,
grasping the principles of taxation to transform those below.
Ministers attend to the month,
reverently carrying out the way to establish treasures.
Teachers and trustworthy officials attend to the day,
displaying various duties
and creating myriad things."
The year, month, and day
constitute unchanging time.
Cultivating affairs requires respecting time
to align with the regulators.
Therefore it is said,
"The sun, moon, stars,
clouds, and rain all arise together."
The Imperial Ultimate (Huángjí 皇極), number five,
is in the center.
The emperor establishes all nations,
residing in the center to distinguish the four directions.
All officials govern accordingly,
all affairs are fully managed,
the seasons bring accomplishments,
and tribute is evenly distributed.
Rent and taxes of five grains
are used to support the king's affairs.
Therefore it is in the center.
The number of the center is fundamentally five.
It is also said,
Earth resides in the center,
corresponding to the number of the Wǔxíng (五行).
If the king's actions are not centered,
then he cannot establish all affairs.
Therefore it is said,
"If the Imperial Ultimate (Huángjí 皇極) is not upheld,
this is called not establishing."
Therefore it is said,
"All officials establish standards,
and governance is carried out by the Dukes and Ministers."
The three virtues, number six,
are in the northwest.
The three virtues are rectitude, hard coercion, and soft coercion. Qián (乾) represents the position of Heaven,
an emblem of the ruler.
As it passes five, its number is six.
It is also said,
Qián (乾) is in the northwest;
Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) energies are distributed in the northwest,
thus corresponding to the number of the six pitches.
The northwest is where Qián (乾) resides,
hence the ruler dwells there.
Rectitude is the virtue of humanity.
A noble person is upright and righteous,
without personal bias.
Therefore it is said,
"Peaceful, healthy, and upright,
his virtue is unquestioned."
Hard coercion is the virtue of Heaven.
Laws and regulations are not lost,
and light and heavy crimes are appropriately punished.
Therefore it is said,
"Profound and powerful, hard coercion."
Soft coercion is the virtue of Earth.
The virtuous are granted salaries,
all offices are stabilized,
and rewards are given to all nations.
Therefore it is said,
"Noble and enlightened, soft coercion."
Therefore it is said,
"Suppressing the strong and violent,
determining judgments and litigations."
Consulting the doubtful, number seven,
is in the west.
Consulting the doubtful means
establishing divination by milfoil and tortoise shell,
asking about uncertainties and choosing the good,
observing the phenomena of Heaven and Earth,
to determine auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
The milfoil stalks are round, the hexagrams square.
The tortoise shell and milfoil together reveal what is permissible or not.
When three people divine,
follow the words of two.
In ancient times, the sages
were cautious in planning and meticulous from the start;
in all their actions and undertakings,
in establishing foundations and initiating projects,
and in resolving doubts and settling uncertainties,
they invariably consulted
with the wise and virtuous,
with the aged and experienced,
and supplemented this with milfoil and tortoise shell.
Therefore, they committed no errors in their endeavors,
and had no misguided plans.
Even among barbarians, though lacking a hierarchy of rulers and ministers,
there were means of divination for resolving doubts,
sometimes using metal or stone,
sometimes wood or grass.
Therefore, the practice of consulting the doubtful
was esteemed by the sages.
Because it follows Qián (乾), its number is seven.
It is also said,
Duì (兌) is due west.
Mǎo (卯) and Yǒu (酉) are the gates of Heaven and Earth.
Mǎo (卯) governs beginning,
Yǒu (酉) governs ending.
Therefore, when the Dipper points to Mǎo (卯),
all things emerge;
when it points to Yǒu (酉),
all things enter.
Duì (兌) corresponds to the number of the seven stars.
Duì (兌) represents metal and governs joyful speech,
hence it is in the west.
Therefore it is said,
"Determining auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
distinguishing what is doubtful."
The various verifications, number eight,
are in the northeast.
"Various verifications" means numerous proofs.
From kings to the common people,
none fail to inwardly examine their faults and transgressions
and outwardly observe auspicious omens.
By following the omens and understanding the opportune moment,
there will be no disaster or misfortune.
If one does not scrutinize their faults,
nor contemplate the various omens,
then when calamity arrives, they will not realize it,
and ruin and destruction will be imminent.
When auspicious omens appear,
one must reverently serve Shàngdì,
and by not committing transgressions,
blessed responses will descend.
The Shī says,
“Reverently serve Shàngdì,
and truly harbor abundant blessings.”
If one does not respectfully offer good deeds,
and does not fear Shàngdì,
the host of Shén will become angry,
and there will certainly be reproaches and punishments.
The number eight
comes after seven.
It also says,
“Gèn eight is in the northeast.”
Gèn means “stopping.”
Gèn represents a path.
All things emerge greatly from Zhèn,
and in a minor way from Gèn.
Zhèn is the eldest of the male trigrams;
Gèn is the youngest of the male trigrams.
Therefore, it corresponds to the number of the Bāguà.
Since Gèn means “stopping,”
it commands stopping evil and pursuing good.
Therefore, it is in the northeast.
Hence it says,
“Solemnly revere the virtuous direction;
act wildly, presumptuously, and disorderly.”
The five blessings and six extremes have the number nine
and are in the south.
The five blessings are longevity (shòu), wealth (fù), peace and tranquility (kāngníng), love of virtue (yōuhàodé), and a good end to life (kǎozhōngmìng).
Longevity (shòu) means
having complete filial piety, fraternal deference, and moral virtue,
then cultivating the divine elixir
to extend one's lifespan.
Wealth (fù) means that where one's virtue and transformation reach,
there will be abundant harvests without lack.
Peace and tranquility (kāngníng) means
the nation is transformed into peace and tranquility,
with lasting joy and no troubles.
Love of virtue (yōuhàodé) means
discussing principles, comparing categories,
and promoting good and suppressing evil.
A good end to life (kǎozhōngmìng) means
acting in accordance with the times to accomplish tasks,
which can embody and make manifest good virtue throughout one's lifespan.
The six extremes (liùjí) are
