misfortune (xiōng), early death (duǎnzhé), illness (jí), sorrow (yōu), wickedness (è), poverty (pín), and weakness (ruò).
Misfortune and early death (xiōngduǎnzhé) refer to
the grave crimes of beheading, exposing the head, executing, and tearing apart.
Illness (jí) refers to
whipping, flogging, beating, striking, and then being ill, lying down, and needing care.
Sorrow (yōu) refers to
being tried, working hard, hoping, and competing with the rising sun.
Wickedness (è) refers to
shaving the head, tattooing, marking with red, flaying, execution, humiliation, and permanent abandonment.
Poverty (pín) refers to
compensating for stolen goods, taxing, and confiscating property.
Weakness (ruò) refers to
being separated from one's village and neighborhood, exiled to border regions,
to serve as a warning to posterity.
The principles of these punishments are placed at the end,
hence the number nine.
It also says,
“Since Lí is at Wǔ,
it is taken as the opposite of Zǐ.”
When an extreme is reached, it returns.
Therefore, Lí is at the very end,
serving as the number for the Nine Palaces (Jiǔgōng).
Lí represents brightness;
the ruler faces south to listen to government affairs,
symbolizing the brightness of Lí.
Punishments must be clear,
hence it is in the south.
Hence it says,
“All things are full and complete.”
There are only nine *gōng*.
The reason there are not ten is that
the eight directions and the center,
the number culminates in nine.
Above, it corresponds to the nine heavens, the nine stars, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions;
below, it corresponds to the Five Sacred Mountains (*Wǔyuè*), the Four Great Rivers (*Sìdú*), and the Nine Provinces (*Jiǔzhōu*).
The *Jiǔgōng Jīng* states:
The first *gōng* corresponds to Héngshān,
the second to the Three Rivers (*Sānjiāng*),
the third to Tàishān,
the fourth to the Huái River,
the fifth to Sōnggāo,
the sixth to the Yellow River (*Hé*),
the seventh to Huàshān,
the eighth to the Jì River,
and the ninth to Huòshān.
Furthermore, the first is Jìzhōu,
the second is Jīngzhōu,
the third is Qīngzhōu,
the fourth is Xúzhōu,
the fifth is Yùzhōu,
the sixth is Yōngzhōu,
the seventh is Liángzhōu,
the eighth is Yǎnzhōu,
and the ninth is Yángzhōu.
The names of the Nine Provinces
have changed at times.
The Nine Provinces of the *Yǔ Gòng*
were matched to the Táng dynasty in this way.
Where the names are the same,
it is because Yáo commanded Yǔ
to control the floods and divide the land into nine provinces,
and these were consequently not changed.
Therefore, during the Zhōu and Yú periods, there were twelve provinces,
with Yōu, Bìng, and Yíng added.
Shùn divided Qí by crossing the sea into Yíngzhōu,
taking Qīngzhōu across the sea.
Jìzhōu was too vast from north to south,
so Wèi was divided off as Bìngzhōu.
North of Yān, Yōuzhōu was established.
During the Yīn period, the Nine Provinces included Yōu and Yíng,
but not Qīng and Liáng.
The *Zhōu Guān* Nine Provinces included Yōu and Bìng,
but not Xú and Liáng.
The Hàn dynasty established twelve provinces,
adding Jiāo and Yì.
Regarding Jìzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Jìzhōu takes its name from the land,
which has both difficult and easy terrain, and is the capital of emperors.
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
Jì is near.
Its *qì* is similar.
Its land extends from east of Tàiháng
to Jiéshí, Wángwū, and Dǐzhù.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Jì was already productive.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says,
The area between the two rivers is Jìzhōu.
It is in the true north.
Regarding Jīngzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Jīng means "alert."
The southern barbarians often rebelled,
so the provincial routes were strengthened first,
to be on alert and prepared.
Its land extends north to Jīngshān,
and south to the sunny side of Héngshān.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Jīng and the sunny side of Héng, that is Jīngzhōu.
The *Ěryǎ* says,
South of the Hàn River is Jīngzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
Jīng is Chǔ.
Regarding Qīngzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Qīng is born in the east.
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
The lesser yang is blue (*qīng*),
the beginning of the year and the start of affairs,
thus it is named.
Its land extends northeast to the sea,
and west to Dài.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between the sea and Dài, that is Qīngzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
The eastern corner of the sea, Qīngzhōu, that is Qí.
Regarding Xúzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Xú means "leisurely."
The *qì* of the land is relaxed and slow.
Its land extends east to the sea,
north to Dài,
and south to the Huái River.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between the sea, Dài, and the Huái,
that is Xúzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
Above the Sì River is Xúzhōu, that is Lǔ.
The *Ěryǎ* says,
East of the Jì River is Xúzhōu.
Regarding Yùzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Yù is in the center of the Nine Provinces, it means "peace and comfort."
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
It embodies the *qì* of moderation and harmony, its nature is peaceful and comfortable.
Its land extends south to Jīng,
and north to the Yellow River.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between Jīng and the Yellow River, that is Yùzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
The area between the Yellow River and the Hàn River is Yùzhōu.
The *Ěryǎ* says,
South of the Yellow River is Yùzhōu.
Regarding Yōngzhōu,
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
Yōng occupies the northwest position,
where the *yáng* energy does not reach,
and the *yīn* energy is blocked and accumulated (*yōng è*),
hence it is named after this.
Its land extends west to the Black Water (*Hēishuǐ*),
and east to the Western River (*Xīhé*).
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between the Black Water and the Western River,
that is Yōngzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
Yōngzhōu is Qín.
The *Ěryǎ* says,
West of the Yellow River is Yōngzhōu.
Regarding Liángzhōu,
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
Liáng means "firm."
It takes its name from the firm and strong *qì* of metal in the west.
Its land extends east to Huàshān,
and west to the Black Water.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between Huàyáng and the Black Water,
that is Liángzhōu.
Regarding Yǎnzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
It takes its name from the Yǎn River.
*Tàikāng Dì Jì* says,
It distinguishes the meaning of treading with faith and embodying uprightness.
Its land extends southeast to the Jì River,
and northwest to the Yellow River.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between the Jì River and the Yellow River, that is Yǎnzhōu.
Regarding Yángzhōu,
the *Shì Míng* says,
Yángzhōu has many waters,
and the water waves rise (*yáng*).
Its land extends north to the Huái River,
and east to the sea.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says,
Between the Huái River and the sea, that is Yángzhōu.
Master Lǚ says,
Yángzhōu is Yuè.
The *Ěryǎ* says,
South of the Jiāng River is Yángzhōu.
Now, according to the positions of the Nine *Gōng*:
Jìzhōu is in the true north, in the Kǎn *gōng*.
Jīngzhōu is in the southwest, in the Kūn *gōng*.
Qīngzhōu is in the true east, in the Zhèn *gōng*.
Xúzhōu is in the southeast, in the Xùn *gōng*.
Yùzhōu is in the center, in the Middle *gōng*.
Yōngzhōu is in the northwest, in the Qián *gōng*.
Liángzhōu is in the true west, in the Duì *gōng*.
Yǎnzhōu is in the northeast, in the Gèn *gōng*.
Yángzhōu is in the true south, in the Lí *gōng*.
Its positions are similar to this explanation.
The Tài Yī places Yǎnzhōu in the true north Kǎn position,
Qīngzhōu in the northeast Gèn position,
Xúzhōu in the true east Zhèn position,
Yángzhōu in the southeast Xùn position,
Jīngzhōu in the true south Lí position,
Liángzhōu in the southwest Kūn position,
Yōngzhōu in the true west Duì position,
and Jìzhōu in the northwest Qián position.
These all follow the original *qì* of the Five Phases (*Wǔxíng*).
The northwest is Hài earth,
therefore Kǎn water resides there.
The northeast is Yín earth,
therefore Zhèn wood resides there.
The southeast is Sì earth,
therefore Lí fire resides there.
The southwest is Shēn earth,
therefore Duì metal resides there.
Qián is metal,
therefore it follows its original metal position.
Xùn is wood,
therefore it follows its original wood position.
Kūn and Gèn are both earth,
therefore they take the warp of the earth,
residing in the true south and true north.
These all follow the initial positions of the *Zhōu Lǐ Zhífāng*.
Although the *gōng* positions shift slightly,
the *qì* of the Five Phases remains unified.
These Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu),
correspond to the Nine Heavens (Jiǔtiān) above,
and are divided among the twenty-eight lunar mansions (èrshíbā sù).
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The Central Heaven (Jūntiān) is in the center,
its number is five,
its stars are Jiǎo (角), Kàng (亢), and Dī (氐).
Jiǎo (角) and Kàng (亢) correspond to Hán (韓) and Zhèng (鄭) divisions.
Jūn (鈞) means pole.
It spreads its pole to the four directions,
also called Jítiān (極天).
It is the lord of the four movements,
corresponding to the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) and Yùzhōu (豫州).
The Eastern Heaven (Cāngtiān) is in the east,
its number is three,
its stars are Fáng (房), Xīn (心), and Wěi (尾).
Fáng (房) and Xīn (心) correspond to Sòng (宋) division,
Wěi (尾) corresponds to Yān (燕) division.
The color of the east is green.
It corresponds to the Zhèn Palace (Zhèngōng) and Qīngzhōu (靑州).
The Northeastern Heaven (Biàntiān) is in the northeast,
its number is eight,
its stars are Jī (箕), Dǒu (斗), and Niú (牛).
Jī (箕) corresponds to Yān (燕) division,
Dǒu (斗) corresponds to Wú (吳) division,
Niú (牛) corresponds to Dài (岱) division.
At the end of water,
Yīn qi (yīnqì) is exhausted and Yáng (yáng) begins to stir,
all things are about to change.
It corresponds to the Gèn Palace (Gèngōng) and Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
The Northern Heaven (Xuántiān) is in the north,
its number is one,
its stars are Nǚ (女), Xū (虛), Wēi (危), and Shì (室).
Nǚ (女) corresponds to Yuè (越) division,
Xū (虛) and Wēi (危) correspond to Qí (齊) division,
Shì (室) corresponds to Wèi (衞) division.
The color of water is black,
hence it is called Xuántiān (玄天).
It corresponds to the Kǎn Palace (Kǎngōng) and Jìzhōu (冀州).
The Northwestern Heaven (Yōutiān) is in the northwest,
its number is six,
its stars are Bì (壁), Kuí (奎), and Lóu (婁).
Bì (壁) corresponds to Wèi (衞) division,
Kuí (奎) and Lóu (婁) correspond to Lǔ (魯) division.
At the end of metal,
it is the great Yīn (tàiyīn), obscure and dark.
It corresponds to the Qián Palace (Qiángōng) and Yōngzhōu (雍州).
The Western Heaven (Hàotiān) is in the west,
its number is seven,
its stars are Wèi (胃), Mǎo (昴), and Bì (畢).
Wèi (胃) corresponds to Lǔ (魯) division,
Bì (畢) and Mǎo (昴) correspond to Zhào (趙) division.
The color of metal is white,
hence it is called Hàotiān (昊天).
It corresponds to the Duì Palace (Duìgōng) and Liángzhōu (梁州).
The Southwestern Heaven (Zhūtiān) is in the southwest,
its number is two,
its stars are Zī (觜), Cān (參), and Jǐng (井).
Zī (觜) and Cān (參) correspond to Jìn (晉) division,
Jǐng (井) corresponds to Qín (秦) division.
It is at the end of fire.
The color of Yáng (yáng) is vermilion.
It corresponds to the Kūn Palace (Kūngōng) and Jīngzhōu (荆州).
The Southern Heaven (Yántiān) is in the south,
its number is nine,
its stars are Guǐ (鬼), Liǔ (柳), and Xīng (星).
Guǐ (鬼) corresponds to Qín (秦) division.
Liǔ (柳) and Xīng (星) correspond to Zhōu (周) division.
Fire tends to flare upwards.
Therefore, it is called Yántiān (炎天).
It corresponds to the Lí Palace (Lígōng) and Yángzhōu (揚州).
The Southeastern Heaven (Yángtiān) is in the southeast,
its number is four,
its stars are Zhāng (張), Yì (翼), and Zhěn (軫).
Zhāng (張) corresponds to Zhōu (周) division,
Yì (翼) and Zhěn (軫) correspond to Chǔ (楚) division.
At the end of wood,
it is about to reach the great Yáng (tàiyáng),
hence it is called Yángtiān (陽天).
It corresponds to the Xùn Palace (Xùngōng) and Xúzhōu (徐州).
These Nine Heavens (Jiǔtiān) also belong to the numbers of the nine stars of the Big Dipper (Běidǒu),
hence they correspond to the Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu) below.
Yántiān (炎天) has the number nine,
it belongs to the first pivot star (shūxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Lí Palace (Lígōng) and Yángzhōu (揚州).
Biàntiān (變天) has the number eight,
it belongs to the second revolving star (xuánxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Gèn Palace (Gèngōng) and Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Hàotiān (昊天) has the number seven,
it belongs to the third jade star (jīxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Duì Palace (Duìgōng) and Liángzhōu (梁州).
Yōutiān (幽天) has the number six,
it belongs to the fourth authority star (quánxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Qián Palace (Qiángōng) and Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Jūntiān (鈞天) has the number five,
it belongs to the fifth balance star (héngxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) and Yùzhōu (豫州).
Yángtiān (陽天) has the number four,
it belongs to the sixth open-Yáng star (kāiyángxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Xùn Palace (Xùngōng) and Xúzhōu (徐州).
Cāngtiān (蒼天) has the number three,
it belongs to the seventh shimmering light star (yáoguāngxīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Zhèn Palace (Zhèngōng) and Qīngzhōu (靑州).
Zhūtiān (朱天) has the number two,
it belongs to the eighth star (dì bā xīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Kūn Palace (Kūngōng) and Jīngzhōu (荆州).
Xuántiān (玄天) has the number one,
it belongs to the ninth star (dì jiǔ xīng) of the Dipper,
corresponding to the Kǎn Palace (Kǎngōng) and Jìzhōu (冀州).
The eighth and ninth stars (dì bā dì jiǔ èr xīng) of the Dipper,
are Yīn (yīn) and thus not visible,
because they correspond to the Yīn Palaces (yīngōng).
Furthermore, Guō Pú's (Guō Pú) Yì Zhān (Yì Zhān) states:
Qián (qián) is one, Kūn (kūn) is two,
Zhèn (zhèn) is three, Xùn (xùn) is four,
Kǎn (kǎn) is five, Lí (lí) is six,
Gèn (gèn) is seven, Duì (duì) is eight.
When divining for people and things,
all are based on this.
This is probably based on the order of father, mother, son, and daughter.
These are the numbers of the Nine Palaces (Jiǔgōng) and Eight Trigrams (Bāguà).
Therefore, they are explained in full here.
Composed by Shàng Yítóng Sānsī Chéngyáng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng Xiāo Jí (上儀同三司城陽郡開國公蕭吉).
The classics say:
Heaven (Tiān) gave birth to one,
starting with water in the north.
Earth (Dì) gave birth to two,
starting with fire in the south.
Man (Rén) gave birth to three,
starting with wood in the east.
Time (Shí) gave birth to four,
starting with metal in the west.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) gave birth to five,
starting with earth in the center.
It also says:
Heaven (Tiān) giving birth to one
means that Heaven (Tiān) was born from one,
not that Heaven (Tiān) gave birth to one.
Therefore it is said:
One begat two,
two begat three,
three begat all things.
Earth (Dì) giving birth to two
also means that Earth (Dì) was born from two,
man (rén) from three,
and time (shí) from four.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) all originated from one,
and their number reached five.
Earth (tǔ) is the last.
Having obtained five, the Five Phases (wǔxíng) are produced.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) are born at the same time but manifest at different times,
leaving their parent,
and having a spouse.
It is like how human beings are also born from the same primordial qi (yuánqì),
each from a different family,
paired as husband and wife,
and procreating descendants.
Therefore, the Five Phases (Wǔxíng) all depend on each other to be completed.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) are born of the same womb but reside separately,
with a sequence of precedence.
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) all rely on Yīn (yīn) and Yáng (yáng) qi (qì) to be born.
Therefore it is said:
Moist qi (ruqì) gives birth to water,
warm qi (wēnqì) gives birth to fire,
strong qi (qiángqì) gives birth to wood,
hard qi (gāngqì) gives birth to metal,
and harmonious qi (héqì) gives birth to earth.
Thus, we know that the Five Phases (Wǔxíng) arise simultaneously,
and give birth to each other by relying on their principles.
The tradition says:
The Five Phases (Wǔxíng) arise together,
each distinguished by its name.
However, since the Five Phases (Wǔxíng) are distinguished by their names,
they take turns in their functions,
rotating through periods of rest and prosperity.
Hence, they give birth to each other.
Yǐng Róng (Yǐng Róng) says:
Generally, the mutual generation of the Five Phases (Wǔxíng xiāngshēng)
refers to different categories transforming each other.
Just as males and females of different surnames can achieve reproduction.
If water is added to water,
no excellent flavor is produced.
Héjiān Xiànwáng
asked Wēnchéng Xūnjūn,
"Filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven
and the righteousness of Earth. What does this mean?"
He replied,
"Heaven has the Five Phases:
wood, fire, earth, metal, and water.
Wood generates fire,
fire generates earth,
earth generates metal,
metal generates water,
and water generates wood.
Wood is spring.
Spring governs birth,
summer governs growth and nurture,
autumn governs harvest,
and winter governs storage.
Storage is what winter accomplishes.
Therefore, what the father gives birth to,
his son makes it grow;
what the father makes grow,
his son nurtures;
what the father nurtures,
his son brings to completion.
One dares not fail to fulfill the father's wishes,
thereby exhausting the Way of being human.
Thus, the Five Phases are the Five Constants."
The Báihǔ Tōng says,
"Wood generates fire:
wood's nature is warm,
fire is latent within it,
and emerges when drilled and burned.
Therefore, wood generates fire.
Fire generates earth:
fire is hot, hence it can burn wood,
and burned wood becomes ash.
Ash is earth.
Therefore, fire generates earth.
Earth generates metal:
metal resides in rocks,
and is born from mountains, moistened and nourished.
As earth accumulates to form mountains,
mountains must produce rocks.
Therefore, earth generates metal.
Metal generates water:
the energy of lesser yin
moistens and flows,
and molten metal also becomes water.
This is why mountain clouds are followed by moisture.
Therefore, metal generates water.
Water generates wood:
because of water's moisture, wood can grow.
Therefore, water generates wood."
The Yuánmìng Bāo says,
"Yang emits, Yin transforms.
Therefore, water generates wood."
The Chūnqiū Fánlù says,
"The East is wood.
Wood is the foundation of agriculture.
The Sīnóng [Minister of Agriculture]
oversees the five grains and stockpiling,
which the Sīmǎ [Minister of War] consumes.
Therefore, wood generates fire.
Fire is fundamentally the court's Sīmǎ,
who should be discerning.
Before the heavenly omens and manifestations have emerged,
he sees clearly by himself.
Once the world is peaceful,
he pacifies the ruler and ministers.
Therefore, fire generates earth.
Earth is the ruler,
who should be trustworthy.
Through the awe and might of the times, he enforces strong governance to achieve completion.
This is the Dàlǐ [Minister of Justice] and Sītú [Minister of Education].
Therefore, earth generates metal.
Metal represents the Yì [Righteousness] of the Shàngshū [Minister of State].
If the borders are peaceful,
brigands do not rise,
and there are no lawsuits in the cities,
then there is peace.
This is the Zhífǎ Sīkòu [Minister of Law Enforcement].
Therefore, metal generates water.
Water is the Zhífǎ Sīkòu.
He values ritual.
Ruler and ministers have their positions,
and elders and youngsters have their order.
All artisans work in their season,
to complete the year's provisions.
Tools and implements are made and supplied.
This is the Sīnóng Tiánguān [Minister of Agriculture and Field Officer].
Therefore, water generates wood.
Although the affairs and meanings of these two explanations differ,
their mutual generation is the same.
The Five Phases each have established forms.
Only fire, which emerges by drilling and burning,
indicates that fire is the energy of Great Yang.
It is born only when warm.
That it emerges by drilling wood
merely means it is re-entrusted to all things.
Just as a sage has no name,
yet can govern all things,
he is still named by all things.
Yang energy is utterly divine.
Thus, it has both hidden and manifest aspects.
The Five Phases differ in substance,
and their places of birth and death are not the same;
they are present throughout the twelve months and twelve earthly branches, appearing and disappearing.
Wood receives its energy in Shēn,
is conceived in Yǒu,
nurtured in Xū,
born in Hài,
bathed in Zǐ,
capped and belted in Chǒu,
enters officialdom in Yín,
becomes king in Mǎo,
declines in Chén,
becomes ill in Sì,
dies in Wǔ,
and is buried in Wèi.

enters officialdom in Shēn,

enters officialdom in Hài,

Earth receives its energy in Hài,
is conceived in Zǐ,
nurtured in Chǒu,
sojourns in Yín,
is born in Mǎo,
bathed in Chén,
capped and belted in Sì,
enters officialdom in Wǔ,
becomes king in Wèi,
declines and becomes ill in Shēn,
dies in Yǒu,
and is buried in Xū.
Xū (戌) is the tomb of fire.
Fire is its mother,
and mother and son are not buried together.
Proceed to Chǒu (丑).
Chǒu (丑) is the tomb of metal.
Metal is its son,
and this too is not appropriate according to ritual.
Wishing to return to Wèi (未).
Wèi (未) is the tomb of wood.
Wood acts as the ghost of earth.
Fearing and not daring to enter,
it rests at Chén (辰).
Chén (辰) is the tomb of water.
Water is its wife.
This is appropriate according to ritual.
So, it is buried at Chén (辰).
In ancient times, when Shùn (舜) was buried at Cāngwú (蒼梧),
his two consorts did not follow.
Thus, we know that joint burial is not an ancient practice.
However, Jì Wǔzǐ (季武子) said,
"Since Zhōu Gōng (周公),
this has not been changed."
The Shī (詩) says,
"While living, in different rooms;
in death, in the same grave."
This is probably to reinforce its righteousness,
and to unite bones and flesh to return together.
For water and earth to share a tomb,
this is precisely what is taken.
It is also explained by the four seasons.
That which is managed returns to this.
Gāotáng Lóngyǐ (高唐隆以) says,
earth is born at Wèi (未),
flourishes at Xū (戌),
grows strong at Chǒu (丑),
and ends at Chén (辰).
Chén (辰) is the tomb of water and earth.
Therefore, one does not wail on a Chén (辰) day.
This is because a Chén (辰) day signifies a repeated mourning.
The sorrow of baring shoulders and stomping
should not wait for a change of day.
What Gāotáng (高唐) said
is probably shallow.
His meaning regarding the "living and reigning"
is another school of thought entirely.
The Wǔxíng Shū (五行書) says,
although earth has a temporary reign in the land of fire,
is born at Sì (巳),
and buried at Chén (辰),
yet earth reigns in each of the four seasons,
each having its place of birth and death.

The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì (孝經援神契) says,
"The five elements' earth yields benefits,
providing for all under heaven."
The Guī Jīng (龜經) says,
"Wood and earth moving becomes Chén (辰) earth,
fire moving becomes Wèi (未) earth,
metal moving becomes Xū (戌) earth,
water moving becomes Chǒu (丑) earth."
It also says,
"Jiǎ Yǐ (甲乙), Yín (寅) Mǎo (卯) become Chén (辰) earth;
Bǐng Dīng (丙丁), Sì (巳) Wǔ (午) become Wèi (未) earth;
Gēng Xīn (庚辛), Shēn (申) Yǒu (酉) become Xū (戌) earth;
Rén Guǐ (壬癸), Hài (亥) Zǐ (子) become Chǒu (丑) earth."
In general, each of the Five Elements reigns
for seventy-two days.
Earth resides in the last eighteen days of each of the four seasons,
totaling seventy-two days.
This clarifies that earth has different births and deaths in the four directions.
This is likely used in divination.
As for discussing its fixed position, reign, and places of birth and death,
the latter half of the sixth month of summer
is considered the time when earth reigns.
The Lǐjì (禮記) says,
"The central earth."
After the latter half of summer,
this is the middle of the year,
located at the center of the four seasons.
The altars to heaven, earth gods, and human ghosts
are also all at Wèi (未).
Kūn (坤) is also at Wèi (未).
The hexagram governs earth.
Therefore, it says,
"Earth's virtue is at Wèi (未),
and it ends at Chǒu (丑)."
The Yì (易) says,
"In the southwest, one finds friends;
in the northeast, one loses friends."
This clarifies that the reign of earth is fixed at Wèi (未),
and its tomb is fixed at Chén (辰).
All five elements, regarding those born during the "parents in office" period,
take this to mean their flourishing and strong state, capable of giving birth and nurturing.
Only metal, when born in fire,
is because Sì (巳) contains strong earth,
which can generate metal.
Without fire, metal
does not change its form.
Therefore, metal is born in the position of fire.
It also says that metal is born among ghosts:
metal's father is earth,
and Wù Jǐ (戊己) are temporarily governed by Bǐng Dīng (丙丁).
The father cannot nurture alone;
a mother is also needed.
Metal in the south encounters Sì (巳) fire.
Metal transforms when it gets fire,
and when metal transforms, water is born.
If Wù Jǐ (戊己) earth has transformational water,
then metal does not fear fire.
Jǐ (己) containing water qi
is then the stepmother of metal.
All five elements, concerning the month after burial
when qi is received,
is because after death, they are reborn,

The principles of Xiūwáng
are of three kinds.
The first distinguishes the Xiūwáng of the five elements' bodies,
the second discusses the Xiūwáng of the Zǐgān,
and the third discusses the Xiūwáng of the Bāguà.
For the Xiūwáng of the five elements' bodies,
in spring, Mù is wáng,
Huǒ is xiàng,
Shuǐ is xiū,
Jīn is qiú,
and Tǔ is sǐ.
In summer, Huǒ is wáng,
Tǔ is xiàng,
Mù is xiū,
Shuǐ is qiú,
and Jīn is sǐ.
In the sixth month, Tǔ is wáng,
Jīn is xiàng,
Huǒ is xiū,
Mù is qiú,
and Shuǐ is sǐ.
In autumn, Jīn is wáng,
Shuǐ is xiàng,
Tǔ is xiū,
Huǒ is qiú,
and Mù is sǐ.
In winter, Shuǐ is wáng,
Mù is xiàng,
Jīn is xiū,
Tǔ is qiú,
and Huǒ is sǐ.
For the Xiūwáng of the Zǐgān,
in spring, Jiǎyǐ Yínmǎo are wáng,
Bǐngdīng Sǐwǔ are xiàng,
Rénkuǐ Hàizǐ are xiū,
Gēngxīn Shēnyǒu are qiú,
and Wùjǐ Chénxū Chǒuwèi are sǐ.
In summer, Bǐngdīng Sǐwǔ are wáng,
Wùjǐ Chénxū Chǒuwèi are xiàng,
Jiǎyǐ Yínmǎo are xiū,
Rénkuǐ Hàizǐ are qiú,
and Gēngxīn Shēnyǒu are sǐ.
In the sixth month, Wùjǐ Chénxū Chǒuwèi are wáng,
Gēngxīn Shēnyǒu are xiàng,
Bǐngdīng Sǐwǔ are xiū,
Jiǎyǐ Yínmǎo are qiú,
and Rénkuǐ Hàizǐ are sǐ.
In autumn, Gēngxīn Shēnyǒu are wáng,
Rénkuǐ Hàizǐ are xiàng,
Wùjǐ Chénxū Chǒuwèi are xiū,
Bǐngdīng Sǐwǔ are qiú,
and Jiǎyǐ Yínmǎo are sǐ.
In winter, Rénkuǐ Hàizǐ are wáng,
Jiǎyǐ Yínmǎo are xiàng,
Gēngxīn Shēnyǒu are xiū,
Wùjǐ Chénxū Chǒuwèi are qiú,
and Bǐngdīng Sǐwǔ are sǐ.
For the Xiūwáng of the Bāguà,
at Lìchūn, Gèn is wáng,
Zhèn is xiàng,
Xùn is tāi,
Lí is mò,
Kūn is sǐ,
Duì is qiú,
Qián is fèi,
and Kǎn is xiū.
At Chūnfēn, Zhèn is wáng,
Xùn is xiàng,
Lí is tāi,
Kūn is mò,
Duì is sǐ,
Qián is qiú,
Kǎn is fèi,
and Gèn is xiū.
At Lìxià, Xùn is wáng,
Lí is xiàng,
Kūn is tāi,
Duì is mò,
Qián is sǐ,
Kǎn is qiú,
Gèn is fèi,

At Xiàzhì, Lí is wáng,
Kūn is xiàng,
Duì is tāi,
Qián is mò,
Kǎn is sǐ,
Gèn is qiú,

At Lìqiū, Kūn is wáng,

Each of these guà follows the energy of the eight seasonal nodes,
each lasting forty-five days.
When it is the 'King' (wàng) phase,
it is always the 'Son' (zǐ) that acts as the 'Minister' (xiàng),
because the 'Son' (zǐ) is then vigorous
and can assist in managing affairs.
The 'Parents' (fùmǔ) are in the 'Rest' (xiū) phase,
because the 'Son' (zǐ) is in the 'King' (wàng) phase with its energy flourishing,
while the 'Parents' (fùmǔ) are old and declining,
unable to manage affairs.
This is like Yáo, when old, entrusting the governance of the state to Shùn.
That which is 'Feared' (wèi) becomes 'Dead' (sǐ),
because the ruling body (King) can control and kill it.
That which is 'Carved' (kè) becomes 'Imprisoned' (qiú),
because the 'Son' (zǐ) acts as the 'Minister' (xiàng),
and can imprison enemies.
Liǔ Shìlóng said:
When Wood is in its 'King' (wàng) phase, it is forests, gardens, bamboos, and trees.
When it is in its 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, it is reeds, rushes, and wild grasses.
When it is in its 'Rest' (xiū) phase, it is rafters, pillars, boats, and carts.
When it is in its 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is firewood, kindling, and thorny branches.
When it is in its 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is coffins, outer coffins, and rotting stumps.
When Fire is in its 'King' (wàng) phase, it is pottery, smelting, and fiery radiance.
When it is in its 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, it is lamps and candles.
When it is in its 'Rest' (xiū) phase, it is smoke and vapor.
When it is in its 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is charcoal and cinders.
When it is in its 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is ash.
When Earth is in its 'King' (wàng) phase, it is states, cities, and mountains.
When it is in its 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, it is city walls, altars, and hills.
When it is in its 'Rest' (xiū) phase, it is fields and dwellings.
When it is in its 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is walls and fences.
When it is in its 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is manure and dirt.
When Metal is in its 'King' (wàng) phase, it is gold, jade, and precious vessels.
When it is in its 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, it is silver, copper, and sharp blades.
When it is in its 'Rest' (xiū) phase, it is lead, tin, plows, and hoes.
When it is in its 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is scorched vessels, cauldrons, and mattocks.
When it is in its 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is sand, gravel, and broken iron.
When Water is in its 'King' (wàng) phase, it is seas and rivers.
When it is in its 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, it is lakes, marshes, reservoirs, and springs.
When it is in its 'Rest' (xiū) phase, it is ditches and channels.
When it is in its 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is wine and juice.
When it is in its 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is dry ponds and depleted wells.
In all these cases, when in the 'King' (wàng) phase, the energy is flourishing,
thus they are vast and great things.
In the 'Minister' (xiàng) phase, the energy is inferior,
and their comparison gradually diminishes.
In the 'Rest' (xiū) phase, the energy declines,
so it further turns to the subtle.
In the 'Imprisoned' (qiú) phase, it is increasingly bad,
thus it is the lowest.
In the 'Dead' (sǐ) phase, it is discarded and unusable,
thus it belongs to the category of dry and rotten things.
Zhào Yí said:
Regarding the positions of the Wǔxíng,
obtaining its own direction makes it flourishing,
and encountering that which it fears marks its end.
Therefore, Wood fears Metal.
Jiǎ, with its younger sister Yǐ, weds Gēng.
Gēng receives Wood's energy.
Therefore, Wood is conceived in the land of Metal,
and is born in Water,
flourishes in its own direction,
and declines in the land of Fire.
Within Fire, Metal is produced,
thus it ends in Wèi.
Upon reaching the west, Wood ends.
Because Metal rules.
Bǐng, with its younger sister Dīng, weds Rén.
Rén receives Fire's energy.
Therefore, Fire is conceived in the land of Water,
is born within Wood,
flourishes in its own direction,
and declines in the position of Metal.
Upon reaching the north, it ends.
Because Water rules.
Wù, with its younger sister Jǐ, weds Jiǎ.
Jiǎ receives Earth's energy.
Therefore, Earth is conceived in the land of Wood,
and is born within Fire,
flourishes in its own position,
and declines in the land of Water.
Upon reaching the east, it ends.
Because Wood rules.
Gēng, with its younger sister Xīn, weds Bǐng.
Bǐng receives Metal's energy.
Therefore, Metal is conceived in the land of Wood,
is born in the position of Fire,
flourishes in its own direction,
and declines in the land of Water.
Upon reaching the east, it ends.
With Fire being produced.
Rén, with its younger sister Guǐ, weds Wù.
Wù receives Water's energy.
Therefore, Water is conceived in the land of Earth,
is born within Metal,
flourishes in its own direction,
and declines in the land of Wood.
Upon reaching the south, it ends.
With strong Earth.
This is the principle of mutual generation and mutual fear,
beginning and ending without cease.
The meaning of the Zhīgàn
involves many pairings.
Here, we briefly discuss directions and their corresponding placements.
The Gān (Celestial Stems) do not stand alone,
nor are the Zhī (Terrestrial Branches) set up in vain.
They must be paired,
to determine and be used for years, months, days, and hours.
Just like ruler and minister, husband and wife,
they must be paired to achieve completion.
In summary,
from Jiǎ to Guǐ are Yáng,
are Gān (Stems),
and are days.
From Yín to Chǒu are Yīn,
are Zhī (Branches),
and are hours.
Specifically,
for the Gān, Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, and Rén are Yáng,
while Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, and Guǐ are Yīn.
For the Zhī, Yín, Chén, Wǔ, Shēn, Xū, and Zǐ are Yáng,
while Mǎo, Sì, Wèi, Yǒu, Hài, and Chǒu are Yīn.
Yáng is then rigid,
is the ruler,
is the husband,
is above,
is outside,
is the surface,
is movement,
is advance,
is rising,
is looking up,
is front,
is left,
is virtue,
is bestowal,
and is opening.
Yīn is then soft,
is the minister,
is the wife,
is the concubine,
is wealth,
is below,
is inside,
is the interior,
is cessation,
is retreat,
is lying low,
is position,
is behind,
is right,
is punishment,
is concealment,
and is closing.
The analogies for Yīn and Yáng
are many but briefly stated.
The main outline is thus.
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, Mǎo are Wood.
Their position is in the east.
Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, Wǔ are Fire.
Their position is in the south.
Wù, Jǐ, Chén, Xū, Chǒu, Wèi are Earth.
Their position is in the center,
presiding over the four seasons in turn,
and temporarily governing with Bǐng and Dīng.
Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, Yǒu are Metal.
Their position is in the west.
Rén, Guǐ, Hài, Zǐ are Water.
Their position is in the north.
Jiǎ is the first of the Heavenly Stems,
Zǐ is the first of the Earthly Branches.
The reason they are matched together is:
The energy of the great Yang
moves beneath the Yellow Springs
in the month of jiànzǐ (the 11th lunar month).
The lǜ (pitch pipe) of huángzhōng
is the source of qi in zǐ.
Therefore, zǐ is taken as the foremost.
All things emerge in the month of jiànyín (the 1st lunar month),
all taking visible form.
Jiǎ belongs to this month,
thus jiǎ is taken as the foremost and matched with zǐ.
That which is visible is Yang,
so it follows the Heavenly Stems.
That which is not yet visible is Yin,
so it follows the Earthly Branches.
This is why Jiǎzǐ are used to be matched,
as the beginning of the sixty-day cycle.
Since there are ten Heavenly Stems
and twelve Earthly Branches,
they rotate and are matched,
ending with Guǐhài.
Thus, there are sixty days.
Ten days make one xún (decade),
thus there are six xún.
At the end of one xún, one cycle of Jiǎ to Guǐ is completed.
Then Jiǎ is matched with Zǐ,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐyǒu.
When the Stems are exhausted, there remain the Branches Xū and Hài.
Then Jiǎ starts again, matched with Xū,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐwèi,
with remaining Branches Shēn and Yǒu.
Then Jiǎ starts again, matched with Shēn,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐsì,
with remaining Branches Wǔ and Wèi.
Then Jiǎ starts again, matched with Wǔ,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐmǎo,
with remaining Branches Chén and Sì.
Then Jiǎ starts again, matched with Chén,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐchǒu,
with remaining Branches Yín and Mǎo.
Then Jiǎ starts again, matched with Yín,
and the Stems are exhausted up to Guǐhài.
When the ten Heavenly Stems are matched with the twelve Earthly Branches,
the cycle completes and returns to Jiǎzǐ.
Therefore, the six Jiǎ cycles rotate,
lasting sixty days.
Ten days make one xún.
Within one xún,
the two Branches that have no match
are called gū (solitary).
Those that are directly opposite them
are called xū (void).
This is what divination refers to as kōngwáng (empty and void).
Since the solitary Branches have no Stem,
they are named kōngwáng.
Wáng (亡) means wú (無, nothing).
No Stem, thus wáng.
Those directly opposite
are completely xū,
thus called kōng.
The method of calculation arranges the twelve Earthly Branches horizontally in the four directions,
and the eight Heavenly Stems vertically in the four directions,
placing Wù and Jǐ in the center.
If it is the Jiǎzǐ xún,
take the Stem Jiǎ to match the Branch Zǐ.
Following this order of matching,
until Wùchén.
Its position is in the center.
Earth is the lord of the five elements,
and cannot be moved.
Therefore, the Branches Chén and Sì
are taken into the center
to match Wù and Jǐ.
All others have Stems approaching Branches.
Until Xū and Hài, there are no Stems to match them.
Being singular, they are gū.
The positions of Chén and Sì
have neither Branch nor Stem.
Therefore, they are named xū.
Regarding the kōngwáng Branches,
from the perspective of the Five Elements,
for example, in the Jiǎzǐ xún, there are no Xū and Hài.
This is a partial kōngwáng of Water and Earth.
Because Xū is Earth,
and Hài is Water.
Since Hài and Zǐ are not entirely absent,
it is called partial.
In the Jiǎxū xún, there are no Shēn and Yǒu.
This is a complete kōngwáng of Metal,
because both Metal Branches are absent.
In the Jiǎshēn xún, there are no Wǔ and Wèi.
This is a partial kōngwáng of Fire and Earth,
because Sì and Wǔ are not entirely absent.
In the Jiǎwǔ xún, there are no Chén and Sì, which is also similar.
In the Jiǎchén xún, there are no Yín and Mǎo.
This is also called a complete kōngwáng of Wood.
In the Jiǎyín xún, there are no Zǐ and Chǒu.
This is also a partial kōngwáng of Water and Earth.
In all these cases, both Branches are not entirely absent.
The book of military strategy says:
Yang is born in Jiǎzǐ,
lacking Xū and Hài.
This is still the Heavenly Gate.
Yin is born in Jiǎwǔ,
lacking Chén and Sì.
This is still the Earthly Door.
Yang borders Jiǎyín,
lacking Zǐ and Chǒu.
This is still the Ghost Gate.
Yin borders Jiǎshēn,
lacking Wǔ and Wèi.
This is still the Human Gate.
Yang is dominant in Jiǎchén,
Mǎo acts as a barrier.
Yin rises in Jiǎxū,
Yǒu acts as a barrier.
These are all the kōng Branches of the six Jiǎ cycles.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says:
The earth is insufficient in the southeast.
The right movement ends and enters the void gate.
This clarifies that Jiǎzǐ is gū in Xū and Hài,
and xū in Chén and Sì.
One Stem and one Branch make one day,
because the heavens revolve 365 and one-quarter degrees,
and the sun moves one degree each day.
Therefore, exactly one Stem and one Branch are used
to govern one day.
Three xún make one month,
the moon travels thirteen and one-quarter degrees daily,
and completes its circuit in three xún.
Twelve months make one year,
the four seasons each have three months,
the work of creation and destruction is complete,
covering all twelve Branches.
One year totals 360 days,
which is six times sixty, the number of the six Jiǎ cycles.
The six Jiǎ cycles account for two months less than a full year,
this is because the odd and even numbers of Yin and Yang are complete.
Yang is odd,
Yin is even.
The principles of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
for all myriad things and categories
are thus made clear.
The Earthly Branches and Heavenly Stems
are matched similarly for years, months, days, and hours.
The beginning of a year
starts from the first Jiǎzǐ of the upper epoch.
The beginning of a month
starts from the eleventh month of a Jiǎ or Jǐ year, on a Jiǎzǐ day.
The beginning of a day
for the sixty-day cycle starts from Jiǎzǐ.
The beginning of an hour
after the winter and summer solstices,
when it is a Jiǎ or Jǐ day, at midnight,
starts from Jiǎzǐ.
All four matters take Jiǎzǐ as their head.
Its upper part corresponds to the Nine Stars,
and its lower part corresponds to the Nine Provinces.
The *Huángdì Bīngjué* says:
Jiǎzǐ starts from the first star of the Northern Dipper's Qúi,
counting clockwise to Gēngwǔ,
which is at the seventh Gāng star.
Upon reaching Xīnwèi,
it reverts, counting counter-clockwise from the sixth star to Bǐngzǐ.
Then it counts clockwise again from the first star, completing all sixty Jiǎ.
Regarding its lower part corresponding to the Nine Provinces,
historical records state:
Jiǎ is Qí,
Yǐ is Dōngyí,
Bǐng is Chǔ,
Dīng is Nányí,
Wù is Wèi,
Jǐ is Hán,
Gēng is Qín,
Xīn is Xīyí,
Rén is Yān,
Gǔi is Běiyí.
The *Hànshū Wǔxíng Zhì* says:
Jiǎ and Yǐ are overseas,
where the sun and moon do not govern.
Bǐng and Dīng are Jiānghuái and Hǎidài.
Wù and Jǐ are Zhōngzhōu and Héjì.
Gēng and Xīn are west of Huàshān.
Rén and Gǔi are north of Chángshān.
Zǐ is Zhōu,
Chǒu is Zhái,
Yín is Chǔ,
Mǎo is Zhèng,
Chén is Hándān,
Sì is Wèi,
Wǔ is Qín,
Wèi is Zhōngshān and Sòng,
Shēn is Qí,
Yǒu is Lǔ,
Xū is Yuè,
Hài is Yān.
The *Lóngshǒu Jīng* says:
Zǐ is Qí and Qīngzhōu,
Chǒu is Wú-Yuè and Yángzhōu,
Yín is Yān and Yōuzhōu,
Mǎo is Sòng and Yùzhōu,
Chén is Jìn and Yǎnzhōu,
Sì is Chǔ and Jīngzhōu,
Wǔ is Zhōu and Sānhé,
Wèi is Qín and Yōngzhōu,
Shēn is Shǔ and Yìzhōu,
Yǒu is Liángzhōu,
Xū is Xúzhōu,
Hài is Wèi and Bìngzhōu.
Regarding the positions of the earthly branches,
the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū* are closer.
In terms of star-sequences,
the *Lóngshǒu* is more appropriate.
For its correspondence to the human body:
Jiǎ and Yǐ are the head,
Bǐng and Dīng are the chest and ribs,
Wù and Jǐ are the heart and abdomen,
Gēng and Xīn are the thighs,
Rén and Gǔi are the hands and feet.
Then Zǐ is the head,
Chǒu and Hài are the chest and arms,
Yín and Xū are the hands,
Mǎo and Yǒu are the waist and ribs,
Chén and Shēn are the buttocks and upper arms,
Sì and Wèi are the shins,
Wǔ is the feet.
All these have the beginning as the head,
and the end as the feet.
For its correspondence to the Five Organs:
The heavenly stems assign Jiǎ and Yǐ to the liver,
Bǐng and Dīng to the heart,
Wù and Jǐ to the spleen,
Gēng and Xīn to the lungs,
Rén and Gǔi to the kidneys.
The earthly branches assign Yín and Mǎo to the liver,
Sì and Wǔ to the heart,
Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi to the spleen,
Shēn and Yǒu to the lungs,
Hài and Zǐ to the kidneys.
These are all based on the Five Phases correspondence.
Furthermore, the heavenly stems assign Jiǎ and Yǐ to the skin and hair,
Bǐng and Dīng to the claws and tendons,
Wù and Jǐ to the flesh,
Gēng and Xīn to the bones,
Rén and Gǔi to the blood vessels.
The earthly branches assign Yín and Mǎo to the skin and hair,
Sì and Wǔ to the claws and tendons,
Chén, Xū, Chǒu, and Wèi to the flesh,
Shēn and Yǒu to the bones,
Hài and Zǐ to the blood vessels.
Wood grows on the ground,
hence it represents skin and hair.
Fire is fierce and resolute,
hence it represents tendons and claws.
Earth supports and carries,
hence it represents flesh.
Metal is firm and rigid by nature,
hence it represents bones.
Water inherently flows and moistens,
hence it represents blood vessels.
These are the correspondences for both heavenly stems and earthly branches,
thus they are fully explained.
Generally, the Five Phases are evenly distributed,
present throughout all things,
and cannot be confined to a single path.
Now, let's first discuss the intermingling nature of the Five Phases.
Their *qì* flows continuously,
applied according to circumstances.
If one says they are not intermingled,
Water should only be one.
Why then is it called five and becomes six?
Fire, Metal, Wood, and Earth are all similar.
It should be known that the generating number is fundamental,
and the completing number is intermingled.
Since there is intermingling,
one phase, when embodied,
possesses five meanings.
For example, Wood has straightness and crookedness;
this is Wood itself.
If Wood contains fire,
then it is Fire.
If Wood can be used as a weapon,
having the ability to strike and touch,
then it is Metal.
If Wood contains moisture,
then it is Water.
If Wood sprouts flowers, leaves, and fruits,
then it is Earth.
Fire's external Yang is Fire itself.
Its internal Yin is Water.
Its ability to kill is Metal.
Its ability to ripen is Wood.
Its ability to generate is Earth.
Earth's ability to generate is Earth itself.
Its ability to contain is Water.
Its ability to complete is Wood.
Its ability to defend is Metal.
Its containing Yang is Fire.
Metal's ability to sever is Metal itself.
Its adaptability is Wood.
Its containing fire is Fire.
Its possessing impurities is Water.
Its ability to generate is Earth.
Water's external Yin is Water itself.
Its internal Yang is Fire.
Its containing nourishment is Wood.
Its moistening and generating is Earth.
Its ability to kill is Metal.
These all explain that by their meaning, one phase generally contains all five *qì*.
When discussing principles based on actual phenomena,
then it is not so.
Sometimes there is, sometimes there isn't.
For those with a weak constitution,
the substances are compatible.
For those with a strong constitution,
the substances are incompatible.
There is no wood in metal,
and no metal in wood.
This is because metal and wood directly harm each other.
There is no fire in water,
and no water in fire.
This is because the two elements directly harm each other.
Similarly, there is no metal in water,
but there is water in metal.
There is also water in wood,
and fire in wood,
and fire in stone.
Since water can generate wood,
then there is water in wood.
Water is born from metal,
so there is water in metal.
Fire is born from wood,
so there is fire in wood.
Water is again born from metal,
so there is water in metal.
Water can generate wood.
There is fire in wood.
Fire khắc [kè] metal;
how then can stone also contain fire?
This is because fire's nature is weak,
hence the weak can penetrate the strong.
However, there is no metal in fire,
meaning the strong cannot penetrate the weak.
Wood is born from water,
so wood contains water.
Metal can generate water,
so metal contains water.
Therefore, regarding why there is no metal or wood in water:
metal and wood are in water,
but one cannot say that the body of water contains metal or wood.
When moisture is in wood and stone,
wood and stone then can be said to have the principle of water.
This also illustrates that the weak can penetrate the strong,
but the strong cannot penetrate the weak.
In Yánzhōu [Yánzhōu] there are trees
that grow in fire.
This is not because fire can generate trees.
It is that fire cannot burn the trees.
Nor is fire in the trees;
rather, the trees are in the fire,
and their substances do not intermingle.
It is no different from metal in water
which cannot intermingle with the body of water.
It is also like the hidden fires burning in the sea.
In this case, there is fire in water,
but the body of water is not mixed with fire.
This somewhat involves spiritual wonders [língqí],
and is not a constant standard of the Five Phases.
Furthermore, there is fire in wood,
and fire in turn burns wood.
This is when the generating fire is flourishing,
hence it can burn wood.
There is fire in stone,
but fire does not burn stone.
This is because when fire reaches the region of metal,
its qi [qì] is already declining,
hence it cannot burn stone.
As for fire dissolving metal,
this also refers to its flourishing state,
hence it can melt metal.
It does not refer to declining fire,
just as metal can overcome wood,
but lead and tin cannot cut it.
This is metal that is not strong.
The nature of earth is inclusive,
receiving everything.
Therefore, earth contains all of water, metal, wood, and fire.
Fire is not solely yang [yáng] qi [qì];
for example, the burning ground of Fànyáng [Fànyáng]
is yin [yīn].
Earth and fire do not harm each other.
Although it is not always so,
one cannot say it never happens.
These are all four elements,
why is it uniquely so?
Since earth occupies the ground,
the ground is yin.
Fire is the qi [qì] of the great yang,
so it cannot always be present.
Regarding the intermingling of the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches [zhīgān zácè]:
The Five Phases texts say:
Jiǎ [Jiǎ] gives his younger sister Yǐ [Yǐ]
in marriage to Gēng [Gēng].
Hence Yǐ [Yǐ] contains mixed metal.
At the beginning of spring, wood thrives.
Jiǎ [Jiǎ] summons Yǐ [Yǐ] back,
and Yǐ [Yǐ] returns bearing the qi [qì] of metal.
Therefore, in mid-spring, the elm pods whiten.
Bǐng [Bǐng] gives his younger sister Dīng [Dīng]
in marriage to Rén [Rén].
Dīng [Dīng] contains mixed water.
At the beginning of summer, fire thrives.
Bǐng [Bǐng] summons Dīng [Dīng] back,
and Dīng [Dīng] returns bearing the qi [qì] of water.
Therefore, in mid-summer, mulberries ripen and turn black.
Wù [Wù] gives his younger sister Jǐ [Jǐ]
in marriage to Jiǎ [Jiǎ].
Jǐ [Jǐ] contains mixed wood.
In late summer, earth thrives.
Wù [Wù] summons Jǐ [Jǐ] back,
and Jǐ [Jǐ] returns bearing the qi [qì] of wood.
Therefore, in late summer, fruits are green.
Gēng [Gēng] gives his younger sister Xīn [Xīn]
in marriage to Bǐng [Bǐng].
Xīn [Xīn] contains mixed fire.
At the beginning of autumn, metal thrives.
Gēng [Gēng] summons Xīn [Xīn] back,
and Xīn [Xīn] returns bearing the qi [qì] of fire.
Therefore, in mid-autumn, dates ripen and turn red.
Rén [Rén] gives his younger sister Guǐ [Guǐ]
in marriage to Wù [Wù].
Guǐ [Guǐ] contains mixed earth.
At the beginning of winter, water thrives.
Rén [Rén] summons Guǐ [Guǐ] back,
and Guǐ [Guǐ] returns bearing the qi [qì] of earth.
Therefore, in mid-winter, all grasses and trees turn yellow.
Jiǎ [Jiǎ], Bǐng [Bǐng], Wù [Wù], Gēng [Gēng], and Rén [Rén] are male,
strong and firm.
Therefore, they possess their own virtue and are not mixed.
Yǐ [Yǐ], Dīng [Dīng], Jǐ [Jǐ], Xīn [Xīn], and Guǐ [Guǐ] are female,
soft and weak.
They do not act independently but follow their husbands.
Therefore, they are mixed.
Just like a married woman,
who takes her husband's surname,
when she returns home for a visit,
she brings her children,
and thus the family lineage becomes mixed.
The text "Five Phases Ten Mixtures" says:
Jiǎ [Jiǎ] is wood,
Yǐ [Yǐ] is timber,
Bǐng [Bǐng] is fire,
Dīng [Dīng] is ash,
Wù [Wù] is earth,
Jǐ [Jǐ] is mud,
Gēng [Gēng] is metal,
Xīn [Xīn] is a furnace or antimony,
Rén [Rén] is water,
Guǐ [Guǐ] is turbid impurity.
These all represent the meaning of mixing.
Yín [Yín] and Mǎo [Mǎo] are wood,
spring contains fire;
therefore Mǎo [Mǎo] is pure wood,
and Yín [Yín] is mixed wood.
Sì [Sì] and Wǔ [Wǔ] are fire,
summer contains earth;
therefore Wǔ [Wǔ] is pure fire,
and Sì [Sì] is mixed fire.
Shēn [Shēn] and Yǒu [Yǒu] are metal,
autumn contains water;
therefore Yǒu [Yǒu] is pure metal,
and Shēn [Shēn] is mixed metal.
Hài [Hài] and Zǐ [Zǐ] are water,
winter contains wood;
therefore Zǐ [Zǐ] is pure water,
and Hài [Hài] is mixed water.
Earth resides in the center,
governing the four qì [qì] separately;
therefore Chén [Chén] contains residual wood,
Wèi [Wèi] contains residual fire,
Xū [Xū] contains residual metal,
Chǒu [Chǒu] contains residual water,
each for twelve days.
Thus, the four Mèng [Mèng] are where generative qi [qì] is conceived and nurtured,
the four Zhòng [Zhòng] are where it thrives and is strong,
and the four Jì [Jì] are where it is buried and ends.
Conception, nurturing, and burial
all have the meaning of mixing.
The Wǔxíng are not merely inherently mixed.
Within each direction, there is also a meaning of mixing.
The Dōngfāng corresponds to Jiǎ, Yǐ, Yín, Mǎo, Chén.
Jiǎ is Mù.
Within Yǐ, there is mixed Jīn.
Within Yín, there is generating Huǒ.
Chén is Tǔ.
Within Mǎo, there is decaying Shuǐ.
The Nánfāng corresponds to Bǐng, Dīng, Sì, Wǔ, Wèi.
Bǐng is Huǒ.
Within Dīng, there is mixed Shuǐ.
Within Sì, there is generating Jīn.
Wèi is Tǔ.
Within Wǔ, there is decaying Mù.
The Xīfāng corresponds to Gēng, Xīn, Shēn, Yǒu, Xū.
Gēng is Jīn.
Within Xīn, there is mixed Huǒ.
Within Shēn, there is generating Shuǐ.
Xū is Tǔ.
Furthermore, within Yǒu, there is embryonic Mù.
The Běifāng corresponds to Rén, Guǐ, Hài, Zǐ, Chǒu.
Rén is Shuǐ.
Within Guǐ, there is mixed Tǔ.
Within Hài, there is generating Mù.
Within Zǐ, there is embryonic Huǒ.
Within Chǒu, there is decaying Jīn.
Thus, each direction separately contains the Wǔxíng.
Yín, Wǔ, Xū are the positions of Huǒ.
Within Yín, there is generating Huǒ,
in the Dōngfāng.
Within Wǔ, there is flourishing Huǒ,
in the Nánfāng.
Within Xū, there is decaying Huǒ,
in the Xīfāng.
Hài, Mǎo, Wèi are the positions of Mù.
Within Hài, there is generating Mù,
in the Běifāng.
Within Mǎo, there is flourishing Mù,
in the Dōngfāng.
Within Wèi, there is decaying Mù,
in the Nánfāng.
Shēn, Zǐ, Chén are the positions of Shuǐ.
Within Shēn, there is generating Shuǐ,
in the Xīfāng.
Within Zǐ, there is flourishing Shuǐ,
in the Běifāng.
Within Chén, there is decaying Shuǐ,
in the Dōngfāng.
Sì, Yǒu, Chǒu are the positions of Jīn.
Within Sì, there is generating Jīn,
in the Nánfāng.
Within Yǒu, there is flourishing Jīn,
in the Xīfāng.
Within Chǒu, there is decaying Jīn,
in the Běifāng.
Thus, the substance of one element
is mixed across three directions.
Wèi, Chén, Chǒu, Xū are the positions of Tǔ.
Within Wèi, there is flourishing Tǔ,
within Chén, there is decaying Tǔ,
within Chǒu, there is weakening Tǔ,
within Xū, there is vigorous Tǔ.
Thus, the substance of Tǔ is mixed across four directions.
Zhào Yí said,
the Wǔxíng mix with each other,
like brocade and embroidered silk.
This statement
is apt.
Dé means "to obtain."
It benefits things,
each according to its desire,
without regret or stinginess,
therefore it is called Dé.
The Wǔxíng books say,
if there is one Dé,
it can ward off a hundred calamities.
Whenever Yīnyáng are active,
encountering Dé is good,
it is called Fúdé.
As there is assistance,
all matters are auspicious,
and disasters vanish.
There are four types of Dé.
Three types are discussed based on the Zhīgān (Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches),
and one type is discussed based on the monthly qi.
The three types of Zhīgān are:
first, Gāndé (Stem Virtue);
second, Zhīdé (Branch Virtue);
third, Zhīgān Hédé (Combined Stem and Branch Virtue).
As for the Virtues of the Heavenly Stems (Gāndé):
The Virtue of Jiǎ is self-residing.
The Virtue of Yǐ is in Gēng.
The Virtue of Bǐng is self-residing.
The Virtue of Dīng is in Rén.
The Virtue of Wù is self-residing.
The Virtue of Jǐ is in Jiǎ.
The Virtue of Gēng is self-residing.
The Virtue of Xīn is in Bǐng.
The Virtue of Rén is self-residing.
The Virtue of Guǐ is in Wù.
Among these ten Heavenly Stems:
Jiǎ, Bǐng, Wù, Gēng, and Rén are Yang.
Being esteemed, their Virtues reside in themselves.
Yǐ, Dīng, Jǐ, Xīn, and Guǐ are Yin.
Being subordinate, their Virtues are paired with Yang,
embodying the principle of "following the husband."
This is why they do not have self-residing Virtues.
Yángzǐ said:
"In the Way of pairing the days,
there are exactly five pairs of days:
Jiǎ and Jǐ for Wood;
Bǐng and Xīn for Fire;
Wù and Guǐ for Earth;
Yǐ and Gēng for Metal;
Dīng and Rén for Water."
The principles of Yin and Yang
must be paired,
in accordance with the meaning of ruler and minister, husband and wife.
Jiǎ is the ruler
and the husband;
Jǐ is the minister
and the wife.
The ruler's position is self-residing;
the minister's position depends on the ruler.
Therefore, the Virtue of Jǐ is in Jiǎ,
and the Virtue of Yǐ is in Gēng.
All other four pairs are similar,
following the principle of Yin following Yang.
As for the Virtues of the Earthly Branches (Zhīdé):
The Virtue of Zǐ is in Sì.
The Virtue of Chǒu is in Wǔ.
The Virtue of Yín is in Wèi.
The Virtue of Mǎo is in Shēn.
The Virtue of Chén is in Yǒu.
The Virtue of Sì is in Xū.
The Virtue of Wǔ is in Hài.
The Virtue of Wèi is in Zǐ.
The Virtue of Shēn is in Chǒu.
The Virtue of Yǒu is in Yín.
The Virtue of Xū is in Mǎo.
The Virtue of Hài is in Chén.
All these are based on the places where their husbands generate and assist them.
As for Zǐ taking Sì as its Virtue:
Zǐ is Water,
taking Earth as its husband.
Within Sì, there is nascent Earth.
As for Chǒu taking Wǔ as its Virtue:
Chǒu is Earth,
taking Wood as its husband.
Within Wǔ, there is dead Wood.
As for Yín taking Wèi as its Virtue:
Yín is Wood,
taking Metal as its husband.
Within Wèi, there is "crowned and belted" Metal.
As for Mǎo taking Shēn as its Virtue:
Mǎo is Wood,
taking Metal as its husband.
Within Shēn, there is "prime" Metal.
As for Chén taking Yǒu as its Virtue:
Chén is Earth,
taking Wood as its husband.
Within Yǒu, there is "fetus" Wood.
As for Sì taking Xū as its Virtue:
Sì is Fire,
taking Water as its husband.
Within Xū, there is "crowned and belted" Water.
As for Wǔ taking Hài as its Virtue:
Wǔ is Fire,
taking Water as its husband.
Within Hài, there is "prime" Water.
As for Wèi taking Zǐ as its Virtue:
Wèi is Earth,
taking Wood as its husband.
Within Zǐ, there is "bathing" Wood.
As for Shēn taking Chǒu as its Virtue:
Shēn is Metal,
taking Fire as its husband.
Within Chǒu, there is "nurtured" Fire.
As for Yǒu taking Yín as its Virtue:
Yǒu is Metal,
taking Fire as its husband.
Within Yín, there is nascent Fire.
As for Xū taking Mǎo as its Virtue:
Xū is Earth,
taking Wood as its husband.
Within Mǎo, there is "flourishing" Wood.
As for Hài taking Chén as its Virtue:
Hài is Water,
taking Earth as its husband.
Within Chén, there is dead Earth.
Someone might ask:
"In the principle of 'following the husband,'
the living have Virtue,
capable of harmony and nourishment,
hence they follow.
The dead, however, are separated and alienated,
unable to harmonize or follow.
How can the dead still be considered a Virtue?"
The answer is:
"A woman does not remarry;
once married to a man,
she is called by her husband's clan name.
Even after death, she still follows his lineage.
How can she be called by it while alive
and then abandoned upon death?
Therefore, the Yin's following of Yang
persists in both life and death."
As for the combined Virtues of Stems and Branches (Gānzhī Hédé):
The Virtue of Zǐ is in Jiǎ.
The Virtue of Chǒu is in Xīn.
The Virtue of Yín is in Bǐng.
The Virtue of Mǎo is in Dīng.
The Virtue of Chén is in Gēng.
The Virtue of Sì is in Jǐ.
The Virtue of Wǔ is in Wù.
The Virtue of Wèi is in Xīn.
The Virtue of Shēn is in Rén.
The Virtue of Yǒu is in Guǐ.
The Virtue of Xū is in Gēng.
The Virtue of Hài is in Yǐ.
All these are taking the son as Virtue.
This means that the son can support and assist his mother,
possessing the nature of filial piety and nurturing,
and thus is considered a Virtue.
Generally, Heavenly Stems (Gān) are Yang,
and Earthly Branches (Zhī) are Yin.
The Yang entity is strong and self-residing;
the Yin entity is gentle and compliant, following Yang.
Women have the ritual of three obediences.
They never have the right to act independently.
If the husband dies, she follows the son,
hence taking the son as Virtue.
If the Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches each had their own Virtues,
they would all follow their husbands.
But since the Stems and Branches now share a combined Virtue,
they leave their husband's position
and thus follow the son.
As for the Virtue of Zǐ being in Jiǎ,
this is because Water is the mother of Wood.
All other cases follow this pattern.
In another case, taking the monthly qi as Virtue:
Virtue does not stand alone;
it is contrasted with Punishment (Xíng).
Virtue is Yang,
thus following Qián (Heaven);
Punishment is Yin,
thus following Kūn (Earth).
This is also like human governance,
where both Punishment and Virtue are applied.
Virtue involves rewards, bestowals of rank, and praise,
hence it is paired with Yang.
Punishment involves killing, penalties, reductions, and deprivation,
hence it is paired with Yin.
Therefore, when a ruler experiences
a solar eclipse, he cultivates Virtue;
when a lunar eclipse, he cultivates Punishment.
Dǒng Zhòngshū, in the Chūnqiū Fánlù, said:
"The constant Way of Heaven
is one Yang and one Yin.
Yang is the Virtue of Heaven;
Yin is the Punishment of Heaven.
By observing the year-long course of Yin and Yang,
one can discern what Heaven cherishes and entrusts,
and thus understand the function of Virtue and Punishment.
However, Heaven entrusts Yang, not Yin;
it favors Virtue, not Punishment.
Therefore, Yang emerges and accumulates in summer,
entrusting Virtue for the year's affairs;
Yin emerges and accumulates in winter,
placing Punishment in an empty position."
Tàigōng said:
"When a ruler undertakes affairs,
if good, Heaven responds with Virtue;
if evil, Heaven responds with Punishment."
These all illustrate that Yin and Yang are opposed,
and Virtue does not rule alone,
but requires Punishment as its complement.
Following the *qì* of the two *guà* of *Qián* and *Kūn*:
In the tenth month, the *Kūn* *guà* is in charge.
From the eleventh month, the *yáng* *qì* stirs,
and the *yīn* lines change.
In the fourth month, the *Qián* *guà* is in charge.
From the fifth month, the *yīn* *qì* stirs,
and the *yáng* lines change.
Thus, *huángzhōng* and *ruíbīn*
are the beginning of the *qì* of *yīn* and *yáng*.
Favor and punishment are therein.
In the month of *Jiànzǐ*,
the first *yīn* line (初六) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
The *Fù* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* stirs beneath the Yellow Springs,
and the *yīn* *qì* spreads above the azure sky.
Favor is in the inner chambers,
and punishment is in the wilderness.
In the month of *Jiànchǒu*,
the second *yīn* line (六二) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
The *Lín* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* gradually emerges,
all things sprout their teeth (buds),
the *yīn* *qì* is about to descend,
and its fierce anger has already waned.
Favor is in the hall,
and punishment is in the street.
In the month of *Jiànyín*,
the third *yīn* line (六三) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
The *Tài* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* has reached its peak,
the *yīn* *qì* has descended,
and *yīn* and *yáng* are in auspicious communion (*jiāotài*).
All things sprout their shoots and leaves.
Favor is in the courtyard,
and punishment is in the alley.
In the month of *Jiànmǎo*,
the fourth *yīn* line (六四) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
The *Dàzhuàng* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* ascends to heaven,
the *yīn* *qì* descends into the earth,
the *qì* of *yīn* and *yáng* intermingle,
and all things develop and emerge.
Favor and punishment both meet at the gate.
In the month of *Jiànchén*,
the fifth *yīn* line (六五) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
The *Guài* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* reaches its height,
and the *yīn* *qì* dwindles.
Favor is in the alley,
and punishment is in the courtyard.
In the month of *Jiànsì*,
the top *yīn* line (上六) of *Kūn*
changes to *yáng*.
Pure *yáng* (*qiányáng*) is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* is greatly abundant,
the *yīn* *qì* is eliminated,
all things are joyous and robust,
there is no more punishment or killing.
Favor is in the street,
and punishment is in the hall.
In the month of *Jiànwǔ*,
the first *yáng* line (初九) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*.
The *Gòu* *guà* is in charge.
The *yīn* *qì* stirs beneath the Yellow Springs,
and the *yáng* *qì* spreads above the azure sky.
Favor is in the wilderness,
and punishment is in the inner chambers.
In the month of *Jiànwèi*,
the second *yáng* line (九二) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*.
The *Dùn* *guà* is in charge.
The *yīn* *qì* gradually rises,
the *yáng* *qì* is about to diminish,
all things reach their peak of robustness,
and then all decline into old age.
Favor is in the street,
and punishment is in the hall.
In the month of *Jiànshēn*,
the third *yáng* line (九三) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*.
The *Pǐ* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* recedes and retreats,
the *yīn* *qì* advances and rises,
*yīn* and *yáng* are blocked off from each other (*pǐgé*),
and the power of killing is flourishing.
Favor is in the alley,
and punishment is in the courtyard.
In the month of *Jiànyǒu*,
the fourth *yáng* line (九四) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*.
The *Guān* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* withdraws inward,
the *yīn* *qì* spreads outward,
*yīn* and *yáng* contend together,
and all things transform and decay.
Favor is at the gate,
and punishment again meets at the gate.
In the month of *Jiànxū*,
the fifth *yáng* line (九五) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*.
The *Bō* *guà* is in charge.
The *yáng* *qì* is about to be exhausted,
the *yīn* *qì* reaches its height,
all things wither and fade,
and killing and harming prevail.
Favor is in the courtyard,
and punishment is in the alley.
In the month of *Jiànhài*,
the top *yáng* line (上九) of *Qián*
changes to *yīn*,
and pure *Kūn* (*chúnkūn*) returns to its position.
The *yáng* *qì* is eliminated,
the *yīn* *qì* is greatly abundant,
all things are stored away,
and no crimes are seen.
Favor is in the hall,
and punishment is in the street.
These two matters of punishment and favor,
their coming and going, their directions and inclinations,
are all to be utilized.
Lest one forget to grasp the chisel.
Encountering favor brings auspiciousness,
meeting punishment brings misfortune,
hence it is explained here.
Kǒngzǐ said,
*Qián* is *yáng*,
*Kūn* is *yīn*;
*yīn* and *yáng* combine their virtues.
The origin of the Five Phases
receives birth from Heaven,
then receives completion from Earth.
It obtains its *qì* from *yáng*,
and its form is determined by *yīn*.
The body does not stand alone,
thus each has its counterpart.
Generally speaking,
the celestial stems (*gān*) belong to *yáng* and Heaven,
the terrestrial branches (*zhī*) belong to *yīn* and Earth.
Specifically speaking,
the celestial stems themselves have *yīn* and *yáng*.
*Jiǎ* is *yáng*,
*Yǐ* is *yīn*,
*Bǐng* is *yáng*,
*Dīng* is *yīn*,
*Wù* is *yáng*,
*Jǐ* is *yīn*,
*Gēng* is *yáng*,
*Xīn* is *yīn*,
*Rén* is *yáng*,
*Guǐ* is *yīn*.
The terrestrial branches also have their own *yīn* and *yáng*.
*Zǐ* is *yáng*,
*Chǒu* is *yīn*,
*Yín* is *yáng*,
*Mǎo* is *yīn*,
*Chén* is *yáng*,
*Sì* is *yīn*,
*Wǔ* is *yáng*,
*Wèi* is *yīn*,
*Shēn* is *yáng*,
*Yǒu* is *yīn*,
*Xū* is *yáng*,
*Hài* is *yīn*.
Each symbolizes Heaven and Earth,
and they combine with each other,
following the way of husband and wife.
As for the Heavenly Stem combinations:
Jǐ is the wife of Jiǎ,
therefore Jiǎ combines with Jǐ.
Xīn is the wife of Bǐng,
therefore Bǐng combines with Xīn.
Guǐ is the wife of Wù,
therefore Guǐ combines with Wù.
Yǐ is the wife of Gēng,
therefore Yǐ combines with Gēng.
Dīng is the wife of Rén,
therefore Rén combines with Dīng.
Jì Shì's theory of Yīn and Yáng states:
Wood, associated with eight, fears Gēng, associated with nine.
Therefore, its younger sister Yǐ is married to Gēng.
Gēng's qi is in autumn,
harmonizing with wood's qi.
This is why shepherd's purse and wheat grow in autumn,
which is called "the meaning of the wife coming."
Fire, associated with seven, fears Rén, associated with six.
Therefore, its younger sister Dīng is married to Rén.
Rén obtains the hot qi of fire,
thus colt's foot blossoms in winter.
Metal, associated with nine, fears Bǐng, associated with seven.
Therefore, its younger sister Xīn is married to Bǐng.
Bǐng obtains the qi of metal,
thus at the beginning of summer, the wild grasses and shepherd's purse die.
Therefore, after the summer solstice,
the three Gēng days constitute the 'hiding' (伏, fú) period,
out of fear of fire.
Earth, associated with five, fears Jiǎ, associated with eight.
Therefore, its younger sister Jǐ is married to Jiǎ.
Earth carries the harmony of Yīn and Yáng,
marrying the female to wood.
Thus it can generate all things.
Water, associated with six, fears Wù, associated with five.
Therefore, its younger sister Guǐ is married to Wù.
When the Five Phases harmonize with each other,
this is their combination.
As for Earthly Branch combinations:
These are the combinations of the sequential movements of the sun and moon.
In the first month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Zuīzī.
Zuīzī is Hài.
It is also called Shǐwéi.
The Dipper points to Yín,
therefore Yín combines with Hài.
In the second month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Jiànglóu.
Jiànglóu is Xū.
The Dipper points to Mǎo,
therefore Mǎo combines with Xū.
In the third month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Dàliáng.
Dàliáng is Yǒu.
The Dipper points to Chén,
therefore Chén combines with Yǒu.
In the fourth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Shíshěn.
Shíshěn is Shēn.
The Dipper points to Sì,
therefore Sì combines with Shēn.
In the fifth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Qúnshǒu.
Qúnshǒu is Wèi.
The Dipper points to Wǔ,
therefore Wǔ combines with Wèi.
In the sixth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Qúnhuǒ.
Qúnhuǒ is Wǔ.
The Dipper points to Wèi,
therefore Wèi combines with Wǔ.
In the seventh month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Qúnwěi.
Qúnwěi is Sì.
The Dipper points to Shēn,
therefore Shēn combines with Sì.
In the eighth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Shòuxīng.
Shòuxīng is Chén.
The Dipper points to Yǒu,
therefore Yǒu combines with Chén.
In the ninth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Dàhuǒ.
Dàhuǒ is Mǎo.
The Dipper points to Xū,
therefore Xū combines with Mǎo.
In the tenth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Zhémù.
Zhémù is Yín.
The Dipper points to Hài,
therefore Hài combines with Yín.
In the eleventh month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Xīngjì.
Xīngjì is Chǒu.
The Dipper points to Zǐ,
therefore Zǐ combines with Chǒu.
In the twelfth month, the sun and moon meet in the mansion of Xuánxiāo.
Xuánxiāo is Zǐ,
also called Tiānyuán.
The Dipper points to Chǒu,
therefore Chǒu combines with Zǐ.
As for Xuánxiāo:
Xuán means black,
Xiāo means consumption.
The Yīn qi is abundant,
thus all things begin to stir,
yet have not yet emerged.
The world is empty and void,
called consumption.
As for Xīngjì:
Jì means to govern.
It governs the beginning and end of all things.
As for Zhémù:
All things begin to sprout,
distinguishing water and wood.
As for Dàhuǒ:
It is the wood of the East.
The heart constellation (Xīn Sù) is in Mǎo,
fire emerges from the heart of wood.
As for Shòuxīng:
All things begin to reach their destiny,
each fulfilling its fate.
As for Qúnwěi:
It is the constellation of the Vermilion Bird of the South,
being the tail of Zhěn.
As for Qúnhuǒ:
The Yáng qi is greatly abundant,
the star of fire (Mars) sets at dusk in the middle (of the sky),
located in the Seven Stars (constellation) of the Vermilion Bird.
As for Qúnshǒu:
It is the constellation of the South,
its shape resembles a bird,
with Jǐng as its crown,
and Liǔ as its mouth.
As for Shíshěn:
The Yīn qi is heavy and profound,
manifesting itself in things.
As for Dàliáng:
It means strong.
White Dew has fallen,
all things are firm and strong.
As for Jiànglóu:
Jiàng means to descend,
Lóu means curved.
The Yīn qi invades from above,
all things wither and curve.
As for Zuīzī:
Yīn is dominant and Yáng is hidden,
all things are sad and sorrowful.
In general, when Yīn and Yáng are paired,
good and evil are equally balanced.
Bad fortune is not entirely bad,
good fortune is not solely good.
When good ends, bad follows;
when bad ends, good follows.
Therefore, combination is not solely combination,
there is also the meaning of separation.
When Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches are paired with days and hours,
there are Five Combinations and Five Separations.
As for the Five Combinations,
the Hétú says:
Jiǎ Yín and Yǐ Mǎo are the combination of Heaven and Earth.
Bǐng Yín and Dīng Mǎo are the combination of Sun and Moon.
Wù Yín and Jǐ Mǎo are the combination of People.
Gēng Yín and Xīn Mǎo are the combination of Metal and Stone.
Rén Yín and Guǐ Mǎo are the combination of Rivers and Seas.
As for the Five Separations:
Jiǎ Shēn and Yǐ Yǒu are the separation of Heaven and Earth.
Bǐng Shēn and Dīng Yǒu are the separation of Sun and Moon.
Wù Shēn and Jǐ Yǒu are the separation of People.
Gēng Shēn and Xīn Yǒu are the separation of Metal and Stone.
Rén Shēn and Guǐ Yǒu are the separation of Rivers and Seas.
Yín and Mǎo are where Yáng ascends,
capable of generating all things.
The sun rises daily,
the moon, when full, also emerges.
The East is the place of lesser Yáng and growth,
where things joyfully gather,
hence it is considered a combination.
Shēn and Yǒu are where Yīn gathers,
the direction of severity and killing.
The sun and moon both set in this place.
The West is the place of lesser Yīn and decline,
what things dislike,
hence it is considered a separation.
Jiǎ and Yǐ are called the heads of the Stems,
their hexagrams belong to Qián and Kūn,
therefore they are compared to Heaven and Earth.
Bǐng and Dīng are the height of Yáng sunlight,
therefore they correspond to the Sun and Moon.
Wù and Jǐ are in the center,
capable of bringing all things to completion,
therefore they are likened to People.
Gēng and Xīn are inherently Metal and Stone.
Rén and Guǐ are naturally Rivers and Seas.
In all matters,
if auspicious, follow combinations;
if inauspicious, follow separations.
Encountering a combination is auspicious;
encountering a separation is inauspicious.
For selecting days and fixing times,
and for the use of divination,
these are extensively applied.
Fú (扶)
takes aiding and assisting as its meaning.
Yì (抑)
is named for stopping and retreating.
Once the Five Phases (wǔxíng) are formed,
their flourishing and decline have their times,
and their venerability and inferiority alternate.
Thus, there are those that mutually aid (fú) and restrain (yì) each other.
This refers to their encounter with each other.
When the mother obtains the son, it is fú (扶);
when the son encounters the mother, it is yì (抑).
The son has the principle of filial piety, nurturing, obedience, and assistance,
which is why it is fú (扶).
The mother has the way of dignity, strictness, instruction, and control,
which is why it is yì (抑).
Those that mutually aid (fú) are:
Wood aids Water (mù fú shuǐ),
Water aids Metal (shuǐ fú jīn),
Metal aids Earth (jīn fú tǔ),
Earth aids Fire (tǔ fú huǒ),
Fire aids Wood (huǒ fú mù).
These are all cases where the mother obtains the son.
Those that mutually restrain (yì) are:
Wood restrains Fire (mù yì huǒ),
Fire restrains Earth (huǒ yì tǔ),
Earth restrains Metal (tǔ yì jīn),
Metal restrains Water (jīn yì shuǐ),
Water restrains Wood (shuǐ yì mù).
These are all cases where the son encounters the mother.
Liǔ Shìlóng's (柳世隆) Guī Jīng (龜經) says:
Fú (扶) brings longevity,
Yì (抑) brings misfortune;
Fú (扶) brings rising,
Yì (抑) brings stopping;
Fú (扶) brings looking up,
Yì (抑) brings looking down;
Fú (扶) brings advancement,
Yì (抑) brings retreat;
Fú (扶) brings movement,
Yì (抑) brings stopping;
Fú (扶) brings auspiciousness,
Yì (抑) brings inauspiciousness.
For this, further discernment is required.
Generally, if parents have qi (qì), they are true parents;
if they have no qi (qì), they are ancestral spirits (zōngmiào guǐshén).
Having qi (qì) means assistance and blessings for the son;
having no qi (qì) means wealth and meritorious deeds.
Therefore, fú (扶) is necessarily good,
and yì (抑) is bad.
During the time of flourishing (shēng wàng),
there is qi (qì);
during the time of death and decay (sǐ mò),
there is no qi (qì).
Having qi (qì) or not having qi (qì)
further has two types.
If one encounters a harmonious combination (hé dé),
even restraint (yì) is not harmful.
If one encounters punishment and overcoming (xíng kè),
it is inauspicious.
A further, more serious question is asked:
The mother's way of instruction and control
over her son
is called inauspicious.
This is not understandable.
With dignity and strict instruction,
teaching with righteousness,
desiring the son to become an accomplished person,
how can it be considered evil?
The answer is:
The previous explanation already has two types.
If one encounters a harmonious combination (yī dé hé),
even restraint (yì) is not harmful.
Having qi (qì) means true parents;
this is desiring the son to become an accomplished person.
However, during the time of instruction,
if the interaction with the son does not go as desired,
it is also an obstruction,
let alone encountering punishment and overcoming (xíng kè).
Even Shùn's (舜) extreme filial piety
still led him to flee when his father used a large staff.
Wáng Xiáng (王祥) knocked on the ice,
Mèng Zōng (孟宗) wept for bamboo shoots.
How could these be teachings of righteousness?
No qi (qì) means ancestral spirits (guǐshén).
When ancestral spirits (guǐshén) come,
they often desire to cause trouble.
Only through earnest entreaties and prayers
can blessings be obtained.
What does this 'misfortune and restraint (fǒu yì)' mean?
Question:
The explanation says having qi (qì) means parents, and no qi (qì) means ancestral spirits (guǐshén).
This also raises doubts.
Although ancestral spirits (guǐshén) dwell in the subtle and obscure,
they are still entities.
Spiritual efficacy connects,
and fortune and misfortune respond accordingly.
If one says there are none,
upon what do ancestral temple sacrifices
rely?
Answer:
What is spoken of as 'having' or 'not having'
precisely discusses life and death.
Alive, the form exists, so it is 'having';
dead, the qi (qì) disperses, so it is 'not having'.
It does not speak of the subtle and obscure;
what is there to doubt?
Question:
If death is explained this way,
then it is 'not having'.
What is there to worry about,
that it can still cause restraint (yì)?
Answer:
Although ancestral spirits (guǐshén) have no visible form,
there are good and bad things that can be sought.
Therefore, they can cause restraint (yì).
Question:
If they can cause restraint (yì),
then they must be entities.
Answer:
In terms of restraint (yì), they exist;
in terms of form, they do not.
The current explanation of 'not having'
is discussed in terms of qi (qì);
it does not mean entirely non-existent.
Rather, there is no qi (qì) of flourishing and prime (wàng xiàng),
but there is qi (qì) of death and decay (sǐ mò).
When qi (qì) of flourishing and prime (wàng xiàng) comes, it is auspicious;
when qi (qì) of death and decay (sǐ mò) comes, it is inauspicious.
What is meant by 'no qi (qì)'
is merely 'no qi (qì) of flourishing and prime (wàng xiàng)'.
Although the Five Phases (wǔxíng) represent ruler and minister, father and son,
their flourishing and prime (shēng wàng) differ.
They naturally oppose and overcome each other.
'Overcoming' (kè)
means to control and punish.
Because the strong can control the weak,
Wood overcomes Earth (mù kè tǔ),
Earth overcomes Water (tǔ kè shuǐ),
Water overcomes Fire (shuǐ kè huǒ),
Fire overcomes Metal (huǒ kè jīn),
Metal overcomes Wood (jīn kè mù).
Bái Hǔ Tōng (白虎通) says:
Wood overcomes Earth (mù kè tǔ) means
concentration triumphs over dispersion.
Earth overcomes Water (tǔ kè shuǐ) means
solidity triumphs over emptiness.
Water overcomes Fire (shuǐ kè huǒ) means
multitude triumphs over few.
Fire overcomes Metal (huǒ kè jīn) means
essence triumphs over hardness.
Metal overcomes Wood (jīn kè mù) means
rigidity triumphs over softness.
Chūnqiū Fánlù (春秋繁露) says:
Wood (mù) is the farmer.
If the farmer is disobedient like a rebel,
the Sītú (司徒) punishes their leader.
Thus, Metal overcomes Wood (jīn shèng mù).
Fire (huǒ) is the court where slander and evil exist.
If they confuse the ruler,
the law punishes them.
Thus, Water overcomes Fire (shuǐ shèng huǒ).
Earth (tǔ) is the ruler.
If there is excessive extravagance and disrespect,
the people rebel and are impoverished.
Thus, Wood overcomes Earth (mù shèng tǔ).
Metal (jīn) is the Sītú (司徒).
If they are weak and cannot command the multitude,
the Sīmǎ (司馬) punishes them.
Thus, Fire overcomes Metal (huǒ shèng jīn).
Water (shuǐ) is the law enforcement.
If they are partial and unjust,
the Sīkòu (司寇) punishes them.
Thus, Earth overcomes Water (tǔ shèng shuǐ).
The victor (shèng zhě) is the ruler,
the husband,
the official,
the clerk,
the spirit.
The vanquished (fù zhě) is the minister,
the wife,
the wealth.
The ruler with majesty and high esteem;
the husband with virtue and great importance;
the official with the ability to reward and punish;
the clerk with the power to judge through law;
the spirit with the power to overcome, kill, sicken, and cause loss.
All these are the victors.
The minister submits to his superior in awe;
the wife respectfully follows her husband;
wealth is consumed and utilized.
All these are the vanquished.
When the superior overcomes the inferior, it is called shùn (顺, obedience/compliance).
When the inferior overcomes the superior, it is called bō (剝, stripping away/peeling off).
This is analogous to a ruler having the power to punish a minister,
but a minister having no right to offend a ruler;
a father having the way to instruct a son,
but a son having no means to teach a father.
Therefore, when the superior overcomes the inferior,
it is in accordance with reason;
when the inferior overcomes the superior,
it is contrary to reason.
Thus, the Bái Hǔ Tōng (白虎通) states:
Yáng (阳) is the ruler,
Yīn (阴) is the minister.
Water, with its tài yīn (太阴) energy,
restrains the tài yáng (太阳) fire.
Metal, with its shǎo yīn (少阴) energy,
restrains the shǎo yáng (少阳) wood.
This is analogous to a ruler who has lost the Way,
such as Yīn Tāng (殷汤) banishing Jié (桀),
or Zhōu Wǔ (周武) attacking Zhòu (纣).
These all involve punishing the guilty.
