Generally, in divination, to obtain that which one overcomes is inauspicious;
to obtain that which is restrained by one is auspicious.
According to the Way of the Wǔ Xíng (五行),
a child can save a parent from calamity.
Thus, when Metal goes and overcomes Wood,
Fire will avenge it.
Once Fire melts Metal,
Water will wash away its disgrace.
However, when in a state of declining energy,
one is instead restrained by the dominant one.
Just as water in a tripod cauldron is boiled by fire.
The Bái Hǔ Tōng (白虎通) states:
Fire is hot, water is cold.
Why is there warm water
but no cold fire?
This illustrates that a minister can become a ruler,
but a ruler cannot become a minister.
When fire boils water into soup,
it does not change its form,
but merely transforms its name.
When water extinguishes fire into charcoal,
both its form and name are completely lost.
This is also like a ruler being deposed and ceasing to exist,
or a minister being guilty and resigning from office.
In the Wǔ Xíng xiāng kè (五行相剋, mutual overcoming of the Five Phases):
Wood penetrates Earth but does not destroy it;
Fire burns Metal but does not destroy it.
This is because Yáng (阳) energy is benevolent
and loves life.
Metal fells Wood and harms it;
Water extinguishes Fire and harms it.
This is because Yīn (阴) energy is greedy
and loves killing.
As for mountains collapsing and rivers drying up,
wood and stone causing disasters,
heavenly fire flowing down,
human fire burning upwards,
floods and droughts occurring together,
wind and frost causing harm –
these are all due to human misgovernance,
and Heaven and Earth inflict warnings.
When the Wǔ Xíng (五行) xiāng lì (相沴, mutually injure),
it signifies disharmony and contention.
Because their qì (气) clash and injure each other,
it is not called kè (剋, overcoming).
Lì (沴) also means destruction.
For Wood, it is the extreme tremor in the Nán Gōng (南宫).
For Water, it is the drying up of the Three Rivers.
For Fire, it is disaster in palaces and houses.
For Metal, it is the tremor of the Jiǔ Dǐng (九鼎).
For Earth, it is the collapse of mountains in Qí (齐) and Chǔ (楚).
When Wood, Metal, Water, and Fire all lì (沴) Earth,
it means earthquakes and fragmentation.
This is it.
Thus, when the qì (气) of the Wǔ Xíng (五行) clash,
there are six kinds of lì (沴).
Roughly, it is like this.
Indeed, xíng (刑, punishment)
is named for killing and chastising.
It is to punish injustice,
not to mutually punish without cause.
Each of the Wǔ Xíng (五行) occupies a direction,
cold and heat move and change,
acting in accordance with the seasons,
not losing their proper timing,
each not violating the others,
and none receiving punishment solely without cause.
One must merely use them, not strictly but with governance.
They cannot be abandoned and left unused.
Thus, they all still mutually punish.
For example, using metal to process metal
then forms its vessel;
using people to govern people
then forms national governance.
The Lǚ Shì Chūn Qiū (吕氏春秋) states:
“Punishments cannot be abolished in a state,
and beating and scolding cannot be abandoned in a family.”
Therefore, the three thousand categories of the Wǔ Xíng (五刑)
are all rooted in the Wǔ Xíng (五行).
The Zhōu Shū (周书) says:
“Based on the Wǔ Xíng (五行) xiāng kè (相剋),
the Wǔ Xíng (五刑) were created.”
Mò (墨), Yì (劓), Fèi (剕), Gōng (宮), Dà Pì (大辟) are these.
Fire can change the color of metal,
thus tattooing (Mò) changes the flesh.
Metal can overcome Wood,
thus amputation (Fèi) removes bones and joints.
Wood can overcome Earth,
thus cutting off the nose (Yì) removes the nose.
Earth can block Water,
thus castration (Gōng) severs sexual depravity.
Water can extinguish Fire,
thus capital punishment (Dà Pì) cuts off life.
Up to Hàn Wén (汉文),
he abolished these physical punishments,
replacing them with whipping and caning.
Thereafter, xiāo (枭, exposing head), zhǎn (斩, beheading), liú (流, banishment), jiǎo (绞, strangulation), tú (徒, penal servitude)
all did not exceed the five categories.
The Shàng Shū (尚书) says:
“Banishment pardons the Wǔ Xíng (五刑).”
Furthermore, the five types of banishment are separated
by five hundred lǐ (里) each.
The number of lashes for whipping and caning
starts from ten
and accumulates to one hundred,
also following the numbers of the Shí Gān (十干).
The Shàng Shū Xíng Dé Kǎo (尚书刑德攷) states:
“Capital punishment (Dà Pì) symbolizes heavenly punishment.”
The number of redemptions is three thousand,
corresponding to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
The punishments of the Rì Chén (日辰) Zhī Gān (支干)
also have three types.
Therefore, the punishments of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity
have one principle.
The three types are:
one, the Earthly Branches mutually punish each other;
two, the Earthly Branches punish the Heavenly Stems;
three, the Heavenly Stems punish the Earthly Branches.
As for the Earthly Branches mutually punishing each other:
Zǐ (子) punishes Mǎo (卯),
Mǎo (卯) punishes Zǐ (子);
Chǒu (丑) punishes Xū (戌),
Xū (戌) punishes Wèi (未),
Wèi (未) punishes Chǒu (丑);
Yín (寅) punishes Sì (巳),
Sì (巳) punishes Shēn (申),
Shēn (申) punishes Yín (寅);
Chén (辰), Wǔ (午), Yǒu (酉), Hài (亥) punish themselves.
Hàn Shū (汉书) Yì Fèng (翼奉) Zòu Shì (奏事) states:
“Wood falls and returns to its root,
thus the positions of Hài (亥), Mǎo (卯), Wèi (未) of Wood
punish in the north.
Hài (亥) punishes itself,
Mǎo (卯) punishes Zǐ (子),
Wèi (未) punishes Chǒu (丑).
Water flows towards its end,
thus the positions of Shēn (申), Zǐ (子), Chén (辰) of Water
punish in the east.
Shēn (申) punishes Yín (寅),
Zǐ (子) punishes Mǎo (卯),
Chén (辰) punishes itself.
Metal is strong and Fire is powerful,
each returning to its own region.
Thus the positions of Sì (巳), Yǒu (酉), Chǒu (丑) of Metal
punish in the west.
Sì (巳) punishes Shēn (申),
Yǒu (酉) punishes itself,
Chǒu (丑) punishes Xū (戌).
The positions of Yín (寅), Wǔ (午), Xū (戌) of Fire
punish in the south.
Yín (寅) punishes Sì (巳),
Wǔ (午) punishes itself,
Xū (戌) punishes Wèi (未).”
As for the *gān* (天干) inflicting *xíng* (刑) on *zhī* (地支):
Yín (寅) inflicts *xíng* on Gēng (庚);
Mǎo (卯) inflicts *xíng* on Xīn (辛);
Chén (辰) inflicts *xíng* on Jiǎ (甲);
Sì (巳) inflicts *xíng* on Guǐ (癸);
Wǔ (午) inflicts *xíng* on Rén (壬);
Wèi (未) inflicts *xíng* on Yǐ (乙);
Shēn (申) inflicts *xíng* on Bǐng (丙);
Yǒu (酉) inflicts *xíng* on Dīng (丁);
Xū (戌) inflicts *xíng* on Jiǎ (甲);
Hài (亥) inflicts *xíng* on Jǐ (己);
Zǐ (子) inflicts *xíng* on Wù (戊);
Chǒu (丑) inflicts *xíng* on Yǐ (乙).
As for the *zhī* (地支) inflicting *xíng* (刑) on *gān* (天干):
Jiǎ (甲) inflicts *xíng* on Shēn (申);
Yǐ (乙) inflicts *xíng* on Yǒu (酉);
Bǐng (丙) inflicts *xíng* on Zǐ (子);
Dīng (丁) inflicts *xíng* on Hài (亥);
Wù (戊) inflicts *xíng* on Yín (寅);
Jǐ (己) inflicts *xíng* on Mǎo (卯);
Gēng (庚) inflicts *xíng* on Wǔ (午);
Xīn (辛) inflicts *xíng* on Sì (巳);
Rén (壬) inflicts *xíng* on Chén (辰) and Xū (戌);
Guǐ (癸) inflicts *xíng* on Chǒu (丑) and Wèi (未).
These all consider that which is overcome as being *xíng*.
In all divination,
encountering *xíng* is not good.
However, for the matter being sought,
it cannot be obtained without *xíng*.
*Shǐ Sū Guī Jīng* (史蘓龜經) says:
"When something should be accomplished but is not,
look at the *xiàng xíng* (相刑) of the omen."
It also asks:
"The Six Combinations (*liù hé*, 六合) are merely auspicious.
What is meant by Shēn (申) mutually overcoming (相剋)?"
The reply is:
"Metal carries water and is born in fire.
Fire is the ghost of metal,
water is the ghost of fire.
Metal together with water is born in fire,
this is the body of the ghost's mother and son."
Shēn (申) is the position of metal,
and furthermore contains water.
Sì (巳) is the position of fire,
and again gives birth to metal.
They are still mutually hostile;
therefore, it is considered *xíng*.
However, *xíng* has upper and lower.
For example, Yín (寅) inflicts *xíng* on Sì (巳);
Sì (巳) is the upper *xíng*,
Yín (寅) is the lower *xíng*;
all other cases are similar.
Therefore, the *Bīng Zhòu* (兵晝) says:
"When wind comes from the upper *xíng*,
those sitting must quickly rise,
those walking must quickly stop."
This refers to this.
When it mentions the Three *Xíng* (三刑),
it is like Yín (寅) inflicting *xíng* on Sì (巳),
and Sì (巳) inflicting *xíng* on Shēn (申).
On a Yín (寅) day, at the Shēn (申) hour,
if wind arises from the direction of Sì (巳),
or if a prodigy is seen in the direction of Sì (巳),
this is called the Three *Xíng*.
Other cases follow this example.
There is another type of *xíng* that derives from *qì* (氣),
which is opposite to *dé* (德);
this has already been explained previously,
so it will not be re-explained.
As for mutual harm (*xiāng hài*, 相害),
it is when they meet each other in reverse order among the twelve earthly branches (*shí èr chén*, 十二辰),
two by two mutually harming each other,
named the Six Harms (*liù hài*, 六害).
Xū (戌) and Yǒu (酉),
Hài (亥) and Shēn (申),
Zǐ (子) and Wèi (未),
Chǒu (丑) and Wǔ (午),
Yín (寅) and Sì (巳),
Mǎo (卯) and Chén (辰) —
these are the Six Harms.
This is the meaning of killing and injuring.
Now, these Six Harms,
whether it is ruler and minister, father and son,
or husband and wife,
logically should not harm each other.
The *Xiào Jīng* (孝經) says:
"Not loving one's own parents,
but loving others,
is called perverse virtue (*bèi dé*, 悖德)."
Since their nature of love and compassion is violated,
there is a reason for anger and punishment.
That which the Five Phases (*wǔ xíng*, 五行) dislike,
lies in destruction and冲 (*chōng*, 衝).
The current mutual harm,
because it aligns with destruction and *chōng*,
results in a father losing his compassion,
a son violating his filial piety,
a wife being disrespectful,
a husband abandoning harmony and unity.
All lead to hatred and resentment,
logically forming mutual harm.
It is like having to wait for a bear's paw (熊蹯) for one's fate,
or a hungry person seeking a nestling sparrow (雀鷇);
Chóng Ěr (重耳) fleeing abroad,
Shēn Shēng (申生) being granted a letter;
in Hénèi (河內), husband and wife mutually destroy each other;
beyond the frontier, ruler and minister kill and seize from each other.
Are these not harms?
As for Chén (辰) and Mǎo (卯) being harmful:
Mǎo (卯) combines with Xū (戌),
Xū (戌) is broken by Chén (辰);
Chén (辰) Earth is the wife of Mǎo (卯) Wood,
Xū (戌) and Chén (辰) are mutual enemies.
Mǎo (卯) combining with Xū (戌)
means abandonment.
Chén (辰) combines with Yǒu (酉),
Yǒu (酉) clashes with and breaks Mǎo (卯);
Chén (辰) is the wife of Mǎo (卯),
Yǒu (酉) is the enemy of Mǎo (卯).
When Chén (辰) combines with Yǒu (酉),
Yǒu (酉) can overcome Mǎo (卯).
This is the image of a wife committing adultery with an outsider,
killing her original husband.
Sì (巳) combines with Shēn (申),
Shēn (申) clashes with Yín (寅);
Sì (巳) is the child of Yín (寅),
Shēn (申) can overcome Yín (寅).
When Sì (巳) combines with Shēn (申),
the child acts rebelliously.
As for Chǒu (丑) and Wǔ (午) mutually harming:
Chǒu (丑) combines with Zǐ (子),
Zǐ (子) clashes with and breaks Wǔ (午);
Wǔ (午) combines with Wèi (未),
Wèi (未) is broken by Chǒu (丑).
This is also the meaning of father and son mutually harming.
As for Wèi (未) and Zǐ (子) mutually harming:
Wèi (未) combines with Wǔ (午),
Wǔ (午) clashes with and breaks Zǐ (子).
Wèi (未) Earth is the ruler,
Zǐ (子) Water is the minister;
Wǔ (午) Fire is the wealth of Zǐ (子) Water.
This is the image of the ruler harming the minister for wealth.
Zǐ (子) combines with Chǒu (丑),
Chǒu (丑) is broken by Wèi (未);
Chǒu (丑) is also Earth.
When Zǐ (子) combines with Chǒu (丑),
it desires to attract an external ruler to jointly harm its own lord.
This is the image of a minister having to flee.
As for Shēn (申) and Hài (亥) mutually harming:
Hài (亥) combines with Yín (寅),
Yín (寅) clashes with Shēn (申);
Shēn (申) combines with Sì (巳),
Sì (巳) clashes with Hài (亥).
This is also the meaning of father and son mutually harming.
Generating is not necessarily generating,
and harming is not necessarily harming.
It is like fire being able to burn things,
yet there is the fire of Yánzhōu
that cannot burn things.
Water can moisten and promote growth,
but when a sudden flood comes,
it also makes grass, trees, and crops wither.
This is an instance of generating instead harming,
and harming instead generating.
Drilling wood produces fire,
and clouds, rain, and lightning
occur in sequence.
This is an instance of harming instead generating.
Water fundamentally harms fire,
but when oil soaks a lamp wick,
the lamplight becomes brighter.
This is also an instance of harming instead generating.
The Yīnyáng and Wǔxíng are what all myriad things depend on.
The responses of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
are each spoken of according to their category.
Sometimes there is inauspiciousness within auspiciousness,
and auspiciousness within inauspiciousness.
In the case of inauspiciousness, one looks at what saves it;
in the case of auspiciousness, one observes what harms it.
If there is inauspiciousness with a savior,
it will not lead to calamity.
If there is auspiciousness with a harm,
it will not reach the full extent of good fortune.
Pure inauspiciousness leads to great calamity;
pure auspiciousness leads to profound blessings.
For example, if Chǒu and Wǔ harm each other,
and Zǐ clashes and breaks Wǔ,
since Zǐ has the 'royal water' (Wángshuǐ),
this is pure inauspiciousness.
If Wèi is broken by Chǒu,
and Chǒu has the 'desired wood' (yù xiāng zhī mù),
which can control Wèi earth,
this is considered having a savior.
If Wèi and Zǐ harm each other,
and Wèi clashes and breaks Zǐ,
since Zǐ is the 'royal water' (Wángshuǐ),
and water controls Wǔ fire,
this is inauspiciousness within auspiciousness.
If Zǐ and Chǒu combine,
Chǒu earth in turn controls Zǐ water,
which is auspiciousness within inauspiciousness.
The principles of generating and harming
are all like this.
Clashing and breaking (chōngpò) means
that their qì confront each other.
Clashing (chōng) qì is light,
and breaking (pò) qì is heavy.
The Heavenly Stems (gān) and Earthly Branches (zhī) each confront each other.
Thus, each has clashing and breaking.
For the Heavenly Stems (gān) in clashing and breaking:
Jiǎ and Gēng clash and break,
Yǐ and Xīn clash and break,
Bǐng and Rén clash and break,
Dīng and Guǐ clash and break.
Wù, Rén, Jiǎ, Wù, Yǐ, Jǐ
also clash and break.
These are all opposite clashing and breaking.
They also inherently mutually restrain,
making them even heavier.
For the Earthly Branches (zhī) in clashing and breaking:
Zǐ and Wǔ clash and break,
Chǒu and Wèi clash and break,
Yín and Shēn clash and break,
Mǎo and Yǒu clash and break,
Chén and Xū clash and break,
Sì and Hài clash and break.
This also takes the opposite positions.
Their lightness and heaviness
are all spoken of in terms of 'life' (shēng) and 'death' (sǐ).
The Four Cardinal Branches (Sìmèng) have 'life' but no 'death',
so they only clash directly but do not break.
The Four Seasonal Branches (Sìjì) have 'death' but no 'life',
so they only break directly but do not clash.
The Four Central Branches (Sìzhòng) have both 'death' and 'life' simultaneously,
thus they both clash and break.
The Four Cardinal Branches (Sìmèng) have 'life' but no 'death',
meaning they only clash but do not break.
Yín has 'life' fire,
Sì has 'life' metal,
Shēn has 'life' water,
and Hài has 'life' wood.
The Four Central Branches (Sìzhòng) have both 'death' and 'life' simultaneously:
Mǎo has 'royal' wood and 'dead' water,
Wǔ has 'royal' fire and 'dead' wood,
Yǒu has 'royal' metal and 'dead' fire,
and Zǐ has 'royal' water and 'dead' metal.
The Four Seasonal Branches (Sìjì) have 'death' but no 'life':
Chén has 'dead' water,
Wèi has 'dead' wood,
Xū has 'dead' fire,
and Chǒu has 'dead' metal.
'Dead' qì is heavy,
thus it can break.
'Life' qì is light,
thus it clashes.
Furthermore, Jiǎ moving towards Gēng is clashing,
and Gēng moving towards Jiǎ is breaking.
This is the stronger controlling the weaker.
Their clashing and breaking
are all opposing clashes in opposite positions,
which is most inauspicious.
They also face each other in clashing positions.
I should be in Gēng while the enemy is in Jiǎ.
This is because the strong controls the weak.
Question:
The 'disastrous qì' (lìqì) is clashing,
but in the current explanation it is 'clashing and breaking' (chōngpò),
and not called 'disastrous' (lì).
This cannot be understood.
Answer:
The mutual disastrous influence (xiāng lì) of the Wǔxíng
becomes severe due to specific circumstances;
it is not always so.
If there is an attack, it appears;
if there is no disaster, it ceases.
What is explained now
refers directly to the positions of the Heavenly Stems (gān) and Earthly Branches (zhī).
They inherently confront each other,
and the rigid and the yielding clash.
This is not asking about unusual changes,
so how could it be called 'disastrous'?
Written by Xiāo Jí, the Senior Yítóng Sānsī, Founding Duke of Chéngyáng Prefecture.
In the Zuǒshì Zhuàn,
Zǐchǎn said,
"Hair is of five colors."
Cài Bójiē said,
"What can be seen through the eyes are the five colors."
The Huángdì Sùwèn says,
"The nature of herbs has five aspects."
The meaning of "manifesting as five colors" is:
Eastern wood is cyan,
the color of the myriad things generating and growing,
and of gentleness.
Southern fire is red,
symbolizing the state of flourishing yáng and intense flames.
Central earth is yellow;
yellow is the color of the earth.
Therefore, it is said, "Heaven is dark, and earth is yellow."
Western metal is white;
autumn is the 'killing qì',
and white dew becomes frost.
White is the symbol of mourning.
Northern water is black;
viewed from afar, it is dark and indistinct.
It is the symbol of yin and darkness.
The vast sea stretches boundlessly,
dark and infinite.
Water is the substance of extreme yin,
hence it is dark.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshén Qì says,
The essence of earth is yellow,
the essence of wood is cyan,
the essence of fire is red,
the essence of metal is white,
the essence of water is black.
The Chūnqiū Kǎoyìyóu says,
The qì of the Northern Dí arises in Yōudū.
Its color is black,
like herds of animals in felt yurts.
The qì of the Southern Yí arises in Jiāozhǐ.
Its color is red,
gathered in corners like banners and bird heads.
The qì of the Eastern Yí arises in Càizhù.
Its color is cyan,
scattered and spread out,
like a forest.
The qì of the Western Yí arises in Shāqiū.
Its color is white,
sharp and accumulated like the floating edge of a blade.
Central earth gathers,
its color is yellow,
like the shape of a city wall.
Yellow qì fills the four directions,
and the essence of earth spreads.
These five are the primary colors.
Their changing colors are also five.
Yǐng Zǐyán's Chūnqiū Shìlì says:
The *Jīng* has Red Dís and White Dís.
Thus, Eastern azure,
Northern black,
and Central yellow
are all "correct" colors.
Earth (Wù) is restrained by Wood,
hence Mèijǐ is married to Jiǎ;
yellow enters azure,
thus the Eastern "intermediate" color is green.
The *Shī* says:
"Green is the robe, green!"
This satirizes intermediate colors disturbing correct colors.
Metal (Gēng) is restrained by Fire,
hence Mèixīn is married to Bǐng;
white enters red,
thus the Southern intermediate color is crimson.
The *Lúnyǔ Xiāngdǎng* says:
"Crimson and purple are not used for informal wear."
Wood (Jiǎ) is restrained by Metal,
hence Mèiyǐ is married to Gēng;
azure enters white,
thus the Western intermediate color is sky-blue.
Fire (Bǐng) is restrained by Water,
hence Mèidīng is married to Rén;
red enters black,
thus the Northern intermediate color is purple.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I detest purple for usurping vermilion."
Water (Rén) is restrained by Earth,
hence Mèiguǐ is married to Wù;
black enters yellow,
thus the central intermediate color is
dark yellow.
The *Wǔxíng Shū* says:
Jiǎ is azure,
Jǐ is green,
Bǐng is red,
Xīn is crimson,
Gēng is white,
Yǐ is sky-blue,
Rén is black,
Dīng is purple,
Wù is yellow,
Guǐ is dark yellow.
In all these cases, the husband represents the primary color,
and the wife represents the mixed color.
Liǔ Shìlóng said:
Each of the Eight Trigrams has its color:
Zhèn is azure,
Lí is red,
Duì is white,
Kǎn is black.
These are all correct colors for their respective directions.
Qián is purple,
Gèn is crimson,
Xùn is green,
Kūn is yellow.
These are all intermediate colors.
Kūn takes the correct color of *wèi* (Earth).
The *Jiǎyǐ Jīng* says:
Azure like kingfisher feathers,
black like crow feathers,
red like a rooster's comb,
yellow like a crab's belly,
white like pig's fat.
These five colors indicate the presence of vital *qì*.
Azure like flourishing grass,
black like water moss,
yellow like the fruit of *Zhǐ* (trifoliate orange),
red like clotted blood,
white like withered bones.
These five colors indicate the presence of death *qì*.
The *Xiāng Jīng* says:
When azure *qì* first appears,
it is like sprouting wheat;
when it is strong and flourishing,
it is like green tree leaves;
when it is about to depart,
it is like moss on water.
When red *qì* first appears,
it is like an ochre pillar;
when it is strong and flourishing,
it is like vermilion cinnabar;
when it is about to depart,
it is like dried blood.
When yellow *qì* first appears,
it is like a silkworm spitting silk;
when it is strong and flourishing,
it is like a wide foundation (for a wall);
when it is about to depart,
it is like withered leaves.
When white *qì* first appears,
it is like a seal or jade disc;
when it is strong and flourishing,
it is like a gleam on powder;
when it is about to depart,
it is like tarnished money.
When black *qì* first appears,
it is like a dead horse's liver;
when it is strong and flourishing,
it is like the luster of lacquer;
when it is about to depart,
it is like mossy grime.
The *Lǐjì* says:
When a *jūnzǐ* wears mourning clothes,
he has a sorrowful countenance;
when wearing a ceremonial cap and robes, he has a respectful countenance.
When wearing armor and helmet, he has an unassailable countenance.
The *Dàdài Lǐ* says:
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A *jūnzǐ* has three countenances:
Clearly joyful and pleased,
the countenance of bells and drums.
Calm and tranquil in spirit,
the countenance of grief and loss.
Angry and agitated,
the countenance of weapons and armor."
The *Dàdài Lǐ Guānrén Piān* says:
"Humans have five natures:
joy, anger, desire, fear, and sorrow.
When joy *qì* is stored within,
even if one wishes to hide it,
outer joy will surely be revealed.
The same is true for all four *qì*.
When the five *qì* are truly within,
they manifest in outward form.
Human emotions cannot be hidden.
Joy appears freely,
anger erupts insultingly,
desire glows with pleasure,
fear shrinks lowly,
and the countenance of sorrow and grief
is apprehensive and still.
True wisdom must have a countenance difficult to exhaust;
true benevolence must have a countenance worthy of respect;
true courage must have a countenance difficult to control;
true loyalty must have a countenance that inspires closeness;
true purity must have a countenance difficult to defile.
True sincerity must have a countenance worthy of trust.
Their essential countenance is clear and thus peaceful;
a false countenance is tangled and vexing.
Joyful countenances are yellow,
angry countenances are red,
sorrowful countenances are azure,
mourning countenances are white,
and grieved countenances are black.
These are all the colors of the Five Constants,
stirred by the Five Organs,
and appearing outwardly,
corresponding to their good or bad, flourishing or declining states.
These are observed by the *jūnzǐ*,
hence explained here."
Zǐchǎn said:
"Zhāng" refers to the five sounds.
Cài Bójī said:
"Shēng" (sound) is what reaches the ear.
Green creates the jué sound,
white creates the shāng sound,
black creates the yǔ sound,
red creates the zhǐ sound,
and yellow creates the gōng sound.
The Lǜlìzhì says:
Jiao (角) means "to touch."
The yang qi stirs and moves,
and all myriad things touch the earth and are born.
Zhǐ (徴) means "blessing" or "flourishing."
All myriad things are greatly flourishing and blessed.
Gōng (宮) means "center."
It resides in the center, extending to the four directions,
initiating creation and giving birth,
and serves as the warp (foundation) of the four sounds.
Shāng (商) means "chapter" or "pattern."
Things form patterns and become clear.
Yǔ (羽) means "space" or "shelter."
Things hide, gather, and are covered by a shelter.
The Yuèwěi says:
When the spring qi is harmonious, the jué sound is in tune.
When the summer qi is harmonious, the zhǐ sound is in tune.
When the late summer qi is harmonious, the gōng sound is in tune.
When the autumn qi is harmonious, the shāng sound is in tune.
When the winter qi is harmonious, the yǔ sound is in tune.
The Yuèjì says:
Gōng is the sovereign.
Therefore, if gōng is disordered, there is desolation,
and the sovereign is arrogant.
Shāng is the minister.
If shāng is disordered, there is deviation,
and the ministers are corrupt.
Zhǐ is affairs.
If zhǐ is disordered, there is sorrow,
and affairs are toilsome.
Yǔ is things.
If yǔ is disordered, there is danger,
and wealth is depleted.
Jué is the people.
If jué is disordered, there is worry,
and the people are resentful.
If these five are not disordered,
then the world is peaceful and harmonious,
with no sounds of ruin or failure.
The Sùwèn says:
The wood sound is jué,
which in vocalization is a cry.
The fire sound is zhǐ,
which in vocalization is laughter.
The earth sound is gōng,
which in vocalization is a song.
The metal sound is shāng,
which in vocalization is weeping.
The water sound is yǔ,
which in vocalization is a groan.
The Yuèjì says:
Music is where sounds originate from.
Its root lies in the human heart's response to things.
Therefore, when a sorrowful heart responds,
its sound is thin and sharp.
When a joyful heart responds,
its sound is expansive and slow.
When a happy heart responds,
its sound is rising and scattered.
When an angry heart responds,
its sound is coarse and forceful.
When an upright heart responds,
its sound is direct and pure.
When a loving heart responds,
its sound is harmonious and gentle.
These six are not inherent nature,
but move after being affected by things.
By examining sounds, one understands tones.
By examining tones, one understands music.
By examining music, one understands governance.
And thus, the Way of governing is complete.
Therefore, the Shīxù says:
When sounds form patterns,
they are called tones.
The tones of a well-governed age
are peaceful and joyful;
its governance is harmonious.
The tones of a disordered age
are resentful and angry;
its governance is perverse.
The tones of a doomed state
are sorrowful and pensive;
its people are distressed.
The Dàdài Lǐ Guānrén Piān says:
What is sincere within
will certainly be manifested outwardly.
From what is manifested, discern what is hidden.
From what is small, discern what is great.
Sound resembles its reality.
Qi first gives rise to things.
When things are born, they have sound.
Sounds have hardness and softness, clarity and muddiness, pleasing and displeasing qualities,
all emanating from sound.
Therefore, those whose heart-qi is boisterous and extravagant
have scattered and flowing sounds.
Those whose heart-qi is compliant and faithful
have regulated and orderly sounds.
Those whose heart-qi is vulgar and perverse
have foul and unpleasant sounds.
Those whose heart-qi is broad and gentle
have warm and harmonious sounds.
Therefore, the sages listen to their sounds
and observe their appearance
to know their good and evil.
What is emitted alone is called shēng (sound);
what is combined and harmonized is called yīn (tone).
The Máoshī Xù says, "When sounds form patterns, they are called tones."
Therefore, from the five sounds, there are eight musical instruments.
The Yuèwěi says:
Things are completed by three
and established by five.
Three and five make eight.
Therefore, tones are by eight.
The eight instruments are metal, stone, silk, bamboo, earth, wood, gourd, and leather,
used to produce gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
Metal is the bell,
stone is the chime,
silk is the string,
bamboo is the pipe,
earth is the xun,
wood is the zhu and yu,
gourd is the sheng,
and leather is the drum.
The drum presides over Zhèn,
the sheng over Xùn,
the zhu and yu over Qián,
the xun over Gèn,
the pipe over Kǎn,
the string over Lí,
the chime over Kūn,
and the bell over Duì.
The chapter "Jīntúzhēng" of the *Yuèwèi* says:
*Kǎn* governs the winter solstice.
*Gōng* represents the sovereign;
when humans have a sovereign,
then all things are perfected.
When the *qì* has the *huángzhōng* mode of *gōng*,
then all things are harmonized,
thus rectifying all under heaven from the start.
Those who can be in accord with the patterns of Heaven and Earth,
and whose virtues combine with the spirits,
will find that the seven beginnings and eight endings
each obtain their proper place,
and the Son of Heaven will be majestic and solemn,
with all four quarters taking him as their beginning.
Therefore, *guǎn* is used in music.
*Gèn* governs the beginning of spring.
The *yáng* *qì* begins to emerge.
It is said that thunder moves for a hundred *lǐ*,
and the sage bestows land upon the people;
it also does not exceed one hundred *mǔ*.
This is the division of Heaven and Earth,
the measure of *huángzhōng*.
The nine are harmonized to tune the eight sounds.
Therefore, the sage uses nine *qǐng*
to establish eight households,
so that the superior farmer can feed nine mouths,
the mediocre seven mouths,
and the inferior five mouths.
This means the wealthy do not have enough for extravagance,
and the poor have no worries of hunger or starvation.
In three years, there is a surplus of one year's storage;
in nine years, a surplus of three years' storage.
This is what *huángzhōng* accomplishes,
by the harmony of ebb and flow.
Therefore, *xūn* is used in music.
*Zhèn* governs the spring equinox.
*Yīn* and *yáng* in Heaven and Earth are equally divided.
Therefore, the sagely king, following the laws of Heaven,
establishes the Five Equalities.
The Five Equalities
are also the equalities by which the *lǜ* harmonizes the Five Sounds.
Although sounds are numerous,
they are no more than five.
Although things are abundant,
their equalities are no more than five.
Caring for the poor among the rich,
the strong not encroaching on the weak,
the wise not deceiving the foolish,
markets having no dual prices,
all things being equally distributed,
the four seasons always being well-ordered,
the public coffers having surplus,
grace extending to all under heaven,
and sharing the virtues of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, *gǔ* is used in music.
*Xùn* governs the beginning of summer.
It is said that all things, long or short, have their differences.
Therefore, the sagely king, following the laws of Heaven,
assigns duties according to law.
The noble and the humble each have their ranks,
among scholars there is righteousness, deference, and propriety,
between ruler and minister there is distinction,
and all above and below are in their proper order.
Thus the way of governance is practiced.
Therefore, *shēng* is used in music.
*Lí* governs the summer solstice.
*Yáng* begins to descend,
and *yīn* again brings forth things.
Therefore, the sagely king, following the laws of Heaven,
establishes systems of clothing and regulations according to law,
thereby clarifying propriety and righteousness, distinguishing the noble and the humble,
illuminating their virtues,
and guiding them with measures.
Then women's crafts have their distinctions,
and men's conduct has its rituals.
Therefore, *xián* is used in music.
*Kūn* governs the beginning of autumn.
The *yáng* *qì* is entering,
and the *yīn* *qì* is taking charge.
Insects begin to burrow and desire to hibernate.
Therefore, the sagely king takes this as a model,
establishing measures for palaces and dwellings.
Moreover, the regulations are appropriate,
large and small have their laws,
noble and humble have their distinctions,
and superior and inferior have their proper order.
Therefore, *qìng* is used in music.
*Duì* governs the autumn equinox.
The works of Heaven, Earth, and man are all established.
Therefore, the sagely king, following the laws of Heaven,
establishes ranks and emoluments.
Ranks and emoluments do not exceed one's ability.
*Gōng* is for the sovereign,
*shāng* for the minister.
*Shāng* means "to display."
It means the minister displays and clarifies the merits and virtues of the sovereign.
The noble and the humble have their positions,
positions have their things,
and things have their appropriateness.
Those who succeed in their accomplishments are rewarded with titles,
those who fail are punished by law.
Therefore, *zhōng* is used in music.
*Qián* governs the beginning of winter.
*Yīn* and *yáng* end and begin anew;
all things die and revive.
Therefore, the sagely king, following the laws of Heaven,
establishes penal laws.
Executing one moves a thousand;
killing one affects ten thousand.
This ensures the dead have no regrets,
and the living no resentment.
Therefore, *zhùwú* is used in music.
*Guóyǔ* says:
Pottery and silk instruments like *qín* and *sè* honor *gōng*;
bells and metals honor *yǔ*;
stone instruments honor *jué*;
gourds and bamboo instruments honor *zhǐ*;
leather and wood instruments honor *shāng*.
The *lǚ* harmonizes music,
the *lǜ* balances sounds.
Metal and stone instruments activate it,
silk and bamboo instruments carry it,
songs chant it,
gourds declare it,
pottery instruments praise it,
leather and wood instruments regulate it.
When things attain their regularity, it is called *yuè* (music);
what is taken is called *jī* (striking);
what preserves each other is called *hé* (harmony);
when small and large do not exceed limits, it is called *píng* (balance).
Pottery and silk are both fire,
hence they honor *gōng*.
This is the principle of mother and child corresponding.
Bells and metals honoring *yǔ* is also similar.
That stone instruments honor *jué* means
stone is metal.
It is the meaning of male and female harmonizing with *jué*.
Gourd is earth.
Bamboo is wood.
Honoring *zhǐ* is also mother and child corresponding.
Leather and wood are both *jué*,
honoring *shāng* is also through male and female harmonizing.
The *gōng* sound is harmonious and expansive,
its harmony broad and soft,
moving the spleen.
The *shāng* sound is scattered and clear,
its harmony warm and empty,
moving the lungs.
The *jué* sound is defensive and restrained,
its harmony quiet and clear,
moving the liver.
The *zhǐ* sound is forceful and swift,
its harmony even and balanced,
moving the heart.
The *yǔ* sound is swift and empty,
its harmony short and dispersed,
moving the kidneys.
*Huángdì Bīngjué* says:
When two enemies are facing each other,
send someone to the enemy camp,
one hundred twenty paces away,
to listen through a pipe.
If one hears a rumbling sound like chariots,
like thunder or drums, it is *gōng*.
Their general is lenient, harmonious, and trustworthy.
If one hears metal and stone harmonizing,
a clanging sound of striking and attacking,
like bells, *qìng*, and thunderbolts, it is *shāng*.
Their general is fierce, angry, and fond of killing;
it is advisable to provoke them repeatedly.
If one hears a sound like galloping horses, raging cannons, or tearing apart, it is *zhǐ*.
Their general is fierce, brave, and difficult to contend with.
If one hears a rustling and whispering sound,
like trees swaying,
or people sighing mournfully, it is *jué*.
Their general is benevolent and popular, not to be deceived.
If one hears a rushing sound like flowing water, rising waves,
or gasping and laughing, it is *yǔ*.
Their general is greedy, ambitious, and full of treacherous schemes.
By discerning these five sounds, one can know the enemy's character.
Listening to the sound of the wind
also provides similar indications.
These all discuss the characteristics of sounds,
therefore they are described in full.
Zǐchǎn (子產) said,
“Qì (氣) produces the five flavors.”
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said,
“What passes through the mouth constitutes the five flavors,
and what passes through the nose constitutes the five odors.”
The Lǐjì Yuèlìng (禮記月令) says,
“On the days of spring,
its flavor is sour,
its odor is rancid [shān (羶)].
This is the odor and flavor of wood.”
The Shuōwén (說文) says,
“Rancid [shān (羶)] is the odor of sheep.”
The qì (氣) of spring objects
is similar to that of sheep.
The reason wood is sour
is to symbolize the birth of all things in the East.
“Sour” (suān) means “to drill” (zuān).
It means all things drill through the earth to be born.
When the five flavors obtain sourness,
they can reach (their full potential).
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“The word for ‘sour’ (suān) is ‘beginning’ (duān).”
When qì (氣) begins to be concentrated,
the heart itself is correct (duān).
The Lǐjì (禮記) says,
“On the days of summer,
its flavor is bitter,
its odor is scorched.”
The reason fire is bitter
is that the South governs growth and nourishment.
Bitterness is what nourishes it.
The five flavors require bitterness
to nourish them.
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“One must be diligent and hardworking (kǔ)
to be able to nourish.”
In Fāngyán (方言),
“bitter” (kǔ) is “fast” (kuài).
“Scorched odor”
refers to the yang qì (陽氣) steaming and moving,
which is the qì (氣) of blazing fire.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) said,
“‘Scorched’ means fire burning things,
having the qì (氣) of scorching and burning.”
The qì (氣) of summer is the same.
The Lǐjì (禮記) says,
“On the days of late summer,
its flavor is sweet,
its odor is fragrant.”
This is why the flavor of earth is sweet.
The center is harmony.
Sweet is beautiful.
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“Sweet (gān) means regular food (shícháng),
meaning one is content with its flavor.”
Sweet flavor is the lord of the five flavors,
just as the harmony of earth is completed by the four elements.
“Fragrant odor”
is the homeland qì (鄉氣) of earth,
with fragrance as its essence.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) said,
“Earth obtains its central harmonious qì (氣),
thus it is fragrant.”
The Lǐjì (禮記) says,
“On the days of autumn,
its odor is raw/fishy (xīng),
its flavor is pungent.”
The West
is the qì (氣) of killing, raw/fishy.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) said,
“The qì (氣) of something unripe
is raw/fishy.”
The qì (氣) of Metal in the West
is symbolized by this. Pungent flavor means
that when things obtain pungency,
they wilt and die.
It is also said,
therefore “new” (xīn) is also “pungent” (xīn).
When all old things are gone,
new things are already formed,
thus it is called “new.”
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“Because yin (陰) harms, it is pungent (xīn);
because it has the meaning of killing, it is pungent (xīn);
it is to pierce the yin qì (陰氣) to make it so.”
The Lǐjì (禮記) says,
“On the days of winter,
its flavor is salty,
its odor is rotten.”
“Rotten” is the qì (氣) of water.
As if existing and not existing,
it means the qì (氣) is subtle.
It is also said,
“Water receives dirt and turbidity,
thus its odor is putrid and rotten.”
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) said,
“The qì (氣) of rotting and decaying,
is the same as the qì (氣) of the North.”
This salty flavor is a northern thing.
Saltiness is used to solidify things,
just as the five flavors become firm when they obtain saltiness.
Xǔ Shèn (許愼) said,
“Salty (xián) means to hold (hán).”
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“Salty (xián) is ‘scythe’ (lián).”
“Scythe” (lián) is “clear” (qīng).
The qì (氣) of extreme cold
thus makes it clear and salty.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said,
“The five flavors are vinegar (xī) (sour),
wine (bitter),
honey (sweet),
ginger (pungent),
salt (salty).”
The Huángdì Jiǎyǐ Jīng (黃帝甲乙經) says,
“Among grains, rice is sweet,
hemp is sour,
soybeans are salty,
wheat is bitter,
and millet is pungent.”
One source says,
“Paddy rice is pungent.”
Among fruits, dates are sweet,
plums are sour,
chestnuts are salty,
apricots are bitter,
peaches are pungent. Among vegetables, mallow is sweet,
chives are sour,
bean leaves are salty,
rakkyo is bitter,
onions are pungent.
Among livestock, cattle are sweet,
dogs are sour,
pigs are salty,
sheep are bitter,
chickens are pungent.
The Běncǎo (本草) says,
“Among stones, jade is sweet,
gold is pungent,
realgar is bitter,
azurite is sour,
and red ochre is salty.”
Among herbs, Poria is sweet,
cassia bark is pungent,
Asparagus root is bitter,
Schisandra is sour,
and Scrophularia is salty.”
Among insects, dung beetles are sweet,
millipedes are pungent,
snakes are bitter,
silverfish are sour,
and lizards are salty.
There are many examples of medicinal and edible items,
so we will only give a general outline.
The matching of the five flavors is as above.
All are generated by the qì (氣) of the Five Elements,
and the qì (氣) has biases,
thus their flavors differ.
In summary,
for the five grains (wǔgǔ), spikes (máng) are correlated with wood (mù),
loose grains (sǎn) with fire (huǒ),
pods (fáng) with metal (jīn),
legumes (jiá) with water (shuǐ),
and compact grains (cuì) with earth (tǔ).
Spikes (máng) are things like wheat (dàxiǎomài),
loose grains (sǎn) are things like millet (jǐshǔ),
pods (fáng) are things like sesame (húmá),
legumes (jiá) are things like beans (dàxiǎodòu),
and compact grains (cuì) are things like foxtail millet (jìsù).
Spikes (máng) are so called because of their sharp points and slender length,
resembling wood (mù) sprouting from the earth
like sharp points.
Loose grains (sǎn) refers to scattering.
They resemble the warm qi (qì) of fire (huǒ),
causing things to spread out.
Pods (fáng) means square.
They resemble metal (jīn) being cut and shaped,
having a square and regular form.
Legumes (jiá) means narrow.
They resemble water (shuǐ) flowing long and narrow.
Compact grains (cuì) means gathering.
They resemble all myriad things gathering in the earth (tǔ)
to be useful.
For the five fruits (wǔguǒ), seeds (zǐ) are correlated with wood (mù),
pits (hé) with fire (huǒ),
peels (pí) with metal (jīn),
shells (ké) with water (shuǐ),
and capsules (fáng) with earth (tǔ).
Seeds (zǐ) are things like pears (lí) and hawthorns (hóngzǐ),
pits (hé) are things like peaches (táo) and plums (lǐ),
peels (pí) are things like oranges (gān) and tangerines (jú),
shells (ké) are things like walnuts (hútáo) and chestnuts (lì),
and capsules (fáng) are things like grapes (pútáo).
Seeds (zǐ) are so called because they contain moisture,
like wood (mù) growing lustrous and moist,
and its fruits flourishing.
Pits (hé) are so called because they are inside the flesh
and inedible,
like the yin (yīn) quality of fire (huǒ) being internal
and unable to be contained.
Peels (pí) are so called because they are thick and tight,
like the metal (jīn) qi (qì) being in decline and old age,
things reaching the west and contracting tightly.
Shells (ké) are so called because their flesh is inside and edible,
like the yang (yáng) quality of water (shuǐ) being internal
and capable of containing.
Capsules (fáng) are so called because they are clustered together,
like all things of earth (tǔ) gathering here.
This is a general discussion of grains (gǔ) and fruits (guǒ),
and their correlation with the five flavors (wǔwèi)
is generally as explained before.
The Yuèlìng says:
In spring, one eats wheat and lamb.
Wheat has sprouts and husks,
hence it belongs to wood.
Lamb is a fire animal;
as spring qi is still cold,
this calms one's nature.
In summer, one eats beans and chicken.
Beans have sprouts and husks, and are firm,
which aligns with water.
Chicken is a wood animal.
Therefore, it is eaten in hot times.
In the center, one eats millet and beef.
Millet is the chief of grains.
Cattle are earth animals;
because they are sweet and harmonizing,
they are likened to the season.
In autumn, one eats sesame and dog meat.
Sesame belongs to metal,
and dogs are also metal animals,
hence they follow autumn.
In winter, one eats broomcorn millet and pork.
Broomcorn millet is expansive and belongs to fire.
Pork is a water animal.
Combining its water and fire
makes it suitable for winter food.
These five types of food
have different meanings.
Spring is still cold, so one eats warm food;
summer is hot, so one eats cold food.
This meaning is understandable.
Bitter and sweet flavors harmonize,
hence they are applied according to the season;
this is also understandable.
Regarding the autumn and winter foods,
which should ideally be hot,
why are they not hot?
What is the reason for this?
If one follows Cài Yōng's explanation,
which simply says that the flavors of the food are suitable,
then there would be no further doubt.
If one follows Zhèng's explanation,
then it is truly incomplete.
Now, I will expand on Zhèng's words.
Shàoyáng and Dàyáng,
their qi is expansive and scattered.
Shàoyīn and Dàyīn,
their qi is restrained and closed.
Therefore, Héshànggōng,
in explaining Lǎozǐ's words, says:
When agitated qi is above,
and yang qi is hidden below,
it is consequently cold.
When calm qi is above,
and yin qi is hidden below,
it is consequently hot.
The yin and yang of the human body
also follow this principle.
In spring and summer, there is expansion and scattering,
and yang qi is developing.
It is appropriate to use warm food to harmonize yin qi.
In autumn and winter, there is closure and restraint,
and yang qi is inside.
It is appropriate to use cold food
to regulate yang qi.
Winter combines water and fire,
which is different from autumn.
Precisely because it is a time of deep storage and closure,
which is more severe than autumn,
it harmonizes with water and fire.
Now, let's take Jiǎyǐ's explanation
and juxtapose it with Zhèng's meaning;
there is a slight discrepancy.
Jiǎyǐ holds that lamb and wheat are both bitter,
both being fire flavors.
Zhèng Xuán says lamb is a fire animal, which is similar.
But wheat belongs to wood.
This takes its sprouted form.
The use of warmth is still the same.
Jiǎyǐ states
that beans are salty and chicken is pungent.
Zhèng Xuán says beans align with water, which is similar,
but chicken belongs to wood, which is different.
This is based on its crowing near dawn, which is close to yín (wood).
Also, it flaps its wings,
having a yang nature.
However, it is a yóu (酉) bird,
which truly belongs to metal.
Jiǎyǐ holds that sesame and dog meat are both sour.
Zhèng says sesame and dog meat both belong to metal.
Sour is a wood flavor,
used to regulate metal qi.
To regulate shàoyīn qi with shàoyáng qi and flavor
is logically sound.
However, regulating metal with metal
might disrupt harmony and appropriateness.
Jiǎyǐ states
that broomcorn millet is pungent and pork is salty.
Zhèng Xuán says pork aligns with water, which is similar,
but broomcorn millet belongs to fire, which is different.
He states that broomcorn millet is red and hot in nature,
hence he considers it fire.
If one follows Zhèng's intention,
it is as explained before.
If one considers the meaning of the Jiǎyǐ Míngtáng Yuèlìng,
summer food being cold
is intended to regulate the qi of disaster, heat, and accumulated toxins.
Winter food also being cold
is to remove hidden heat from within the organs.
Spring cold uses warmth.
These two intentions are not different.
Autumn uses shàoyáng to harmonize shàoyīn.
Because there is killing qi,
living flavors are used to supplement it.
Zhèng's explanation is entirely contrary.
The Zhōulǐ Tiānguān says:
In general, when harmonizing, spring should have more sour,
summer more bitter,
autumn more pungent,
winter more salty,
and be balanced with slippery and sweet.
There are two interpretations.
One says:
It should follow the seasonal qi,
so spring food should be mostly sour,
and summer food should be mostly bitter.
The other says:
"More" means excess.
If spring food is excessively sour,
one should reduce its salty flavor.
If summer food is excessively bitter,
one should reduce its sour flavor.
This is why the latter sentence says,
"balanced with slippery and sweet."
Now, following the former interpretation,
the flavors of the four seasons
each correspond to what is appropriate for the time.
Thus, according to the seasonal saltiness and bitterness,
it is suitable for nourishing the body.
Since earth is in the center,
it broadly supports the four elements.
Therefore, the flavors of the four seasons
also need to be balanced with sweet flavors.
It also says:
Regarding the suitability of meals,
beef goes well with tǔ (稌),
tǔ is rice.
Lamb goes well with shǔ,
pork goes well with jì,
dog meat goes well with liáng,
birds go well with wheat,
and fish goes well with gū.
Gū is diāohú.
Generally, a jūnzi's food always follows these guidelines.
In general, sour medicine nourishes bones,
bitter nourishes qi,
sweet nourishes flesh,
pungent nourishes sinews,
and salty nourishes blood vessels.
These all represent the principle of mutual support.
The Hétú 河圖 states:
If a person consumes excessively salty food,
it will cause kí shèng 腎氣盛 (kidney qi to flourish)
and xīn qì shuāi 心氣衰 (heart qi to decline),
leading to madness,
a tendency to nosebleeds and vomiting blood,
and unstable mental state.
Excessively pungent [food]
causes fèi qì shèng 肺氣盛 (lung qi to flourish)
and gān qì shuāi 肝氣衰 (liver qi to decline),
leading to cowardice, sadness,
blindness, and white hair.
Excessively sweet [food]
causes pí qì shèng 脾氣盛 (spleen qi to flourish)
and shèn qì shuāi 腎氣衰 (kidney qi to decline),
leading to foolishness, licentiousness,
seminal emission, lower back pain,
and discharge of pus and blood.
Excessively bitter [food]
causes xīn qì shèng 心氣盛 (heart qi to flourish)
and fèi qì shuāi 肺氣衰 (lung qi to decline),
leading to boldness, a disregard for death,
coughing with reversed qi, and chest fullness.
Excessively sour [food]
causes gān qì shèng 肝氣盛 (liver qi to flourish)
and pí qì shuāi 脾氣衰 (spleen qi to decline),
leading to indigestion,
deafness, and solid masses.
These explain the principle of mutual restraint and overcoming among the five zàng 臟 organs.
The Huángdì Yǎngshēng Jīng 黃帝養生經 states:
Sour enters the gān 肝 (liver),
pungent enters the fèi 肺 (lungs),
bitter enters the xīn 心 (heart),
sweet enters the pí 脾 (spleen),
and salty enters the shèn 腎 (kidneys).
If the disease is in the sinews,
do not eat sour.
If the disease is in the qi,
do not eat pungent.
If the disease is in the bones,
do not eat salty.
If the disease is in the blood,
do not eat bitter.
If the disease is in the flesh,
do not eat sweet.
If one craves and eats them,
they should not be in large quantities,
otherwise they will certainly harm oneself.
Therefore, they are called the "Five Thieves."
It also states:
For gān 肝 (liver) disease, pungent is forbidden;
for xīn 心 (heart) disease, salty is forbidden;
for pí 脾 (spleen) disease, sour is forbidden;
for fèi 肺 (lung) disease, bitter is forbidden;
for shèn 腎 (kidney) disease, sweet is forbidden.
These are all tastes that are disliked,
hence forbidden.
It also states:
For fèi 肺 (lung) disease, glutinous rice,
beef, and jujubes and mallow are suitable.
For xīn 心 (heart) disease, wheat, lamb, almonds, and Chinese leek are suitable.
For shèn 腎 (kidney) disease, soybeans, yellow millet, pork, and bean sprouts are suitable.
For gān 肝 (liver) disease, hemp seeds, dog meat, plums, and chives are suitable.
For pí 脾 (spleen) disease, chicken meat, peaches, millet, and scallions are suitable.
These are the five suitable foods.
When the gān 肝 (liver), xīn 心 (heart), and shèn 腎 (kidney) three zàng 臟 organs are full (excess),
they are supplemented by their original flavors.
When the pí 脾 (spleen) and fèi 肺 (lungs) are deficient,
they are nourished by their "mother-child" relationships.
The Chūnqiū Qiántán Bā 春秋潛潭巴 states:
The five flavors generate the five zàng 臟 organs:
Salty generates the gān 肝 (liver),
sour generates the xīn 心 (heart),
bitter generates the pí 脾 (spleen),
sweet generates the fèi 肺 (lungs),
and pungent generates the shèn 腎 (kidneys).
The Yǎngshēng Jīng 養生經 states:
The gān 肝 (liver) color is blue,
and salty food,
rice, beef, and jujubes are suitable.
The xīn 心 (heart) color is red,
and sour food,
dog meat, and plums are suitable.
The fèi 肺 (lung) color is white,
and sweet food,
wheat, lamb, and almonds are suitable.
The pí 脾 (spleen) color is yellow,
and bitter food,
soybeans, pork, and millet are suitable.
The shèn 腎 (kidney) color is black,
and pungent food,
millet, and chicken meat are suitable.
All these five foods are based on what they generate,
and can nourish their "children."
It also states:
When the five flavors enter the mouth,
each has a particular path it takes,
and each causes a particular illness.
Sour goes to the sinews;
eating too much
causes urinary retention.
Salty goes to the blood;
eating too much
causes thirst.
Pungent goes to the qi;
eating too much
causes internal agitation.
Bitter goes to the bones;
eating too much
causes changes [in the body].
Sweet goes to the skin;
eating too much
causes nausea.
Pungent disperses,
sour astringes,
sweet moderates,
bitter hardens,
and salty softens.
The five grains provide nourishment,
the five fruits assist,
and the five domesticated animals benefit.
Their qi and flavors are combined and consumed
according to what is suitable for the four seasons and the five zàng 臟 organs.
It also states:
People with a yellow complexion should eat sweet;
those with a blue complexion should eat sour;
those with a black complexion should eat salty;
those with a red complexion should eat bitter;
and those with a white complexion should eat pungent.
These are all based on what is suitable for one's inherent constitution.
The Jiāyǔ 家語 says:
Those who eat water
are good swimmers and resistant to cold.
Those who eat earth
are unthinking and restless.
Those who eat wood
are strong but difficult to govern.
Those who eat grass
are good runners but foolish.
Those who eat mulberry [leaves]
spin silk and become moths.
Those who eat meat
are brave.
Those who eat qi
are enlightened and long-lived.
Those who eat grains
are intelligent and skillful.
Those who eat nothing
are immortal and divine.
These are all categories related to qi and flavors,
thus they are attached and described here.
The explanations for the five flavors are numerous,
so most are not listed.
What the classical texts clearly explain is as stated above.
The zàng-fǔ
are formed by the Five Phases and the Six Qì.
There are five zàng,
which inherently follow the Five Phases, becoming the Five Natures.
There are six fǔ,
which depend on the Six Qì.
These are called the Six Sentiments.
The Sentiments, Natures, and Qì
will be explained separately later.
Now,
we will discuss the meaning of the zàng-fǔ pairings.
The Five Zàng are
the gān, xīn, pí, fèi, and shèn.
The Six Fǔ are
the dàcháng, xiǎocháng, dǎn, wèi, sānjiāo, and pángguāng.
The gān is paired with wood.
The xīn is paired with fire.
The pí is paired with earth.
The fèi is paired with metal.
The shèn is paired with water.
The pángguāng is yáng.
The xiǎocháng is yīn.
The dǎn is wind.
The dàcháng is rain.
The sānjiāo is gloom.
The wèi is brightness.
Therefore, Dù Zǐ Chūnqiū Yī Hé said:
"Yīn excess causes cold illnesses.
Yáng excess causes hot illnesses.
Wind excess causes distal illnesses."
"Distal" refers to the four limbs.
"Rain excess causes abdominal illnesses.
Gloom excess causes bewildering illnesses.
Brightness excess causes heart illnesses."
As for the zàng,
because they are stored within the physical body,
they are called zàng.
They can also store and receive the Five Qì,
hence they are named zàng.
As for the fǔ,
because they transmit, circulate, receive, and contain,
they are called fǔ.
The Bái Hǔ Tōng says:
"The word gān means to guard."
"The word fèi means to expend."
"When emotions move, order is obtained."
"The word xīn means to undertake,
to undertake thought."
"The word shèn means guest,
for expelling through orifices."
"The word pí means to differentiate,
by which essence receives qì."
The Yuán Mìng Bāo says:
"The pí differentiates."
"The xīn obtains it and becomes noble.
The gān obtains it and thrives.
The fèi obtains it and becomes great.
The shèn obtains it and transforms."
The gān is benevolent.
The fèi is righteous.
The xīn is礼 (lǐ).
The shèn is wise.
The pí is trustworthy.
Why is the gān benevolent?
The gān is the essence of wood.
The benevolent love life.
The East is yáng.
All things begin to grow,
therefore the gān resembles wood.
Its color is green and it possesses gentleness.
Why is the fèi righteous?
The fèi is the essence of metal.
The righteous are decisive.
The West slays and completes all things,
therefore the fèi resembles metal.
Its color is white and it possesses firmness.
Why is the xīn禮 (lǐ)?
The xīn is the essence of fire.
The South honors yáng above
and lowly yīn below.
禮 (Lǐ) involves honor and lowliness,
therefore the xīn resembles fire.
Its color is red and it shines.
Why is the shèn wise?
The shèn is the essence of water.
The wise advance without deviating
and are free from doubt.
Water also advances without confusion.
Therefore the shèn resembles water.
Its color is black; water is yīn,
hence the shèn is double.
Why is the pí trustworthy?
The pí is the essence of earth.
Earth governs trustworthiness.
It nurtures all things
and serves as their image.
It gives birth to things without partiality,
which is the height of trustworthiness.
Therefore the pí resembles earth,
and its color is yellow.
Yì Fèng says:
"The gān's nature is calm;
Jiǎ and Jǐ govern it.
The xīn's nature is restless;
Bǐng and Xīn govern it.
The pí's nature is strong;
Wù and Guǐ govern it.
The fèi's nature is firm;
Yǐ and Gēng govern it.
The shèn's nature is reverent;
Dīng and Rén govern it."
In Xǔ Shèn's (許愼) *Wǔjīng Yìyì* (五經異義),
the *Shàngshū* (尚書) according to the Xiàhóu (夏侯) and Ōuyáng (歐陽) schools says:
The liver is wood,
the heart is fire,
the spleen is earth,
the lungs are metal,
the kidneys are water.
This is the same as before.
The *Gǔwén Shàngshū* (古文尚書) says:
The spleen is wood,
the lungs are fire,
the heart is earth,
the liver is metal.
These four *zàng* (藏) are different.
Upon examination, the *Lǐjì Yuèlìng* (禮記月令) says:
In spring, offer sacrifices with the spleen;
in summer, offer sacrifices with the lungs;
in late summer, offer sacrifices with the heart;
in autumn, offer sacrifices with the liver;
in winter, offer sacrifices with the kidneys.
If all
the five seasons correspond to each other naturally,
then the *Gǔ Shàngshū* (古尚書) is correct.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) rebutted, saying:
This text has differing accounts and conflicting matters,
without having investigated its original intent.
The five sacrifices in the *Yuèlìng* (月令) all speak of "first,"
and none speak of "after."
Any mention of "first" implies a "later."
In spring, the household (hù 戶) is sacrificed to;
in that sacrifice,
the spleen is offered first,
then the kidneys.
In summer, the stove (zào 竈) is sacrificed to;
in that sacrifice,
the lungs are offered first, then the heart and liver.
In late summer, the central hearth (zhōngliú 中霤) is sacrificed to;
in that sacrifice,
the heart is offered first,
then the lungs.
In autumn, the gate (mén 門) is sacrificed to;
in that sacrifice,
the liver is offered first,
then the heart and lungs.
In winter, the path (háng 行) is sacrificed to;
in that sacrifice,
the kidneys are offered first,
then the spleen.
The meaning of all this
is based on the positions of the four seasons
and the superior-inferior positions of the five *zàng*,
arranged in order.
Winter is positioned in the rear,
and the kidneys are below.
Summer is positioned in front,
and the lungs are above.
Spring is positioned slightly in front,
hence the spleen is sacrificed first.
Autumn is positioned slightly behind,
hence the liver is sacrificed first.
The liver, kidneys, and spleen are all below the *gé* (鬲) (diaphragm);
the lungs and heart are all above the *gé* (鬲).
There must be three offerings in a sacrifice,
hence there is a "first" and "last."
This meaning is not the same as the circulation of *qì* (氣).
The *Bāshíyī Wèn* (八十一問) says:
If all five *zàng* (藏) are equal,
why are the heart and lungs uniquely above the *gé* (鬲)?
The reply is:
The heart governs *qì* (氣),
the lungs govern blood.
Blood circulates within the vessels,
*qì* (氣) circulates outside the vessels.
They follow each other up and down,
hence they are called *róngwèi* (榮衞) (nutritive *qì* and defensive *qì*),
thus the heart and lungs are above the *gé* (鬲).
The *Jiǎyǐ Jīng* (甲乙經) says:
Huángdì (黃帝)
asked Qíbó (岐伯), saying:
Man has five *zàng* (藏),
and each *zàng* (藏) has five transformations.
The liver is a male *zàng* (藏),
its color is green,
its season is spring,
its days are *jiǎyǐ* (甲乙).
The heart is a male *zàng* (藏),
its color is red,
its season is summer,
its days are *bǐngdīng* (丙丁).
The spleen is a female *zàng* (藏),
its color is yellow,
its season is late summer,
its days are *wùjǐ* (戊己).
The lungs are a female *zàng* (藏),
their color is white,
their season is autumn,
their days are *gēngxīn* (庚辛).
The kidneys are a female *zàng* (藏),
their color is black,
their season is winter,
their days are *rén guǐ* (壬癸).
The *Sùwèn* (素問) says:
The liver is where the *hún* (魂) (ethereal soul) resides,
the minor *yáng* (陽) within *yīn* (陰).
Therefore, it communicates with the *qì* (氣) of spring.
The heart is the root of life,
where the *shén* (神) (spirit) resides,
the great *yáng* (陽) within *yáng* (陽).
Therefore, it communicates with the *qì* (氣) of summer.
The spleen is the root of granaries,
named "promoting transformation,"
able to transform dregs,
and convert tastes for intake and output,
a type of extreme *yīn* (陰).
Therefore, it communicates with the *qì* (氣) of earth.
The lungs are the root of *qì* (氣),
where the *pò* (魄) (corporeal soul) resides,
the minor *yīn* (陰) within *yáng* (陽).
Therefore, they communicate with the *qì* (氣) of autumn.
The kidneys govern hibernation,
the root of storage and concealment,
where the *jīng* (精) (essence) resides,
the great *yīn* (陰) within *yīn* (陰).
Therefore, they communicate with the *qì* (氣) of winter.
It also says:
In spring, do not eat liver;
in summer, do not eat heart;
in late summer, do not eat spleen;
in autumn, do not eat lungs;
in winter, do not eat kidneys.
The *Zhōulǐ Jíyī* (周禮疾醫),
who manages the diseases of all people,
by taking the liver as wood,
the heart as fire,
the spleen as earth,
the lungs as metal,
and the kidneys as water,
then most diseases are cured;
if he reverses his methods,
then there is death.
The rituals for the central hearth (zhōngliú 中霤) in the *Yuèlìng* (月令)
are sequenced by the advance and retreat of *yīn* (陰) and *yáng* (陽).
The *Báihǔ Tōng* (白虎通) and medical books like the *Sùwèn* (素問)
use the practical application of the Five Phases for verification.
Therefore, their correlations are correct.
The *Báihǔ Tōng* (白虎通) also says:
Why does wood float and
metal sink?
It is the principle of the child being born from the mother.
Why does the liver sink and
the lungs float?
It is that the conscious one
honors its mother.
One theory says:
Jiǎ (甲) wood fears metal,
so Yǐ (乙) marries Gēng (庚),
and undergoes Gēng's (庚) transformation.
Wood follows its root nature,
being directly *jiǎ* (甲) so it floats.
The liver follows its transformation,
being directly *yǐ* (乙) so it sinks.
Gēng (庚) metal fears fire,
so Xīn (辛) marries Bǐng (丙),
and undergoes Bǐng's (丙) transformation.
Metal follows its root nature,
being directly *gēng* (庚) so it sinks.
The lungs follow its transformation,
being directly *xīn* (辛) so they float.
Héshàng Gōng
annotated Lǎozǐ saying:
The liver stores the hún (ethereal soul);
the lungs store the pò (corporeal soul);
the heart stores the shén (spirit);
the kidneys store the jīng (essence);
the spleen stores the zhì (will).
If the five zàng (viscera) are all injured,
then the five shén will depart.
The Dàojīng Yì says:
The hún resides in the liver;
the pò is in the lungs;
the shén is in the heart;
the jīng is stored in the kidneys;
the zhì is entrusted to the spleen.
This is consistent with the Sùwèn.
The hún is wood qi;
the shén is fire qi;
the zhì is earth qi;
the pò is metal qi;
the jīng is water qi.
The hún connects to the eyes;
the shén connects to the tongue;
the zhì connects to the mouth;
the pò connects to the nose;
the jīng connects to the ears.
The Jiǎyǐ Jīng says:
The nose is the official of the lungs;
the eyes are the official of the liver;
the mouth and lips are the official of the spleen;
the tongue is the official of the heart;
the ears are the official of the kidneys.
Therefore, lung disease causes wheezing and flaring nostrils;
liver disease causes closed eyes and blue canthi;
spleen disease causes yellow, dry mouth and lips;
heart disease causes a curled, short tongue and a red complexion;
kidney disease causes dark yellow cheeks and face, and deafness.
These are called the five officials.
Physiognomy books also call them the five hòu (manifestations).
Taking the philtrum of the nose as one official,
it governs the heart.
The rest are the same.
As for hòu,
it is when the good or bad color of the five zàng manifests in the five officials,
through which one can prognosticate good or bad fortune.
The philtrum of the nose
is still a part of the mouth.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshén Qì says:
The liver is benevolent,
hence the eyes see.
The lungs are righteous,
hence the nose perceives.
The heart is礼 (propriety),
hence the ears preside.
The kidneys are trustworthy,
hence the orifices excrete.
The spleen is wise,
hence the mouth instructs.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says:
The eyes are the emissary of the liver;
the liver's qi is benevolent and illuminates outwards.
The Guǎnzǐ says:
The spleen manifests as the nose;
the liver manifests as the eyes;
the kidneys manifest as the ears;
the lungs manifest as the mouth;
the heart manifests as the lower orifices.
The Daoist Tàipíng Jīng says:
If the liver shén is absent,
the eyes will have no brightness.
If the heart shén is absent,
the lips will be pale blue/white.
If the lung shén is absent,
the nose will be blocked.
If the kidney shén is absent,
there will be deafness.
If the spleen shén is absent,
the tongue will not know sweet tastes.
Another theory says:
The eyes govern the liver;
the ears govern the kidneys;
the nose governs the heart;
the tongue governs the spleen;
the mouth governs the lungs.
For the liver and kidneys,
all scriptures agree.
The reason the liver governs the eyes is that
the liver is a wood zàng;
wood is yang,
the bright place of the East;
the eyes also shine brightly and clearly.
Therefore, it connects to the eyes.
The Daoist Dàshì Jīng says:
Heaven is called "insightful vision,"
governing the eyes;
the eyes govern the liver.
Heaven is yang;
the liver is also yang;
the bright essence of the eyes is also yang.
The shining clarity of the eyes,
moreover, has a constant rule,
like the sun's yang essence, bright and without defect.
The reason the kidneys govern the ears is that
the kidneys are a water zàng;
water is yin,
the dark place of the North;
the ears can hear sounds;
sound is a subtle yin phenomenon;
therefore, it connects to the ears.
The Dàshì Jīng says:
Earth is called "insightful hearing,"
governing the ears;
the ears govern the kidneys.
Earth is yin.
The ears function by being empty to receive sounds.
Water governs emptiness;
yin governs emptiness;
yin governs the deep dark.
Sound is also not constant,
like the waxing and waning of the moon.
For the three zàng of the spleen, heart, and lungs, and their manifestations,
there are different theories.
The Jiǎyǐ connects the nose to the lungs;
Daoists connect the nose to the heart;
the Guǎnzǐ connects it to the spleen.
The Jiǎyǐ's connection of the nose to the lungs is because
the nose is empty to receive qi,
and the lungs are also empty to receive qi.
The Daoist view that the nose governs the heart is because
it is yang.
The Lǎozǐ Jīng says:
Heaven's qi of the five phases
enters the heart from the nose.
The nose is empty and allows breath to enter and exit.
Its height symbolizes heaven,
thus it communicates with heaven,
and qi is stored in the heart.
The Guǎnzǐ views the spleen as earth,
and the nose is in the middle of the face,
hence it is its manifestation.
The Jiǎyǐ connects the spleen to the mouth.
Daoists connect the lungs to the mouth,
which is the same as the Guǎnzǐ.
The Jiǎyǐ's connection of the spleen to the mouth is because
the mouth is the gate of receiving and giving,
and the spleen is the place of reception and containment.
The mouth can speak and articulate,
the spleen can digest and transform.
Therefore, they are connected.
The Daoist connection of the lungs to the mouth is because
the lungs are metal;
metal can cut and divide,
and the mouth has teeth,
which also can make judgments and decisions,
which is a metal attribute.
The Guǎnzǐ's intention
is probably also like this.
The Jiǎyǐ connects the tongue to the heart;
Daoists connect the tongue to the spleen;
the Guǎnzǐ connects the heart to the lower orifices.
The Jiǎyǐ's connection of the tongue to the heart is because
in sustaining life,
nothing surpasses the five flavors;
in distinguishing and knowing,
nothing surpasses the heart.
The entry of the five flavors
is known by the tongue.
The right and wrong of myriad affairs
are judged by the heart.
When the heart wishes to express something,
the tongue will surely speak it.
Therefore, the heart corresponds to the tongue.
The Daoist connection of the tongue to the spleen is because
the spleen is yin.
The Lǎozǐ Jīng says:
Earth feeds people with the five flavors,
entering the mouth and storing in the stomach.
What the tongue receives
has moisture and substance.
The earth's body is indeed substantial.
All flavors are produced by the earth.
Therefore, the tongue communicates with the earth.
The Guǎnzǐ's connection of the heart to the lower orifices is because
the heart can distinguish good from evil,
hence it connects to the lower orifices
to eliminate waste.
The manifestations of the five zàng are in the five officials.
The two officials of the mouth and tongue
are in the same place;
for the others that are not together,
the mouth is the manifestation of the spleen;
the spleen is earth;
the tongue is the manifestation of the heart;
the heart is fire.
Their being together is because
earth resides temporarily in the realm of fire.
The tongue being inside the mouth is because
fire among the five phases
is not always visible.
It appears when needed,
in use, it is hidden,
like the tongue inside the mouth.
Opening the mouth, it is immediately seen;
closing the mouth, it is hidden.
Moreover, the heart (mind) is the body's noble master,
therefore it is inside.
Earth flourishes in the four seasons,
therefore it is called the four convergences.
The `Jiǎ Yǐ` and `Sù Wèn` (texts)
are books on diagnosis.
Therefore, one distinguishes based on actual practice.
The Daoist classics, the `Guǎnzǐ`,
each with the unique approach of its own school.
The six fǔ (viscera) are defined in
the Hétú, saying:
The Fèi (lungs) correspond to the Dàcháng (large intestine);
the Dàcháng is the fǔ for transmitting the Dao.
The Xīn (heart) corresponds to the Xiǎocháng (small intestine);
the Xiǎocháng is the fǔ for receiving and holding.
The Gān (liver) corresponds to the Dǎn (gallbladder);
the Dǎn is the fǔ for concentrating essence.
The Pí (spleen) corresponds to the Wèi (stomach);
the Wèi is the fǔ for the five grains.
The Shèn (kidneys) correspond to the Pángguāng (bladder);
the Pángguāng is the fǔ for jinye (body fluids).
The Sānjiāo stands alone as the fǔ for the inner waterway.
The Jiǎyǐ Sùwèn
states the same.
The Dàcháng being the fǔ for transmitting the Dao means that
the Fèi connects to the nose;
the nose inhales and exhales qi.
The Dàcháng transmits the qi of the five grains,
hence it is its fǔ.
The Xiǎocháng being the fǔ for receiving and holding means that
the Xīn connects to the tongue;
the tongue takes in the five flavors.
The Xiǎocháng receives them,
hence it is the fǔ for receiving and holding.
The Dǎn being the fǔ for concentrating essence means that
the Gān connects to the eyes;
the eyes are organs of clear essence
and also the master of jing-shen (spirit and essence),
hence it is called the fǔ for concentrating essence.
The Wèi being the fǔ for the five grains means that
the Pí connects to the mouth;
the mouth takes in the five grains,
and the Wèi receives them,
hence it is its fǔ.
The Pángguāng being the fǔ for jinye means that
the Shèn is the water zàng (organ).
The Pángguāng is empty and receives water.
Clear water-qi becomes jinye;
turbid qi becomes nasal mucus and saliva.
Hence it is considered its fǔ.
The Sānjiāo being the fǔ for the central waterway means that
each of the five zàng corresponds to one fǔ.
The Sānjiāo alone has no corresponding zàng,
hence it is said to stand alone.
It is situated in the midst of the five zàng,
circulating qi upwards and downwards,
hence it is the fǔ for the central waterway.
The five zàng having six fǔ
is also like the six qì arising from the five elements.
Furthermore,
it is like the five xìng (natures) giving rise to the six qíng (emotions).
The Sùwèn says:
The skin corresponds to the Dàcháng;
its luster is the hair,
governed by the Xīn.
The blood vessels correspond to the Xiǎocháng;
its luster is the complexion,
governed by the Shèn.
The sinews correspond to the Dǎn;
its luster is the nails,
governed by the Fèi.
The flesh corresponds to the Wèi;
its luster is the lips,
governed by the Gān.
The couli (skin texture) and fine body hair
correspond to the Sānjiāo and Pángguāng;
their luster is the head hair,
governed by the Pí.
The skin corresponding to the Dàcháng,
its luster being the hair,
and governed by the Xīn, means that
the Xīn is the ruler of the body,
the skin is the city wall of the body,
the hair is the protective feathers of the body,
and the Dàcháng is the pathway of qi.
Therefore, they are all connected.
The Xīn is a fire zàng,
the Dàcháng is a metal fǔ,
hence they are matched.
This is what Bǐng-Xīn governs.
The blood vessels corresponding to the Xiǎocháng,
its luster being the complexion,
and governed by the Shèn, means that
the Shèn is water.
The blood vessels are the channels for blood,
through which water-qi flows.
The complexion is a person's radiance.
If blood and qi are abundant,
the complexion is robust and pleasant.
If blood and qi are weak,
the countenance is withered and haggard.
The Shèn is a water zàng.
The Xiǎocháng,
being able to receive and hold,
contains water-qi,
and is also a fire fǔ,
hence they are matched.
This is what Dīng-Rén governs.
The sinews corresponding to the Dǎn,
its luster being the nails,
and governed by the Fèi, means that
the sinews are the inner rigidity of the skin,
the nails are the outer sharpness of the skin.
The Fèi is a metal zàng.
The Dǎn has the nature of rigid essence,
and
is a wood fǔ,
hence they are matched.
This is what Yǐ-Gēng governs.
The flesh corresponding to the Wèi,
its luster being the lips,
and governed by the Gān, means that
the Wèi can digest the five grains.
Their refined qi becomes flesh.
The five grains enter through the mouth,
hence the luster and moisture are in the lips.
The Gān is a wood zàng,
benevolent and capable of generation.
The Wèi is an earth fǔ,
hence they are matched.
This is what Jiǎ-Jǐ governs.
The couli and fine body hair
corresponding to the Sānjiāo and Pángguāng,
their luster being the head hair,
and governed by the Pí, means that
the fine body hair relies on jin (fluid) and run (moisture),
and the couli are inherently open.
The Pí receives the nourishment of flavors.
Through this nourishment of flavors,
it obtains jin and run, and becomes open.
Through jin and run, and being open,
hair grows.
The book says:
Hair is the surplus of blood.
The Pí is an earth zàng.
The Sānjiāo and Pángguāng
are both water fǔ,
hence they are matched.
This is what Wù-Guǐ governs.
The Pí is matched with two fǔ,
while the other four zàng
are each matched with one fǔ. This is because
the Pí is an earth zàng,
earth is the way of the ruler.
The ruler is yang.
The number of yang is one,
so a zàng is not paired with two.
The Sānjiāo and Pángguāng are both water fǔ.
Water is the way of the minister.
The minister is yin.
The number of yin is even,
so there are two fǔ.
Guǎnzǐ says:
The Pí generates bones,
the Shèn generates sinews,
the Fèi generates skin,
the Xīn generates flesh,
the Gān generates nails and hair.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says:
The Gān generates sinews.
That the Pí generates bones means
the Pí is earth,
and earth can generate wood.
Bones are the foundation of the body,
like wood standing on the ground,
capable of forming houses,
hence the Pí generates them.
That the Shèn generates sinews means
sinews are the meridians and collaterals of bones,
through which blood flows,
and by which joints are connected,
all circulating blood and qi.
The Shèn is water,
hence it generates them.
That the Fèi generates skin means
the Fèi is metal,
metal can cut and divide,
and skin also delimits and divides,
hence the Fèi generates it.
That the Xīn generates flesh means
the Xīn is fire.
Flesh is the earth of the body,
hence the Xīn generates it.
That the Gān generates nails and hair means
the Gān is wood.
Nails are the surplus of bones,
hair is the surplus of blood,
both are qi of water and wood,
hence the Gān generates them.
The Yuánmìng Bāo saying that the Gān generates sinews
also follows the meaning of wood-qi,
as sinews have branches and resemble wood.
The Hétú 河圖 states:
Benevolence, compassion, generosity, and charitable giving
are the essence of the liver.
Excessive grief and sorrow
injure the liver.
When the liver is injured,
it causes vision to become blurry.
Propriety, discipline, and uprightness
are the essence of the heart.
Intense anger and joy injure the heart.
When the heart is injured,
nosebleeds and vomiting occur.
Harmony, generosity, sincerity, and trustworthiness
are the essence of the spleen.
Excessive indulgence and gluttony
injure the spleen.
When the spleen is injured,
accumulation and lack of transformation occur,
leading to abdominal distension and結jié (mass) diseases.
Righteousness, kindness, firmness, and decisiveness
are the essence of the lungs.
Worry, anxiety, and indignation
injure the lungs.
When the lungs are injured,
coughing, reversed qi, and loss of voice occur.
Wisdom, discernment, and strategy
are the essence of the kidneys.
Overexertion, excessive desires, and suppressed anger
injure the kidneys.
When the kidneys are injured,
essence is lost and life is shortened.
This not only violates the Five Constants
and shortens one’s lifespan,
but also destroys the Six Emotions,
leading to the ruin of families and states.
Take, for example, the two emperors Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂:
both lost their states due to greed and indulgence.
The two officials Liáng 梁 and Dòu 竇
also ruined their families due to extravagance.
Although Pángzǐ 彭子 prolonged his life through sexual activity,
and King Qí 齊 cured his illness through anger,
these are different paths,
but all involve appropriate regulation.
When regulated, the four great elements (body components) achieve peace;
when indulged, the five zàng 臟 organs become diseased.
The Sùwèn 素問 states:
The liver is the official of the general,
from which planning and deliberation arise.
The heart is the official of the sovereign,
from which spirit and clarity arise.
The spleen is the official of the granary,
from which the five flavors arise.
The lungs are the official of the prime minister,
from which governance and regulation arise.
The kidneys are the official of strength and vigor,
from which skill and ingenuity arise.
The liver is the official of the general,
from which planning and deliberation arise:
the nature of wood is benevolence.
A benevolent person must be able to think deeply and plan for the long term,
always wishing to benefit and bring peace to all beings.
A general is the master of deploying troops,
and must prioritize planning and deliberation.
Therefore, the military classics say:
If an army is raised with benevolence,
there is nothing it cannot obtain;
if it distributes with benevolence,
there is no one who will not be pleased.
It also says:
If a general lacks strategy,
the soldiers will be anxious;
if a general lacks deliberation,
the soldiers will desert.
Therefore, the liver is the general,
and gives rise to planning and deliberation.
The heart is the official of the sovereign,
from which spirit and clarity arise:
fire corresponds to the south, to the brilliance of the sun,
