an image of a monarch.
The spirit is the monarch of the body,
just as a monarch faces south to govern.
The Yìjīng 易經 takes Lí 離 as fire,
occupying the position of great yang,
an image of a monarch.
All human movements,
and the generation of emotions and nature,
come from the heart.
Therefore, it is the official of the sovereign,
from which spirit and clarity arise.
The spleen is the official of the granary,
from which the five flavors arise:
all things are born from the earth when alive,
and return to it when dead.
The five grains that enter [the body],
are received by the spleen.
Therefore, the production of the five flavors
also originates from this.
The lungs are the official of the prime minister,
from which governance and regulation arise:
metal can cut and decide.
The duty of the prime minister
is to be clear about the way of governance,
so that superiors and subordinates follow instructions,
and all things have propriety and order.
Among the five zàng 臟 organs, the lungs
are also where governance and regulation arise.
The Yuèwěi 樂緯 states:
Shāng 商 (the musical note) means zhāng 章 (to be manifest or clear).
A minister manifests and clarifies the monarch's virtue,
thereby regulating superiors and subordinates.
This is the role of the prime minister.
The kidneys are the official of strength and vigor,
from which skill and ingenuity arise:
the nature of water is wisdom.
The wise are certainly multi-talented,
hence possessing skill and ingenuity.
Ingenuity leads to unceasing self-strengthening.
The Bāshíyī Wèn 八十一問 asks:
Each zàng 臟 organ is singular,
why are the kidneys uniquely dual?
The left is the kidney,
and the right is the Mìngmén 命門.
The Mìngmén 命門
is where essence and spirit converge.
The Hétú 河圖 states:
The liver and heart appear on the left,
the spleen and lungs appear on the right,
and the kidneys and Mìngmén 命門
both appear in the chǐbù 尺部 (cubit region of the pulse).
This is pulse diagnosis.
Question:
The previous explanation
said the kidneys are yin, hence dual.
Now,
it says the left is the kidney and the right is the Mìngmén 命門.
Is this not self-contradictory?
Answer:
Mìngmén 命門 and the kidneys,
though different in name, are similar in form.
As water organs, their physical substance is not distinct,
hence they are dual.
But when primarily named by their yin aspect,
they are differentiated into left and right,
each having its own primary function.
This is similar to the Sānjiāo 三焦 and the bladder,
both being water residences,
which does not prevent them from having two names.
In the Lǎozi Jīng and Sùwèn,
it is said that the heart stores shén.
Shén is defined by its bright and illuminating comprehension.
It means the heart can clearly understand all things.
Shén is the ruler of the body,
symbolizing fire,
as previously explained.
That the kidneys store jīng
is based on jīng being called the essence of intelligence and wisdom.
It is also the essence of intelligent qi,
kidney water.
Because of its skill and ingenuity,
jīng is stored there.
That the spleen stores zhì
is because zhì is earth.
Earth encompasses the four elements
and has many inclinations.
Zhì is defined by the heart's aspirations and inclinations,
hence it is stored in the spleen.
That the liver stores hún
is because hún is named for movement.
The liver is shàoyáng,
and yáng nature is movement.
Wood nature is benevolence,
so hún also governs goodness,
hence it is stored in the liver.
That the lungs store pò
is because pò is named for attachment.
The lungs are shàoyīn,
and yīn nature is calm and quiet.
Metal governs killing,
and pò also governs evil.
Therefore it is stored there.
The functions governed by the five zàng
are the five kinds of shén, jīng, zhì, hún, and pò.
Discussing them in terms of yīnyáng,
there are only two distinctions.
Yáng is called hún,
and yīn is called pò.
Héshànggōng Zhāngjù says:
The five pure and subtle qì
constitute the essence, spirit, intelligence,
voice, and five natures.
Their guǐ is called hún,
and hún is masculine.
It governs entering and exiting through the nose,
communicating with Heaven.
The five turbid and moist flavors
constitute the form, bones, flesh,
blood vessels, and six emotions.
Their guǐ is called pò,
and pò is feminine.
It enters and exits through the mouth,
communicating with Earth.
Jiāyǔ says:
Zǎiwǒ
asked Kǒngzǐ,
"I have heard the names guǐ and shén,
but I don't know what they mean."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"When a person is born, they have qì.
Hún qì
is the flourishing of shén.
Pò qì
is the flourishing of guǐ.
When a person is born, they will die.
Upon death, they must return to the earth;
this is called guǐ.
Hún qì returns to Heaven;
this is called shén.
To combine guǐ and shén and offer sacrifices to them
is the ultimate teaching.
The bones and flesh perish below,
transforming into wild earth.
Their qì rises and spreads above;
this is the manifestation of shén.
The Sages, based on the nature of things and people,
clearly defined guǐ and shén
to serve as a standard for the people.
Burning and roasting fragrant offerings
is how qì is repaid.
Offering millet and grains,
cultivating the lungs and liver,
and adding fragrant herbs
is how pò is repaid.
Hànshū Wǔxíng Zhì says:
When a person dies and their form is buried,
their jīngshén disperses.
The Sages established ancestral temples for them
to collect hún qì.
Spring and autumn sacrifices
are performed to cultivate filial piety.
Shīzǐ says:
Guǐ means 'to return'.
In ancient times, the deceased
were called 'returners'.
Huáinánzǐ says:
A person's jīngshén
belongs to Heaven.
Their bones and flesh
belong to Earth.
The jīng qì enters its gate,
and the bones return to their root.
It also
says:
Heavenly qì is hún,
Earthly qì is pò.
Lǐjì Jiāotèshēng says:
All sacrifices should be mindful of this.
Hún qì returns to Heaven,
and xíng pò returns to Earth.
Therefore, sacrifices seek the meaning of yīnyáng.
Thus, the pure qì is called shén,
which is yáng hún.
The turbid qì is called guǐ,
which is yīn pò.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ,
when burying his son between Yíng and Bó, said:
"Bones and flesh return to the earth;
this is fate.
Hún qì goes everywhere."
Yuèjì says:
The King
asked Fànzǐ,
"I have heard that
one who loses their hún and pò dies,
and one who gains their hún and pò lives.
All things have this;
is it true for humans?"
Fàn Lǐ replied,
"Pò is a container,
and hún is the source of vital qì."
It also
says:
Hún is the essence of vital qì;
pò is the dwelling of dead qì.
Hánshī says:
There are two rivers, Còuwěi.
On the third month, Shàngsì day,
the state of Zhèng often performed rituals on these waters
to summon hún and restore pò.
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo, 25th year:
Duke Sòng was feasting and drinking,
and had Zhāozǐ act as his right attendant.
They conversed, weeping and laughing.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Now both the Duke and Zǐshū will die, won't they?"
The pure essence of the heart
is called hún and pò.
If hún and pò leave it,
how can it last long?
These all clarify that the human body has the two distinctions of hún and pò.
The Lǎozi Jīng
says hún is stored in the liver,
and pò is stored in the lungs.
Since hún belongs to Heaven,
Heavenly qì is yáng,
yáng governs goodness and favors the left.
The liver is located in the eastern wood position.
Since pò belongs to Earth,
Earthly qì is yīn,
yīn governs evil and favors the right.
Therefore, the lungs are located in the western metal position.
Lǎozi says:
"Auspicious matters favor the left,
inauspicious matters favor the right."
It also says the five qì are stored in the heart,
and the five flavors are stored in the stomach.
This theory is that
qì is yáng,
and is received by the zàng.
The heart is the fire zàng,
where yáng qì resides.
Flavor is yīn,
and is received by the fǔ.
The stomach is the fǔ of the five grains,
where flavors reside.
The heart governs jīngshén,
and the stomach governs reception and containment,
which does not contradict the principle of hún, pò, yīnyáng.
It also
says hún has three [parts],
and pò has seven.
Yáng numbers are odd,
yīn numbers are even.
Odd numbers begin with one,
and one is the primordial qì.
Although hún is yáng,
it is not called primordial origin;
the number after one is three,
so hún has three.
It also says
that humans are born from the combination of the two qì of Heaven and Earth,
and humans also have one qì.
The Three Powers each have one qì,
thus hún has three.
Yīn numbers are two,
and two is also the beginning of yīn.
Although pò is yīn,
Also, it is not Yuánshǐ,
second, then fourth.
Yīn does not stand alone,
it must rely on Yáng.
When the three Hún
combine, they become seven.
Another explanation says:
Hún resides in the East,
taking Zhèn's number three.
Pò resides in the West,
taking Duì's number seven.
Three Hún
and seven Pò
combine to make ten.
This corresponds to the five phases of Heaven
and the five phases of Earth.
The two fives combine to make ten,
collectively forming a human being.
The five are the five Qì of Heaven
and the five flavors of Earth.
The Chūnqiū Wěi says:
Humans are conceived from the ten,
thus they are born after ten months.
Also,
regarding those who speak of six Pò,
this comes from the Dàojiā's Sānhuáng Jīng,
which takes the spirits of the five Zàng as five Hún,
and the spirits of the six Fǔ as six Pò.
This also reflects the meaning of the five phases and six Qì.
Hún and Pò are fundamental to humans,
and since they are associated with the Fǔ and Zàng,
they are explained here.
Jiǎyǐ says:
Hún belongs to Jīng,
Pò belongs to Shén.
The five constants (wǔcháng) are
Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì, and Xìn.
They are practiced permanently and enduringly,
and cannot ever be absent,
hence they are called "constants" (cháng).
They are also called the five virtues (wǔdé),
because by constantly practicing these,
one can achieve virtue,
hence they are called the five virtues.
And these five virtues are matched with the five phases.
Zhèng Xuán,
in his commentary on the Zhōngyōng chapter of the Lǐjì, says:
The spirit of Wood is Rén,
the spirit of Metal is Yì,
the spirit of Fire is Lǐ,
the spirit of Water is Xìn,
the spirit of Earth is Zhì.
The Shī Wěi and other texts say the same.
Máo Gōng's teachings,
and the teachings of Jīng Fáng and others,
all take Earth as Xìn
and Water as Zhì.
The Hànshū Tiānwén Zhì says:
Regarding the Suìxīng in humans,
the five constants are Rén,
the five affairs are Mào.
If Rén is deficient and Mào is lost,
it goes against the spring order,
harms the Wood Qì,
and the punishment is seen in Suìxīng.
Regarding Yínghuò in humans,
the five constants are Lǐ,
the five affairs are Shì.
If Lǐ is deficient and Shì is lost,
it goes against the summer order,
harms the Fire Qì,
and the punishment is seen in Yínghuò.
Regarding Tàibái in humans,
the five constants are Yì,
the five affairs are Yán.
If Yì is deficient and Yán is lost,
it goes against the autumn order,
harms the Metal Qì,
and the punishment is seen in Tàibái.
Regarding Chénxīng in humans,
the five constants are Zhì,
the five affairs are Tīng.
If Zhì is deficient and Tīng is lost,
it goes against the winter order,
harms the Water Qì,
and the punishment is seen in Chénxīng.
Regarding Zhènxīng in humans,
the five constants are Xìn,
the five affairs are Sī.
Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì,
take Xìn as their foundation.
Mào, Yán, Shì, Tīng,
take Sī as their correctness.
If all four affairs are lost,
Zhènxīng will move accordingly.
According to Máo Gōng, Jīng Fáng, and the Hàn History,
all take Earth as Xìn,
which can be considered accurate.
The reason for this is as follows:
Regarding the meaning of the five constants,
Rén takes compassion as its essence,
and extensive benevolence as its function.
Lǐ takes distinction as its essence,
and adhering to norms as its function.
Zhì takes clear wisdom as its essence,
and bright insight as its function.
Yì takes suitability as its essence,
and decisive judgment as its function.
Xìn takes honesty as its essence,
and trustworthiness as its function.
Regarding the five phases,
Wood has covering, enveloping, nourishing, and proliferating;
this is its compassion and extensive benevolence.
Fire has extinguishing darkness and illuminating brightness;
this is its distinction and adherence to norms.
Water has containing, moistening, and flowing;
this is its clear wisdom and bright insight.
Metal has hardness, rigidity, and sharpness;
this is its suitability and decisive judgment.
Earth has supporting, carrying, and containing;
it generates myriad things in due season;
this is its trustworthiness and honesty.
Zhèng Xuán and the Shī Wěi,
who take Earth as Zhì,
do so because no one surpasses Zhì
in being able to understand all things,
and no one surpasses Earth
in being able to generate all things,
hence they take it as Zhì.
As for Water being Xìn,
the tides of water
arrive according to schedule,
hence water is taken as Xìn.
This reasoning has limited evidence and is narrow,
and deviates from Fú Xī's principles.
As for the Five Classics (Wǔjīng),
benevolence (rén) is matched with the Changes (Yì),
its position is the East.
Rites (lǐ) are matched with Fire,
its position is the South.
Righteousness (yì) is matched with the Commentaries (zhuàn),
its position is the West.
Wisdom (zhì) is matched with the Odes (Shī),
its position is the North.
Trustworthiness (xìn) is matched with the Documents (Shàngshū),
its position is the Center.
The Changes (Yì) are matched with the East and benevolence (rén) because
the Changes (Yì) is a book of creation,
encompassing all existence,
with the meaning of change and transformation.
The East is the beginning of the four seasons,
the transformation of benevolence (rén) can give rise to life,
thus the Changes (Yì) lead to renewal.
Moreover, the Di appeared from Zhèn,
first creating the Eight Trigrams (bāguà),
hence it is matched with benevolence (rén).
Rites (lǐ) are matched with the South because
rites (lǐ) can regulate the laws for superiors and inferiors,
differentiate between the noble and the humble,
and lords and ministers, fathers and sons,
are all regulated by rites (lǐ).
Just as fire can accomplish the five flavors,
and brightly illuminate all things,
therefore the South is matched with rites (lǐ).
The Commentaries (zhuàn) are matched with the West and righteousness (yì) because
the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū) is the history of Lǔ,
praising the deserving and criticizing the undeserving.
At that time, the Way of the King (Wáng Dào) had declined,
the various feudal lords (zhūhóu) contended for power,
and matters of war and conquest
were all recorded.
Those who conformed to righteousness (yì) were praised,
those who lost virtue were criticized,
just as metal cuts with righteousness (yì),
regulating all things,
hence it is matched with righteousness (yì).
The Odes (Shī) are matched with the North and wisdom (zhì) because
the Odes (Shī) express one's aspirations,
serving as satire,
containing subtle and profound words,
harmonizing and moistening human emotions,
moving spirits and deities (guǐshén) and affecting heaven and earth.
Through matters of good and evil,
recited in song and music,
they cause listeners to benefit in their conduct,
and the authors to be free from blame.
Just as water flows secretly, moistening everything,
therefore it is matched with wisdom (zhì).
The Documents (Shàngshū) are matched with the Center and trustworthiness (xìn) because
this is a book of high antiquity,
transmitting the words of emperors and kings,
and matters of pledges and oaths
are all preserved therein.
It can be revered and honored,
just as earth has trustworthiness (xìn),
giving birth to things according to the seasons,
and is honored by the four seasons.
Therefore it is matched with trustworthiness (xìn).
Jīng means constancy,
it also means origin,
it also means law.
It describes matters originating,
hence it is called origin.
Its principles can serve as laws,
hence it is called law.
It serves as a constant canon of instruction,
hence it is constancy.
However, the nature of the Jīng is already constant law,
and its essence is equipped with the Five Constants (Wǔcháng),
each specializing in certain matters.
But as it primarily focuses on one aspect,
without discussing its textual meaning,
it is not fully explained.
The practice of the Five Constants (Wǔcháng)
is elucidated through the Jīng,
hence this matching explanation.
As for the Five Matters (Wǔ Shì),
the "Grand Norm" (Hóngfàn) of the Documents (Shàngshū) says:
"Reverently employ the Five Matters (Wǔ Shì),"
which means matching human affairs with the Five Elements (Wǔ Xíng).
First is appearance (mào),
matched with Wood.
matched with Metal.
Second is speech (yán),
matched with Fire.
Fourth is hearing (tīng),
matched with Water.
Fifth is thought (sī),
matched with Earth.
The "Grand Norm" (Hóngfàn) of the Documents (Shàngshū) says: "Appearance (mào) is called reverence (gōng),
speech (yán) is called compliance (cóng),
sight (shì) is called clarity (míng),
hearing (tīng) is called acuity (cōng),
thought (sī) is called sagacity (ruì)."
Reverence (gōng) leads to solemnity (sù),
compliance (cóng) leads to order (yì),
clarity (míng) leads to insight (zhé),
acuity (cōng) leads to planning (móu),
sagacity (ruì) leads to wisdom (shèng).
"Appearance (mào) is called reverence (gōng)" means
the reverence (gōng) of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ)
is called majestic and dignified (mùmù).
If superiors are reverent and solemn (gōngsù),
then inferiors will be respectful.
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"In his personal conduct, he is reverent (gōng);
in serving his superiors, he is respectful (jìng)."
He also said:
"In one's person, it is called reverence (gōng);
when applied to others,
and manifested in affairs, it is called respect (jìng)."
If one's appearance (mào) is not reverent (gōng),
this is called not solemn (sù),
and solemnity (sù) means respect (jìng).
Among the Five Matters (Wǔ Shì) presented in the "Grand Norm" (Hóngfàn),
appearance (mào) is first because
in the Changes (Yì), appearance (mào) is Zhèn,
Zhèn is Wood,
and Wood is visible.
Therefore, the classics list three virtues,
and outward demeanor (fú) is at their head.
The Odes (Shī) say:
"Be reverent and careful in your awe-inspiring demeanor (wēiyí),
for it is the standard for others."
To have majesty (wēi) that inspires fear
is called majesty (wēi);
to have an exemplary bearing (yí)
is called demeanor (yí).
If a ruler has majesty and demeanor (wēiyí),
his ministers will fear and love him,
taking him as their standard and example,
hence he can long possess his state.
If ministers have majesty and demeanor (wēiyí),
they can long maintain their positions.
If a gentleman in office is awe-inspiring,
amiable in giving and receiving,
measured in advancing and retreating,
exemplary in his movements,
admirable in his deportment,
a model in his actions,
an example in his virtue,
pleasant in his speech,
cultured in his movements,
and eloquent in his words,
then his rule over his subordinates
is called majesty and demeanor (wēiyí).
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"If he sets right his clothes and cap,
and dignifies his gaze,
so that people look at him with awe,
is this not majesty without ferocity?"
He also said:
"If one does not preside with strictness,
then people will not be respectful."
Therefore, losing the moderation of majesty and demeanor (wēiyí),
being lazy, arrogant, and self-indulgent
is called madness (kuáng).
If mad (kuáng), inferiors will not be solemn (sù).
If inferiors are not respectful,
then superiors will have no majesty (wēi).
If one does not respect his ruler,
and does not comply with his governance,
then the yin (yīn) qi prevails.
If the yin (yīn) qi prevails,
then the phenomenon of water arrives.
Therefore it is said:
"Its punishment is constant rain."
If it rains, then hunger and cold arrive.
If hunger and cold arrive,
then superiors and inferiors do not trust each other.
Ministers engage in wicked schemes,
and the people become bandits and thieves.
If many people are punished,
then their clothing becomes unnatural (fúyāo).
Unnatural clothing (fúyāo) means
light, strange, decadent, violent, and insolent clothing,
symbolizing the transformation of the climate.
Those who speak of the Way of the *Yì* say *Duì*,
*Duì* refers to the image of speech from the mouth.
When the ruler's words issue forth,
if his commands are executed, people will follow.
Therefore, the *Yì* says,
"By pleasing the people, you make them forget their toil;
by pleasing them to face danger,
you make them forget their death."
For this reason, an enlightened ruler
levies light taxes and grants generous salaries,
rewards generously in case of doubt,
and punishes leniently in case of doubt.
This aligns with the people's will.
Thus, his teachings succeed without severity,
and his governance is orderly without strictness.
This is how he gains the people's hearts.
When the people's hearts are gained,
the multitude returns to him.
When the multitude returns to him,
the people, even in death,
will not forget him.
How much more so will they obey his commands!
If the ruler loses the hearts of the multitude,
his political commands will not be followed,
the soaring *yáng* will dissipate on its own,
and the mass of *yīn* will not attach itself.
And if the lower classes fear the ruler's heavy punishments,
then the *yáng* energy will be dominant.
When *yáng* energy is dominant, there is drought.
Therefore, it is said,
"Its punishment is constant *yáng*."
Constant *yáng* leads to hunger and poverty,
and insufficiency.
When there is insufficiency, people dare not speak out directly,
then it first manifests through the mouths of songs and ballads.
When *qì* is rebellious, evil words arrive,
and insect plagues arise;
these are all matters of the mouth.
Seeing refers to the south,
the image of the eye.
Seeing is called *míng* (brightness/discernment).
*Míng* takes knowing people as its foundation.
In the *Yì*, it is *Lí*.
*Lí* represents fire and the eye.
If one's vision is unclear,
weak and not knowing whom to trust,
one will inevitably serve a faction for a long time.
Enemies and kin, all treated the same.
In such a case, the worthy will not be promoted.
If the worthy are not promoted,
then the unworthy will not be retired.
If the unworthy are not retired,
then those who offend superiors will not be punished,
the innocent will be unjustly penalized,
all offices will be neglected and damaged,
all affairs will be stalled and blocked,
and teaching and governance will be lax.
Therefore, it is said,
"Its punishment is constant warmth."
Warmth leads to winter leakage (*xiè*),
and when winter *qì* leaks, it is not cold.
When spring and summer *qì* are disordered,
diseases and epidemics arise.
If those who offend superiors are not punished,
then grass will defy frost and not die.
If the people's wealth is avariciously seized,
then locusts and armyworms will also eat human food.
These are all images related to seeing.
Listening resides in the ear.
The ear, in the *Yì*, is *Kǎn*.
In ancient times, sagely kings had banners for promoting good deeds,
drums for encouraging remonstrance,
and consulted with woodcutters and grass gatherers,
all to widely extend and broadly listen.
If the ruler does not like to deliberate,
then the lower classes will not dare to speak.
If the lower classes do not dare to speak,
then the superiors will hear nothing.
If the superiors hear nothing,
then they do not listen.
Not listening
stems from not deliberating on political affairs,
hence it is called not listening.
With no knowledge or information,
all affairs are suppressed and thwarted,
resentment is in the heart and mouth,
and joy and anger are unrestrained.
Therefore, it is called urgency (*jí*).
Cold is a constricted thing,
all winter things are dry and constricted.
Dry and constricted,
hence it is said,
"Its punishment is constant cold."
Constant cold means no grains grow,
and no grains growing
means the people are impoverished.
Therefore, omens (*yāo*) arise in the ear.
When things move according to their kind,
there are sounds of drum omens and similar phenomena.
*Kǎn* represents the pig.
If ear *qì* is harmed, there is a disaster related to pigs.
The color of water is black;
there are black disasters.
These are all related to listening.
Thinking refers to the heart being the master of the five affairs,
just as the earth element is the master of the five phases.
In the *Yì*, it is *Kūn*.
The *qì* of the eight proper directions
also arises from the eight winds.
Wind is the master of the four seasons.
To have one's thinking heart attained is called *róng* (tolerance/capacity).
A *róng* person is capable of accommodating and nurturing ministers and sons,
hence called a sage.
If the thinking heart is not attained,
all four other affairs are lost,
then one cannot accommodate and nurture ministers and sons.
Therefore, it is said,
"If the thinking heart is intolerant,
this is called not being a sage."
The fault lies in confusion and disorder, losing discipline.
Therefore, wind in the *Yì* is *Xùn*.
In the third and fourth months, it is purely *yáng* and governs.
In *yáng*, it becomes *yīn*;
in *yīn*, it becomes *yáng*.
It is the image of a high minister.
Once the ruler is confused and disordered,
the high ministers become autocratic and arbitrary.
When high ministers are autocratic and arbitrary,
the *yīn* *qì* becomes dominant.
When *yīn* *qì* is dominant, it resonates.
Hence, "Its punishment is constant wind."
When *yīn* *qì* is abundant,
it is cloudy but does not rain—
this is its extremity.
Constant overcast darkness
is nurtured and accumulated in the heart,
and if the heart's *qì* is harmed,
it leads to dark omens.
The *Yì* says,
*Kūn* represents the ox.
*Kūn* is earth.
If earth *qì* is harmed,
many oxen die.
It also says,
earth represents internal affairs,
if internal affairs are chaotic,
there will be noxious growths (*huá niè*).
These are all affairs of thinking.
The manifestations of the five affairs are extremely numerous.
Only a brief summary is given here.
Thus.
Composed by Shàng Yí Tóng Sān Sī Chéngyáng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng Xiāo Jí.
The *Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* says,
"*Lǜ* (pitch-pipe) as a word means *shuài* (to lead/govern)."
The *Xù Hàn Shū* says,
"*Lǜ* is a method."
The *Lǜ Shū* says,
"*Lǚ* is an order/sequence."
It orders and describes the *qì* of the four seasons,
and determines the positions of the twelve months.
*Yīn* and *yáng* each have six,
totaling twelve.
The six *yáng* are the *lǜ*,
the six *yīn* are the *lǚ*.
The six *lǜ* are
Huángzhōng, Dàcù, Gūxǐ, Ruíbīn, Yízé, Wúshè.
The six *lǚ* are
Línzhōng, Nánlǚ, Yìngzhōng, Dàlǚ, Jiázhōng, Zhònglǚ.
The *Shǐjì* says,
"*Lǜlì* (pitch-pipes and calendar) are how Heaven operates the *qì* of the five phases and eight proper directions,
to bring all things to maturity."
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
Huángdì sent Línglún to the west of Dàxià,
to the north side of Kūnlún,
to fetch bamboo from a valley.
Those with uniform thickness and openings,
he cut between two joints,
and blew them to make pipes for the Huángzhōng,
imitating the call of the phoenix.
There were six male and six female,
to establish the lǜlǚ,
and to divide the celestial stations.
Língzhōujiū said:
The lǜ are for establishing musical standards and setting measures.
Therefore it is said:
To record by threes,
to equalize by sixes,
and to complete by twelves.
This is the Way of Heaven.
This is the origin among the six [pitches].
Ancient divine blind musicians,
examined the central sound and measured it to regulate,
to measure the lǜ and harmonize the bells.
Thus it was named Huángzhōng.
It is used to circulate and nourish the six qì.
The second is Dàcù,
used for metal instrument performances,
to assist the yang in releasing stagnation.
The third is Gūxǐ,
used to purify all things,
to examine spirits and receive guests.
The fourth is Ruíbīn,
used to tranquilize spirits and people,
and to present and return toasts.
The fifth is Yízé,
used to sing the nine principles,
so that the common people have no doubts.
The sixth is Wúshè,
used to proclaim the excellent virtues of wise men,
and to show the people proper conduct.
And there are six auxiliary pitches,
to elevate what is hidden and suppress what is scattered or excessive.
The first auxiliary pitch is Dàlǚ,
which assists in the manifestation of things.
The second auxiliary pitch is Jiázhōng,
which brings forth the subtleties of the four gaps.
The third auxiliary pitch is Zhōnglǚ,
which circulates the central qì.
The fourth auxiliary pitch is Línzhōng,
which harmonizes and unfolds all affairs,
ensuring all are reverent, pure, and conscientious.
The fifth auxiliary pitch is Nánlǚ,
which aids the flourishing of yang.
The sixth auxiliary pitch is Yìngzhōng,
which harmonizes the utility of instruments,
so they may respond and repeat.
When the lǜlǚ do not change,
there are no corrupting influences.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng says:
Lǜ means law.
It refers to the fact that when yang qì manifests life,
each has its own law.
Lǚ means assistance.
It assists in the flourishing of success.
Another interpretation says:
Lǜ means leader.
It leads and guides the yang qì,
enabling it to reach everywhere.
Lǚ means companion.
It corresponds to yang,
and accompanies it.
It also means lǚjù (resistance).
When harmonizing the qì of yin and yang,
they sometimes oppose each other.
Clearly, when yang emerges, yin recedes;
when yin ascends, yang diminishes.
Thus, there is the meaning of opposition.
The Xù Hànshū says:
Yang takes the circle as its form,
and its nature is active.
Yin takes the square as its structure,
and its nature is still.
The number for active is three,
the number for still is two.
Yang generates yin and accompanies it,
yin generates yang and halves it.
All are based on the ratio of three to one.
Yang generating yin is called "xiàshēng" (downward generation).
Yin generating yang is called "shàngshēng" (upward generation).
All are structured like "three heavens and two earths",
with a round covering and a square foundation.
This is the way of six even numbers supporting odd numbers.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
Numbers begin with one,
but one cannot generate.
Therefore, it divides into yin and yang.
Yin and yang combine to generate all things.
Therefore, one generates two,
two generates three,
and three generates all things.
Thus, three months constitute one season.
Therefore, sacrifices include three servings of rice,
mourning rituals include three leaps,
and military has three commands.
All take three as their principle.
Three times three is nine.
Therefore, the lǜ of Huángzhōng,
is nine cùn, and the Gōng note is tuned.
Consequently, multiplying by nine,
nine times nine is eighty-one,
thus establishing the number for Huángzhōng.
The qì of Huángzhōng is in zǐ,
established in the eleventh month,
its celestial division is Xīngjì,
and it generates Línzhōng downward.
The number for Línzhōng is fifty-four,
its qì is in wèi,
established in the sixth month,
its celestial division is Qúnhuǒ,
and it generates Dàcù upward.
The number for Dàcù is seventy-two,
its qì is in yín,
established in the first month,
its celestial division is Zōuzī,
and it generates Nánlǚ downward.
The number for Nánlǚ is forty-eight,
its qì is in yǒu,
established in the eighth month,
its celestial division is Shòuxīng,
and it generates Gūxǐ upward.
The number for Gūxǐ is sixty-four,
its qì is in chén,
established in the third month,
its celestial division is Dàliáng,
and it generates Yìngzhōng downward.
The number for Yìngzhōng is forty-two,
its qì is in hài,
established in the tenth month,
its celestial division is Zhémù,
and it generates Ruíbīn upward.
The number for Ruíbīn is fifty-six,
its qì is in wǔ,
established in the fifth month,
its celestial division is Qúnshǒu,
and it generates Dàlǚ upward.
The number for Dàlǚ is seventy-six,
its qì is in chǒu,
established in the twelfth month,
its celestial division is Xuánxiāo,
and it generates Yízé downward.
The number for Yízé is fifty-one,
its qì is in shēn,
established in the seventh month,
its celestial division is Qúnwěi,
and it generates Jiázhōng upward.
The number for Jiázhōng is sixty-eight,
its qì is in mǎo,
established in the second month.
Its celestial division is Jiànglóu,
and it generates Wúshè downward.
The number for Wúshè is forty-five,
its qì is in xū,
established in the ninth month,
its celestial division is Dàhuǒ.
And it generates Zhōnglǚ upward.
The number for Zhōnglǚ is sixty,
its qì is in sì,
established in the fourth month,
its celestial division is Shíshén.
The celestial divisions and the established months are intertwined as inner and outer.
This is how they naturally combine and generate each other.
It is based on the six hexagrams of Qiánkūn.
Huángzhōng (beginning with nine),
generates Línzhōng (beginning with six) downward.
And further, it generates Dàcù upward.
The Yuèwěi says:
Huángzhōng is the central Gōng note,
its number is eighty-one,
using the numbers of Heaven one, Earth two, and Human three.
By increasing and decreasing,
the lǜ forms the harmonious qì of the five notes.
Increasing creates upward generation,
decreasing creates downward generation.
For upward generation,
one-third is added.
For downward generation,
one-third is subtracted.
For adding, multiply by four,
and divide by three.
For subtracting, multiply by two,
and divide by three.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
The pipe for Huángzhōng (黃鐘)
is originally nine inches long.
The reason it is nine
is that nine is the extreme of the yang numbers.
The origin of numbers
begins with three.
The principles of the Three Powers (sāncái)—Heaven, Earth, and Humanity—
combine to form numbers.
Therefore, it is called the Sāncái (三才).
Thus, Heaven, Earth, and Humanity each have three numbers.
Yang can encompass three,
hence it is called nine.
Yin only encompasses two,
hence it is called six.
Since yang obtains qi (氣) encompassing three,
it is therefore multiplied by three.
Three times three makes nine.
Thus, the yang number nine is the extreme.
The reason the pipe uses nine inches
is to measure the yang qi (陽氣).
The yang qi (陽氣) manifests according to the seasons.
This is a natural and divine verification.
Further, upward it generates Dàcù (大蔟) nine-two;
further, downward it generates Nánlǚ (南呂) six-two;
further, upward it generates Gūxǐ (姑洗) nine-three;
further, downward it generates Yìngzhōng (應鐘) six-three;
further, upward it generates Ruíbīn (蕤賓) nine-four;
further, downward it generates Dàlǚ (大呂) six-four;
further, upward it generates Yízé (夷則) nine-five;
further, downward it generates Jiázhōng (夾鐘) six-five;
further, upward it generates Wúshè (無射) upper nine;
further, downward it generates Zhōnglǚ (中呂) upper six.
The reason same positions symbolize husband and wife,
and different positions symbolize mother and child
is the so-called "lǜ (律) takes a wife,
and lǚ (呂) bears a child."
The Báihǔ Tōng (白虎通) says:
What is Huángzhōng (黃鐘)?
Huáng (黃) refers to the central harmony (zhōnghé, 中和) of qi (氣),
and zhōng (鐘) means movement.
It means that yang, from beneath the Yellow Springs (Huángquán, 黃泉),
moves all things.
The Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Huáng (黃) is the color of earth,
and zhōng (鐘) is where qi (氣) moves.
Huángzhōng (黃鐘) is the ruler,
obtained at the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì, 冬至).
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Zhōng (鐘) is "response."
It means that the yang qi (陽氣) subtly moves beneath the Yellow Springs (Huángquán, 黃泉),
responding to nurture all things,
as buds and sprouts desire to emerge.
Dàlǚ (大呂):
Dà (大) means "great" or "supreme."
Lǚ (呂) means "to hinder" or "to resist."
It means that the yang qi (陽氣) desires to emerge, but the yin (陰) resists and makes it difficult.
The Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Lǚ (呂) is "to travel" (lǚ, 旅).
To travel and support.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Lǚ (呂) is "to assist."
In the twelfth month, yang is just beginning to grow,
and yin qi (陰氣) assists it.
The功 of giving birth and nurturing
is vast and great.
Therefore, one explanation says:
Lǚ (呂) is "companion" (lǚ, 侶).
It is a companion to yang,
and together they give birth to all things.
Dàcù (大蔟) means that all things begin to grow large
and gather from the earth to emerge.
The Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
All things gather but have not yet emerged.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Cù (蔟) has the meaning of "to gather" (còu, 湊).
At the time of the first month,
all things begin to grow large,
gathering from the earth to emerge.
Jiázhōng (夾鐘) means that all things sprout and develop shells,
and species emerge.
The Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Seeds begin to be enclosed.
The Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Jiá (夾) means "to assist" (zuǒ, 佐).
In the second month,
not all things have emerged.
Yin assists the yang qi (陽氣),
responding to things and causing them to emerge.
One explanation says:
Jiá (夾) means "to hold" or "to confine" (xiá, 俠).
It means that all things are confined by their shells,
and only at this point do they break free
and emerge in response to the bell.
Gūxǐ (姑洗) is
Gū (姑) meaning "old,"
xǐ (洗) meaning "fresh."
All things shed the old and embrace the new;
none are not fresh and bright.
Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Gūxǐ (姑洗) is when the old departs
and the new arrives.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Gū (姑) means "withered."
It has the meaning of washing and cleansing.
In the third month, things grow,
fresh and clean, washing away their withered state.
Zhōnglǚ (中呂) is when
all things emerge from within.
Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Zhōng (中) means "full."
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Lǚ (呂) has the meaning of resisting and obstructing.
It means that the yin (陰) desires to emerge,
but the yang (陽) energy is within,
resisting and holding it back.
Another saying is:
Lǚ (呂) is the time of the fourth month,
when yang (陽) energy is strong and growing,
and yin's (陰) auxiliary power is weak.
Therefore, it is said so.
Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is
ruí (蕤) meaning "to hang down,"
bīn (賓) meaning "to revere."
It means the yang (陽) energy descends.
Therefore, it is revered.
Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) says:
Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is peaceful and submissive.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Ruí (蕤) has the meaning of hanging down.
Bīn (賓) means "subtle" or "humble."
In the fifth month, yang (陽) energy descends,
and yin (陰) energy begins to rise,
mutually revering each other.
Línzhōng (林鐘) is
lín (林) meaning "numerous."
All things mature,
and species are numerous.
Huáinánzǐ (淮ánzǐ) says:
Línzhōng (林鐘) pulls and stops them.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Lín (林) means "lush and flourishing."
In the middle of the sixth month,
all things are flourishing and thriving,
gathered and accumulated in the fields.
Therefore, it is called lín (林).
Yízé (夷則) is
yí (夷) meaning "to injure,"
zé (則) meaning "law."
It means that all things begin to be injured,
subjected to punishment and law.
Huáinánzǐ (淮ánzǐ) says:
Yízé (夷則) changes its rule.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Yí (夷) means "even,"
zé (則) means "law."
In the seventh month, all things are about to complete,
evenly bearing fruit,
all having their rules and laws,
virtuous and auspicious.
Nánlǚ (南呂) is
nán (南) meaning "to bear" or "to be responsible for."
It means that yang (陽) energy has the responsibility to generate
and grow.
Huáinánzǐ (淮ánzǐ) says:
Nánlǚ (南呂) is
to bear and embrace greatness.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Nán (南) means "to bear."
In the middle of the eighth month,
all things contain their essence,
having the image of bearing and nurturing,
assisting in the completion of achievements.
Wúshè (無射) is
shè (射) meaning "to end."
It means that all things end by following yang (陽),
and will rise again by following yin (陰).
There is no end.
Huáinánzǐ (淮ánzǐ) says:
Wúshè (無射) is
human insatiability.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
Shè (射) means "to be weary of."
It means "to dislike."
In the ninth month, all things ripen,
nothing to be weary of.
Yìngzhōng (應鐘) means
all things respond to the season and descend to be stored.
Huáinánzǐ (淮ánzǐ) says:
Responds to what is gathered.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng (三禮義宗) says:
At the time of the tenth month,
the year's achievements are all complete,
the function of yin (陰) energy
responds to the achievement of yang (陽),
collecting and accumulating;
therefore it is called zhōng (鐘).
It also says:
Yìng (應) has the meaning of responding and harmonizing.
It means that at this time, it will again respond to the yang (陽) energy
and move below.
Yuèwěi (樂緯) says:
Huángzhōng (黃鐘) is gōng (宮),
Línzhōng (林鐘) is zhǐ (徵),
Dàcù (大蔟) is shāng (商),
Nánlǚ (南呂) is yǔ (羽),
Gūxǐ (姑洗) is jué (角),
Yìngzhōng (應鐘) is biàngōng (變宮),
Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is biànzhǐ (變徵).
Arranged in this order,
the five notes are complete.
Huángzhōng (黃鐘) gives birth to Línzhōng (林鐘) below it.
Therefore, Línzhōng (林鐘) is zhǐ (徵),
next to Huángzhōng (黃鐘).
Línzhōng (林鐘) gives birth to Dàcù (大蔟) above it.
Therefore, Dàcù (大蔟) is shāng (商),
next to Línzhōng (林鐘).
Dàcù (大蔟) gives birth to Nánlǚ (南呂) below it.
Therefore, Nánlǚ (南呂) is yǔ (羽),
next to Dàcù (大蔟).
Nánlǚ (南呂) gives birth to Gūxǐ (姑洗) above it.
Therefore, Gūxǐ (姑洗) is jué (角),
next to Nánlǚ (南呂).
Gūxǐ (姑洗) gives birth to Yìngzhōng (應鐘) below it,
therefore Yìngzhōng (應鐘) is biàngōng (變宮),
next to Gūxǐ (姑洗).
Yìngzhōng (應鐘) gives birth to Ruíbīn (蕤賓) above it.
Therefore, Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is biànzhǐ (變徵).
There are seven notes in total,
which circularly serve as gōng (宮).
As for the seven notes,
it is probably because the number of mutual generation is seven.
Starting from Huángzhōng (黃鐘) generating Línzhōng (林鐘),
from the twelfth month to the sixth month,
it is seven months in total.
Fú Qián's (服虔) explanation says:
The seven lǜ (律) are the seven notes.
Wàichuán's (外傳) explanation says:
When King Wǔ (武王) conquered Shāng (商),
the year was in Quánhuǒ (鶉火),
the day was in Tiānsì (天駟).
From Quánhuǒ (鶉火) to Tiānsì (天駟),
there are seven constellations in total.
Also, the earthly branch day was jiǎzǐ (甲子),
from zǐ (子) to wǔ (午) is also seven.
The celestial phenomena and earthly branches,
their numbers are all seven.
The sages used the lǜ (律) to match their numbers
and used sounds to call them forth.
Therefore, there are seven notes.
Music uses the seven lǜ (律) to match the seven beginnings.
Therefore, it establishes the three origins and four seasons.
Thus, Huángzhōng (黃鐘) is matched with heaven,
Línzhōng (林鐘) is matched with earth,
Dàcù (大蔟) is matched with humanity,
Gūxǐ (姑洗) is matched with spring,
Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is matched with summer,
Nánlǚ (南呂) is matched with autumn,
Yìngzhōng (應鐘) is matched with winter.
As for the three origins:
The Zhōu (周) dynasty took the jiànzǐ (建子) month as the heavenly proper (天正).
Therefore, the Huángzhōng (黃鐘) tube is matched with it.
The Yīn (殷) dynasty took the jiànchǒu (建丑) month as the earthly proper (地正).
It should be matched with the Dàlǚ (大呂) tube.
However, yin (陰) numbers are even.
Wèi (未) is the king of earth.
It is also the heavenly altar.
Therefore, its opposite is taken,
responding to the energy of earth,
and the Línzhōng (林鐘) tube is matched with it.
The Xià (夏) dynasty took the jiànyín (建寅) month as the human proper (人正).
Therefore, the Dàcù (大蔟) tube is matched with it.
The virtue of yang (陽) naturally occupies its place.
Therefore, the enthronement is taken as the proper.
The virtue of yin (陰) is in others.
Therefore, its opposite is taken.
The “Lǜlì Zhì” (Treatise on Harmonics and the Calendar) of the
Hànshū states: The Sān Yuán are
the records of Heaven's bestowal, Earth's transformation, and human affairs.
In the eleventh month, at qián zhī chū jiǔ,
the yang essence is hidden beneath the earth,
beginning to manifest as one.
All things stir and sprout,
culminating in the great yin.
Therefore, Huángzhōng is the Tiānyuán.
Its pitch pipe is nine cun long.
The number nine is used to exhaust the utmost harmony,
serving as the origin of all things.
The Yì Jīng says:
"Establishing the way of Heaven
is called yin and yang."
This is it.
In the sixth month, at kūn zhī chū liù,
the yin essence receives its charge from the great yang,
continuing to nurture and transform softly.
All things grow and flourish,
at their peak before the end,
making the seeds strong and firm.
Therefore, Línzhōng is the Dìyuán,
its pitch pipe is six cun long.
The number six
is for yin to receive the bestowal of yang,
establishing it within the six directions (liùhé),
making the hard and soft have form.
Establishing the way of Earth
is called soft and hard.
This is it.
Qián knows the great beginning;
Kūn accomplishes the creation of things.
In the first month, at qián zhī jiǔ sān,
all things spread and connect,
clustering forth in yín.
Humans uphold and complete them,
nurturing them with benevolence,
and acting upon them with righteousness,
causing all things to obtain their proper principles.
Yín is wood,
representing benevolence.
Its sound is shāng,
representing righteousness.
Therefore, Dàcù is the Rényuán,
its pitch pipe is eight cun long.
Eight corresponds to the trigrams.
This is how Fúxī Shì harmonized Heaven and Earth, communicated with spirits,
and classified the natures of all things.
Establishing the way of humanity
is called benevolence and righteousness.
This is it.
In Heaven, images are formed;
on Earth, forms are completed.
Later rulers then cut and complete the ways of Heaven, Earth, and humanity.
These are the Sān Yuán,
the beginning of the lǜ (pitch pipes).
The Gǎnjīng Fúyún states:
In the eleventh month, jiànzǐ,
is the beginning of Heaven's bestowal,
called Tiāntǒng.
The Zhōu dynasty, for its first month, favored red clothing,
symbolizing the red color of sprouting things.
The twelfth month, jiànchǒu,
is the beginning of Earth's transformation,
called Dìtǒng.
The Yīn dynasty, for its first month, favored white clothing,
symbolizing the white color of plant shoots.
The first month, jiànyín,
is the beginning of humanity's transformation,
called Réntǒng.
The Xià dynasty, for its first month, favored black clothing,
symbolizing the black color of things being born.
These three proper lǜ
also succeeded each other according to the Wǔdé,
taking the former Sān Huáng as proper,
namely Tiānhuáng, Dìhuáng, and Rénhuáng.
All took Heaven, Earth, and humanity as their model,
cyclically repeating.
The names written at the beginning of the year
were therefore taken from these.
Wishing to embody the way of the Sān Cái (three powers)
and rule over all nations,
therefore, a king who received the Mandate of Heaven
must adjust the liùlǜ,
and reform the calendar (zhèngshuò),
receive the Wǔqì and change the color of clothing,
emulating the way of the Sān Zhèng.
The Zhōu dynasty, using Tiāntǒng, favored red clothing because
the yang path favors the left,
thus Heaven rotates to the left.
The Zhōu ruled with the virtue of wood,
fire is its child,
the color of fire is red,
so it moves left and uses its red color.
The Yīn dynasty, using Dìtǒng, favored white clothing because
the yin path favors the right,
its movement turns right.
The Yīn ruled with the virtue of water,
metal is its mother,
the color of metal is white,
so it moves right and uses its white color.
The Xià dynasty, using Réntǒng, favored black clothing because
humanity also favors the left.
The Xià ruled with the virtue of metal,
water is its child,
the color of water is black,
so it moves left and uses its black color.
It also says:
The rise of emperors and kings
often comes with auspicious omens.
The Zhōu was moved by a red sparrow,
thus it favored red.
The Yīn attracted a white wolf,
thus it favored white.
The Xià was granted a dark jade tablet (xuánguī),
thus it favored black.
These are all preliminary signs.
The omens of a king,
the meaning of child and mother mutually assisting,
like the Hàn with the virtue of fire.
The essence of the planet Zhèn Xīng (Saturn)
descended as a yellow stone,
bestowing military stratagems upon Zǐfáng,
assisting Pèigōng in destroying Chǔ.
It is the colors of the Wǔ Yùn (Five Phases)
mutually assisting each other in their function.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Xià dynasty obtained Heaven."
This means it obtained the qi of the four seasons according to the way of Heaven,
corresponding to the cycles of birth and death of the Bā Jié (eight seasonal nodes).
Therefore, it says:
"Implement the time of Xià,
ride in the carriage of Yīn,
wear the cap of Zhōu."
It combines the three dynasties as a model.
This is probably to take what is enduring.
The Qín dynasty made the month of jiànhài
its new year.
The early Hàn followed Qín's calendar (zhèngshuò).
From the Wèi dynasty onwards,
they used the Xià calendar (Xià Zhèng),
and it has not changed since,
because it obtained the qi of Heaven.
Furthermore, Dùnjiǎ, Tàiyī, Jiǔgōng, Yuánchén,
all have Sān Yuán,
all starting with jiǎzǐ.
The first is Tiānyuán,
lasting six jiǎ;
the next jiǎzǐ is Dìyuán;
and the subsequent jiǎzǐ is Rényuán.
Dùnjiǎ takes the jiǎjǐ day at midnight
after the winter and summer solstices as the jiǎzǐ head of the yuán.
The Sān Yuán are each divided into three.
Therefore, one hundred eighty days constitute a yuán,
completing the two paths of yin and yang,
exhausting the functions of one year.
Tàiyī takes the first yuán's sixty-year jiǎzǐ cycle as one jì;
the next jiǎzǐ is the second jì;
six jì totaling three hundred sixty years complete one cycle (zhōu).
Jiǔgōng specifically takes jǐhài as the head of the yuán,
divided into Wǔ Yuán.
The first sixty-year jǐhài is Tiānyuán;
the next sixty-year jǐhài is Dìyuán;
the subsequent sixty-year jǐhài is Rényuán;
the next sixty-year jǐhài is Héyuán;
and the next sixty-year jǐhài is Hǎiyuán.
Nine years make one cycle,
four nines are thirty-six,
also completing the great number of six jiǎ.
The Sān Yuán and the calendar (zhèngshuò)
all follow the lǜlǚ,
corresponding to historical records and fixed times,
all aligned with the Wǔ Xíng.
Thus, this explanation is the same.
As for the Qī Zhèng (seven regulators),
they are the beginning of the dark celestial images,
regulating the celestial degrees.
Kings look up to them
to govern.
Thus, they are called zhèng.
The number seven is seven.
There are three interpretations in total.
One says:
The sun, moon, and five planets
together make the Qī Zhèng.
The second says:
The seven stars of the Běidǒu (Big Dipper) are the Qī Zhèng.
The third says:
The Èrshíbā Xiù (twenty-eight mansions),
distributed in the four directions,
with seven mansions per direction,
together constitute the Qī Zhèng.
These three types of Qī Zhèng
are all aligned with the Wǔ Xíng.
They are all the heads of the Sān Chén (three luminaries).
The sun, moon, and five planets are the seven regulators because
the Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào (尚書考靈耀) says of the seven regulators:
"The sun and moon
are the masters of time.
The five planets
are the records of time."
Therefore it says:
"In the xuánjī yùhéng (璇璣玉衡),
to regulate the seven regulators."
The seven regulators and five regulators refer to the governance of the five phases (wǔxíng).
The seven regulators are precisely the sun, moon, and five planets.
Regarding the sun,
the Hétú Wūguāng Piān (河圖汙光篇) says:
"The sun is the beginning of yang essence (yángjīng);
the sun is substantial."
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says:
"Yang begins with one."
Therefore, the sun travels one degree each day.
"Yang completes at three."
Hence, there is a three-legged crow.
The crow is yang essence.
Its call is "lúhū" (僂呼).
Common people see that "lúhū" resembles a crow,
hence they named it as such.
It also says:
"It is the essence of fire (huǒjīng) and yang energy (yángqì).
Therefore, it is hot outside and dark inside,
resembling a crow."
The sun is honored, hence full;
full, hence it bestows;
bestowing, hence benevolent.
Benevolent, hence it has essence;
its essence is on the outside.
On the outside, hence it is large;
the sun is hot outside.
Hot outside, hence yang essence emits outwards.
Heaven has three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees,
spread across the four directions.
The sun daily traverses them without error or delay,
making the four directions coalesce as one.
Therefore, its character (日) is a combination of four (四) and one (一).
The Báihǔtōng (白虎通) says:
"The sun is a thousand lǐ (里) in diameter,
three thousand lǐ in circumference,
and seven thousand lǐ below heaven."
The Tàixuánjīng (太玄經) says:
"When the sun is completely in the south, all things die;
when the sun is completely in the north, all things live."
The Wùlǐlùn (物理論) says:
"In summer, yang is ascendant and yin is descendant,
hence days are long and nights are short.
In winter, yin is ascendant and yang is descendant,
hence days are short and nights are long.
When traveling the yang path, the days are long,
rising and setting north of mǎo (卯) and yǒu (酉).
When traveling the yin path, the days are short,
rising and setting south of mǎo and yǒu.
In spring and autumn, yin and yang are equal.
Therefore, it travels the middle path,
and days and nights are equal."
The Kǎolíngyào (考靈耀) says:
"On the first day of spring,
the sun rises at mǎo (卯) and sets at yǒu (酉).
The Mǎo constellation (Mǎoxīng) is at one degree,
it is central at dusk;
the Dǒu constellation (Dǒuxīng) is at twelve degrees,
it is central at dawn.
On the first day of mid-summer,
the sun rises at yín (寅) and sets at xū (戌).
The Xīn constellation (Xīnxīng) is at five degrees,
it is central at dusk;
the Yíngshì constellation (Yíngshì) is at ten degrees,
it is central at dawn.
On the first day of autumn,
the sun rises at mǎo (卯) and sets at yǒu (酉).
The Xūnǚ constellation (Xūnǚ) is at four degrees,
it is central at dusk;
the Dōngjǐng constellation (Dōngjǐng) is at eleven degrees,
it is central at dawn.
On the first day of mid-winter,
the sun rises at chén (辰) and sets at shēn (申).
The Kuí constellation (Kuíxīng) is at one degree,
it is central at dusk;
the Dǐ constellation (Dǐxīng) is at nine degrees,
it is central at dawn."
Mǎo (卯) and yǒu (酉) are where yin and yang converge;
the sun and moon reach this point as the middle path.
It is the place where all things flourish and decline, rise and set.
Therefore, it is called the "Gate of Two Eights,"
corresponding to the second and eighth months.
Hence, the Shī (詩) in "Tuīdùzāi" (推度災) says:
"The juncture of mǎo (卯) and yǒu (酉) is where governance changes."
The Hànshū Tiānwénzhì (漢書天文志) says:
"The sun is the image of the ruler.
If the ruler acts hastily, the sun moves quickly;
if the ruler acts slowly, the sun moves slowly.
If quickness or slowness deviates from its norm, there is an eclipse.
An eclipse is on the intersection path."
"An eclipse is the image of yin encroaching upon yang,
and a minister transgressing against the ruler."
Therefore, during a solar eclipse, one cultivates virtue to avert it.
Regarding the moon,
the Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo (春秋元命苞) says:
"The moon is yin essence (yīnjīng);
its name is 'què' (闕), meaning 'deficient'."
"Within it are a toad and a rabbit;
yin and yang reside together, mutually dependent.
They suppress and contract, combining with yang to form and govern."
"Its inner light is a torch;
its internal qi resembles markings."
"The rabbit is good at running, symbolizing the movement of yang."
The rabbit's sound is "xīhū" (僖呼);
"xīhū" is the name for warmth.
The moon is the essence of water.
Therefore, it is bright inside but cold in its qi.
"Yin is born incomplete" means
it is subdued by the ruler.
"It becomes full at the full moon" means
its qi and affairs align.
"It wanes after being full" means
it bows to the revered.
"Its qi is humble."
Humble, hence it forms the warp and weft.
Yin receives yang essence,
so its essence is within.
This is why metal and water are internal reflections.
Internal reflections, hence yin essence is submerged and does not move.
The moon is yin essence;
its body inherently has no light.
It relies on the sun's illumination to be bright,
just as a minister inherently has no authority,
but borrows the ruler's power
to establish his authority.
In the beginning of the month, the moon is not aligned directly opposite the sun.
Therefore, it is without light and crescent-shaped.
At mid-month, it is directly opposite the sun.
Therefore, its light is full.
After the sixteenth day, it gradually wanes,
also gradually no longer being opposite the sun.
The Hànshū Tiānwénzhì (漢書天文志) says:
"The moon travels thirteen and one-quarter degrees each day."
"At Lìchūn (立春) and Chūnfēn (春分),
it follows the Green Path from the east.
At Lìqiū (立秋) and Qiūfēn (秋分),
it follows the White Path from the west.
At Lìdōng (立冬) and Dōngzhì (冬至),
it follows the Black Path from the north.
At Lìxià (立夏) and Xiàzhì (夏至),
it follows the Red Path from the south.
In mid-summer, it travels the middle path."
"The red and green paths emerge from the yang path;
the white and black paths emerge from the yin path."
"When it is seen in the west during the dark of the moon,
it is called tiǎo (朓).
When it is seen in the east during the new moon,
it is called nuò (朒)."
"If the ruler is leisurely and relaxed,
the ministers are arrogant and complacent.
Therefore, the sun moves slowly,
and the moon moves quickly.
If the ruler is solemn and urgent, the ministers are fearful.
Therefore, the sun moves quickly,
and the moon moves slowly,
not daring to approach the ruler's position."
"If its movement, whether slow or fast,
deviates from its proper measure, there is also an eclipse."
"An eclipse occurs when there is a dark void
opposing the sun.
If the dark void opposes the moon,
there is a lunar eclipse; if it opposes a star,
the star disappears."
A lunar eclipse is yang encroaching upon yin.
Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒) says:
"It is the image of consorts, queens, high ministers, and feudal lords among humans.
The moon represents punishment."
Therefore, during a lunar eclipse, one reforms punishments to avert it.
Regarding the five planets,
the Shuōwén (說文) says:
"Stars are the essence of all things."
Or it says:
"The sun divided to become stars."
Therefore, its character (星) has "sun" (日) below "birth" (生).
The Shǐjì (史記) says:
"Stars are the scattered essence of metal.
Falling stars become stones."
This refers to metal.
The Chūnqiū (春秋) says:
"Stones fell in Sòng (宋),"
meaning falling stars.
It also says:
"Stars are yin essence."
Metal is also yin.
Speaking separately,
each corresponds to one of the five phases,
not solely governing metal.
Suìxīng (Jupiter) is the essence of wood.
Its position is in the East, presiding over spring.
It is the son of Cāngdì,
the image of the human sovereign,
the chief of the Five Planets,
the official overseeing agriculture,
and presides over blessings and good fortune.
It has six names:
The first is Shè tí;
the second is Chónghuá;
the third is Yìngxīng;
the fourth is Móxīng;
the fifth is Jìxīng;
and the sixth is Xiūrénxīng.
The states it presides over are Wú and Qí.
If it goes beyond its lodging and moves forward, it is called Yíng.
If it retreats from its lodging, it is called Suō.
If its movement is crooked, it indicates crookedness.
If its movement is straight, it indicates rectitude.
If governance is urgent, its movement is swift.
If governance is relaxed, its movement is slow.
If cruel, its movement is dark.
If harmonious, its movement is bright.
If its movement is bright, there is drought.
If its movement is dark, there is flooding.
If there is good governance, it follows its course.
If there is disorder, it moves in reverse.
Because it presides over the year,
it is named Suìxīng.
Yínghuò (Mars) is the essence of fire.
Its position is in the South, presiding over summer.
It is the son of Chìdì,
the image of the Regional Lord,
and the paramount of the Five Planets.
It receives commands from Tàiyī above,
and below oversees the human ruler,
meaning it governs the Son of Heaven.
It spies on those without the Way,
appearing and disappearing irregularly,
acting as Heaven's spy and observer.
Wherever it goes, it indicates war, rebellion, death, famine, and sickness.
It has two names:
The first is Fáxīng;
the second is Zhífǎ.
The states it presides over are Jīng and Yuè.
It is the male counterpart to Tàibái.
When it appears in the south, it is called Yínghuò.
When it stays in the west, it is called Tiānlǐ.
When it is in the east, it is called Xuánxī.
Because of its irregular appearance and disappearance,
it is named Yínghuò.
Zhènxīng (Saturn) is the essence of earth.
Its position is in the center, presiding over the four seasons.
It is the image of the female sovereign.
It presides over virtue and is the king of the Five Planets.
It has one name, Dìhóu.
It observes the rectitude or wickedness of the female sovereign.
If it enters the yang position, it signifies external affairs.
If it enters the yin position, it signifies internal affairs.
If all four other planets are amiss,
Zhènxīng then moves.
Because it remains stable in its lodging,
it is named Zhènxīng.
Tàibái (Venus) is the essence of metal.
Its position is in the West, presiding over the beginning of autumn.
It is the son of Báidì,
the image of the great general,
and presides over military misfortunes.
When the sun is in the south and Tàibái is in its south,
or when the sun is in the north and Tàibái is in its north, it is called Yíng.
When the sun is in the south and Tàibái is in its north,
or when the sun is in the north and Tàibái is in its south, it is called Suō.
If it should not appear in the east,
but appears in the east,
it is named Chónghuá.
If it should not descend in the east,
but descends in the east,
it is named Shàosuì.
If it should not appear in the west,
but appears in the west,
it is named Tàibái.
If it should not descend in the west,
but descends in the west,
it is named Báixiào.
It has six names:
The first is Tiānxīang;
the second is Tiānzhèng;
the third is Dàchén;
the fourth is Dàhào;
the fifth is Míngxīng;
and the sixth is Dà'āo.
The Shī says:
"In the east, it is called Qǐmíng.
In the west, it is called Chánggēng."
The states it presides over are Qín, Jìn, and Zhèng.
Tàibái is the male counterpart to Suìxīng.
Tàibái presides over military affairs.
Military affairs are associated with the West and the color white.
Therefore, it is called Tàibái.
Chénxīng (Mercury) is the essence of water.
Its position is in the North, presiding over winter.
It is the son of Hēidì,
the image of the chancellor, and presides over punishments.
If governance is cruel, it does not enter.
If governance is harmonious, it does not appear.
It has six names.
The first is Āndiào;
the second is Xìjí;
the third is Xióngxīng;
the fourth is Gōuxīng;
the fifth is Sìnóng;
and the sixth is Miǎnxīng.
The states it presides over are Zhào and Dài.
Chénxīng presides over virtue.
It is Heaven's enforcer of rectitude.
Its appearance and disappearance are regular.
Therefore, it is named Chénxīng.
The Xīngjīng says:
"To the northwest of Wǔchē,
the first star is called Tàibái.
Next to it, to the north, is a star called Chénxīng.
Next to it, to the northeast, is a star called Suìxīng.
Next to it, to the southeast, is a star called Zhènxīng.
Next to it, to the southwest, is a star called Yínghuò."
This is when the Five Planets divide their qi.
It also says:
"Suìxīng transforms into a comet, chán yún, qiāng yún, or tiāngǒu.
Yínghuò transforms into a comet, Chīyóuqí, or gézé.
Zhènxīng transforms into yùhàn, tiānfèi, xúnshǐ, or hóngní.
Tàibái transforms into a comet, jí sǎo.
Chénxīng transforms into kuángshǐ, tiānqiāng, or tiānpàng."
These are all the qi of the Five Planets,
seen as abnormal, ominous stars.
The ruler observes them
to understand gains and losses.
The Kǎolíngyào says:
"Suìxīng is the compass.
Yínghuò is the square.
Zhènxīng is the plumb line.
Tàibái is the balance arm.
Chénxīng is the balance weight."
The balance weight, balance arm, compass, square, and plumb line
all have their origins,
and complete a cycle to begin again.
Therefore, if governance fails in spring,
Suìxīng swells and lies flat,
not staying in its usual position.
If governance fails in summer,
Yínghuò moves in reverse.
If governance fails in late summer,
Zhènxīng deviates from its course.
If governance fails in autumn,
Tàibái deviates from its movement,
appearing and disappearing improperly.
If governance fails in winter,
Chénxīng does not manifest its direction.
If all five administrations fail,
the Five Planets are not bright.
If the spring administration does not fail,
the five grains multiply.
If the summer administration does not fail,
sweet rain comes in time.
If the late summer administration does not fail,
there are no disasters in due season.
If the autumn administration does not fail,
the people prosper.
If the winter administration does not fail,
there is little sickness and death.
If the five administrations do not fail,
the sun and moon are bright.
This means the sun, moon, and Five Planets
together form the Way of the Seven Regulators.
They are also named the Seven Luminaries.
Because they shine brightly and move.
The Běidǒu 斗 (Northern Dipper) serves as the Qīzhèng 七政 (Seven Regulators) because
the Běidǒu is the Tiānshū 天樞 (Heavenly Pivot).
Heaven has seven celestial courses,
and the Dipper has seven stars.
The first to fourth stars form the Kuí 魁 (Dipper Head),
the fifth to seventh stars form the Piáo 瓢 (Dipper Ladle),
making a total of seven.
The Shàngshū Wěi 尚書緯 says:
The Xuánjī 璇璣 (Revolving Jade) and Dǒukuí 斗魁 (Dipper Head) are four stars,
the Yùhéng 玉衡 (Jade Transverse) and Jūhéng 拘橫 (Restraining Transverse) are three stars,
totaling seven.
These regulate the four seasons and the Wǔwēi 五威 (Five Majesties).
The Wǔwēi are the Wǔxíng 五行 (Five Phases).
In humans, the Wǔwēi manifest as the five Fates,
and the seven stars manifest as the seven Germs of virtue.
The Běidǒu is located in the center of Heaven,
directly above Kūnlún 崑崙.
Its rotating pointer
corresponds to the twenty-four qi (solar terms),
governs the twelve chén 辰 (Earthly Branches),
and establishes the twelve months.
Furthermore, regarding the allocation of regions, states, years, and destinies,
there is nothing it does not govern.
Therefore, it is called the Qīzhèng.
The Yúlù 虞錄 says:
The Běidǒu's seven stars,
relying on the Xuánjī and Yùhéng,
regulate the Qīzhèng.
The 'zhèng' refers to the emperor's rule over the world.
Thus, a true king
receives Heaven's mandate to implement laws.
The Héchéngtú 合誠圖 says:
The Běidǒu has seven stars,
and the Son of Heaven has seven regulators.
The Dipper resides in the Yin and distributes the Yang,
hence it is called the Běidǒu.
Its seven stars each have four names.
The Héchéngtú says:
The first star of the Dipper is named Shū 樞,
the second Xuán 璇,
the third Jī 璣,
the fourth Quán 權,
the fifth Héng 衡,
the sixth Kāiyáng 開陽,
and the seventh Biāoguāng 標光.
The Huángdì Dǒutú 黃帝斗圖 says:
The first is named Tānláng 貪狼,
to which people born in the zǐ 子 hour belong.
The second is named Jùmén 巨門,
to which people born in the chǒu 丑 and hài 亥 hours belong.
The third is named Lùcún 祿存,
to which people born in the yín 寅 and xū 戌 hours belong.
The fourth is named Wénqǔ 文曲,
to which people born in the mǎo 卯 and yǒu 酉 hours belong.
The fifth is named Liánzhēn 廉貞,
to which people born in the chén 辰 and shēn 申 hours belong.
The sixth is named Wǔqǔ 武曲,
to which people born in the sì 巳 and wèi 未 hours belong.
The seventh is named Pòjūn 破軍,
to which people born in the wǔ 午 hour belong.
The Kǒngzǐ Yuánchén Jīng 孔子元辰經 says:
The first is named Yángmíng Xīng 陽明星,
the second Yīnjīng Xīng 陰精星,
the third Zhēnrén Xīng 真人星,
the fourth Xuánmíng Xīng 玄冥星,
the fifth Dānyuán Xīng 丹元星,
the sixth Běijí Xīng 北極星,
and the seventh Tiānkāi Xīng 天開星.
The Dùnjiǎ Jīng 遁甲經 says:
The first is named Kuízhēn Xīng 魁眞星,
the second Kuíyuán Xīng 魁元星,
the third Quánjiǔjí Xīng 權九極星,
the fourth Kuíxì Xīng 魁細星,
the fifth Bìgāng Xīng 魓剛星,
the sixth Yāojì Xīng 𩳐紀星,
and the seventh Piāoxuányáng Xīng 飄玄陽星.
The first star is Water,
the second Water and Earth,
the third Wood and Earth,
the fourth Metal and Wood,
the fifth Metal and Earth,
the sixth Fire and Earth,
and the seventh Fire.
The reason zǐ and wǔ each belong to only one star,
while the others are shared by two chén,
is that zǐ and wǔ are the meridians of Heaven and Earth.
The Dipper's first and seventh stars, Kuí and Gāng,
are also the meridians of the Dipper.
They are used for pointing and establishing.
The rest are not for pointing.
Therefore, they are each shared by two.
Thus, the sixty jiǎzǐ 甲子 start from the first star,
beginning with jiǎzǐ to match them,
and circulating back and forth
until their number is complete.
The Běidǒu leads the twenty-eight xiù 宿 (lunar mansions).
Each star presides over four seasons.
The Kuí begins with Shì 室,
the Gāng begins with Jiǎo 角,
and they are successively assigned.
If a person's annual cycle
reaches Shì and the five planets are moving,
and they arrive at this mansion,
then the fortune or misfortune follows that star.
The Héchéngtú says:
The Shū star is Yōngzhōu 雍州,
the Xuán star is Jìzhōu 冀州,
the Jī star is Qīngzhōu 靑州 and Yǎnzhōu 兗州.
The Quán star is Xúzhōu 徐州 and Yángzhōu 楊州,
the Héng star is Jīngzhōu 荆州,
the Kāiyáng star is Liángzhōu 梁州,
and the Biāoguāng star is Yùzhōu 豫州.
These represent the Way of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, Man).
All are governed by the Dipper.
The twenty-eight xiù are the Qīzhèng
because they delineate and establish countries and states,
and appoint officials and positions.
The Yùn Dǒushū 運斗樞 says:
Heaven has the positions of generals and ministers,
assisting the arrayed mansions as guards.
All rely on the Xuánjī and Yùhéng
to regulate the Qīzhèng.
The four seasons spread their virtue,
and the three Ways rectify qi.
The Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào 尚書考靈耀 says:
The twenty-eight xiù
circumnavigate Heaven, covering three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees.
Therefore, they harmonize with the seasons and months,
and rectify the degrees of the sun and stars.
The twenty-eight xiù are matched with the Wǔxíng
in two distinct ways.
First, the general matching;
second, the specific matching.
For the general matching:
The seven mansions of the Eastern Azure Dragon:
Jiǎo 角, Kàng 亢, Dī 氐, Fáng 房, Xīn 心, Wěi 尾, Jī 箕 are Wood.
They total thirty-two stars and seventy-five degrees.
The seven mansions of the Southern Vermilion Bird:
Dōngjǐng 東井, Yú 輿, Guǐ 鬼, Liǔ 柳, Qīxīng 七星, Zhāng 張, Yì 翼, Zhěn 軫 are Fire.
They total sixty-five stars and one hundred twelve degrees.
The seven mansions of the Western White Tiger:
Kuí 奎, Lóu 婁, Wèi 胃, Mǎo 昴, Bì 畢, Zī 觜, Cān 參 are Metal.
They total fifty-one stars and eighty degrees.
The seven mansions of the Northern Black Tortoise:
Dǒu 斗, Qiānniú 牽牛, Xūnǚ 須女, Xū 虛, Wēi 危, Yíngshì 營室, Dōngbì 東壁 are Water.
They total thirty-five stars and ninety-eight degrees.
Those belonging to Earth:
In the east are Jiǎo and Kàng;
in the south are Jǐng and Guǐ;
in the west are Kuí and Lóu;
in the north are Dǒu and Niú (Qiānniú).
All reside in the four seasons as Earth.
Zēngzǐ 曾子 said:
At the vernal equinox, the Bird Star (Zhāng 張) sets at dusk.
The one presiding over spring
indicates the opportune time for planting millet.
At the summer solstice, the Heart Star (Xīn 心) sets at dusk.
The one presiding over summer
indicates the opportune time for planting broomcorn millet and beans.
At the autumnal equinox, the Void Star (Xū 虛) sets at dusk.
The one presiding over autumn
indicates the opportune time for planting wheat.
At the winter solstice, the Pleiades (Mǎo 昴) set at dusk.
The one presiding over winter
indicates that people in the mountains can fell trees for tools.
Households can gather reeds and accumulate provisions for hunting.
The ruler, by observing the center of these four stars,
understands the urgency of the people.
If urgent, then corvée labor is not levied.
Therefore, it is said, "Respectfully grant the people their seasons."
This is the general matching.
Concerning the separate allocation to the Wǔxíng (Five Phases):
The two stars of Jiǎo (Horn) constitute the path of the three lights of the Tiānmén (Celestial Gate).
Twelve dù (degrees).
At this time, it is in Chén (Dragon),
and is allocated to Wood by Zhèng.
The four stars of Kàng (Neck) constitute the Tiāntíng (Celestial Court) and the Office of Shàngshū (Minister).
Nine dù.
At this time, it is in Chén,
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Zhèng,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The four stars of Dī (Root) constitute the Sùgōng (Lodging Palace), the place where the lùqǐn (road-bed) stops.
Fifteen dù.
At this time, it is in Mǎo (Rabbit),
and is allocated to Metal for spring and summer by Sòng,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The six stars of Fáng (Chamber) constitute the Míngtáng (Bright Hall) and the path of government and teaching.
Five dù. At this time, it is in Mǎo,
and is allocated to Earth by Sòng.
The three stars of Xīn (Heart) constitute the position of the Tiānwáng (Heavenly King).
Five dù.
At this time, it is in Mǎo,
and is allocated to Wood for spring and summer by Sòng,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The nine stars of Wěi (Tail) constitute the Hòugōng (Rear Palace) and the residence of concubines.
Eighteen dù.
At this time, it is in Yín (Tiger),
and is allocated to Water by Yān.
The four stars of Jī (Winnowing Basket) constitute the residence of the Wánghòu (Queen) and the sleeping chambers for imperial favors.
Eleven dù.
At this time, it is in Yín,
and is allocated to Wood by Yān.
For spring and summer, it is allocated to Metal,
and for autumn and winter, to Earth.
The six stars of Dǒu (Dipper) are in charge of juelù (titles and emoluments),
praising the virtuous and advancing scholars.
Twenty-six dù.
At this time, it is in Chǒu (Ox),
and is allocated to Wood by Wú.
The six stars of Qiānniú (Draught Ox) are in charge of bridges,
the beginning of the Qīzhèng (Seven Regulators).
Eight dù.
At this time, it is in Chǒu,
and is allocated to Wood by Wú.
The four stars of Xūnǚ (Weaving Girl) are in charge of cloth and silk,
the celestial inner storehouse.
Twelve dù.
At this time, it is in Zǐ (Rat),
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Yuè,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The two stars of Xū (Emptiness) constitute the Yàntáng (Banquet Hall), in charge of sacrificial rites.
Eleven dù.
At this time, it is in Zǐ,
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Qí,
and to Metal for autumn and winter.
The three stars of Wēi (Rooftop) constitute tombs,
to identify ancestors.
Seventeen dù.
At this time, it is in Zǐ,
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Qí,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The two stars of Yíngshì (Encampment) are in charge of military provisions,
to supply soldiers.
Sixteen dù.
At this time, it is in Hài (Pig),
and is allocated to Wood for spring and summer by Wèi,
and to Earth for autumn and winter.
The two stars of Dōngbì (East Wall) constitute the storehouse of literature and books.
Nine dù.
At this time, it is in Hài,
and is allocated to Metal for spring and summer by Wèi,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The sixteen stars of Kuí (Legs) constitute the arsenal of the Wǔbīng (Five Weapons),
to prohibit and suppress rebellion.
Sixteen dù.
At this time, it is in Xū (Dog),
and is allocated to Metal for spring and summer by Lǔ,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The three stars of Lóu (Bond) constitute the imperial parks and pastures,
in charge of providing for sacrifices.
Twelve dù.
At this time, it is in Xū,
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Lǔ,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The three stars of Wèi (Stomach) constitute granaries,
where the five grains are gathered.
Fourteen dù.
At this time, it is in Yǒu (Rooster),
and is allocated to Wood for spring and summer by Zhào,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The seven stars of Mǎo (Pleiades) are in charge of prison affairs,
presiding over trials and judgments.
Eleven dù.
At this time, it is in Yǒu,
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Zhào,
and to Metal for autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Bì (Net) constitute border troops to guard against barbarians.
Ten dù.
At this time, it is in Yǒu,
and is allocated to Metal for spring and summer by Zhào,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The three stars of Zǐyuàn (Beak and Turtle) constitute a treasury,
for collecting and inspecting autumn goods.
Two dù.
At this time, it is in Shēn (Monkey),
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Jìn,
and to Earth for autumn and winter.
The ten stars of Cānfá (Orion's Belt and Scabbard) constitute the celestial great general,
for reaping and harvesting.
Nine dù.
At this time, it is in Shēn,
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Jìn,
and to Earth for autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Dōngjǐng (East Well) are in charge of water management,
to ensure fairness according to law.
Thirty-three dù.
At this time, it is in Wèi (Goat),
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Qín,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The five stars of Yúguǐ (Wagon and Ghost) are for clear observation,
in charge of investigating treacherous schemes.
Four dù.
At this time, it is in Wèi,
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Qín,
and to Fire for autumn and winter.
The eight stars of Liǔ (Willow) constitute the imperial cuisine,
in charge of harmonizing flavors.
Fifteen dù.
At this time, it is in Wǔ (Horse),
and is allocated to Water for spring and summer by Zhōu,
and to Fire for autumn.
The seven stars of Xīng (Star) constitute clothing,
in charge of covering the body.
Seven dù.
At this time, it is in Wǔ,
and is allocated to Fire for spring and summer by Zhōu,
and to Water for autumn and winter.
The six stars of Zhāng (Extended Net) are in charge of guests,
granting gifts and entertainment.
Eighteen dù.
At this time, it is in Wǔ,
and is allocated to Water by Zhōu.
The twenty-two stars of Yì (Wings) constitute the celestial singer,
in charge of entertainment.
Eighteen dù.
At this time, it is in Sì (Snake),
and is allocated to Wood for spring and summer by Chǔ,
and to Metal for autumn and winter.
The four stars of Zhěn (Chariot) are for death and mourning, to know disaster and misfortune.
Seventeen dù.
At this time, it is in Sì,
and is allocated to Wood for spring and summer by Chǔ,
and to Earth for autumn and winter.
The "Tiānwénzhì" (Treatise on Astronomy) of the Hànshū (Book of Han) states:
Jiǎo, Kàng, Dī are the divisions of Hán, Zhèng, and Yǎnzhōu.
Fáng, Xīn are the divisions of Sòng and Yùzhōu.
Wěi, Jī are the divisions of Yān and Yōuzhōu.
Jǐng, Guǐ are the divisions of Qín and Yǒngzhōu.
Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng are the divisions of Sānhé.
Yì, Zhěn are the divisions of Chǔ and Jīngzhōu.
Kuí, Lóu, Wèi are the divisions of Lǔ and Xúzhōu.
Mǎo, Bì are the divisions of Zhào and Jìzhōu.
Zǐ, Cān are the divisions of Wèi and Liángzhōu.
Dǒu is the division of Jiānghú.
Qiānniú, Xūnǚ are the divisions of Wú and Yángzhōu.
Xū, Wēi are the divisions of Qí and Qīngzhōu.
Shì, Bì are the divisions of Wèi and Bìngzhōu.
All these are what the respective divisions govern,
to correct the good and evil of their states and kingdoms.
Thus, it is for governance.
The commentary on the Heavenly Offices by Shí Shì (石氏) states:
The two stars of Jiǎo (角) are the upper horns of the head of the Azure Dragon.
The path of Heaven lies between the two horns,
where the sun, moon, and five planets travel,
hence it is named Jiǎo.
Kàng (亢) represents the imperial court,
offering praise and advice to the king.
Day and night, it deliberates and consults on matters within the four seas,
hence it is named Kàng.
Dǐ (氐) is the chamber for official rest, where ice melts,
hence it is named Dǐ.
Fáng (房) is where the Son of Heaven resides during the four seasons,
hence it is named Fáng.
The one star in front of Xīn (心) is the Crown Prince,
the middle star is the Son of Heaven,
and the one star behind is the庶子 (shùzǐ, son of a concubine).
Just as the heart is central and the master of the body,
hence it is named Xīn.
Wěi (尾) is the tail of the Eastern Azure Dragon constellation,
hence it is named Wěi,
resembling its shape.
Jī (箕) is near Dǒu (斗),
resembling the winnowing and scattering of five grains,
hence it is named Jī.
Dǒu (斗) is a measuring vessel;
it measures and dispenses爵祿 (juélù, titles and emoluments).
Its shape resembles a Dǒu,
hence it is named Dǒu.
Niú (牛) also resembles ox horns,
being the beginning of the seven luminaries,
hence it is named Niú.
Nǚ (女) has the image of squareness and cutting,
resembling maids and concubines,
hence it is named Nǚ.
