Xū (虛) means deficiency.
The space within it resembles an empty temple hall,
hence it is named Xū.
Wēi (危) resembles a dwelling,
and also a tomb,
hence it is named Wēi.
Yíng Shì (營室) has six stars,
forming a detached palace,
resembling a palace or residence,
hence it is named Shì.
Bì (壁) stands upright like a wall.
Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) hid books in a wall,
following this meaning,
hence it is named Bì.
Kuí (奎) is the master of the arsenal, overseeing military affairs.
Its image is that of a secure and complete arsenal.
Hence Kuí means "different" or "contrary."
Military action is taken due to differences and defiance,
therefore it is named Kuí.
Lóu (婁) is like a pavilion,
also like a bell tower,
hence it fosters sacrificial animals,
and is named after this.
Wèi (胃) is the granary of the five grains within the storage.
It presides over granaries,
hence it is named after this.
Mǎo (昴) is clustered like prisoners in a jail,
hence it presides over prison affairs.
It is the Mǎo star,
and when clustered, there is worry,
hence it is named Mǎo.
Bì (畢) represents border barbarians and shaggy-haired peoples.
It is like the Son of Heaven giving an alarm: "Bì!" (Finish!)
The shaggy-haired ones respond.
It is finished.
The call is to alert the populace,
hence it is named after this.
Zī (觜) means "gathered."
It is the nose of the White Tiger.
It is gathered in the tiger's muzzle and whiskers,
hence it is named after this.
Cān (參) means "together."
It mixes the qi of metal and earth,
jointly carrying out killing and punishment,
hence it is named Cān.
Jǐng (井) means "purity."
It holds water, standing still.
Reaching the utmost subtlety,
this star symbolizes laws and standards,
like the flatness of water,
hence it is named Jǐng.
Guǐ (鬼) means "return."
Yang returns to Yin,
which is why one star within it is dim and unclear,
an image of ghosts,
hence it is named after this.
Liǔ (柳) means "to stay."
The Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn (春秋傳) states:
"Some eat at Rèn (任)."
Liǔ is also called Rèn.
It offers sacrifices to ghosts and spirits,
harmonizing the five flavors,
retaining divine spirits.
Hence it is named after this.
Qī Xīng (七星) refers to the number seven.
It is like a bird's covering plumage,
hence it is named after this.
Zhāng (張) means "to open" or "to spread."
It is the crop of the Vermilion Bird,
having capacity to contain,
hence it presides over guests.
Yì (翼) is like six feathers,
resembling a bird's two flying wings,
hence it is named Yì.
Zhěn (軫) resembles a small cart or a four-sided cart.
The rear crossbar is called Zhěn.
It is used for ominous events,
hence it is named after this.
Its concealment and appearance, rectitude and deviance, diminution and eclipse,
scattering into abnormal phenomena,
and flying comets and meteors—
all such events
are observed and interpreted according to their meanings.
Therefore, a detailed account is not provided.
The twenty-eight constellations and seven luminaries,
already associated with the Five Phases,
are briefly explained thus.
Regarding the Bā Guà (八卦):
The Zhōu Yì (周易) states:
"In ancient times, when Bāo Xī Shì (庖羲氏) ruled the world,
he looked up to observe the phenomena in the heavens,
and looked down to observe the patterns on the earth.
He observed the patterns of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land.
He drew close examples from his own person,
and distant examples from external objects.
Thereupon he first created the Bā Guà,
to comprehend the virtues of the divine and intelligent,
and to classify the dispositions of all things.
He combined the three powers and duplicated them.
Thus, six strokes form a guà."
Because the eight directions communicate with the eight winds,
the qi of the eight seasons is formed.
Therefore, there are eight *guà*.
As for their correspondence with the Five Phases:
Qián and Duì are Metal;
Kǎn is Water;
Zhèn and Xùn are Wood;
Lí is Fire;
Kūn and Gèn are Earth.
Each is spoken of in terms of its cardinal direction.
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* says:
Gèn in the northeast governs Lìchūn;
Zhèn in the east governs Chūnfēn;
Xùn in the southeast governs Lìxià;
Lí in the south governs Xiàzhì;
Kūn in the southwest governs Lìqiū;
Duì in the west governs Qiūfēn;
Qián in the northwest governs Lìdōng;
Kǎn in the north governs Dōngzhì.
Kǎn resides in the north because
on the day of Dōngzhì,
yang qi stirs beneath the Yellow Springs.
Although *zǐ* (子) is the position of great yin,
yang qi stirs beneath it.
Therefore, its *guà* is yin on the outside and yang on the inside,
symbolizing water, which is bright on the outside but harbors yang within.
Therefore, it occupies the *zǐ* position
and corresponds to Water.
Gèn is in the northeast because
its *guà* has one yang line at the top,
symbolizing the time of Lìchūn,
when yang qi has already risen
to the surface of the earth.
Below are heavy yin lines,
symbolizing that yin qi is still thick
and yang qi is still weak.
Since Gèn is Mountain,
its heavy yin lines at the bottom represent deep accumulated earth.
Therefore, the *guà* is also at *chǒu* (丑).
*Chǒu* (丑) is opposed to *wèi* (未),
and thus it corresponds to Earth.
Zhèn resides in the east because
Zhèn is the eldest son,
capable of taking on heavy responsibilities,
and therefore resides in a prominent and bright place.
The east is spring.
All things emerge and grow,
becoming clear and manifest.
Zhèn is Thunder;
when thunder moves, all things emerge.
At the time of Chūnfēn,
heavenly qi descends,
earthly qi ascends,
heaven and earth harmonize,
and all things sprout and stir.
Therefore, Zhèn resides at *mǎo* (卯).
*Mǎo* (卯) is the position of lesser yang wood;
thus it corresponds to Wood.
Xùn resides in the southeast because
its *guà* has heavy yang lines at the top,
symbolizing the time of Lìxià,
when yang qi is already strong at the top,
and yin qi is weak at the bottom.
As for wood,
it penetrates the earth the least
and emerges from the earth the most.
The Xùn *guà* has two yang lines at the top,
symbolizing the abundance of wood emerging from the earth.
One yin line resides at the bottom,
symbolizing the scarcity of wood penetrating the earth.
The body of wood is yang,
and it should also be manifest.
Therefore, it is in the southeast,
corresponding to Wood.
Lí resides in the south because
at the time of Xiàzhì,
yin stirs beneath the Yellow Springs.
*Wǔ* (午) is the position of flourishing yang,
yet yin qi stirs.
Therefore, its *guà* is yang on the outside and yin on the inside,
symbolizing fire, which is bright on the outside but dark within,
harboring yin qi.
Therefore, it is in the south,
corresponding to Fire.
Kūn resides in the southwest because
the Kūn *guà* is an image of pure yin,
and nothing nourishes all things
more than the earth.
The body of yin is humble and yielding,
not daring to take the lead.
Yin stirs at *wǔ* (午),
and only begins to manifest at *wèi* (未).
Therefore, Kūn follows the *wǔ* (午) position.
The earth's body is accumulated yin,
and Kūn, being pure yin, symbolizes the earth.
According to ritual, the central earth is at *wèi* (未),
and earth is soil.
Therefore, it is in the southwest,
corresponding to Earth.
Duì is in the west because
the Duì *guà* has one yin line at the top,
symbolizing the time of Qiūfēn,
when yang qi is already deep.
Metal is lesser yin,
thus one yin line resides at the top.
*Yǒu* (酉) is the position of Metal.
Therefore, it is in the west,
corresponding to Metal.
Qián resides in the northwest because
the Qián *guà* is an image of pure yang,
and nothing generates all things
more than Heaven.
Qián is the origin of all living things.
Yang qi arises at *zǐ* (子),
and Qián is the root of yang qi.
Therefore, it precedes the *zǐ* (子) position.
Being pure yang and firm and strong,
it is in the northwest,
corresponding to Metal.
The *Yì Zhuàn* says:
Zhèn governs Chūnfēn and Gǔyǔ.
If Gǔyǔ obtains the *qi* of Heavenly Duì,
then all things will fully grow.
Duì is the *guà* of the west.
At this time, the sun is in Mǎo,
and Mǎo is a western constellation.
Since the sun is in the west,
it is called Heavenly Duì.
If one's countenance is compliant with Wood's attainment,
then Heavenly Duì brings harmony.
If one's countenance is lost and Wood is rebellious,
then Heavenly Duì brings harm,
and constant rain is the punishment.
Duì governs Qiūfēn and Shuāngjiàng.
If Shuāngjiàng obtains the stirring *qi* of Heavenly Zhèn,
then frost covers the world,
and all things die.
Zhèn is the *guà* of the east;
at this time, the sun is in Fáng,
and Fáng is an eastern constellation.
Since the sun is in the east,
it is called Heavenly Zhèn.
If one's speech is compliant with Metal's attainment,
then Heavenly Zhèn brings harmony.
If one's speech is lost and Metal is rebellious,
then Heavenly Zhèn brings harm and drought is the punishment.
The reason why a lost countenance brings rain and lost speech brings drought is that
Zhèn is yang and Duì is yin;
yang brings drought and yin brings rain.
The reason why Wood brings rain and Metal brings drought is that
if human affairs involve a lost countenance,
then the common people resent, and yin qi flourishes,
hence rain.
If speech is lost, then the support of the multitude is lost;
solitary yang stands alone,
and the multitude of yin does not attach,
hence drought.
During the two seasons of spring and autumn,
Zhèn and Duì face each other,
and the qi of heaven and earth is harmonious,
which is why there is no extreme cold or heat.
Kǎn governs Dōngzhì and Dàhán.
If Dàhán obtains the *qi* of Heavenly Kǎn,
then there is great cold throughout the world.
At this time, the sun is in Xū,
and Xū is a northern constellation.
Therefore, it is called Heavenly Kǎn.
If one's listening is compliant with Water's attainment,
then Heavenly Kǎn brings harmony.
If one's listening is lost and Water is rebellious,
then Heavenly Kǎn brings punishment.
Therefore, it is constantly cold.
Lí governs Xiàzhì and Dàrè.
When Dàrè extends,
and again obtains the *qi* of Heavenly Lí,
then there is great heat throughout the world,
and all things fully emerge.
At this time, the sun is in the Seven Stars,
and the Seven Stars are the seven southern constellations.
Therefore, it is called Heavenly Lí.
If one's seeing is compliant with Fire's attainment,
then Heavenly Lí brings harmony.
If one's seeing is lost and Fire is rebellious,
then Heavenly Lí brings punishment,
and therefore it is constantly scorching hot.
During the two seasons of winter and summer,
the qi of heaven and earth combine,
and Kǎn and Lí each occupy their respective directions,
which is why there is extreme cold and heat.
Now, dividing the Bāguà,
to correspond with the cardinal directions:
Kǎn, Lí, Zhèn, Duì
are each in the celestial branch of their respective directions.
For the four corners and their four guà,
Chǒu and Yín belong to Gèn;
Chén and Sì belong to Xùn;
Wèi and Shēn belong to Kūn;
Xū and Hài belong to Qián.
The Bāguà are thus connected to the eight winds.
The eight directions regulate the qi of the eight seasons.
Thus, Kǎn generates the Guǎngmò Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Gèn generates the Tiáo Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Zhèn generates the Míngshù Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Xùn generates the Qīngmíng Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Lí generates the Jǐng Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Kūn generates the Liáng Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Duì generates the Chānghé Fēng,
which arrives in forty-five days.
Qián generates the Bùzhōu Fēng,
which arrives, after forty-five more days, back to Kǎn.
The yang qi is born from the five extremes and nine,
five times nine is forty-five.
Thus, it moves forty-five days to the left,
and then transforms.
The Guǎngmò Fēng
means vastness.
Mò means desert.
The cold qi is vast and far-reaching,
coming from the desert.
It is also said
that at this time the yang qi is below,
and the yin is vast.
The Tiáo Fēng
means flourishing.
At this time, it causes myriad things to grow.
The Míngshù Fēng
means multitude.
At this time, yang bestows its benevolent virtue,
and all things clearly emerge.
The Qīngmíng Fēng
means the weather is clear, bright, and cool.
At this time, a clear wind blows over myriad things,
making them lush, bright, and beautiful to behold.
The Jǐng Fēng
means Jǐng is high.
Myriad things reach their height at this point.
It also means
Jǐng is an end.
The way of yang reaches its conclusion here.
The Liáng Fēng
is the cool autumn wind.
At this time, the yin qi is desolate and cool,
harvesting myriad things.
The Chānghé Fēng
means flourishing.
At this time, myriad things flourish and are stored away.
The Bùzhōu Fēng
means pervasive.
Myriad things are fully mature.
Bùzhōu means closed and blocked.
It means that at this time, it is pure yin without yang,
closed off and impassable.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
The northeast direction is called Cāngmén,
generating the Tiáo Fēng.
The east direction is called Kāimíng Mén,
generating the Míngshù Fēng.
The southeast direction is called Yáng Mén,
generating the Qīngmíng Fēng.
The south direction is called Shǔ Mén,
generating the Jǐng Fēng.
The southwest direction is called Bái Mén,
generating the Liáng Fēng.
The west direction is called Chānghé Mén,
generating the Chānghé Fēng.
The northwest direction is called Yōudū Mén,
generating the Bùzhōu Fēng.
The north direction is called Hán Mén,
generating the Guǎngmò Fēng.
Cāngmén
is where wood in the northeast is about to take charge,
the beginning of spring,
thus it is called Cāngmén.
Kāimíng Mén
means bright yang.
Where the sun rises,
thus it is called Kāimíng Mén.
Yáng Mén
is where the lunar branch is Sì,
pure yang takes charge,
thus it is called Yáng Mén.
Jǐng Mén
is the time of flourishing and decline,
thus it is called Shǔ Mén.
Bái Mén
is where the lunar branch is Shēn,
the beginning of metal qi,
thus it is called Bái Mén.
Chānghé Mén
is where the eighth month's branch is Yǒu,
myriad things are about to be harvested.
Chāng means great, hé means closed,
the time of gathering and closing,
thus it is called Chānghé Mén.
Yōudū Mén
means dark and obscure.
Xuánmíng is about to take charge,
yin gathers and thus it is obscure,
thus it is called Yōudū Mén.
Hán Mén
is where accumulated cold resides,
thus it is called Hán Mén.
These are the directions of the eight extremes.
These are the places where the eight winds originate.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
The east wind is Tāofēng,
the southeast wind is Dòngfēng,
the south wind is Jùfēng,
the southwest wind is Qīfēng,
the west wind is Piāofēng,
the northwest wind is Lìfēng,
the north wind is Hánfēng,
the northeast wind is Yánfēng.
The meaning here is also the same as before.
Tài Gōng’s Bīngshū says:
Kǎn is called “Great Strong Wind,”
Qián is called “Breaking Wind,”
Duì is called “Small Strong Wind,”
Gèn is called “Inauspicious Wind,”
Kūn is called “Conspiracy Wind,”
Xùn is called “Small Weak Wind,”
Zhèn is called “Infant Wind,”
Lí is called “Great Weak Wind.”
“Great Strong Wind”
is the great Yīn energy, fond of killing,
hence strong.
“Breaking Wind”
is metal's strength, capable of destroying objects.
“Small Strong Wind”
is also due to metal's killing nature.
“Inauspicious Wind”
is Gèn, located at the "Ghost Gate,"
a place of harm and misfortune.
“Conspiracy Wind”
is Kūn, representing earth,
the root of great Yīn,
thus implying many Yīn conspiracies.
“Small Weak Wind”
is Xùn, representing the eldest daughter,
hence called weak.
“Infant Wind”
is Zhèn, representing the eldest son,
who is beloved.
Hence it is called an infant.
“Great Weak Wind”
is Lí, representing the middle daughter,
who is even weaker than the eldest daughter.
With Great Strong and Small Strong winds, the guest prevails;
with Great Weak and Small Weak winds, the host prevails.
Inauspicious implies matters of misfortune and harm;
Conspiracy implies people of sedition and treachery.
Breaking signifies impending death;
Infant Wind means the host is strong.
These are all ways for strategists to observe the rise and fall of guest and host,
and to determine the direction from which the wind comes.
Yángquán says:
In spring, the Qi is tender,
its wind is warm and harmonious;
it is a joyful wind.
In summer, the Qi is flourishing,
its wind is bright and upright;
it is a delightful wind.
In autumn, the Qi is vigorous,
its wind is fierce and clear;
it is an angry wind.
In winter, the Qi is cold,
its wind is congealed and harsh;
it is a sorrowful wind.
Furthermore, the winds of the four corners
follow the Qi of generation and growth,
with varying suitabilities in different regions,
each responding according to what it perceives.
However, wind is Heaven's command,
an omen of governance.
If a ruler possesses virtuous decrees,
then the wind does not shake the branches,
but is clear, harmonious, and smoothly flowing.
If decrees are errant,
then the Qi is angry and violent,
sending sand flying and breaking trees.
This is the principle of heavenly and earthly retribution.
These are all the Qi of the Five Phases,
hence all are explained here.
Zuǒzhuàn states that Zǐchǎn said:
“To emulate the brightness of Heaven,”
Heaven has three luminaries,
hence it is called brightness.
“To follow the nature of Earth,”
nature is generation.
It generates myriad things,
hence one follows what it generates and utilizes it.
It generates the six Qi,
and uses the five phases.
The Five Phases
are the five natures.
The Six Qi
pertain to the six emotions.
Yì Fèng says:
The Five Phases in humans are nature (xìng),
the Six Lǜ in humans are emotion (qíng).
Nature comprises benevolence (rén), righteousness (yì), propriety (lǐ), wisdom (zhì), and trustworthiness (xìn).
Emotion comprises joy (xǐ), anger (nù), sorrow (āi), delight (lè), liking (hǎo), and disliking (è).
The five natures reside internally, managing Yáng,
likened to gathering the five zàng organs.
The six emotions reside externally, managing Yīn,
likened to gathering the six tǐ forms.
Therefore, if emotion overcomes nature, there is chaos;
if nature overcomes emotion, there is order.
Nature originates internally;
emotion comes from external sources.
The interaction of emotion and nature
leaves no room for even a hair to pass.
Shuōwén says:
Emotion (qíng) is the Yīn Qi of a person,
having desires and cravings.
Nature (xìng) is the Yáng Qi of a person,
that which is good.
Xiàojīng Yuán Shénqì says:
Nature (xìng) is the essential quality of a person,
that which a person is endowed with and produced.
Emotion (qíng) is the number of Yīn,
transmitted internally and flowing,
connecting to the five zàng organs.
Therefore, nature is the root,
emotion is the branch.
Nature governs tranquility,
calmly maintaining the constant.
Emotion, however, governs activity,
changing upon encountering circumstances.
As activity and tranquility interact,
the space between them is subtle and dense.
Héshànggōng Zhāngjù says:
The ghost of the five natures
is called hún, which is masculine.
The ghost of the six emotions
is called pò, which is feminine.
This clarifies that nature is Yáng and emotion is Yīn.
The six emotions are connected to the six *qì*.
Now, first, according to the commentary of *Fú* on the *Zuǒzhuàn*, it says:
The six *qì* are
yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Yin becomes earth,
yang and wind become wood,
rain becomes metal,
darkness becomes water,
and light becomes fire.
Only the celestial yang remains unchanged.
As for yin becoming earth,
earth is the essence of yin.
Therefore, yin condenses to form the earth.
As for wind becoming wood,
wind is movement.
Wood also moves,
emerging from the earth.
The constellation *Jī* is a mansion in the east,
governing wind.
Furthermore, *Xùn* represents both wood and wind.
As for rain becoming metal,
rain is water.
The nature of water is to dissolve and release,
and the nature of metal can also dissolve and release.
The constellation *Bì* is a mansion in the west,
governing rain.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
“When the moon is in *Bì*,
the rain pours heavily.”
Thus, rain becomes metal.
As for darkness becoming water,
darkness means obscurity.
When it is obscure, water is generated.
Darkness is the color of water.
As for light becoming fire,
light illuminates things.
Therefore, it is fire.
All follow their respective categories.
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* says:
Wood is rain,
metal is yang,
fire is warmth,
earth is wind,
and water is cold.
*Zhèn* governs the vernal equinox;
at the vernal equinox, there is *gǔyǔ*,
and obtaining the celestial *Duì*,
all things are born.
*Duì* is a trigram of the west,
and at this time, the sun is in *Mǎo*.
*Mǎo* is a mansion of the west.
Since the sun is in the west,
it is called celestial *Duì*.
When the appearance accords with the virtue of wood,
then the celestial *Duì* is harmonious,
thus wood is rain.
The *Shī* says:
“Gently blowing valley winds,
with yin and with rain.”
As for metal being yang,
in autumn, the sun travels eastward,
in the mansion of *Fáng*.
It obtains the *qì* of celestial *Zhèn*.
It means that if one accords with the virtue of metal,
then celestial *Zhèn* is harmonious.
*Zhèn* is yang.
In autumn, things mature,
and thus things are roasted;
this is its harmony.
If one goes against the *qì* of metal, there will be punishment by drought,
thus metal is yang.
As for earth being wind,
the *zhuàn* says:
“If the thoughtful mind has failings,
its punishment is constant wind.”
It means that wind is the *qì* of earth.
*Zhuāngzǐ* says:
“The great clod exhales *qì*,
its name is wind.”
Earth is the ruler.
The ruler establishes teachings and commands,
therefore it is wind.
Earth establishes the four seasons.
Therefore, if commands fail, wind becomes a disaster.
Zhèng considers wood to be rain,
while Fú considers wood to be wind.
Fú considers metal to be rain,
while Zhèng considers metal to be yang.
Zhèng considers earth to be wind,
while Fú considers earth to be yin.
The two explanations are convoluted and contradictory,
each having its own meaning.
Now, if we distinguish them based on the Five Phases,
Fú’s view is closer.
The reason for this is that
water is born from metal,
and the body of metal is not yang.
Wood is minor yang,
and should not be rain.
Earth is the ground,
and the ground is inherently yin.
Wind is naturally the *qì* of yin and yang,
not solely born from earth.
Fú considers wood to be wind because
he takes *Xùn* as wood.
Therefore, it is appropriate.
As for the six *qì* connecting to the six emotions:
Fondness is yang,
aversion is yin,
anger is wind,
joy is rain,
sorrow is darkness,
and happiness is light.
As for fondness being yang,
yang *qì* loves to generate life,
hence it is fondness.
As for aversion being yin,
yin *qì* loves to kill,
hence it is aversion.
As for anger being wind,
*Yángquán* says:
“Wind is the breath of yin and yang in the pores,
stirred and rising,
like the internal *qì* of humans,
stirred and rising due to joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.”
Zēngzǐ says:
“Yin and yang become wind when angry.”
As for joy becoming rain,
Zēngzǐ says:
“Yin and yang become rain when harmonious.”
Harmony and moisture are therefore joy.
As for sorrow being darkness,
darkness means obscurity.
When one is worried, things are blocked,
hence dark.
Therefore, it is darkness.
As for happiness being light,
when happy, feelings are relaxed and expansive,
hence light.
The *Hànshū Lǐyuèzhì* says:
“Humans contain the yin and yang *qì* of heaven and earth,
and have the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.”
The *Lùnhéng* says:
“Among the five *zàng* organs of a person, the heart is the master.
The heart generates wisdom,
and the four *zàng* follow it.
The liver causes joy,
the lungs cause anger,
the kidneys cause sorrow,
and the spleen causes happiness.”
Therefore, the sages regulated them,
fearing they would harm one’s nature.
Yì Fèng says:
“Fondness is received by the bladder;
water prefers to advance,
hence it is called fondness.”
“Anger is received by the gallbladder;
minor yang begins to flourish,
and all things sprout forward.”
“Aversion is received by the small intestine.”
“Summer nourishes all things and dislikes falsity.
Hence it is called aversion.”
“Joy is received by the large intestine.”
“Metal is a valuable substance,
hence all rejoice.”
“Happiness is received by the stomach.”
“Earth nourishes all things,
and all above and below are happy.”
“Sorrow is received by the triple burner.”
“It is the palace of yin and yang;
when yang ascends and yin ends,
its palace is exhausted.
Hence it is called the triple burner,
hence there is sorrow and sadness.”
The *Lùnhéng* discusses the *zàng* based on the four seasons,
while Yì Fèng discusses the *fǔ* by connecting wind to the six emotions.
The spleen and kidneys are two types where
the *zàng* and *fǔ* are the same.
The liver and lungs are two *zàng* whose *fǔ* differ because
the *zàng* of the lungs has the nature of killing and punishing,
hence anger.
The *fǔ* is associated with the precious function of lung metal,
hence joy.
The liver, on the other hand, generates the *qì* of spring,
hence joy.
The gallbladder, on the other hand, is associated with fire’s ability to burn,
hence anger.
Both explanations are coherent.
It also says:
“Joy *qì* is warmth, corresponding to spring;
anger *qì* is clear weather, corresponding to autumn;
happiness *qì* is yang, corresponding to summer;
sorrow *qì* is yin, corresponding to winter.”
This aligns with the meaning of the *Lùnhéng*.
Yì Fèng 翼奉 said:
The nature of the East is benevolence, its emotion is anger;
the angry act of insidious malevolence governs it.
The nature of the South is propriety, its emotion is aversion;
the averse act of incorruptible integrity governs it.
The nature of the Below is trustworthiness, its emotion is sorrow;
the sorrowful act of impartiality governs it.
The nature of the West is righteousness, its emotion is joy;
the joyful act of magnanimity governs it.
The nature of the North is wisdom, its emotion is desire;
the desiring act of avarice governs it.
The nature of the Above is wickedness, its emotion is pleasure;
the pleasurable act of treachery and depravity governs it.
Avarice governs the seeking and demanding of wealth and goods.
Since it is called avarice,
it naturally involves seeking and needing.
Insidious malevolence governs robbery.
This too is beyond doubt.
Incorruptible integrity governs the promotion and summoning of high-ranking guests.
As Yín 寅 marks the beginning of yang,
and Wǔ 午 marks the height of yang,
they are therefore called high-ranking guests.
Possessing the nature of incorruptible integrity,
it naturally leads to being summoned and appointed to high positions.
Magnanimity governs banquets and celebrations of good fortune.
Magnanimity encompasses much,
hence there are good fortunes and celebrations.
Good fortunes and celebrations necessarily entail setting out food and drink.
Treachery and depravity govern illness and deceitful promiscuity.
Deceitful promiscuity arises from depravity and wickedness.
Depravity and wickedness necessarily cause illness.
Impartiality governs settling disputes and offering remonstrance against enemies.
Being upright, one can dispute;
being impartial, one can confront enemies.
As for desire:
water is born in Shēn 申 and flourishes in Zǐ 子.
The nature of water is to flow wherever it touches the ground,
and to moisten whatever it touches,
having many desires,
hence it is desire.
Having many desires
leads to insatiable greed.
Hence it is avarice.
Shēn 申 and Zǐ 子 govern it.
As for anger:
wood is born in Hài 亥 and flourishes in Mǎo 卯.
Its nature is born from receiving water energy,
and it penetrates the earth to emerge.
Hence it is anger.
Mǎo 卯 wood is born from Zǐ 子.
Water and Mǎo 卯 mutually punish each other,
and Hài 亥 also punishes itself.
Therefore, yin energy mutually injures,
hence it is insidious malevolence.
Hài 亥 and Mǎo 卯 govern it.
Avarice must attain insidious malevolence before it moves;
insidious malevolence must attain avarice before it can be used.
Two yins proceed together.
Therefore, a king
should avoid the days of Zǐ 子 and Mǎo 卯.
These are days of mutual punishment.
As for aversion:
fire is born in Yín 寅 and flourishes in Wǔ 午.
The nature of fire is fierce and violent,
allowing no compromise,
hence it is aversion.
Its energy is pure, clear, bright, and radiant,
ordering itself with propriety,
hence it is incorruptible integrity.
Yín 寅 and Wǔ 午 govern it.
As for joy:
metal is born in Sì 巳 and flourishes in Yǒu 酉.
Metal is a precious object,
seeing it brings joy,
and it is also joyful to apply sharp blades to all things,
hence it is joy.
Wherever a sharp blade is applied,
there is nothing that is not broadened.
As a vessel, it holds much.
Hence it is magnanimity.
Sì 巳 and Yǒu 酉 govern it.
Two yangs proceed together.
Therefore, a king finds good fortune on the days of Wǔ 午 and Yǒu 酉.
As for pleasure:
it refers to the North and the East,
where yang energy germinates.
Hence it is Above,
and also governs the center.
Chén 辰 is the end of water.
When wood falls, it returns to its root;
when water flows, it returns to its end.
Thus, wood's punishment is in Wèi 未,
and water's punishment is in Chén 辰.
Flourishing and decline each find their place,
hence there is pleasure.
When water reaches its end, it penetrates every crevice.
When wood emerges from its end upward,
it spreads sideways, becoming crooked,
hence it is treachery and depravity.
Chén 辰 and Wèi 未 govern it.
As for sorrow:
it refers to the South and the West,
where yin energy germinates,
hence it is Below.
Xū 戌 is the end of fire.
Chǒu 丑 is the end of metal.
Metal is hard and fire is strong;
each returns to its region.
Thus, fire's punishment is in Wǔ 午,
and metal's punishment is in Yǒu 酉.
The flourishing of metal and fire
are subject to self-punishment.
Reaching the end, with nowhere to return,
hence it is called sorrow.
The nature of fire is selfless;
the nature of metal is resolute,
hence it is called impartiality.
Xū 戌 and Chǒu 丑 govern it.
Therefore it is said,
the Five Natures reside in the root,
the Six Emotions reside in the branch.
Emotions arise from nature,
and nature is influenced by emotion.
Emotions and nature are interdependent.
Therefore, this complete explanation is provided.
As for governance:
To govern (治) means to bring order (治).
The establishment of order (治) is its name.
Government (政) means to be upright (正).
Not being perverse is its designation.
The common people cannot govern themselves.
A ruler is established to govern them.
The myriad people cannot rectify themselves,
so leaders are appointed to rectify them.
Rectification ensures no perversity,
governance ensures no disorder.
No disorder leads to peace,
no perversity leads to goodness.
If good, bandits will not arise;
if peaceful, each will preserve their livelihood.
Thus, one can overcome cruelty and eliminate killing.
People walk in orderly lines on the roads,
vipers and snakes can be stepped upon,
qilin and dragons can be driven.
This is what is called political governance.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"To govern by virtue
is like the North Star dwelling in its place,
while all the other stars pay homage to it."
Dà Dài Lǐ 大戴禮 says:
"The ruler is the root of governance;
without a ruler, how can there be governance?"
To be able to model oneself on the Five Phases
is called conforming to the Way.
Therefore, leniency and strictness are likened to water and fire;
benevolence and righteousness are taken from metal and wood.
Follow the four seasons to instruct the people,
and utilize the five materials for their use.
Employ people and employ strength,
and all principles return to a single standard.
The chapter “Zhìshùn Wǔxíng” of Chūnqiū Fánlù says:
When Wood is ascendant,
its qi is turbid
and green for seventy-two days.
When Fire is ascendant,
its qi is bright and yang
and red for seventy-two days.
When Earth is ascendant,
its qi is warm and turbid
and yellow for seventy-two days.
When Metal is ascendant,
its qi is firm and congealed
and white for seventy-two days.
When Water is ascendant,
its qi is clear and cold
and black for seventy-two days.
When Wood is again ascendant,
then one should practice gentleness and benevolence,
and promote scholars of classical arts.
Upon Lìchūn,
release those lightly imprisoned,
remove those detained,
break fetters,
open closed gates,
clear blockages,
care for the young and orphaned,
and pity widows and the solitary.
These are all in accordance with the spreading influence of spring.
Do not fell trees.
When kindness extends to plants and trees,
then vermillion grass will appear.
This is what poets sing of,
kindness extending to the "walking reeds."
Not felling trees
is so as not to go against the yang qi of heaven's growth.
If a ruler indulges in excessive pursuits,
is immersed in wine and unrestrained,
imposes heavy labor,
takes away people's time,
and collects heavy taxes,
then the people will suffer from rashes and dread,
have foot ailments,
and injure the spring qi.
Thus, these are all "Wood ailments."
When Wood is injured and destroyed,
then dragons hide deep,
and Wood-associated birds fear and do not appear.
Whales and large fish emerge and cause harm.
Scaly creatures have the qi of Metal,
which is why they harm Wood.
When Fire is ascendant,
then one should rectify boundaries
and cultivate fields.
Upon Lìxià,
appoint the worthy and good,
enfeoff the virtuous,
reward the meritorious,
and send envoys in all directions.
This is in accordance with Fire's transforming
and nurturing of all things.
Do not let fire run wild.
If fire follows human use,
sweet dew will descend,
phoenixes will come,
and yellow swans will be seen.
Phoenixes are a kind of Zhūquè,
and appear because they are pleased.
Sweet dew and yellow swans
are both omens of children celebrating their mother.
If a ruler uses sycophants,
separates kin,
alienates loyal ministers,
abandons laws,
and allows women to govern,
then the people will suffer from blood swellings,
the state will become unclear,
fire will become a disaster,
winter geese will not come,
and birds will become omens of ill.
Fire is not benevolent.
Thus, birds show changes and fear,
which is why they do not come.
When Earth is ascendant,
care for the elders,
pity widows and the solitary,
bestow gifts upon the filial and fraternal,
and spread benevolence and grace.
This is in accordance with Earth's virtue of generosity, harmony, and nurture.
Do not undertake earthworks.
If palace and dwelling regulations are kept in order,
and affection for relatives has its proper sequence,
then the five grains will ripen,
auspicious grains will emerge,
and worthy sages will come.
The Earth qi is harmonious,
so the auspicious grains are harmonious and ripened.
The virtue and splendor are great,
so worthy sages are pleased and come.
If a ruler indulges in excessive pleasures,
insults elders,
and oppresses the populace,
then the people will suffer from abdominal and heart diseases.
The heart and abdomen govern Earth,
and when the qi is not harmonious, they fall ill.
Worthy people will hide,
the hundred grains will not grow,
and naked worms will cause disaster.
The nature of Earth is injured,
so crops do not succeed,
and worthy people abhor this,
which is why they do not appear.
Naked worms are of Earth qi.
When injured, they cause transformations.
When Metal is ascendant,
repair city walls,
mend ramparts,
carefully review prohibitions,
adorn weapons,
warn officials,
and punish the lawless.
These are all in accordance with Metal,
with its qi of majestic severity and killing.
Do not burn metal or stone.
If this is followed, the Bái Hǔ will appear.
The tiger is a Metal beast,
and appears because it is pleased.
If a ruler is greedy for bribes
and fond of war,
then the people will suffer from coughing, muscle spasms, and nasal obstruction.
The nose governs the lungs,
and when the lungs are diseased,
therefore there is coughing and nasal obstruction.
These are all Metal-induced ailments.
Hairy creatures, metal, and stone will become omens of ill.
The Metal qi is injured,
so it causes transformations and omens of ill.
When Water is ascendant,
close village gates,
apprehend criminals,
and repair bridges.
These are all in accordance with Water,
and the principle of sealing and storing.
Do not breach ponds or dams,
for fear that the Water qi will leak and overflow.
If this is followed, sweet springs will emerge,
and kindness will extend to birds and insects,
then spiritual turtles will appear.
The Shū Jīng says,
"Kindness extends to insects."
Armored creatures belong to Water,
and appear because they are pleased.
If a ruler neglects sacrifices,
treats ancestral temples lightly,
does not enforce laws properly,
and goes against the qi of heaven,
then the people will suffer from edema, dropsy, and atrophy,
and their orifices will be obstructed.
These are all manifestations of the Water qi being stagnant and blocked.
The sages place Water in the position of Tàiyīn.
Tàiyīn is dark and empty,
compared to ancestral temples,
where the refined qi of deceased persons disperses,
and ancestral temples are established to collect it.
The halls are empty and silent,
dark and uninhabited.
This is likened to Water.
Neglecting sacrifices
goes against the way of filial piety.
Thus, the qi of Tàiyīn
is affected and causes illness in people,
leading to these ailments.
Water causes disasters,
spiritual turtles hide deep,
ghosts cry, and armored insects become omens of ill.
Armored insects belong to Water,
and when their qi is injured,
they hide and do not appear.
When ancestral temples are not offered sacrifices,
the souls and qi are harmed and resentful.
Thus, ghosts cry.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì (Classic of Filial Piety, Assisting the Spirits and Responding to the Numinous) says:
The qi of wood produces wind;
the qi of fire produces locusts;
the qi of earth produces insects;
the qi of metal produces frost;
the qi of water produces hail.
If governance is amiss in relation to wood,
then wind comes in response.
If governance is amiss in relation to fire,
then locusts come in response.
If governance is amiss in relation to earth,
then insects come in response.
If governance is amiss in relation to metal,
then frost comes in response.
If governance is amiss in relation to water,
then hail comes in response.
Injury leads to wind;
invasion leads to locusts;
greed and cruelty lead to insects;
harshness and toxicity lead to frost;
tyranny leads to hail.
All these arise according to their respective categories.
Huánzǐ Xīnlùn (New Discourses of Master Huan) says:
Man embodies the form of Heaven and Earth,
harboring the pure and essential qi,
the most numinous of all living beings.
Therefore, the countenance moves according to wood;
words are trustworthy according to metal;
sight is clear according to fire;
hearing is acute according to water;
thought is sagacious according to earth.
The functions of the Five Phases,
both active and still, correspond with the spirits.
If the countenance is reverent, there is solemnity;
when solemn, timely rain is abundant.
If words are compliant, there is order;
when ordered, timely sunshine is abundant.
If sight is clear, there is wisdom;
when wise, timely warmth is abundant.
If hearing is acute, there is planning;
when planning, timely cold is abundant.
If the heart is severe, there is sagacity;
when sagacious, timely wind is abundant.
Metal, wood, water, and fire are all borne by earth.
Rain, sunshine, warmth, and cold
all originate from wind.
Countenance, speech, sight, and hearing
all arise from the heart.
Shīzǐ (Master Shi) says:
The heart is the ruler of the body.
The Son of Heaven receives orders for All Under Heaven from his heart;
if the heart is not upright, All Under Heaven suffers calamity.
The feudal lords receive orders for their states from their hearts;
if the heart is not upright, the state perishes.
An ordinary man receives orders for his body from his heart;
if the heart is not upright, the body is destroyed.
Therefore, the human heart
is the essence of Heaven and Earth,
the root of all life.
Thus, the order or chaos of government
depends on the ruler's heart.
Therefore, when the sage receives the mandate to rule,
they invariably uphold Heaven and Earth,
model themselves on the Five Phases,
cultivate the Five Affairs,
and govern the universe,
nurturing the common people.
Their institutions and regulations
are all based on the Five Phases.
Carriages, clothing, awe-inspiring demeanor,
courtly bowing and rising,
farming and sericulture, sowing and planting,
bestowing favors and celebrating gifts—these are wood.
Distinction between noble and humble, superior and inferior,
institutions and rituals,
conferring titles and rewarding merit,
residing in high places and seeing far—these are fire.
Palaces and pavilions,
husband and wife, relatives,
spreading virtue and nurturing,
granting emoluments, pardons, and amnesties—these are earth.
Military weapons and implements,
hunting and martial preparations,
punishments and imprisonments—these are metal.
Ancestral temples and sacrifices,
storing and hoarding,
mourning rites and observances,
divination by tortoise shell and milfoil to resolve doubts—these are water.
Through the Five Phases, all officials are appointed;
through all officials, myriad affairs are governed.
When myriad affairs are governed, the four seas are at peace;
this is the origin of political order.
Their dwellings, clothing, and conveyances,
and the use of their implements,
are all rooted in the Five Phases,
thus achieving the Way of governance.
The Lǐjì (Book of Rites) says:
In the months of spring,
the Son of Heaven resides in the Left Chamber of Qīngyáng,
rides a luán chariot,
drives azure dragons,
carries azure banners,
wears azure robes,
and adorns himself with azure jade.
In the months of summer,
he resides in the Left Chamber of the Míngtáng,
rides a vermilion chariot,
drives red horses,
carries red banners,
wears vermilion robes,
and adorns himself with red jade.
For central earth, he resides in the Grand Temple's Grand Chamber,
rides a grand chariot,
drives yellow horses,
carries yellow banners,
wears yellow robes,
and adorns himself with yellow jade.
In the months of autumn,
he resides in the Left Chamber of Zǒngzhāng,
rides a military chariot,
drives white chariots,
carries white banners,
wears white robes,
and adorns himself with white jade.
In the months of winter,
he resides in the Left Chamber of Xuántáng,
rides a dark chariot,
drives iron-black horses,
carries dark banners,
wears dark robes,
and adorns himself with dark jade.
The Kǎolíngyào (Profound Brilliance of Examining Spirits) says:
In spring, issue commands from outside,
practice benevolent governance,
follow the constant principles of Heaven;
at this time, wear azure.
In summer, one may destroy pure copper and melt it,
make preparations for fire,
respect the brightness of Heaven;
at this time, wear red.
For central earth,
elevate virtuous people,
and consult with them on state affairs;
one may execute criminals,
but should not undertake earthworks,
violating the constant principles of earth;
at this time, wear yellow.
In autumn, do not destroy gold or copper,
violating the hardness of yin;
at this time, hold weapons,
it is appropriate to kill fierce beasts;
at this time, wear white.
In winter, do not allow things to remain unhidden,
do not obstruct waterways,
and preserve harmony with the qi;
at this time, wear black.
The Jiāyǔ says:
In the first month of Mèngchūn,
the Eastern Palace wears blue-green silks,
plays the qín and sè,
its weapon is the spear,
and its tree is the willow.
In the second month of Zhòngchūn,
the Eastern Palace wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the apricot.
In the third month of Jìchūn,
the Eastern Palace wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the plum.
In the fourth month of Mèngxià,
the Southern Palace wears red silks,
plays the shēng and yú,
its tree is the peach,
and its weapon is the halberd.
In the fifth month of Zhòngxià,
the Southern Palace wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the elm.
In the sixth month of Jìxià,
the Central Palace wears yellow silks,
beats the great drum,
its tree is the catalpa,
and its weapon is the bow.
In the seventh month of Mèngqiū,
the Western Palace wears white silks,
strikes the great bell,
its tree is the neem,
and its weapon is the sword.
In the eighth month of Zhòngqiū,
it wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the silkworm thorn.
In the ninth month of Jìqiū,
it wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the scholar tree.
In the tenth month of Mèngdōng,
the Northern Palace wears black silks,
strikes the qìng,
its tree is the sandalwood,
and its weapon is the shield.
In the eleventh month of Zhòngdōng,
the Northern Palace wears the same attire, plays the same music, uses the same weapons as before,
and its tree is the oak.
This discusses the seasonal regulations,
to await the suitability of succeeding and storing.
The Zhōuguān says:
For spring, the array is a 'Du' formation,
with bows at the front.
For summer, the array is a square formation,
with halberds at the front.
In the sixth month, the array is a circular formation,
with spears at the front.
For autumn, the array is a 'Pìn' formation,
with swords at the front.
For winter, the array is a 'Fú' formation,
with shields at the front.
These military preparations also follow the five phases.
The Lùtú says:
When a ruler reigns by Wood,
people are blue-green in color,
have long necks and beautiful hair.
Its people have tall bodies and broad shoulders,
and value benevolence.
Tallness
all symbolizes Wood.
Benevolence is the nature of Wood.
If virtuous, seasonal grasses will be lush,
auspicious grains will grow abundantly,
birds will not suffer miscarriage or injury,
as the qi of Wood is strong.
If lacking virtue, the constellations will be extinguished,
colors will be chaotic,
grains will not ripen,
and many people will die from crushing.
Wood grows and emerges upwards;
if it encounters harm from Earth,
it turns blue-green and cannot rise,
hence death by crushing.
When reigning by Fire,
people are red in color,
with large eyes.
Lí represents the eye,
hence great vision and brightness.
Its people have pointed heads and long waists,
are quick and agile, and value filial piety.
The long waist is taken from Duì,
and agility is the nature of Fire.
Lí represents the sun,
and the sun has a crow;
the crow symbolizes filial piety.
If virtuous, worthy people are employed,
government praises are just,
and dappled horses and patterned foxes arrive.
Horses are Fire animals;
they come because of virtue.
Foxes are also similar.
If lacking virtue, there will be summer frost.
The sun is the essence of Fire;
if virtue is lacking, it changes, eclipses, rains soil,
suddenly obscuring the symbol of brightness.
When reigning by Earth,
it features a prominent head;
a large head signifies Earth.
Its people have broad shoulders and large feet.
They enjoy hearty laughter, games, and dancing.
Broadness and largeness symbolize Earth,
and harmony thus brings joy.
If virtuous, sweet dew descends,
and sweet springs respond to its virtue.
If lacking virtue, insect plagues arise,
the heavens rain, and strong winds and mists are chaotic.
All this indicates harm to the qi of Earth,
hence the unusual manifestations.
When reigning by Metal,
people are white in color,
with broad shoulders, square ears, and hairy faces.
Its people have white necks and are tall and large,
valuing righteousness.
All are characteristics of the qi of Metal.
If virtuous, large cowrie shells and bright pearls appear,
and foreign nations present distant tributes of pearls and shells.
The qi of Metal is strong in its function,
able to control distant peoples,
hence they come to offer tribute.
If lacking virtue, fire flies,
the sky roars, the earth splits,
rivers overflow, mountains collapse,
wicked people advance,
and insects and beasts cause disaster.
Fire can overcome Metal;
if Metal suffers a loss,
then Fire attacks it and it flies.
When reigning by Water,
people are black in color,
with large ears.
Kǎn represents the ear and governs the kidneys;
the qi of Water is thus great.
Its people have sharp hearing,
which is Kǎn water.
Passage through openings makes one keen of hearing.
If virtuous, auspicious clouds arrive,
and turtles and dragons appear with patterns;
all are auspicious signs of Water qi.
If lacking virtue, toads leave the moon,
many people drown,
and constant rain causes harm.
These are all troubles of Water.
These all clearly explain the way of governance,
which does not go beyond the Five Phases.
Therefore, this complete explanation is provided.
Composed by Xiāo Jí, Yítóng Sānsī and Kāiguó Gōng of Chéngyáng Jùn.
As for the various spirits (shén),
their spiritual wisdom is boundless,
and their hidden or manifest forms are unfathomable.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The essence-qi of yang becomes shén.”
He also said:
“That which is unfathomable by yin and yang is called shén.”
One interpretation says:
“Shén is shēn (伸, to stretch).”
All myriad things have substance,
they are obstructed and bent, and cannot stretch out.
Shén is the qi of purity and emptiness,
unobstructed by anything,
hence it is called shēn.
Speaking of its shén,
it has myriad names,
the way of the Three Powers,
and the hundred spirits are not one.
All follow the Five Phases,
difficult to fully enumerate.
Now we will discuss what aligns with the Five Phases.
To discern good and ill fortune:
The Dìxìpǔ (帝系譜) says:
When heaven and earth first began,
the Tiānhuáng (天皇) was born.
He ruled by the virtue of wood.
The Sānwǔ Lìjì (三五曆紀) says:
The Tiānhuáng had thirteen heads.
The Dìxìpǔ says:
The Dìhuáng (地皇) ruled by the virtue of fire.
The Sānwǔ Lì (三五曆) says:
There was a divine being
with eleven heads,
named Dìhuáng.
The Chūnqiū Mìnglì Xù (春秋命曆序) says:
The Rénhuáng (人皇) had nine heads.
Sòng Jūn (宋均) notes:
Nine brothers.
The Dòngjì (洞紀) says:
The Rénhuáng divided and governed the Nine Provinces.
Ancient language was plain,
hence it spoke of "heads."
Táo Huáyáng (陶華陽) says:
These three Sovereigns ruled the Zǐwēi Gōng (紫微宮),
their essence becoming Tiānhuáng Tàidì (天皇太帝).
The Shìjì (世紀) says:
Tiānhuáng Tàidì is Yàopòbǎo (曜魄寶);
Dìhuáng is Tiānyī (天一);
Rénhuáng is Tàiyī (太一).
Gān Gōng Xīngjīng (甘公星經) says:
Tiānhuáng Tàidì
originally held the chart of myriad deities.
One star is in the center of Gōuchén (勾陳),
named Yàopòbǎo.
He is the venerable ancestor of the Wǔdì (五帝).
Tiānyī and Tàiyī mainly serve the spirits.
To serve is like attending.
There are two stars,
outside the gates of the Zǐwēi Gōng,
both attending Tiānhuáng Tàidì.
Tiānyī presides over battles
and knows good and ill fortune.
On jiǎ (甲), wù (戊), gēng (庚), and rén (壬) days,
he rules the Yùtáng Gōng (玉堂宮).
On yǐ (乙), jǐ (己), and xīn (辛) days,
he rules the Míngtáng Gōng (明堂宮).
On bǐng (丙), dīng (丁), and guǐ (癸) days,
he rules the Jiàng Gōng (絳宮).
These are the three palace great spirits.
Tàiyī presides over wind, rain, drought, war, famine, epidemics, and disasters,
and further dispatches sixteen deities to roam the Nine Palaces.
Tiānyī nourishes all things,
while Tàiyī observes disasters.
These are the ministers of the Tiāndì (天帝).
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) notes in the Gān Záodù (乾鑿度) that:
Tàiyī is
the name of the god of the Northern Dipper.
When at its dwelling, it is called Tàidì;
when moving between the eight trigrams and day-branches,
it is called Tàiyī,
or sometimes Tiānyī.
Its coming and going
rests outside the Zǐ Gōng (紫宮).
Its star is thus named after it.
The movement of Tiānyī
is like the Son of Heaven inspecting the four directions and mountains;
the human ruler also follows and inspects,
and returns after each circuit.
Tàiyī moves through the palaces of the eight trigrams,
and in each of the four seasons,
it enters the center.
The great division of celestial numbers is that yang emerges,
and yin enters.
Yang rises at zǐ (子),
yin rises at wǔ (午).
Therefore, Tàiyī descends through the Nine Palaces,
starting from kǎn (坎).
The Jiǔgōngjīng (九宮經) says:
The movement of Tiānyī
starts from Lígōng (離宮);
the movement of Tàiyī
starts from Kǎngōng (坎宮).
Tiānyī presides over abundant harvests,
Tàiyī presides over floods, droughts, war, and famine.
Combined, the twelve deities
roam the Nine Palaces.
The twelve positions are from lesser to greater.
The Liùrén Shìjīng (六壬拭經) says:
Among the twelve divine generals,
Tiānyī is the principal.
On jiǎ (甲), wù (戊), and gēng (庚) days,
in the morning it rules Dàjí (大吉),
in the evening it rules Xiǎojí (小吉).
On yǐ (乙) and jǐ (己) days,
in the morning it rules Shénhòu (神后),
in the evening it rules Chuánsòng (傳送).
On bǐng (丙) and dīng (丁) days,
in the morning it rules Wēimíng (微明),
in the evening it rules Cóngkuí (從魁).
On xīn (辛) days,
in the morning it rules Shèngxiān (勝先),
in the evening it rules Gōngcáo (功曹).
On rén (壬) and guǐ (癸) days,
in the morning it rules Tàiyī,
in the evening it rules Tàichōng (太衝).
These are all outside the gates of the Zǐwēi Gōng.
Tiānyī and Tàiyī
are not within Zǐwēi.
The name of the Northern Dipper is Tàidì.
Zhèng Xuán was mistaken.
The sixteen deities of Tàiyī are:
Dìzhǔ (地主) is in zǐ (子).
Yang energy stirs in the Yellow Springs,
all things are born from the earth.
Zǐ is the head of yang energy,
hence it is called Dìzhǔ.
Yángdé (陽德) is in chǒu (丑).
Yang can give birth to all things.
It begins to be born at chǒu,
hence it is called Yángdé.
Hédé (和德) is in the northeast corner.
At this time, yin and yang energies merge,
giving birth to all things,
hence it is called Hédé.
Lǚshēn (呂申) is in yín (寅).
Lǚ means "great."
Shēn means "to extend."
All things gradually extend and grow great,
hence it is called Lǚshēn.
Gāocóng (高藂) is in mǎo (卯).
All things gather and grow tall and great,
hence it is called Gāocóng.
Tàiyáng (太陽) is in chén (辰).
After the stirring of zhèn (震),
yang energy greatly flourishes,
hence it is called Tàiyáng.
Dàhào (大昊) is in the southeast corner.
At this time, yang is already manifest,
illuminating broadly,
hence it is called Dàhào.
Dàshén (大神) is in sì (巳).
All things have ripened,
their qi rises,
hence it is called Dàshén.
Dàwēi (大威) is in wǔ (午).
Yang declines, yin arises.
Form and qi begin to move,
hence it is called Dàwēi.
Tiāndào (天道) is in wèi (未).
All things are complete,
none are without use,
hence it is called Tiāndào.
Dàwǔ (大武) is in the southwest corner.
Yin energy is in charge,
all things are harmed,
hence it is called Dàwǔ.
Wǔdé (武德) is in shēn (申).
Chives and wheat are beginning to grow,
yin contains yang nature,
hence it is called Wǔdé.
Dàzú (大族) is in yǒu (酉).
Yin energy brings great destruction,
all categories of things perish,
hence it is called Dàzú.
Yīnzhǔ (陰主) is in xū (戌).
Yang energy hides below,
yin energy is self-existent above,
hence it is called Yīnzhǔ.
Yīndé (陰德) is in the northwest corner.
Qián (乾) is Heaven.
Yin energy reaches its extreme here,
only then can it give birth to yang,
hence it is called Yīndé.
Dàyì (大義) is in hài (亥).
All things are conceived here.
Yin energy contains yang,
hence it is called Dàyì.
Furthermore, concerning the nine palaces and twelve *shén* (deities):
*Tiānyī* is in the *Lí* palace;
*Tàiyī* is in the *Kǎn* palace;
*Tiānfú* is in the central palace;
*Shètí* is in the *Kūn* palace;
*Xuānyuán* is in the *Zhèn* palace;
*Zhāoyáo* is in the *Xùn* palace;
*Qīnglóng* is in the *Qián* palace;
*Xiánchí* is in the *Duì* palace;
*Tàiyīn* is in the *Gèn* palace.
*Tàiyī* has already been explained above.
The remaining seven *shén*
are all names of stellar palaces.
Along with *Tiānyī* and *Tàiyī*,
they move through the nine palaces,
shifting once each year,
returning to their original position after nine years.
*Tiānyī* governs abundance;
*Tàiyī* governs water and cold;
*Tiānfú* governs famine;
*Shètí* governs illness and suffering;
*Xuānyuán* governs thunder and rain;
*Zhāoyáo* governs wind and clouds;
*Qīnglóng* governs frost and hail;
*Xiánchí* governs soldiers and bandits;
*Tàiyīn* governs conspiracies.
There is also a separate *Qīnglóng*
that travels through the twelve earthly branches (*shí'èrzhēn*).
This is the name for *Tàisuì*.
In ancient times, the year was named *Qīnglóng*.
This *shén* governs blessings and good fortune.
*Tàiyīn* moves once every three years,
traveling clockwise through the twelve earthly branches.
This is the *yīn shén* of *Tàisuì*.
It symbolizes empresses and consorts,
governing water, rain, and private matters.
The malevolent *qì* travels clockwise through the four *mèng* (first months of the seasons),
shifting once each year.
Because it brings harm wherever it arrives,
it is called "malevolent *qì*."
Together, these form the twelve *shén*,
which are used in the nine palaces.
Furthermore, *Xuánnǚ Shìjīng* states:
The twelve *shén* used in *Liùrén* are:
*Shénhòu* governs *zǐ* (Water *shén*);
*Dàjí* governs *chǒu* (Earth *shén*);
*Gōngcáo* governs *yín* (Wood *shén*);
*Tàichōng* governs *mǎo* (Wood *shén*);
*Tiāngāng* governs *chén* (Earth *shén*);
*Tàiyī* governs *sì* (Fire *shén*);
*Shèngxiān* governs *wǔ* (Fire *shén*);
*Xiǎojí* governs *wèi* (Earth *shén*);
*Chuánsòng* governs *shēn* (Metal *shén*);
*Cóngkuí* governs *yǒu* (Metal *shén*);
*Hékuí* governs *xū* (Earth *shén*);
*Wēimíng* governs *hài* (Water *shén*).
Concerning *Zǐ Shénhòu*:
*Zǐ* is *huángzhōng*,
the Way of the sovereign.
Therefore, it is called *hòu* (queen),
the beginning of *yáng*.
*Yáng* moves internally but has not yet taken shape,
hence it is called *shén*.
Concerning *Chǒu Dàjí*:
When all things reach *chǒu*,
they all sprout and receive *yáng* to be born,
hence it is *Dàjí* (great auspiciousness).
Concerning *Yín Gōngcáo*:
When all things reach *yín*,
their merit is already manifest.
*Cáo* means multitude.
The merit of all things is already manifest in *yín*.
Concerning *Mǎo Tàichōng*:
When all things reach *mǎo*,
they all *tàichōng* their core and the outer skin extracts the calyx.
Concerning *Chén Tiāngāng*:
It is situated at the handle of the Dipper star,
and its *shén* is strong and firm.
Concerning *Sì Tàiyī*:
Pure *qián* is at work,
and *tiāndé* (heavenly virtue) resides there,
hence it is *Tàiyī Shénhòu*.
Concerning *Wǔ Shèngxiān*:
The *yáng qì* is greatly powerful,
and *yīn qì* moves at this time.
Only *yáng* being first is victorious.
Concerning *Wèi Xiǎojí*:
All things are fully ripe and complete,
hence it is *Xiǎojí* (small auspiciousness).
Concerning *Shēn Chuánsòng*:
It transmits the completed things
and sends them for winter storage.
Concerning *Yǒu Cóngkuí*:
It follows the second star of the Dipper's *kuí* (bowl).
Concerning *Xū Hékuí*:
*Hé* means head.
It is at the head of the Dipper's *kuí*.
Concerning *Hài Wēimíng*:
The water body is bright within,
but not visible externally.
Its *yáng qì* is subtle until *zǐ* square becomes bright.
*Shénhòu* governs women;
*Dàjí* governs fields and agriculture;
*Gōngcáo* governs relocation of states;
*Tàichōng* governs facing officials;
*Tiāngāng* governs killing and punitive expeditions;
*Tàiyī* governs gold and treasures;
*Shèngxiān* governs ancestral rites;
*Xiǎojí* governs marriages and gatherings;
*Chuánsòng* governs arrests and captures;
*Cóngkuí* governs death and mourning;
*Wēimíng* governs summons and recruitment.
Furthermore, concerning the twelve generals (*shí'èrzhàng*):
*Tiānyī* is an Earth general;
The first ahead, *Téngshé*, is a Fire general;
The second ahead, *Zhūquè*, is a Fire general;
The third ahead, *Liùhé*, is a Wood general;
The fourth ahead, *Gōuchén*, is an Earth general;
The fifth ahead, *Qīnglóng*, is a Wood general;
The first behind, *Tiānhòu*, is a Water general;
The second behind, *Tàiyīn*, is a Metal general;
The third behind, *Xuánwǔ*, is a Water general;
The fourth behind, *Tàishang*, is an Earth general;
The fifth behind, *Báihǔ*, is a Metal general;
The sixth behind, *Tiānkōng*, is an Earth general.
*Tiānyī* has already been explained above.
*Téngshé* governs fear and panic;
*Zhūquè* governs documents;
*Liùhé* governs celebrations;
*Gōuchén* governs restraint and obstruction;
*Qīnglóng* governs blessings and assistance;
*Tiānhòu* is still *Shénhòu*,
the consort of *Tiānyī*.
*Tàiyīn* governs private matters;
*Xuánwǔ* governs death and illness;
*Tàishang* governs gifts and rewards;
*Báihǔ* governs disputes and lawsuits;
*Tiānkōng* governs emptiness and depletion.
The nine spirits of Dùnjiǎ are:
Tiānféng is in Kǎn,
also named Zǐjīng,
a wood spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Pòjūn star.
Tiānnèi is in Kūn,
also named Zǐchéng,
a water spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Pòjūn star.
Tiānchōng is in Zhèn,
also named Zǐqiáo,
a metal spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Pòjūn star.
Tiānfǔ is in Xùn,
also named Zǐwén,
an earth spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Wǔqǔ star.
Tiānqín is in Kūn,
also named Zǐgōng,
a fire spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Liánzhēn star.
Tiānxīn is in Qián,
also named Zǐxiāng,
a wood spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Wénqǔ star.
Tiānzhù is in Duì,
also named Zǐwéi,
a water spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Lùcún star.
Tiānrèn is in Gèn,
also named Zǐjīn,
a metal spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Jùmén star.
Tiānyīng is in Lí,
also named Zǐshā,
an earth spirit.
In the Big Dipper, it resides in the Tānláng star.
From Tiānféng downwards,
these are all names of stars.
Zǐjīng means
that Zǐ and Wǔ form the warp and weft of heaven and earth.
Since its position is in Kǎn,
it is therefore named Jīng.
Tiānnèi Zǐchéng means
Kūn is Earth.
It can bring all things to completion.
Tiānchōng Zǐqiáo means
Qiáo describes movement.
Qiáo is the image of movement in Zhèn.
Tiānfǔ Zǐwén means
Xùn is the command,
possessing elegant writing.
Tiānqín Zǐgōng means
it resides in the position of the five earths,
affiliated with Kūn.
Earth is the father of all things,
hence it is called Gōng.
Tiānxīn Zǐxiāng means
Xiāng is goodness.
Qián is Heaven,
it bestows mercy, hence it is good.
Tiānzhù Zǐwéi means
Duì governs metal.
Metal has the quality of killing and cutting,
thus it deviates from the way of Heaven.
Tiānrèn Zǐjīn means
Gèn is in Chǒu,
Chǒu is the origin of metal.
Tiānyīng Zǐshā means
Lí is fire.
Fire has the meaning of burning.
The Dùnjiǎ Classic says:
Tiānféng is suitable for settling borders and ensuring stability.
Tiānnèi is suitable for following the Way and making friends.
Tiānchōng is suitable for leading armies and ambushing enemies.
Tiānfǔ is suitable for performing rituals and establishing teachings.
Tiānqín is suitable for praying for blessings and removing evil.
Tiānxīn is suitable for avoiding illness and seeking medicine.
Tiānzhù is suitable for hiding troops and holding fast to defenses.
Tiānrèn is suitable for celebrating audiences and facilitating wealth.
Tiānyīng is suitable for long journeys and making merry.
The names of the nine spirits
all begin with "Tiān" above,
and all have "Zǐ" below because
these spirits belong to the Northern Dipper,
and are all subordinate to Heaven.
Zǐ is an honorific title,
because these spirits are esteemed and beautiful.
Kǒngzǐ Yuánchén says:
The first spirit of the Northern Dipper
is named Xīshénzǐ.
The second spirit
is named Zhēnwénzǐ.
The third spirit
is named Lùcúnzǐ.
The fourth spirit
is named Shìhuìzǐ.
The fifth spirit
is named Wèibùlínzǐ.
The sixth spirit
is named Wēihuìzǐ.
The seventh spirit
is named Dàjǐngzǐ.
These are also all called Zǐ.
Chūnqiū Zuǒzhùqī says:
The first star spirit is named Zhíyīn,
surname Jǐngliáng.
The second star spirit is named Dǒuliàng,
surname Yīyúdāng.
The third star spirit is named Jùlǐ,
surname Yīngwǎnglíngxǔ.
The fifth star spirit is named Fángwǔ,
surname Jīyǐndǔ.
The sixth star spirit is named Kāibǎo,
surname Chī,
also named Cāng'érbù.
The seventh star spirit is named Zhāo,
surname Féituōluòpéng.
The names of these seven stars
are all related to a person's birth year,
and should be constantly remembered and recited
to seek blessings.
The Huángdì Bāshéntú says:
The Qián spirit Xuānyuán,
the minister and envoy of Heaven,
resides in the planet Chén.
The Duì spirit Shíxíng,
the envoy of the Northern Dipper,
resides in the Niú star,
and governs carriages and grindstones.
The Kūn spirit Zhāoyáo,
the Grand Duke's envoy of Heaven,
resides in the Jiǎo star,
and governs killing and harm.
The Lí spirit Hàoshí,
the wandering and fierce envoy of Heaven,
resides in the Yì star.
The Xùn spirit Tiānhòu,
the law-enforcing envoy of Heaven,
resides in the Zī star.
The Zhèn spirit Léigōng,
the surveillance envoy of Tàiyīn,
resides in the Qī star.
The Gèn spirit Qǔlóng,
the envoy of the Eastern Brightness of the Celestial Lord,
resides in the Kuí star.
The Kǎn spirit Xiánchí,
the Rain Master's envoy of Heaven,
resides in the Jǐng star and governs rain.
These are the spirits of the eight envoys.
When women give birth,
it is forbidden to face downwards towards them.
These are also the spirits of the Nine Palaces.
Since spirits are pure and ethereal,
they wander without a fixed abode.
Therefore, within the palaces,
their appearances vary at different times.
Since the Eight Trigrams are associated with the Five Elements,
the methods of divination for these various spirits are recorded here.
Each has its own separate annotations,
so there is no need here
for a detailed explanation of the meanings of their names.
Thus, it is only briefly discussed.
As for the sun, moon, stars,
wind, rain, thunder, lightning,
mountains, rivers, and sacred peaks,
wells, stoves, and humble gates,
as well as the numerous spirits within the human body,
those venerated and sacrificed to by emperors,
and those prayed to by the common people,
such examples
are very many in number and name.
Regarding their relationship to the Five Elements,
there is no separate meaning.
Therefore, they are not fully explained.
Moreover, the various spirits used in divination and calendrical calculations,
which are precisely those influencing the past and present years and months,
and the turning points of the seasons,
also do not require a comprehensive discussion,
nor a laborious interpretation.
These preceding spirits
are the guiding principles for divination
and the essential theories of the Three Powers.
Therefore, they are described in sequence.
From ancient times until now,
the Five Dì (五帝) discussed
are generally of three types.
The Hétú (河圖) says:
The Eastern Qīngdì (青帝) is
Líng Wēiyǎng (靈威仰),
the Wood Dì.
The Southern Chìdì (赤帝) is
Chì Biāonù (赤熛怒),
the Fire Dì.
The Central Huángdì (黃帝) is
Hán Shūniǔ (含樞紐),
the Earth Dì.
The Western Báidì (白帝) is
Bái Zhāojù (白招拒),
the Metal Dì.
The Northern Hēidì (黑帝) is
Yè Guāngjì (叶光紀),
the Water Dì.
Táo Huáyáng (陶華陽) says:
There are five brothers: Huáng Bó (皇伯), Huáng Zhòng (皇仲), Huáng Shū (皇叔), Huáng Jì (皇季), and Huáng Shǎo (皇少).
These are Líng Wēiyǎng (靈威仰) and the others;
these Wǔdì (五帝) are all celestial deities.
They descend to govern the world,
overseeing deities and spirits,
succeeding each other in order,
and governing the Tàiwēi Gōng (太微宮).
Their essence forms the seats of the Wǔdì (五帝).
The five planets receive their qi (氣) according to the reigning king.
These are those worshipped in the Míngtáng (明堂).
Therefore it is said:
"Wénwáng (文王) is worshipped in the Míngtáng (明堂),
paired with Shàngdì (上帝)."
The Lǐjì (禮記) says:
"In the months of spring,
its Dì (帝) is Dàhào (大暭).
In the months of summer,
its Dì (帝) is Yándì (炎帝).
For the central earth,
its Dì (帝) is Huángdì (黃帝).
In the months of autumn,
its Dì (帝) is Shàohào (少暭).
In the months of winter,
its Dì (帝) is Zhuānxū (顓頊)."
The Eastern Dàhào Páo Xīshì (大昊庖羲氏) presides over spring,
he is the lord of the verdant essence.
The Southern Yándì Shénnóngshì (炎帝神農氏) presides over summer,
he is the lord of the crimson essence.
The Central Huángdì Xuānyuánshì (黃帝軒轅氏) presides over the four seasons,
he is the lord of the yellow essence.
The Western Báidì Jīntiānshì (白帝金天氏) presides over autumn,
he is the lord of the white essence.
The Northern Hēidì Zhuānxūshì (黑帝顓頊氏) presides over winter,
he is the lord of the black essence.
The Yì (易) says:
"The Dì (帝) emerges from Zhèn (震)."
This likely refers to the beginning of human Dì (帝),
starting with Fúxī (伏羲).
In the order of the Wǔxíng (五行),
Wood comes first.
The four seasons alternate,
with spring as the head.
Therefore, Páo Xī (庖羲) is the first of the Wǔdì (五帝).
Furthermore, various historians consider Shàohào (少昊), Zhuānxū (顓頊), Gāoxīn (高辛), Táng (唐), and Yú (虞)
to be the Wǔdì (五帝).
This likely refers to the Dì (帝) who succeeded each other according to the Wǔxíng (五行) before Shùn (舜).
The Yìjīng (易經) takes Fúxī (伏羲) at the top,
and Yú Shùn (虞舜) at the bottom,
but does not mention the three Dì (帝) in between,
because they followed existing practices and made no original creations.
How could they be spoken of?
Therefore, they are not discussed.
Dàhào Dì Páo Xī (大昊帝庖羲)
had the surname Fēng (風).
His mother, Huáxū (華胥),
stepped in a giant's footprint
and gave birth to the Dì (帝) in Chéngjì (成紀).
He had the body of a serpent and the head of a human.
With the virtue of Wood, he reigned over All Under Heaven,
becoming the first of all kings.
The Yì (易) says:
"The Dì (帝) emerges from Zhèn (震)."
Zhèn (震) is Wood,
the East presides over spring,
symbolizing the brightness of the sun.
Therefore, he is called Dàhào (大昊).
Following the patterns of turtle shells,
he drew the Bāguà (八卦).
He created nets and snares for hunting and fishing.
In ancient times,
humans and animals ate each other,
causing much harm.
The Dì (帝) observed spiders' webs,
and taught the people to capture sacrificial animals
to fill their kitchens.
Therefore, he is called Páo Xī (庖犧).
He is known as Xīhuáng (羲皇).
Later generations distorted the sound,
calling him Fú Xī (伏犧),
or sometimes Mì Xī (宓羲).
Another name for him is Xiónghuángshì (雄皇氏).
The Xiàojīng Gōumìngjué (孝經鈎命決) says:
"Fúxī (伏羲) had a 'sun-horn' forehead, 'pearl-balance' eyebrows, and wore a 'victory crown'."
The Lǐ Hánwénjiā (禮含文嘉) says:
"Fúxī's (伏羲) virtue permeated heaven and earth.
Heaven responded with patterns of birds and beasts,
and earth responded with turtle scripts.
Fúxī (伏羲) then imitated these patterns to create the Bāguà (八卦)."
Yándì Shénnóngshì (炎帝神農氏)
had the surname Jiāng (姜).
His mother, Rèn Sì (任姒),
was named Nǚ Dēng (女登).
She was moved by a divine dragon and gave birth to the Dì (帝) at Chángyáng (常羊).
He had the body of a human and the head of an ox.
Succeeding Wood with Fire,
his position was in the South, presiding over summer.
Therefore, he is called Yándì (炎帝).
He created the plow and plowshare,
and first taught the people agriculture.
He tasted and distinguished various herbs and trees,
teaching people to eat grains,
replacing the need for sacrificial animals.
Therefore, he is called Shénnóng (神農).
Another name for him is Kuíwěishì (魁㠕氏).
He is known as Nónghuáng (農皇).
The Lǐ Hánwénjiā (禮含文嘉) says:
"Shénnóng (神農) established the way of farming,
using plows and plowshares.
Heaven responded with auspicious grains,
and earth brought forth sweet springs."
Huángdì Xuānyuánshì (黃帝軒轅氏)
had the surname Jī (姬).
His mother, Fù Bǎo (附寶),
saw a great flash of lightning encircling the pivot star of the Běidǒu Shū Xīng (北斗樞星),
brightly illuminating the countryside.
Moved by this, she gave birth to the Dì (帝) at Shòuqiu (壽丘).
Succeeding Fire with Earth,
his position was in the center.
Therefore, he is called Huángdì (黃帝).
He regulated the five qi (氣) and established the five planets.
He was the first to institute clothing,
create boats and chariots,
and build houses.
In ancient times, people lived in nests and caves.
Huángdì (黃帝) changed this,
using upper beams and lower eaves,
to shelter from wind and rain.
Therefore, he is called Xuānyuán (軒轅).
It is also said
that he lived on Xuānyuán Qiū (軒轅之丘).
Thus, he was named after it.
Another name for him is Dìhóngshì (帝鴻氏),
or Guīcángshì (歸藏氏),
or Yǒuxióngshì (有熊氏).
The Chūnqiū Wényàogōu (春秋文燿鈎) says:
"Huángdì (黃帝) had a dragon-like face and received the Tiāntíng (天庭).
He patterned himself on the central constellations,
and took Wénchāng (文昌) as his emblem."
The Lǐ Hánwénjiā (禮含文嘉) says:
"Huángdì (黃帝) cultivated military prowess.
With his virtuous conduct,
a yellow dragon arrived,
and phoenixes came in stately procession."
Shàohào Jīntiānshì (少昊金天氏)
had the surname Jī (姬).
His given name was Zhì (摯),
and his courtesy name was Qīngyáng (靑陽).
His mother, Nǚ Jié (女節),
saw a great star, like a rainbow, descend to Huázhǔ (華渚).
She dreamt she conceived and, moved by this, gave birth to the Dì (帝).
Succeeding Earth with Metal.
Therefore, he is called Jīntiān (金天).
He is the Báidì Zhū Xuān (白帝朱宣) mentioned in the Túchèn (圖讖).
His position was in the West, presiding over autumn.
Metal possesses brightness,
occupying the Xiǎoyīn (小陰) position.
Therefore, he is called Shàohào (少昊).
The Wényàogōu (文燿鈎) says:
"Dì Kù (帝嚳) carried the shield,
this is called 'clear brightness'.
He initiated regulations and changed the measures.
This likely symbolizes Zhāoyáo (招搖)."
Zhuānxū Gāoyángshì (顓頊高陽氏)
had the surname Jī (姬).
His mother, Jǐng Pú (景僕),
saw the Yáoguāng Xīng (搖光星) pierce the moon like a rainbow.
Moved by this, she gave birth to the Dì (帝) by the Ruò Shuǐ (若水).
Succeeding Metal with Water,
his position was in the North, presiding over winter.
Therefore, he is called Zhuānxū (顓頊).
The Wényàogōu (文燿鈎) says:
"Zhuānxū (顓頊) combined the gàn (幹),
patterning himself above on the moon and the constellation Cān (參),
gathering majesty to establish the records,
to govern Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽)."
These Wǔdì (五帝) are thus those associated with the five directions in the rites.
Dì Kù Gāoxīn-shì was surnamed Jī.
He was born with divine peculiarities,
and called himself Qūn by name.
He made wood succeed water,
and named officials according to the Five Phases,
hence he was called Gāoxīn.
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
Gāoxīn had prominent teeth
and possessed sagely virtue.
He was able to follow the three luminaries.
Dì Yáo Táotáng-shì was surnamed Qí.
His mother, Qìngdū,
encountered a red dragon at Luòzhǔ,
conceived, and after fourteen months,
gave birth to the Emperor in Dānlíng.
His given name was Fàngxūn.
He made fire succeed wood.
His elder brother, Dì Zhì,
was enfeoffed in Táng.
Therefore, he was called Táotáng-shì.
The Wényào Gōu says:
Yáo had eight-colored eyebrows,
which was called 'penetrating brightness'.
He calendared the sun and moon,
and established and measured achievements.
The Lǐ Hán Wénjiā says:
Yáo's influence spread widely to the four extremities,
reaching even the tortoises and dragons.
Dì Shùn Yǒuyú-shì was surnamed Yáo.
His mother, Wòdēng, saw a great rainbow,
conceived, and gave birth to the Emperor at Yáoxū.
His given name was Chónghuá,
and his courtesy name was Dūjūn.
His eyes had double pupils,
hence he was named Chónghuá.
He made earth succeed fire.
Yáo enfeoffed him in Yú,
hence he was called Yǒuyú-shì,
and he established garments of five colors.
The Wényào Gōu says:
Shùn had double pupils.
This was called 'penetrating integrity',
corresponding above to Shè tí
to govern the three luminaries.
The Lǐ Wénjiā says:
Shùn diminished himself
to bring peace to the common people,
attracting birds and beasts to gather,
and phoenixes to come in stately procession.
These three Emperors, along with Shǎohào and Zhuānxū,
are collectively the Five Emperors.
The Shǐjì considers Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng as the Three August Ones,
and Huángdì and those after him as the Five Emperors.
The Dìwáng Shìjì
considers Xī Huáng, Shénnóng, and Huángdì as the Three August Ones,
and Shǎohào and those after him as the Five Emperors.
Now, examining the Lǐjì,
the suburban sacrifice matches the Five Virtues.
From Fúxī to Zhuānxū are the Five Emperors.
This is their correct position.
The reason for this is
that the Yì states that the Emperor emerges from Zhèn.
This is the beginning of the Five Virtues.
Following the sequence,
when it reaches Zhuānxū,
the number of the Five Virtues is complete.
If Shǎohào is taken as the beginning,
then Metal is not the first of the Five Virtues.
If Huángdì is taken as the beginning,
Earth resides in the center,
fundamentally not the originator.
Therefore, starting with Wood as the first,
Fúxī is the head of the Five Virtues.
The Yì's statement is correct.
From Dì Kù downwards,
they all succeeded each other in sequence.
There are five Heavenly Emperors.
The surnames and deeds of Língwēiyǎng and others,
and the distant年代 of Fúxī,
are lost in historical records,
and cannot be fully explained.
However, the Five Virtues succeeding each other
means receiving the bright mandate of Heaven,
which must be preceded by auspicious omens
to illuminate a prosperous era.
If the rulers who receive the mandate
all inherit the essence of the Five Emperors of Tàiwēi,
and are born into the world,
there must be prior signs
to show their omens.
When Wood reigns, it is the son of Cāngdì.
When Fire reigns, it is the son of Chìdì.
When Earth reigns, it is the son of Huángdì.
When Metal reigns, it is the son of Báidì.
When Water reigns, it is the son of Hēidì.
Therefore, the Lùtú says:
The Cāngdì of the East
has the form of a Azure Dragon.
His person has a long head,
a face with prominent large horn-like bones,
and broad and full eyebrows and back.
He follows Metal and grants Fire.
The Chìdì of the South
has the form of a Vermilion Bird.
His person has a pointed head,
a round face, square jaw, wide eyes,
small above and broad below,
and a beard and mustache reaching his chest.
He follows Water and grants Earth.
The Huángdì of the Center
has the form of Xuānyuán.
His person has a square face, broad forehead,
a sharp chin, slack lips,
and a broad and thick back.
He follows Wood and grants Metal.
The Báidì of the West
has the form of a White Tiger.
His person has a square forehead,
a straight face, pointed mouth,
a large nose, and small horns.
He follows Fire and grants Water.
The Hēidì of the North
has the form of Xuánwǔ.
His person has a narrow face, pointed head,
deep eyes, thick ears,
a hanging belly, and upward-turned wings.
He follows Earth and grants Wood.
These all symbolize the energies of the Five Phases,
and are transmitted in their sequence.
The Gǎnjīng Fú says:
The Cāngdì appears broad when viewed from a distance,
and extensive when seen up close.
The Chìdì appears fiery when viewed from a distance,
resplendent,
and pointed at the top when seen up close.
The Huángdì appears small when viewed from a distance,
and large,
broad, thick, and squarely proportioned when seen up close.
The Báidì appears bright when viewed from a distance,
and flourishing when seen up close.
The Hēidì appears gigantic when viewed from a distance,
and delicate when seen up close.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says:
When the Azure Essence is in charge,
it resembles the Jupiter star.
When the Red Essence is in charge,
it resembles the Mars star.
When the Yellow Essence is in charge,
it resembles the Saturn star.
When the White Essence is in charge,
it resembles the Venus star.
When the Black Essence is in charge,
it resembles the Mercury star.
These are all the Five Virtues relying on the Five Phases,
transmitted from parent to child.
If they are not in the correct sequence,
there will inevitably be conquest and destruction,
and they will not endure.
Qín, with the virtue of Metal, conquered Zhōu,
but perished after two generations.
Hàn, with the virtue of Fire, succeeded Zhōu,
and conquered the false Metal of Qín.
Therefore, its dynasty lasted long.
If it follows this sequence,
then there will be auspicious omens.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says:
Yáo was the essence of Fire,
thus Qìngdū conceived by encountering a red dragon and gave birth.
The Hàn dynasty, when Kǒngzǐ captured a Qílín,
obtained diagrams and writings that said:
The Jī-Zhōu will perish,
the radiance of Fire (Liú) will rise,
and the Emperor will be Mǎo Jīn.
Therefore, Gāozǔ killed a white snake,
and the divine mother cried out:
