"The son of the Red Emperor has killed my son of the White Emperor!"
Guāngwǔ revived the dynasty by being moved by the Chìfú Fú.
These are all signs of the virtue of Fire.
The responses to the other four phases
are all similar.
The auspicious omens for emperors of past dynasties are numerous,
and cannot be fully recounted.
Now, we briefly discuss the Five Emperors,
and their correspondence to the Five Phases as such.
Since the Three Sovereigns (Sān Huáng) and Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì),
the records of officials have not been consistent.
This is all due to auspicious omens [fúruì],
and different appellations [mínghào].
Sometimes they were named after birds and dragons,
sometimes after clouds and fire.
They all looked up and observed, and looked down and examined,
establishing offices based on events.
Although the eras were not uniform,
the Five Phases [wǔxíng] were never mistaken.
As for Zhuānxū,
he recorded officials based on human affairs.
The Southern Magistrate Chóng (Nánzhèng Chóng) supervised the heavens, attributing them to the spirits,
and the Northern Magistrate Lí (Běizhèng Lí) supervised the earth, attributing it to the people.
Thus, spirits and people were not separated.
The Gāoxīn Clan (Gāoxīn Shì) established officials named after the Five Phases.
They made Gōumáng the Magistrate of Wood (Mùzhèng),
Zhùróng the Magistrate of Fire (Huǒzhèng),
Rùshōu the Magistrate of Metal (Jīnzhèng),
Xuánmíng the Magistrate of Water (Shuǐzhèng),
and Hòutǔ the Magistrate of Earth (Tǔzhèng),
each managing their respective duties.
The Shàohào Clan (Shàohào Shì) had four sons:
Chóng, Gāi, Xiū, and Xī.
Chóng became Gōumáng,
the spirit of the Wood Office.
Gāi became Rùshōu,
the spirit of the Metal Office.
Xiū and Xī together became Xuánmíng,
the spirit of the Water Office.
A son of the Zhuānxū Clan (Zhuānxū Shì) was named Lí,
who became Zhùróng,
the spirit of the Fire Office.
A son of the Gònggōng Clan (Gònggōng Shì) was named Gōulóng,
who became Hòutǔ,
the spirit of the Earth Office.
These five spirits, when alive, served as high dukes,
and after death, became honored spirits.
They are also called the Five Sacrifices (Wǔ Sì),
and are already matched with the Five Phases.
The Book of Zhōu (Zhōu Shū) says:
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) was building Luòyì, but it was not yet completed.
The spirits of the four seas all gathered and said,
"The King of Zhōu (Zhōu Wáng) is divine and sagely,
he should know our names.
If he does not, we will ruin him with floods and droughts."
The next year, it rained and snowed for more than ten *xún* (ten-day periods),
with a depth of more than one *zhàng*.
Five *dàfū* rode in chariots,
followed by two riders, and stopped at the king's gate.
Tàigōng said,
"The chariots and riders leave no tracks;
this signifies a transformation of men."
He then sent someone to offer them gruel and said,
"We do not know the rank of our esteemed guests."
The accompanying riders said,
"First to enter is the Controller of the South Sea (Nánhǎi Yù),
next is the Controller of the East Sea (Dōnghǎi Yù),
next is the Controller of the North Sea (Běihǎi Yù),
next is the Controller of the West Sea (Xīhǎi Yù),
next is Hébó,
next is Fēngbó,
next is Yǔshī."
King Wǔ asked Tàigōng,
"What are all their names?"
Tàigōng replied,
"The spirit of the South Sea is named Zhùróng,
the spirit of the East Sea is named Gōumáng,
the spirit of the North Sea is named Xuánmíng,
the spirit of the West Sea is named Rùshōu."
The Lǐjì Yuèlìng says:
In the months of spring,
their spirit is Gōumáng;
in the months of summer,
their spirit is Zhùróng;
for the central earth,
its spirit is Hòutǔ;
in the months of autumn,
their spirit is Rùshōu;
in the months of winter,
their spirit is Xuánmíng.
This is correct.
These are the spirits of the five directions,
matched with the Five Phases.
Furthermore, the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) established the offices of the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng),
symbolizing the three stars of the Sāntái constellation.
Fēnghòu was assigned to the Upper Platform (Shàngtái),
Tiānlǎo to the Middle Platform (Zhōngtái),
and Wǔshèng to the Lower Platform (Xiàtái).
He also established two supervisors, Left and Right.
This also refers to the Five Phases.
The Four Stewards (Sì Sī) divided the management of the four directions,
which is the method of the four seasons.
Yáo had the four sons of Yìhé [Yìhé Sìzǐ],
who were assigned to manage the duties of the four seasons and four sacred mountains,
and were called the Four Sacred Mountains (Sì Yuè).
Tàigōng said:
The Grand Tutor (Tàishī)
is a minister of the heart and belly,
the person he employs is an outstanding individual.
Therefore, he is called "Pre-Doubter" (Qiányí),
always standing in front,
resolving doubtful matters.
The Grand Historian (Tàishǐ)
is a minister of the ears and eyes,
the person he employs observes and listens,
he is a successor.
Therefore, he is called "Post-Receiver" (Hòuchéng),
always standing at the back,
receiving the lord's transgressions,
and seeking verification from heaven.
The Grand Guardian (Tàifù)
is a minister of claws and teeth,
the person he employs guards and protects,
he is a hero.
Therefore, he is called "Left Supporter" (Zuǒfǔ),
assisting the lord in lacking matters,
standing on the left,
warding off difficulties for the sovereign.
The Grand Protector (Tàibǎo)
is a minister of feathers and wings,
the person he employs observes and investigates,
he is a cautious individual.
Therefore, he is called "Right Helper" (Yòubì),
always standing on the right,
assisting the lord against evil.
Once the Four Assistants (Sì Fǔ) are established,
the king is secure and does nothing,
and the common people are aided and unharmed.
If the Four Assistants are not complete,
it is like fighting a tiger without preparation,
or crossing a river without a boat.
If the king
does not know the affairs of ancient and modern times,
or the strategies of distant lands,
does not consult with the feudal lords,
does not understand speech,
or acts not in accordance with regulations,
the Grand Tutor contends with him.
If he does not know the changes in heaven, the movements of stars and calendars,
the movements and stillness of celestial officials,
the sounds of bells and pitches,
the strange phenomena of mountains and rivers,
or the inauspicious disasters,
the Grand Historian presents celestial patterns
to contend with him.
If he issues edicts
that do not conform to the laws and regulations of the former kings,
is impolite to his great ministers,
perverts the Way for the people,
or administers punishments unfairly,
only trusts himself and acts arbitrarily,
is not solemn in governing,
or does not care for his ministers and servants,
the Grand Guardian contends with him.
If he ascends the chariot without the harmony of the phoenix bells,
bows and yields not in accord with the jade pendants,
engages in excessive banquets and reckless riding,
is immersed in wine and women,
is disrespectful in the ancestral temple,
lacks proper decorum in carriages and attire,
or has no moderation in court,
the Grand Protector contends with him.
These are the officials of the four seasons,
the divided duties of the Four Sacred Mountains.
The "Pre-Doubter" presides over summer,
the "Post-Receiver" presides over winter,
the "Left Supporter" presides over spring,
and the "Right Helper" presides over autumn.
During the time of Táng-Yú,
official titles already numbered one hundred.
The Shàngshū says:
"The hundred officials are well-ordered."
The Xià and Yīn dynasties set the number
at one hundred and twenty,
in accordance with the great numbers of Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang.
Thus there were the Sān Gōng (Three Dukes), Jiǔ Qīng (Nine Ministers), twenty-seven Dàfū (Grand Masters), and eighty-one Yuánshì (Primary Scholars).
Three multiplying three
altogether made one hundred and twenty.
The Dìwáng Shìjì says:
Yīn Tāng asked Yī Zhì,
"In ancient times, why were the Sān Gōng, Jiǔ Qīng, Dàfū, and Lièshì established?"
Zhì replied:
"The Sān Gōng participate with the ruler in royal affairs;
the Jiǔ Qīng participate with the Sān Gōng;
the Dàfū participate with the Jiǔ Qīng;
the Yuánshì participate with the Dàfū.
Thus, they participate and participate again.
This is called 'venerating affairs.'
If 'venerating affairs' is not lost,
then internal and external are as one."
He also asked:
"How far apart are they?"
Zhì replied:
"The Sān Gōng possess wisdom that penetrates Heaven and Earth,
responding to changes without limit,
and discerning the nature of all things.
Their words are sufficient to regulate Yin and Yang and the four seasons,
and to moderate wind and rain.
Those who are like this
are elevated to be Sān Gōng.
Therefore, the affairs of the Sān Gōng
are always rooted in the Way (Dào).
The Jiǔ Qīng
do not neglect the four seasons,
they clear canals,
repair dikes,
plant five grains,
understand geography,
and are able to make beneficial what is not beneficial.
Those who are like this
are elevated to be Jiǔ Qīng.
Therefore, the affairs of the Jiǔ Qīng
are always rooted in Virtue (Dé).
The Dàfū
enter and exit sharing the same image with the people,
taking and giving sharing the same understanding with the people.
They understand human affairs,
act within the bounds of propriety,
do not injure with their words.
Their words are sufficient to serve as a model for the world,
and do not harm themselves.
They open passes and bridges, and fill granaries and treasuries.
Those who are like this
are elevated to be Dàfū.
Therefore, the affairs of the Dàfū
are always rooted in Benevolence (Rén).
The Yuánshì
understand righteousness and do not miss opportunities,
they achieve merit without acting selfishly.
They are upright and offer strong remonstrance,
without deceit or fraud.
In private, they uphold public good,
and can establish laws and regulations.
Those who are like this
are elevated to be Yuánshì.
Therefore, the affairs of the Yuánshì
are always rooted in Righteousness (Yì).
When Dào, Dé, Rén, and Yì are established,
then the world is set right."
He also said:
"The Sān Gōng are ministers like the thighs and arms;
the Jiǔ Qīng are ministers like the hands and feet;
the Dàfū are ministers like the sinews and veins;
the Yuánshì are ministers like the muscles and flesh."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Sān Gōng resemble the Five Great Mountains (Wǔ Yuè);
the Jiǔ Qīng are modeled after the rivers and seas (Héhǎi);
the twenty-seven Dàfū are modeled after hills and mounds (Shānlíng);
the eighty-one Yuánshì are modeled after valleys and peaks (Gǔfù).
The Sān Gōng in heaven are the Sān Néng stars;
the Jiǔ Qīng are the Běidǒu (Northern Dipper);
the likes of Shàowēi are the Dàfū;
the likes of Lángwèi are the Yuánshì.
Altogether, the great number of one hundred and twenty exists."
The Héchén Tú says:
"Heaven does not stand alone;
Yin and Yang move together,
assisting and establishing order,
combining into two sixes,
taking three as the elevation point.
Therefore, the Sān Néng six stars,
two by two,
become the Sān Gōng.
Three times three makes nine,
and the Yang essence arises.
Therefore, the Běidǒu nine stars
become the Jiǔ Qīng.
Three nines are twenty-seven,
hence there are Shètí, Shàowēi, Sīkōng, Zhífǎ, and the Wǔ Zhūhóu.
Their stars number twenty-seven,
making up the Dàfū.
Nine nines are eighty-one.
Hence the inner array, Bèi Wèi,
Gédào Lángwèi,
and those who assist and support the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),
eighty-one stars, become the Yuánshì.
In total there are one hundred and twenty officials.
Below, they correspond to the twelve months.
Their numbers, warp and weft,
are all established by the flowing qi of the five essences to form the official court."
The Shàngshū says:
"Establish the Tàishī, Tàifù, and Tàibǎo;
these are the Sān Gōng.
They discuss the Way, manage the state,
and harmonize Yin and Yang.
Officials are not necessarily complete [in number],
but depend solely on the person."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Elevate the noblest in the world
to be Sān Gōng.
The noblest of a state
to be Jiǔ Qīng.
The noblest of a district
to be twenty-seven Dàfū.
The noblest of a community
to be eighty-one Yuánshì."
The Gǎnjīng Fú says:
"If the Sān Gōng are not the right people,
then mountains collapse and the Sān Néng stars shift.
If the Jiǔ Qīng are not the right people,
then rivers burst their banks and Fǔxīng Jiǎo stars are disturbed.
If the Dàfū are not the right people,
then hills and mounds collapse and the Shàowēi stars, etc., have anomalies.
If the Yuánshì are not the right people,
then valleys and peaks are destroyed and Fúkuāng is lost.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler
looks up to Heaven for its images,
and looks down to Earth for its laws.
In between, he selects the worthy and capable
to appoint them.
If the right people are appointed,
then the country prospers and the people are at peace.
If the wrong people are appointed,
then the state is in danger and the people suffer."
The Yì says:
"The tripod breaks a leg,
overturning the duke's broth."
This metaphor for the Sān Gōng,
losing the right person is like a tripod breaking a leg,
unable to hold anything.
The *Zhōu Guān* says:
The Heavenly Officer is the *Zhǒngzǎi*,
The Earthly Officer is the *Sītú*,
The Spring Officer is the *Zōngbó*,
The Summer Officer is the *Sīmǎ*,
The Autumn Officer is the *Sīkòu*,
The Winter Officer is the *Sīkōng*.
The *Zhǒngzǎi* presides over accounts,
The *Sītú* presides over land,
The *Zōngbó* presides over rites and music,
The *Sīmǎ* presides over military affairs,
The *Sīkòu* presides over punishments,
The *Sīkōng* presides over construction.
Kǒngzǐ said:
The office of *Zhǒngzǎi*
serves to perfect the *dào*,
The office of *Sītú*
serves to perfect virtue,
The office of *Zōngbó*
serves to perfect benevolence,
The office of *Sīmǎ*
serves to perfect sagacity,
The office of *Sīkòu*
serves to perfect righteousness,
The office of *Sīkōng*
serves to perfect rites.
When the *dào* is applied, the state is well-governed;
When virtue is applied, the state is secure;
When benevolence is applied, the state is harmonious;
When sagacity is applied, the state is tranquil;
When rites are applied, the state is stable;
When righteousness is applied, the state is successful.
Therefore, when subordinates are not managed,
and the division of duties is unclear,
the laws and regulations are not uniform,
and all affairs lose their order—this is called disorder.
If there is disorder, the *Zhǒngzǎi* is to be embellished.
When the land is not cultivated,
wealth and goods do not multiply,
the myriad people suffer from hunger and cold,
education and transformation are not carried out,
customs are scattered and chaotic,
and the people are displaced and scattered—this is called peril.
If there is peril, the *Sītú* is to be embellished.
When fathers and sons are not close,
the order between elders and youths is lost,
and rulers and ministers, superiors and subordinates,
are estranged and have differing intentions—this is called disharmony.
If there is disharmony, the *Zōngbó* is to be embellished.
When the worthy and capable lose their official positions and titles,
meritorious service goes unrewarded,
soldiers harbor resentment,
and the military is weak and useless—this is called injustice.
If there is injustice, the *Sīmǎ* is to be embellished.
When punishments are violent and chaotic,
and the treacherous and evil are not overcome—this is called unrighteousness.
If there is unrighteousness, the *Sīkòu* is to be embellished.
When measures are not accurate,
undertakings are unreasonable,
cities and villages are not maintained,
and resources are mismanaged—this is called poverty.
If there is poverty, the *Sīkōng* is to be embellished.
Thus, the ancient kings
would regularly, in the last month of winter,
examine virtue and rectify laws,
to observe governance and disorder.
If virtue was abundant, they would amend the laws;
If virtue was not abundant, they would adjust the administration.
Thus, laws and administration flourished and did not decline.
The *Huáinánzǐ*, "Tiānwén Piān," says:
The East is the Field Officer,
The South is the *Sīmǎ*,
The West is the *Dàlǐ*,
The North is the *Sīkōng*,
The Center is the Metropolitan Officer.
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* says:
Wood is the *Sīnóng*,
Fire is the *Sīmǎ*,
Earth is the *Sīkōng*,
Metal is the *Sītú*,
Water is the *Sīkòu*.
These are all matched with the Five Phases.
The *Zhōu Guān* assigns the *Zhǒngzǎi* to accounting,
and the *Sītú* to land,
both having the meaning of the center,
which is consistent with the ideas in *Huáinánzǐ* and *Fánlù*.
The Spring Officer presides over rites and music;
Rites equalize superiors and subordinates,
music harmonizes human emotions.
All these are benevolence.
Therefore, it is said:
The office of *Zōngbó* serves to perfect benevolence.
Benevolence belongs to Wood and the East.
The *Huáinánzǐ* and *Fánlù*
both assign the agricultural officer,
taking spring as the origin of agriculture.
The Summer Officer presides over military affairs;
The fierce and violent nature of fire
is the image of warfare.
However, punishments are assigned to the *Sīkòu*.
The *Sīmǎ* regulates through rites,
presiding over but not applying punishments.
The *Huáinánzǐ* and *Fánlù* are consistent here.
The Autumn Officer presides over punishments;
The intrinsic nature of metal
is to govern killing and cutting.
The *Dàlǐ* in *Huáinánzǐ*
also governs punishments.
For the *Fánlù* to have the *Sītú* (in this context)
is a different name but the same function.
Therefore, it is said:
By the awe of the season,
the *Dàlǐ* and *Sītú* are perfected.
The Winter Officer presides over construction;
In winter, all things are stored away,
and all artisans return to their places.
Thus, implements are made
to supply the king's affairs.
The *Huáinánzǐ*'s explanation is similar.
The *Fánlù* considers it the *Sīkòu*,
meaning an officer who enforces laws,
requiring an impartial person,
just as water can be level and balanced.
Therefore, it is said:
If the law enforcer is partial,
and not impartial, he is punished.
Thus, Earth overcomes Water.
This means its Water takes the meaning of impartiality.
Although the Five Movements succeed each other,
and official titles change with the generations,
the functioning of the Five Phases,
and their principles remain consistent.
This is why Yǔ pacified the great flood,
personally taking on the role of *Sīkōng*;
the nine regions submitted tribute,
and Bó Yí was *Zhìzōng*,
surely performing the three rites;
Xìe became *Sītú*,
reverently spreading the five teachings;
Gāoyáo was *Shìshī*,
clearly applying the penal code.
With such divisions of duties,
the *Zhōu Guān*'s ministers are examples of this.
From ancient times,
the number of officials started from three,
and reached a maximum of eighty-one,
because yang completes at three,
and reaches its extreme at nine.
Thus, there were three *gōng* and nine *qīng*.
Nine times nine is eighty-one,
the extreme number of the *huángzhōng* pitch pipe.
Therefore, senior officials take the initial numbers,
while junior officials use the final numbers.
The reason one is not mentioned is that
one is the primordial *qì*,
belonging to the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven is called the "primordial head,"
because there is one and no second.
The *Shàngshū* says:
How bright is the primordial head!
A minister is not the primordial one.
Thus, it starts from three.
The *Zhōu* stopped at six *qīng*
to encompass the six directions.
According to the six *qì*, six treasuries were established.
This is due to different eras,
and does not go beyond the Five Phases.
Furthermore, during the three dynasties, official appointments
all stopped at nine.
Thus, there were three grades of *shì*.
A lower *shì* had one *mìng*,
a middle *shì* had two *mìng*,
an upper *shì* had three *mìng*.
There were three grades of *dàfū*.
A lower *dàfū* had four *mìng*,
a middle *dàfū* had five *mìng*,
an upper *dàfū* had six *mìng*.
Those above *qīng* also had three.
A junior *qīng* had seven *mìng*,
a grand *qīng* had eight *mìng*,
a *gōng* had nine *mìng*.
Three times three is nine,
also using the proper number of yang.
In later generations, *mìng* was taken as *pǐn*,
and also did not exceed nine.
But one was taken as the senior official,
and nine as the junior official.
Taking *mìng* as originating from a superior command,
it ranks lower official titles.
Therefore, a higher number indicated a higher *pǐn*.
This is the order of *pǐn*,
where one comes first.
Therefore, one is considered noble.
These are all the assignments of directions and numbers to the Five Phases.
Now we will discuss this.
Regarding the Tiāngān and Dìzhī as officials,
the Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn says:
Jiǎ is the Cāngcáo,
in charge of agricultural taxes.
Yǐ is the Hùcáo,
in charge of household numbers.
Bǐng is the Cícáo,
in charge of lawsuits.
Dīng is the Fùcáo,
in charge of prisons and arrests.
Wù is the Gōngcáo,
in charge of appointing and dismissing officials.
Jǐ is the Tiáncáo,
in charge of livestock.
Gēng is the Jīncáo,
in charge of money and currency.
Xīn is the Wèicáo,
in charge of the original envoys.
Rén is the Shícáo,
in charge of government and education.
Guǐ is the Jícáo,
in charge of collections and remittances.
Zǐ is the Chuánshè,
regarding comings and goings, respect and taboos.
Chǒu is the Sīkōng,
managing generals and governance.
Yín is the Shìguān,
for balancing prices and sales.
Mǎo is the Xiāngguān,
for personal affairs and the five teachings.
Chén is the Shǎofǔ,
for gold, copper, money, and currency.
Sì is the Yóutíng,
for delivering letters and relay stations.
Wǔ is the Wèiguān,
for chasing and arresting.
Wèi is the Chúguān,
where all a hundred flavors are prepared.
Shēn is the Kùguān,
for weapons and implements of war.
Yǒu is the Cāngguān,
for the five grains and accumulated stores.
Xū is the Yùguān,
where prohibitions and interrogations are fully equipped.
Hài is the Zǎiguān,
for storing things securely.
The Tiāngān and Dìzhī are assigned to offices,
all following their original Wǔxíng essence.
The meaning is generally understandable,
so there is no need for lengthy elaboration.
Yì Fèng said:
The office of the liver is the Wèicáo.
The nature of wood is benevolence.
The Wèicáo is in charge of soldiers,
and should therefore be benevolent.
The office of the heart is the Hùcáo.
The nature of fire is yang.
The Hùcáo is in charge of the rituals of marriage.
The office of the lungs is the Jīncáo.
The nature of metal is firmness.
It is in charge of copper and iron.
The office of the kidneys is the Cāngcáo.
The nature of water is yin, congealing and storing things;
the Cāngcáo performs autumn harvests.
The former kings, at the winter solstice, closed the passes,
not allowing merchants to travel.
This was to be cautious about yin qi.
The office of the spleen is the Gōngcáo.
The nature of earth is trustworthiness,
producing and receiving from the four directions.
The Gōngcáo serves the ruler with trustworthiness,
and imparts teachings to the four directions.
The Wèicáo, with the Yù and Sīkōng as its office,
is in charge of soldiers;
the prison detains fugitives.
If there is corruption,
then locusts will appear.
The nature of wood is quietness;
if it communicates with the common people,
then fish will be consumed by the people,
thus insects will follow their kind.
The Hùcáo, with the Chuánshè as its office,
is in charge of household registers.
The Chuánshè is in charge of guests.
If there is corruption,
then the people will leave their hometowns.
The Hùcáo is in charge of the people's benefits and households,
and gathers the people's benefits.
Therefore, all these are removed.
The Cāngcáo, with the Chú as its office,
is in charge of granaries and loans.
The Chú is in charge of receipts and payments.
If there is corruption,
then robbers will arise.
The Cāngcáo collects taxes from the people;
if they infringe upon and exploit the common people, they will become poor.
The Gōngcáo, with the Xiǎofǔ as its office,
is responsible for accounting with the four offices.
The Xiǎofǔ is also used together with the four offices.
Therefore, the Xiǎofǔ, as a granary, is in charge of receipts and payments, provisions and seeds.
The Gōngcáo has two offices.
This is why there are five offices and six treasuries.
The Yóujī, Tíngzhǎng, and external officials
all belong to the Gōngcáo.
If there is corruption,
then tigers and wolves will devour people.
The Gōngcáo's duty is in punishments.
If there is internal corruption,
then tigers, wolves, and robbers
will kill and plunder among the people.
Corruption above leads to chaos below.
The Jīncáo, with the Bīngzéi Sèfū as its office,
is in charge of suppression and arrests.
If there is corruption,
then there will be robbers in the city walls.
This arises from favoritism.
The Jīncáo is in charge of market taxes and infringement.
Therefore, the upper and lower levels collude.
Thus, market prices are unfair.
These are all derived from the Wǔxíng,
assigning the five zàng to the six fǔ.
Since they are all named offices,
they are explained here.
The Lǐjì, in the Lǐyùn chapter, states:
Humans are the virtue of heaven and earth,
the intersection of yin and yang,
the gathering of ghosts and spirits,
and the finest qi of the Wǔxíng.
Wénzǐ said:
Humans are the heart of heaven and earth,
the beginning of the Wǔxíng.
Therefore, they are born by receiving the qi of heaven, earth, and the Wǔxíng,
become the masters of all things,
and are paired with the two principles (heaven and earth) to form the three powers.
However, those who receive qi
each receive varying amounts.
Those who receive much wood qi
have a firm and upright nature, and harbor benevolence.
Those who receive much fire qi
have a fierce and ardent nature, and value propriety.
Those who receive much earth qi
have a broad and harmonious nature, and are trustworthy.
Those who receive much metal qi
have a resolute and decisive nature, and contain righteousness.
Those who receive much water qi
have a profound and hidden nature, and are full of wisdom.
The five qi gather and combine,
jointly forming their bodies.
If the qi is clear and sharp,
then the person is intelligent, quick-witted, and bright.
If it is murky and dull, then the person is foolish and stubborn.
Lǎozi said:
Yīn and Yáng's essential *qì* form humans.
Where *qì* is thick or thin,
those who receive a balanced and nourishing essence
give birth to worthy and wise people.
Those who receive disordered, turbid, and defiled *qì*
give birth to greedy and licentious people.
The Book of Destiny says:
Metal people are strong and self-reliant.
Wood people are often splendid and refined.
Water people are open and intelligent.
Fire people value themselves and are quick-tempered.
Earth people are loyal, trustworthy, and straightforward.
The Zhōu Shū says:
Humans are born when ten elements resonate:
the five elements of Heaven and the five elements of Earth,
which combine to make ten.
The five elements of Heaven become the Wǔcháng.
The five elements of Earth become the Wǔzàng.
Therefore, the Yì says:
They form images in Heaven,
and shapes on Earth.
The Jiāyǔ says:
Heaven is one, Earth is two, humans are three.
Three times three is nine.
Nine times nine is eighty-one.
One presides over the sun.
The sun's number is ten.
Therefore, humans are born in ten months.
Wénzi says:
Humans receive the transformations of Heaven and Earth and are born.
In one month, it becomes a paste.
In two months, it forms脉 (*mài*).
In three months, it becomes a fetus.
In four months, muscles form.
In five months, sinews form.
In six months, bones form.
In seven months, the form is complete.
In eight months, it moves.
In nine months, it becomes restless.
In ten months, it is born.
Once the physical body is formed,
the Wǔzàng take shape.
The outside is the exterior;
the inside is the interior.
The head is round, following the pattern of Heaven.
The feet are square, resembling Earth.
Heaven has four seasons, five elements, nine stars, and three hundred and sixty days.
Humans also have four limbs, five *zàng*, nine orifices, and three hundred and sixty joints.
Heaven has wind, rain, cold, and heat.
Humans also have joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.
Huáinánzi and Wénzi both say:
The gallbladder is like clouds.
The lungs are like *qì*.
The spleen is like wind.
The kidneys are like rain.
The liver is like lightning.
They are similar to Heaven,
with the heart as the master.
The ears and eyes are the sun and moon.
Blood and *qì* are wind and rain.
The Sùwèn says:
Humans pattern themselves after Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, the Sages align with Heaven above to nourish the head,
resemble Earth below to nourish the feet,
and imitate human affairs in the middle to nourish the Wǔzàng.
Heavenly *qì* connects to the lungs.
Earthly *qì* connects to the throat.
Wind *qì* connects to the liver.
Thunder *qì* connects to the heart.
Grain *qì* connects to the spleen.
Rain *qì* connects to the kidneys.
The six channels are like rivers.
The intestines and stomach are like the sea.
The nine orifices are like water.
If one patterns oneself after the principles of Heaven
and uses the logic of Earth,
then disasters and misfortunes will depart.
Zuǒ Cí's Physiognomy Says:
The human head is round, patterning after Heaven.
The feet are square, resembling Earth.
The left eye is the sun.
The right eye is the moon.
The left eyebrow is Qīnglóng.
The right eyebrow is Báihǔ.
The nose is Gōuchén.
The Fúxī is Zhūquè.
The Yùzhěn is Xuánwǔ.
It also says:
The front is Zhūquè.
The back is Xuánwǔ.
The left is Qīnglóng.
The right is Báihǔ.
These are called the Four Bodies.
The head is Gōuchén.
This is the master of the body.
It also says:
Behind the left ear is Tàishān.
Behind the right ear is Huàshān.
The forehead is Héngshān.
The back of the head is Héngshān.
The nose is Sōnggāoshān.
The Secret Physiognomy says:
The forehead is Héngshān.
The chin is Héngshān.
The nose is Sōnggāoshān.
The eyebrows are Dàishān.
The cheekbones are Kūnlúnshān.
The Two Instruments symbolize Heaven and Earth.
The Three Sections follow the Three Talents.
The Four Rivers govern the four seasons.
The Five Officials correspond to the five elements.
The Six Palaces conform to the six *lǜ*.
The Seven Gates match the seven stars.
The Eight Nodes derive from the eight winds.
The Nine Stations compare to the nine regions.
The Ten Fingers correspond to the ten days.
The Twelve Virtues resemble the twelve months.
The Twenty-Eight Sections correspond to the twenty-eight mansions.
The Jiāyǔ says:
Humans, at three months, are vaguely able to see,
and then their eyes can see.
At eight months, teeth emerge,
and then they can eat.
At one year, their kneecaps develop,
and then they can walk.
At three years, the fontanelle closes,
and then they can speak.
When *yīn* reaches its extreme, it reverts to *yáng*.
Therefore, *yīn* transforms with *yáng*.
When *yáng* reaches its extreme, it reverts to *yīn*.
Therefore, *yáng* transforms with *yīn*.
This is why boys grow teeth at eight months,
lose baby teeth at eight years,
and have their essence mature at sixteen,
and then they can reproduce.
Girls grow teeth at seven months,
lose baby teeth at seven years,
and transform at fourteen.
According to the Rites, men are capped at twenty,
having the beginnings of becoming a father.
Women are pinned at fifteen and promised in marriage,
having the way of becoming a mother.
All these follow the great numbers of Heaven, Earth, and the five elements.
Wénzi said:
In ancient times, Zhōnghuángzi said:
Heaven has five elements.
Earth has five peaks.
Sound has five tones.
Things have five flavors.
Colors have five patterns.
Humans have five ranks.
Therefore, between Heaven and Earth,
there are twenty-five kinds of people.
The top five are spirit-people, true-people, Daoist-people, ultimate-people, and sage-people.
The next five are virtuous-people, worthy-people, good-people, ordinary-people, and discerning-people.
The middle five are benevolent-people, ritualistic-people, trustworthy-people, righteous-people, and wise-people.
The next five are officials, commoners, farmers, merchants, and artisans.
The bottom five are multitudes, petty-people, incompetent-people, foolish-people, and flesh-people.
The top five and the bottom five
are like humans and cattle/horses.
A Sage
sees with their eyes,
hears with their ears,
speaks with their mouth,
and walks with their feet.
A True Person
sees clearly without looking,
hears acutely without listening,
speaks without uttering words,
and follows without walking.
Thus, what Sages use to move the world,
True People have never encountered.
What Worthy People use to correct worldly customs,
Sages have never observed.
Those called Daoist-people
have no front and no back,
no left and no right.
All myriad things are profoundly the same.
There is no right and no wrong.
Wénzǐ (文子) spoke of twenty-five types of people,
but the discussion provided only four [types],
which was not a complete explanation.
Now, based on various classics and books, a brief explanation is given.
The first five are called "divine people" (shénrén 神人).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"That which is unpredictable in yin and yang
is called shén (神, divine)."
Zēngzǐ (曾子) said,
"The refined energy of yang becomes shén (神)."
Shén (神) is defined by spiritual wisdom.
It means that their insight is like that of shén (神),
hence they are called shénrén (神人).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"Yáo's (堯) wisdom was like that of a shén (神)."
A "true person" (zhēnrén 真人)
is one whose nature aligns with the Dào (道),
who is as if possessing nothing,
and as if empty in reality.
They clearly understand the Great Simplicity (tàisù 太素),
reaching the ultimate state of effortless non-action (wúwéi 無為),
hence they are called zhēnrén (真人).
A "Dào person" (dàorén 道人)
Kǒngzǐ (孔zǐ) said,
"Their virtue is as vast as Heaven and Earth,
their capacity encompasses the sun and moon,
and no one can fathom them."
Having such virtue and capacity,
they are called dàorén (道人).
A "supreme person" (zhìrén 至人)
is truly straightforward and unadorned,
maintaining unity without wavering.
Good and evil cannot turn their thoughts,
honor and disgrace cannot stir their heart,
hence they are called zhìrén (至人).
A "sage" (shèngrén 聖人)
the Jiāyǔ (家語) states:
"Their virtue accords with Heaven and Earth,
their transformations are boundless,
they comprehend the beginning and end of all things,
they harmonize with the natural order of myriad beings,
they spread their Great Dào (大道),
and thereby complete innate dispositions.
Their brilliance rivals the sun and moon,
their transforming influence operates like shén (神);
people are unaware of their virtue,
and those who observe them do not recognize their goodness.
These are called shèngrén (聖人)."
Zhuāngzǐ (莊子) said,
"Taking Heaven as the origin,
taking virtue as the root,
taking the Dào (道) as the gateway,
and being clear about change,
is called a shèngrén (聖人)."
The next five are "virtuous people" (dérén 德人).
Their virtue extends to all beings,
enabling the common people to each obtain what they desire,
using it daily without knowing it.
They universally benefit without discrimination,
and are in harmony with Heaven and Earth.
The Yì (易) says,
"A great person (dàrén 大人)
is one whose virtue accords with Heaven and Earth,
whose brightness accords with the sun and moon,
and whose auspiciousness and inauspiciousness accord with spirits and deities (guǐshén 鬼神)."
This is called dé (德, virtue).
A "worthy person" (xiánrén 賢人)
is one whose wisdom encompasses all things,
and whose actions and stillness are reasonable.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"Their likes and dislikes share the feelings of the people,
their choices and rejections share the principles of the people,
their actions conform to rules and standards,
their words can serve as models.
They are not resentful as a common man,
nor arrogant as a feudal lord,
their Dào (道) is sufficient to transform the common people,
without harming themselves,
and they distribute wealth throughout the world without becoming poor.
These are xiánrén (賢人)."
A "good person" (shànrén 善人)
sees good as if they cannot reach it,
and their words fill the world without fault.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"They personally practice loyalty and trustworthiness,
yet their heart harbors no resentment.
They do not display benevolence and righteousness,
their aspirations are broad and extensive,
yet their demeanor shows no boastfulness.
Their thoughts are clear and insightful,
yet their words do not contend.
They diligently practice and trust the Dào (道),
striving tirelessly,
as if they can be surpassed,
yet cannot be caught up to.
These are junzǐ (君子, noble people)."
They are also called shànrén (善人).
A "middle person" (zhōngrén 中人)
serves their lord with a single mind,
thinking of giving their utmost loyalty when advancing,
and thinking of remedying faults when retreating.
They assent to what is good and rectify what is bad,
offending without concealment,
putting public before private,
and not boasting of their achievements.
These are zhōngrén (中人).
A "discerning person" (biànrén 辨人)
has inexhaustible wisdom and thought,
discerns good and evil with their emotions,
asks without obstruction or hesitation,
and speaks eloquently like a flowing stream.
They abandon evil and follow righteousness,
with nothing that can be hidden from them.
These are biànrén (辨人).
The middle five are "benevolent people" (rénrén 仁人).
As superiors, they do not boast of their accomplishments;
as subordinates, they are not ashamed of their humble state.
They practice compassionate giving and empathy,
and this does not diminish until the end.
These are rénrén (仁人).
A "ritual person" (lǐrén 禮人)
distinguishes between high and low,
is incorruptible, yielding, humble, and cautious.
They are respectful to their superiors,
and thoughtful in their respect for subordinates.
These are lǐrén (禮人).
A "trustworthy person" (xìnrén 信人)
is sincere and does not deceive.
A single word from them can settle a lawsuit.
When successful, they do not act recklessly;
when in straits, they do not change their principles.
These are xìnrén (信人).
A "righteous person" (yìrén 義人)
makes decisive distinctions,
always acts in accordance with reason,
follows good and rejects evil,
and encounters no obstacles in affairs.
These are yìrén (義人).
A "wise person" (zhìrén 智人)
has clear insight and deliberates thoughtfully,
examining and discerning the nature of things.
They can perceive nascent signs,
and foresee good and evil.
These are zhìrén (智人).
The next five are "officials" (shìrén 士人).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"One's knowledge should not be extensive without careful examination of its origin.
One's words should not be many without careful consideration of what they mean.
The mind has its firm resolves,
and plans have their adherence.
Although one may not fully grasp the fundamentals of Dào (道) and techniques,
one must have principles to follow.
Although one may not encompass all the beauty of a hundred good deeds,
one must have a place to stand.
Once actions are followed accordingly,
wisdom is known accordingly,
and words are understood accordingly,
then one's nature, destiny, form, and body will not be easily altered.
Wealth and honor are not enough to enhance one,
and poverty and lowliness are not enough to diminish one.
These are shìrén (士人)."
A "commoner" (shùrén 庶人)
is one who has not yet entered official positions,
still residing among the fields and furrows,
or who has just shed their common clothes
but has not yet been assigned a rank or title.
The Zhōulǐ (周禮) says,
"Commoners who are officials
are those who have just entered the ranks."
These are called shùrén (庶人).
A "farmer" (nóngrén 農人)
follows the Dào (道) of Heaven,
utilizes the benefits of the Earth,
plows in spring and harvests in autumn,
and is constantly engaged in planting and harvesting.
These are called nóngrén (農人).
A "merchant" (shāngrén 商人)
carries goods and trades in markets,
sells merchandise according to the times,
and exchanges expensive for cheap
to accumulate capital and property.
These are shāngrén (商人).
They are also called gǔrén (賈人).
An "artisan" (gōngrén 工人)
engages in carving, shaping, and skilled crafts,
producing various implements,
creating new ones and repairing old ones,
to earn wealth with their labor.
These are called gōngrén (工人).
Those of the five common folk below,
are all indiscriminately referred to as common folk.
Yù Ràng said,
“The Fàn Zhōngháng clan
treated me as a common person.”
“Xiǎorén” (small person) means
those who are base, vulgar, and act wickedly.
These are called xiǎorén.
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Jié and Zhòu, though emperors,
were still xiǎorén.”
Wénzǐ said,
“Those who conform to the norm are called jūnzǐ (noble persons);
those who do not conform to the norm are called xiǎorén.”
Though a jūnzǐ dies,
their name does not perish.
Though a xiǎorén gains power,
their crimes are not removed.
“Núrén” (dull person) means
dull and slow-witted.
It also refers to those named as criminals and servants.
In ancient times, those who committed crimes became slaves.
The Shàngshū says,
“If you are unprepared, I will enslave and kill you.”
This is to punish them.
Zhòu enslaved Jīzǐ;
this was also a killing and humiliation.
There are nú (dull) horses,
because of their dullness.
“Yúrén” (foolish person) means
arrogant, ignorant, and unknowing.
They cannot distinguish beans from wheat.
These are called Yúrén.
Kǒngzǐ said, “Their wisdom can be attained,
but their foolishness cannot be attained,”
because they are born with a muddled and turbid temperament,
not something gained through learning.
They are also called “yōngrén” (mediocre person).
Kǒngzǐ said,
“One whose heart does not store principles for beginning and end,
whose mouth does not utter words of instruction and regulation,
who does not choose the worthy to entrust their person,
who does not strive to act to establish themselves,
who sees the small and ignores the great,
and does not know what is harmful,
who follows things like a current,
and does not know what to uphold.
This is a yōngrén.”
“Ròurén” (flesh person) means
mad, foolish, and unperceiving;
unable to distinguish pain from itch;
though able to move and be still,
they are no different from mere flesh.
This is called a ròurén.
These twenty-five types of people,
due to receiving the qi of the Wǔxíng (Five Phases),
each have their superior and inferior qualities.
Thus there are many levels,
and good and evil differ.
Now we will temporarily divide them into four grades.
Those of shén, zhēn, dào, zhì, shèng, dé, xián (spirit, true, way, utmost, sage, virtue, worthy) – seven types –
are born from receiving the wángqì (royal qi).
Those of shàn, zhōng, biàn, rén, lǐ, xìn, yì, zhì (good, loyal, discerning, benevolent, polite, trustworthy, righteous, wise) – eight types –
are born from receiving the xiāngqì (ministerial qi).
Those of shì, shù, nóng, shāng, gōng (scholar, commoner, farmer, merchant, artisan) – five types –
are born from receiving the xiūqì (resting qi).
Those of zhòng, xiǎo, nú, yú, ròu (common, small, dull, foolish, flesh) – five types –
are born from receiving the qiúqì (imprisoned qi).
The wángqì is at its flourishing time.
Therefore, it is the most numinous and sacred.
The xiāngqì is slightly inferior to the wángqì.
Therefore, from shàn and zhōng downwards,
they submit to royal governance.
The xiūqì has already declined.
Therefore, it falls into the category of shì and shù.
The qiúqì is the most inferior.
Therefore, it falls into the category of zhòng and xiǎo.
Wénzǐ compares the higher to the lower,
likening people to animals.
This is also close to the truth.
However, these five qi,
have clear and turbid, righteous and evil, initial and final aspects.
If one obtains the righteous qi,
even if in a humble and inferior position,
they will become greatly good.
If one receives the evil qi,
even if in a respected and superior position,
they will give rise to great evil.
As for Jié overthrowing the Xià dynasty,
Zhòu destroying the Yīn clan,
Zhōu declining under Yōu and Lì,
Hàn being extinguished by Huán and Líng –
these are examples of those in respected positions who were evil.
Bearing a tripod in the Yīn ancestral temple,
fishing by Bān Xī,
a merchant in Nányáng,
tending oxen beneath a cart.
At these times,
their goodness was not yet seen,
but when they ascended to become teachers and advisors,
benevolence and sageliness shone forth equally.
Is this not those who were humble and lowly yet able to bring about great salvation?
As for those of xián and dé and above,
their qi is righteous and without evil.
Therefore they occupy the highest position.
However, at the beginning of the qi,
lifespans are long.
At the end of the qi,
fates are short.
These four qi also have four distinctions.
If superior and clear and refined,
spiritual wisdom is even higher.
If superior yet turbid and defiled,
then it requires cultivation and embellishment.
If inferior yet clear and refined,
it can be gradually polished to become an instrument.
If also muddled and turbid,
rotten wood cannot be carved again.
Combined with noble and humble, rich and poor, beautiful and ugly, good and evil, nature and temperament, age and destiny,
there are tens of thousands of paths.
All are caused by the interaction of the Wǔxíng qi.
Now, let us use Wénzǐ
to discuss these twenty-five grades,
as a scale of differences.
Other types beyond these
are difficult to fully distinguish.
“He who knows people is wise.”
“Only the Emperor finds it difficult.”
If not a clear sage,
who can discern them?
The Lù Mìng Jué says,
“Those born within the wángqì,
their human appearance is kingly and suitable for titles and emoluments.”
“Those born within the xiāngqì,
these people often hold official positions.”
“Those born within the sīqì (dead qi),
these people often suffer from illnesses and have short lives.”
These all discuss their birth month being during the flourishing or declining times of the Wǔxíng qi.
Moreover, regarding those who receive *qì*,
their human form, quality, disposition, bones, flesh, and internal organs
all resemble the Five Phases.
The physiognomy books say,
“Wood people are slender, long, and upright;
Fire people have small heads, full lower bodies, and are short;
Earth people have round faces and large bellies;
Metal people have square faces and *Duì* (兌) mouths.
Water people have thin faces, lopsided bodies, and walk like snakes.”
Green is the color of the Wood people;
if there is true white, it is a harmful *qì*.
Red is the color of the Fire people;
if there is true black, it is a harmful *qì*.
Yellow is the color of the Earth people;
if there is true green, it is a harmful *qì*.
White is the color of the Metal people;
if there is true red, it is a harmful *qì*.
Black is the color of the Water people;
if there is true yellow, it is a harmful *qì*.
When correlated with the heavenly stems, *Jiǎ*-*Yǐ* (甲乙) correspond to skin and hair;
*Bǐng*-*Dīng* (丙丁) to claws and tendons;
*Wù*-*Jǐ* (戊己) to flesh;
*Gēng*-*Xīn* (庚辛) to bones;
and *Rén*-*Guǐ* (壬癸) to blood and脉.
When correlated with the trigrams, *Qián* (乾) corresponds to the head;
*Lí* (離) to the eyes;
*Kǎn* (坎) to the ears;
*Duì* (兌) to the mouth;
*Kūn* (坤) to the abdomen;
*Xùn* (巽) to the hands;
*Gèn* (艮) to the thighs and knees;
and *Zhèn* (震) to the feet.
Their internal organs and dispositions
each have separate explanations.
However, people residing within Heaven and Earth,
amidst mountains and rivers,
each follow their directional location,
and their forms and dispositions are not equal.
Therefore, the people of *Dōngyí* (東夷)
have slender and long forms,
long eyebrows and long eyes;
their clothing and caps also prefer narrowness and length.
The people of *Dōnghǎi Gōulì* (東海勾麗)
have high and narrow caps,
adorned with bird feathers,
resembling tree branches.
Those with long eyes,
the eyes are governed by the liver;
the liver is Wood.
Thus, slender and long
all resemble Wood.
The people of *Nánmán* (南蠻)
are short, small, light, and have ravines;
they have high mouths and sparse hair;
their clothing also prefers shortness and lightness.
Those with high mouths,
the mouth and *rénzhōng* (人中) are governed by the heart;
the heart is Fire.
Fire flames upward.
Thus, high and flaming upward,
hence sparse hair.
The people of *Xīróng* (西戎)
have deep-set eyes and high noses;
they wear clothes but no caps.
The nose is governed by the lungs;
the lungs are Metal.
Hence, high.
The eyes are the liver;
the liver is Wood.
It is cut by Metal.
Hence, deep-set.
Metal governs cutting and severing.
Hence, hair is cut, and there are no caps.
The people of *Běidí* (北狄)
have high cheekbones and dishevelled hair;
their clothes are long.
The cheekbones are governed by the kidneys;
the kidneys are Water.
Hence, high cheekbones.
Dishevelled hair resembles flowing water.
Long clothes also resemble the movement of water.
The people of *Zhōngxià* (中夏)
have well-proportioned features,
resembling the peace and harmony of the earth.
Their clothing, caps, carriages, and attire
include all five colors,
resembling the Earth's virtue of encompassing the four elements.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"The people of the eastern border are called *Yí* (夷),
clever and cunning.
The people of the southern border are called *Mán* (蠻),
trustworthy and simple.
The people of the western border are called *Róng* (戎),
stubborn and rigid.
The people of the northern border are called *Dí* (狄),
fat and perverse.
The people of the Central States
live in peace and have harmonious tastes."
*Dìwáng Shìjì* (帝王世紀) says,
"Yáo (堯) banished *Gònggōng* (共工) to *Yōuzhōu* (幽洲)
to repel the *Běidí*.
He moved *Sānxí* (三苗) to *Sānwēi* (三危)
to repel the *Xīróng*.
He exiled *Huāndōu* (驩兜) to *Chóngshān* (崇山)
to repel the *Nánmán*.
He executed *Gǔn* (鯀) at *Yǔshān* (禹山)
to repel the *Dōngyí*."
*Chūnqiū Wényào Gōu* (春秋文燿鈎) says,
"*Qì* follows human form;
thus, the south is extremely warm,
its people have large mouths,
resembling the relaxed and expansive *qì*.
The north is extremely cold,
its people have short necks,
resembling the urgent and contracted *qì*.
The east, where rivers and valleys converge,
its people have small heads and *duì* (兌) shapes,
resembling small wood rising upwards.
The west, with its high earth where the sun and moon set,
its people have hairy faces,
resembling mountains with abundant grass and trees.
The center, where all four directions connect and rain and dew are bestowed,
its people have large faces,
resembling the flat and broad earth."
*Jiāyǔ* (家語) says,
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"People from hard earth are rigid.
People from soft earth are gentle.
People from marshy earth are large.
People from sandy earth are slender.
People from fertile earth are beautiful.
People from barren earth are ugly.
The south has immortal grass;
the north has ice that never melts;
the east has a land of *jūnzǐ* (君子);
the west has mutilated corpses;
the central land has many sages."
All these resemble their *qì*.
Therefore, it is said,
"Mountain *qì* produces many males;
marsh *qì* produces many females;
water *qì* produces many mutes;
wind *qì* produces many deaf people;
stagnant *qì* produces many with urinary retention;
wood *qì* produces many hunchbacks;
damp *qì* below riverbanks produces many with heel pain;
upright *qì* produces great strength;
rugged and dangerous *qì* produces many goiters;
cold *qì* produces longevity;
hot *qì* produces premature death;
valley *qì* produces many with numbness;
hill *qì* produces many mad people;
street *qì* produces many benevolent people;
mound *qì* produces many greedy people;
light earth makes for nimble feet;
heavy earth makes for slowness and dullness.
Fast water makes for light people;
slow water makes for heavy people."
All these are differentiated according to the *qì* of *Yīn* and *Yáng* and the Five Phases,
hence good and evil are distinguished.
The “traveling year” (yóu nián) has three names
but two distinctions.
The three names are:
first, yóu nián;
second, “moving year” (xíng nián);
and third, “standing year” (nián lì).
The name yóu nián
is defined by its continuous movement,
because it travels with the years
and does not settle in one place.
Nián lì is exactly xíng nián.
“Lì” (立) means to stand still,
because this year it stands at the North Star (Běichén).
From a human perspective,
it is constantly moving without rest.
Therefore, it is called xíng (行).
From a yearly perspective,
for this current year,
the year stands here,
hence it is called lì (立).
The two distinctions are:
yóu nián is counted from the eight trigrams (bāguà),
while nián lì proceeds from the sixty Jia-cycles (liùjiǎ).
As for the liùjiǎ:
males start from Bǐngyín (丙寅) and move left;
females start from Rénshēn (壬申) and turn right,
both stopping at their respective year count.
This indicates where the xíng nián arrives
and stands.
If one wishes to calculate and know this:
for males, add two to the actual age (shí nián), calculate, and count left;
for females, add one to the actual age, calculate, and count right.
Both start from the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) cycle
and continue until the calculation is complete.
This is the standing position (lì chù).
So, why do males start from Bǐngyín?
Because the sun is born in Yín (寅).
The sun is the essence of yang (yáng jīng).
Males follow yang.
Therefore, the sun is taken.
Bǐng (丙) is the greater yang (tài yáng).
Therefore, Bǐng is taken to match Yín.
Why do females start from Rénshēn?
Because the moon is born in Shēn (申).
The moon is the essence of yin (yīn jīng).
Females follow yin.
Therefore, the moon is taken.
Rén (壬) is the greater yin (tài yīn).
Therefore, Rén is taken to match Shēn.
Yang thus moves left;
yin thus turns right.
The Kǒngzǐ Yuánchén Jīng (孔子元辰經) states:
For the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) cycle,
males start from Bǐngyín,
females from Rénshēn.
For the Jiǎxū (甲戌) cycle,
males start from Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
females from Rénwǔ (壬午).
For the Jiǎshēn (甲申) cycle,
males start from Bǐngxū (丙戌),
females from Rénchén (壬辰).
For the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) cycle,
males start from Bǐngshēn (丙申),
females from Rényín (壬寅).
For the Jiǎchén (甲辰) cycle,
males start from Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
females from Rénzǐ (壬子).
For the Jiǎyín (甲寅) cycle,
males start from Bǐngchén (丙辰),
females from Rénxū (壬戌).
All these are called xíng nián.
These are methods for diagnosing illness,
not for common use.
As for yóu nián:
for males, one year starts counting from Lí (離).
Moving left through the eight trigrams:
two is at Kūn (坤),
three is at Duì (兌),
four is at Qián (乾),
five is at Kǎn (坎),
six is at Gèn (艮),
seven is at Zhèn (震),
eight is at Xùn (巽).
Xùn does not accept eight,
so it advances to Lí.
Lí then becomes eight,
Kūn becomes nine,
Duì becomes ten.
Counting in this sequence,
if one reaches Kūn,
Kūn does not accept one,
so it retreats to Lí.
Therefore, all counts up to ten
are in the cardinal directions.
For females, one year starts from Kǎn (坎) and moves right.
This is also like the Lí method:
Gèn (艮) does not accept eight,
Qián (乾) does not accept one,
all return to Kǎn.
The reason Xùn does not accept eight and
Kūn does not accept one is:
Kūn and Xùn are positioned
flanking the Lí palace.
Xùn is a yang position,
having the meaning of advance but not of end.
Eight is the final number of the trigrams,
therefore it is not accepted.
It is transferred to Lí.
Kūn is a yin position,
yin has retreat but no advance.
Retreat implies extinction.
It dare not take the number of the yang beginning.
Therefore, it yields and returns to Lí.
The reason Qián does not accept one and
Gèn does not accept eight is:
Qián is yang.
It is also heaven.
It is naturally at its beginning;
beginning is the meaning of one.
If repeated, the number becomes even,
and an even number becomes yin.
Therefore, it is transferred to Kǎn.
Gèn is yin.
Gèn is also mountain.
Mountain signifies the end.
When the yóu nián travels through the eight trigrams,
the trigram count ends at eight,
meaning it stops.
Since it has its own end,
it is illogical to accept it again.
Therefore, it is transferred to Kǎn.
Someone might ask:
In the movement of Tiānyī (天一),
Kǎn is considered the first palace (yī gōng),
and Lí the ninth palace (jiǔ gōng).
Why does the bāguà yóu nián use Lí as the first palace?
The answer is:
Tiānyī concerns the nine regions (jiǔ zhōu) of the world.
Therefore, it starts from one and proceeds.
Yóu nián concerns a person's life year (nián mìng).
Therefore, it starts from the end, nine.
Now, for female yóu nián, it starts from Kǎn;
for males, virtue encompasses beginning and end.
Therefore, both nine and one are counted,
starting from the position of the greater yang (tài yáng).
For females, yin gives birth to yang.
Therefore, it starts from its original yin position and proceeds.
The Kǎn position is fundamentally one,
receiving the number one and starting,
altogether making two,
which is a yin number.
The trigram reached by yóu nián
is then transformed three times.
The first transformation results in "calamity" (huòhài),
the second transformation results in "absolute death" (juémìng),
the third transformation results in "generating qi" (shēngqì).
Shēngqì is auspicious;
huòhài and juémìng are inauspicious.
If auspicious, one can go to that direction;
if inauspicious, one should avoid that place.
Huòhài means
that they mutually overcome and harm each other.
For example, Qián's initial nine Jiǎzǐ water
transforms into Xùn,
Xùn's initial six Xīnchǒu (辛丑) earth.
This means the "flying stellar omen" (fēi chén) comes
to overcome the "hidden stellar omen" (fú chén).
Kǎn's initial six Wùyín (戊寅) wood transforms into Duì,
Duì's initial nine Dīngsì (丁巳) fire.
This is the flying and hidden mutually harming.
Juémìng means
that the trigram body is overcome and restrained.
For example, Zhèn transforms into Duì.
Metal overcomes wood.
Gèn transforms into Xùn.
Wood overcomes earth.
Shēngqì means
that they mutually generate and have the same body.
For example, Qián transforms into Duì,
having the same body as metal.
Zhèn transforms into Lí.
Wood generates fire.
Huòhài and juémìng also have methods of aversion.
According to the trigram reached,
those that restrain it are warded off.
For example, to avoid military disaster (bīng zāi) by clashing fire,
one hangs a cypress wood
to ward off the death of Zhèn.
These are all proven effects of the mutual restraint of the five phases (wǔ xíng).
Yóu nián and nián lì
represent a person's life year.
All are matched with the five phases,
hence they are explained here.
The twenty-fourth chapter
discusses birds and insects (qín chóng), which is divided into two sections here.
All creatures that possess life and stir,
those with sentience,
none do not rely on the five *qì* to form their nature,
and depend on *Yīn* and *Yáng* to establish their form.
Thus, whether they dwell on land or in water,
whether hidden or visible, their paths diverge.
Whether they swim, soar, fly, or walk,
whether they are slow or swift, they differ.
All of this is due to the clarity or turbidity of their *qì*,
and the depth of their inherent nature.
The *Kǎo Yì Yóu* says:
Those with fangs and horns,
those with spurs and dangling barbs,
are all *yīn*.
*Yīn* possesses a killing *qì*.
Therefore, they are equipped with the venom of claws and teeth,
like stinging scorpions.
Those that fly and soar, with feathers and wings, gentle and good beasts,
are all *yáng*.
*Yáng* possesses a benevolent *qì*,
and no killing nature.
The *Jiā Yǔ* says:
Those that bite and swallow have eight orifices and are oviparous.
Those that chew and gnaw have nine orifices and are viviparous.
Those born in the daytime resemble the father;
those born at night resemble the mother.
The most *yīn* are female;
the most *yáng* are male.
All are compelled by *qì*.
All stirring creatures,
are collectively categorized as *chóng* (insects/worms).
Now, we briefly divide them into three types.
First is *qín* (birds),
second is *shòu* (beasts),
third is *chóng* (insects/worms).
Those with wings that fly are *qín*;
those with four legs that walk are *shòu*;
those without wings or legs are *chóng*.
As for the wings of a *fúyóu*,
the wings of a *jiāoliáo*,
flying centipedes,
mosquitoes and gnats with six limbs—
although these have wings and legs,
they are still considered *chóng*.
Those that are born in the morning and die in the evening,
those that arise from decay, filth, *gǔ* (poisonous insects), and dampness—
these are all born through transformation,
following their kind,
and are also all *chóng*.
The *Kǎo Yì Yóu* says:
A *chóng* transforms in eight days.
Thus, the present is shortened.
Furthermore, there are two names: birds and fish.
Regarding these two,
although their designations differ,
birds fly and soar,
which means they are *qín*.
Fish dive and swim,
belonging to the *chóng* category.
The *Jiā Yǔ* says:
Birds and fish are born of *yīn*,
but belong to *yáng*.
Therefore, they are all oviparous.
Fish swim in water,
birds soar in clouds.
Therefore, at the beginning of winter,
swallows and sparrows enter the sea,
transforming into clams.
This is their fundamental kind.
The name *qín* extends to *shòu*,
but the name *shòu* does not extend to *qín*.
Hence, we know that *qín* has the ability to move on the ground,
while *shòu* lacks the function of flying in the air.
However, there are many examples for these three classifications,
which cannot be fully explained here.
Now, let us first discuss the Five Spirits,
then match them with the hexagrams and the thirty-six *qín*.
The *Jiā Yǔ* says:
Among the three hundred and sixty feathered *chóng*,
the Fèng is their chief.
Among the three hundred and sixty hairy *chóng*,
the Qílín is their chief.
Among the three hundred and sixty armored *chóng*,
the Guī is their chief.
Among the three hundred and sixty scaly *chóng*,
the Lóng is their chief.
Among the three hundred and sixty naked *chóng*,
humans are their chief.
It also says:
The essence of hairy *chóng* is the Qílín;
the essence of feathered *chóng* is the Fèng;
the essence of armored *chóng* is the Guī;
the essence of scaly *chóng* is the Lóng;
the essence of naked *chóng* is the Sage.
Hairy *chóng* belong to the West;
feathered *chóng* to the South;
armored *chóng* to the North;
scaly *chóng* to the East;
naked *chóng* to the Center.
These are all referred to as *chóng*.
The Five Spirits are collectively the heads of all *chóng*.
Now we only mention four of them,
as humans are placed in the center,
meaning that among creatures with nature and feelings,
humans are the most important.
“Spirit” (靈) means divine and spiritual.
The five *qín* are the most spiritual among *chóng* and *shòu*,
hence they are called the Five Spirits.
The *Lǐjì Yuèlìng* says:
In spring, its *chóng* are scaly.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
This refers to the *Lóng* and *shé* (snake) species.
In summer, its *chóng* are feathered,
referring to flying birds.
In the center, its *chóng* are naked,
referring to the species of *hǔ* (tiger) and *bào* (leopard) with sparse fur.
In autumn, its *chóng* are hairy,
referring to the species of *hú* (fox) and *hé* (badger).
In winter, its *chóng* are armored,
referring to the species of *guī* (turtle) and *biē* (softshell turtle).
It also says:
When a monarch proceeds, the Zhūquè is in front,
the Xuánwǔ behind,
the Cānglóng to the left,
and the Báihǔ to the right.
The *Shàngshū Xíngdé Fàngyán* says:
The East in spring,
the Cānglóng, whose wisdom is benevolent.
The South in summer,
the Zhūniǎo, who loves ritual.
The West in autumn,
the Báihǔ, who upholds righteousness.
The North in winter,
the Xuánguī, who presides over trustworthiness.
The essence of the central earth converges.
The *Lǐyùn* does not discuss the five virtues,
but only distinguishes the Four Spirits.
The *Gōumìng Jué* says:
If benevolence is lost, the Lóng and Lín will not dance.
If ritual is lost, the Luán and Fèng will not soar.
If wisdom is lost, the Huánglóng will not appear.
If righteousness is lost, the Báihǔ will not emerge.
If trustworthiness is lost, the Xuánguī will not be seen.
The *Lǐjì* says:
The Lín, Fèng, Guī, and Lóng
are called the Four Spirits.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
The Lín and Fèng, the Five Spirits,
are auspicious omens for a king.
The *Lǐ* mentions Lín, Fèng, Guī, Lóng,
but the tiger is not seen.
In the Metal element, it refers to the tiger.
Its righteousness is then incomplete.
The Zhūquè in front
and Xuánwǔ behind are consistent.
The remaining three *chóng* all show discrepancies.
The Yuánmìng Bāo (元命苞) says:
Lí (離) is Fèng (鳳).
It also says:
Fèng (鳳) is the essence of fire.
The spiritual tortoise (靈龜) is born of water.
Xuánwǔ (玄武) belongs to the north.
This is consistent with the Lǐ (禮) texts.
Only the three, Lóng (龍), Lín (麟), and Hǔ (虎), are different.
The Azure Dragon (靑龍) on the left,
the White Tiger (白虎) on the right –
the old saying is not doubted.
The Yǎnkǒng Tú (衍孔圖) considers the Qílín (麒麟) to be the essence of wood,
but the Lóng (龍) is not of wood.
The Dàdài Lǐ (大戴禮) considers the Qílín (麒麟) to be a hairy creature,
and the Qílín (麒麟) further becomes metal.
If the Qílín (麒麟) is metal,
then the Hǔ (虎) is useless.
Gōngyáng Gāo (公羊高) considers the Qílín (麒麟) to be the essence of wood.
Wood is born of fire.
When the Master (夫子) compiled the Chūnqiū (春秋),
he stopped at the Qílín (麒麟).
How could he know it would be an auspicious omen for the Hàn (漢)?
This is not upheld now.
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) Yuèlìng Zhāngjù (月令章句) states:
The five beasts of the celestial officers are:
the Azure Dragon (蒼龍) on the left,
the appearance of Dàchén (大辰).
The White Tiger (白虎) on the right,
the pattern of Dàliáng (大梁).
The Vermilion Bird (朱雀) in front,
the body of Qúnhuǒ (鶉火).
The Dark Warrior (玄武) behind,
the substance of tortoise and serpent (龜虵).
In the center are Dàjiǎo Xuānyuán (大角軒轅),
the omen of Qílín (麒麟).
Also, the Lóng (龍) is born of water
and roams in wood.
The bird (鳥) is born of wood
and roams in fire.
The Qílín (麒麟) is born of fire
and roams in earth.
The Hǔ (虎) is born of earth
and roams in metal.
The tortoise (龜) is born of metal
and roams in water.
Nourishing its mother to bring forth its child
is the nature of the Five Phases.
Therefore, if one's demeanor is reverent and one's body benevolent,
then the Fènghuáng (鳳凰) will come to display themselves.
If one's words follow harmony and righteousness,
then the divine tortoise (神龜) will arrive.
If one's vision is clear and rites are cultivated,
then the Qílín (麒麟) will gather.
If one's wisdom listens to governance,
then the Yellow Dragon (黃龍) will appear.
If one's thoughts are keen and faith is established,
then the White Tiger (白虎) will be tamed.
These words are fitting.
The Lǐdǒu Wēiyí (禮斗威儀) says:
When one rules by metal,
Qílín (麒麟) are in the suburbs.
The Bǎoqián Tú (保乾圖) also says:
The year star (歲星) is Qílín (麒麟).
The Kǎoyì Yóu (考異郵) says:
The Qílín (麟) is the essence of yin.
These are all different.
Now, the explanation is that wood refers to touching.
It has the meaning of impinging and offending.
The Qílín (麟) has fleshy horns,
without anything to strike or butt.
The Lóng's (龍) horns are pointed without flesh,
having the meaning of striking or butting.
The Yì (易) imagery for Zhèn (震) is Lóng (龍).
Therefore, the meaning of wood supports the Lóng (龍).
The celestial officers have the omens of Xuānyuán (軒轅), Yellow Dragon (黃龍), and Qílín (麒麟).
Xìn (信) presides over earth,
cultivating the mother-child response.
This meaning is also consistent.
For those associated with the Hàn (漢),
the Hàn (漢) has the virtue of fire,
thus it is the child's response.
This means the virtue of earth supports the Qílín (麟).
The Yìtōng Guàyàn (易通卦驗) says:
At the beginning of autumn, the Hǔ (虎) first roars.
The Yǎnkǒng Tú (衍孔圖) says:
The Hǔ (虎) is the essence of metal.
The Dàdài Lǐ (大戴禮) says:
The Hǔ (虎) is born in the seventh month.
This corresponds to the yang numbers.
The Kǎoyì Yóu (考異郵) also says:
The striped patterns of the Hǔ (虎)
are a mixture of yin and yang.
The Hǔ (虎) is a hairy creature,
definitely a metal beast.
The Kǎoyì Yóu (考異郵) says:
Cān (參) and Fá (伐) are the virtues of the Hǔ (虎).
Their meaning is to cut down and harvest.
This is why school gates are called Hǔmén (虎門),
and a Hǔ (虎) is drawn on the gate.
Because Duì (兌) resides in the autumn direction.
Duì (兌) means thuyết (說).
It signifies explaining and speaking.
Thus, metal has the awe of killing and attacking,
and the Hǔ (虎) has the ferocity of poisoning and harming.
Therefore, the meaning of metal supports the Hǔ (虎).
Question:
The Yín (寅) position is in the east,
why does the White Tiger (白虎) suddenly reside in the west?
Answer:
Generally, the Five Phases are mixed;
there is no meaning of one existing in a single direction.
The east itself is the movement of wood.
Next, the White Tiger (白虎) resides in the west.
This is the awe of slaughter.
For example, Zhèn (震) is in the east,
directly associated with the Lóng (龍).
All six lines of Qián (乾)
are Lóng (龍) images.
Zhèn (震) takes its movement,
Qián (乾) likens the sage.
The Lóng (龍) itself possesses the virtues of flying and潛ing.
The images vary.
Therefore, there is no fixed standard.
As the Kǎoyì Yóu (考異郵) says, yin and yang are mixed,
it does not prevent them from being divided in the east.
These are all spiritual and connected,
hidden and manifest without fixity.
How can one be adhered to?
Shǐ Sū's (史蘇) Guī Jīng (龜經) says:
The wood spirit is the Azure Dragon (蒼龍),
the essence of the year star (歲星).
The fire spirit is the Vermilion Bird (朱雀),
the essence of the planet Huò (熒惑).
The ash-earth spirit
is named Téngshé (騰虵).
The earth spirit is Gōuchén (勾陣),
the essence of the planet Zhèn (鎭星).
The metal spirit is the White Tiger (白虎),
the essence of the planet Tàibái (太白).
The water spirit is the Dark Warrior (玄武),
the essence of the planet Chén (辰星).
The Azure Dragon (蒼龍) governs the head.
The Vermilion Bird (朱雀) governs the lips and neck.
Téngshé (騰虵) governs the chest and ribs.
Gōuchén (勾陣) governs the waist and abdomen.
The White Tiger (白虎) governs the thighs and knees.
The Dark Warrior (玄武) governs the feet and shins.
Examining these six spirits,
the Vermilion Bird (朱雀), Dark Warrior (玄武), Azure Dragon (蒼龍), and White Tiger (白虎)
are consistent with the Jīngwěi (經緯) texts.
Only the spirit of Gōuchén (勾陣)
has different wording.
However, the celestial officers have the star Gōuchén (勾陣)
within the Zǐwēi (紫微) enclosure,
thus it is the earth spirit.
This is what Cài Yōng (蔡邕) referred to
as the omen of the Qílín (騏驎).
Téngshé (騰虵) is at the end of fire
and at the beginning of earth,
and thus is the ash spirit.
Pairing the snake (虵) with the tortoise (龜),
they together form the Dark Warrior (玄武).
Without a cardinal direction,
it is the ash spirit.
Its pairing with head and feet, etc.,
takes east as the head,
thus the Lóng (龍) is paired with the head.
Turning southward in sequence,
thus the Dark Warrior (玄武) is paired with the feet.
As for animals and birds belonging to the eight trigrams,
the Yì says:
Qián is the horse,
Kūn is the ox,
Zhèn is the dragon,
Xùn is the chicken,
Kǎn is the pig,
Lí is the pheasant,
Gèn is the dog,
Duì is the sheep.
Qián is strong.
The horse is chosen for its strength.
Kūn is yielding.
The ox is chosen for its yielding nature.
Zhèn is movement.
The dragon is chosen for its movement.
Xùn is wind.
The chicken is in charge of commanding calls,
symbolizing the movement of wind.
Kǎn is yīn.
The pig is chosen for its yīn nature.
Lí is yáng.
The pheasant is chosen for its soaring flight.
Gèn is a gate.
The dog is chosen for its guarding and defense.
Duì is joy.
It is speech.
The sheep is chosen for its joy in eating grass.
Furthermore, Qián symbolizes six dragons,
taking the meaning of their concealment and leaping.
The Shuō Guà says:
The horse is chosen for its strong and healthy virtue,
for its strength.
Therefore, it is called a good horse.
Because it is a father, it is called an old horse.
Because it strives diligently without rest,
it is called a lean horse.
Because it has the function of transformation,
it is called a piebald horse.
However, the Kūn trigram
also refers to the constancy of a mare.
This only takes the meaning of compliance.
The meaning of the horse
is not limited to Qián and Kūn;
Zhèn also represents a good-neighing horse.
Because Zhèn has the sound of thunder,
it is the image of Zhèn thunder.
It is also a horse with white hind feet.
It is also said to be white-headed,
a horse with a white forehead.
This takes the meaning of its prominent brilliance.
Kǎn is a horse with a beautiful back.
Because it has an intercalary month in the middle,
therefore, the Shuō Guà pairs the dragon-horse
with many things.
It is believed that nothing travels the sky better than the dragon,
and nothing travels the earth better than the horse;
therefore, they symbolize many things.
Kūn refers to the mother and calf ox
to emphasize its reproduction.
Gèn is both the dog
and the rat.
The dog has the ability to guard.
The dog is what can stop,
the rat is what is stopped.
Both belong to Gèn.
Lí is the turtle, crab, snail, clam, and tortoise.
All are chosen for their armored appearance,
the meaning of yáng on the outside.
These are all coordinated with the Five Elements.
Therefore, they are explained here.
The second part
discusses the thirty-six animals.
The number of types of birds and insects
is very large.
Now, explaining the thirty-six
is generally based on the number of the liù jiǎ.
It is used in the Shì Jīng.
Its twelve categories are assigned to the twelve earthly branches.
Each branch has three animals.
Thus there are thirty-six animals.
The reason each branch has three
is to divide a day into three periods:
morning, daytime, and evening.
If one seeks by intention,
it should be that the twelve categories all occupy the daytime position,
not sometimes morning or sometimes evening.
Now, according to the method of the Shì Jīng,
taken by qì,
the first month (mèng) is in the evening,
the middle month (zhòng) is in the middle,
and the last month (jì) is in the morning.
This means the twelve categories correspond to the twelve earthly branches.
The remaining twenty-four
are assigned animals.
Because they do not occupy the branch position.
The reason the first month (mèng) is in the evening
is that mèng is the beginning of a season.
The qì is initially not strong,
only becoming strong towards zhòng.
Therefore it belongs to it.
Taking the qì near its peak,
thus it is in the evening.
The reason zhòng is in the daytime
is that its qì is strong in the middle.
The reason jì is in the morning
is that jì is the end of a season.
Its qì has already declined,
being initially close to zhòng,
still having royal power,
thus it belongs to the morning.
When it comes to the correct positions,
neither is lost.
Wáng Jiǎn said:
Zǐ morning is the swallow,
daytime is the rat,
evening is the bat.
Chǒu morning is the ox,
daytime is the crab,
evening is the turtle.
Yín morning is the civet cat,
daytime is the leopard,
evening is the tiger.
The Běn Shēng Jīng says:
Morning is living wood.
It also says:
Daytime is the tiger,
evening is the civet cat.
Mǎo morning is the hedgehog,
daytime is the rabbit,
evening is the badger.
One account says:
Morning is the fox.
The Běn Shēng Jīng says:
Evening is the crane.
Chén morning is the dragon,
daytime is the flood dragon,
evening is the fish.
Sì morning is the earthworm,
daytime is the common earthworm,
evening is the watersnake.
One account says:
Evening is the tortoise.
The Běn Shēng Jīng states:
Morning is red earth,
daytime is the snake,
evening is the cicada.
Wǔ morning is the deer,
daytime is the horse,
evening is the muntjac.
The Běn Shēng Jīng states:
Morning is the horse,
daytime is the deer,
evening is the muntjac.
Wèi morning is the sheep,
daytime is the eagle,
evening is the goose.
The Běn Shēng Jīng says:
Evening is old wood.
Shēn morning is the weasel,
daytime is the ape,
evening is the monkey.
One account says:
Morning is jade.
The Běn Shēng Jīng states:
Evening is dead stone.
Yǒu (酉) in the morning becomes a pheasant,
in the daytime it becomes a chicken,
in the evening it becomes a wild goose (yān 焉).
Another says,
in the morning it becomes a chicken,
in the evening it becomes a dead stone.
The Qínbiàn (禽變) says,
in the evening it becomes dead earth.
The Běnshēngjīng (本生經) says,
in the evening it becomes an owl (xiāo 䳒).
Xū (戌) in the morning becomes a dog,
in the daytime it becomes a wolf,
in the evening it becomes a jackal.
Another says,
in the evening it becomes dead metal.
The Qínbiàn (禽變) says,
in the evening it becomes dead fire.
Hài (亥) in the morning becomes a pig,
in the daytime it becomes a monkey (jué 玃),
in the evening it becomes a boar (zhū 猪).
Another says,
in the morning it becomes living wood,
in the daytime it becomes a pig,
in the evening it becomes a snail (yǐyú 蟻蝓).
Another says,
in the morning it becomes a piglet (tún 㹠),
in the daytime it becomes a wild boar (xián 𤠾).
Another says,
in the evening it becomes rotten wood.
Although the Běnshēngjīng (本生經) and Qínbiàn (禽變)
have differences in their original forms,
the positions of day and evening
logically follow the previous interpretations.
Zǐ (子) is for the rat, bat (yǐn 䴏), and flying fox (yì 犾翼),
their colors are all black.
This takes the color of water.
The nature of the rat is
to hide by day and roam by night.
This symbolizes the Yin energy.
It emerges from its hole,
and its head is often seen,
symbolizing the Yang energy beginning to stir at Zǐ (子),
desiring to be seen but still hidden.
The bat (yǐn 䴏) has red under its mouth,
symbolizing Yin containing Yang.
Its tail is split,
as the number of Yin is two.
It arrives at the spring equinox,
appearing with the Yang.
It hibernates at the autumn equinox,
hiding with the Yin.
The Lǐjì (禮記), Yuèlìng (月令) chapter, says,
“In the second month of spring,
the swallows (xuánniǎo 玄鳥) arrive.”
On the day they arrive, with a grand sacrifice (tàiláo 太牢),
they are offered to Gāoméi (高禖)
to pray for descendants.
“At the autumn equinox, the swallows (xuánniǎo 玄鳥) depart.”
This seeing in the second month
is Zǐ (子) punishing Mǎo (卯).
The Yìtōng Guàyàn (易通卦驗) says,
“The swallow (xuánniǎo 玄鳥) is a Yin bird.”
The flying fox (yì 犾翼)
is what an old rat becomes,
called an immortal rat.
The Fāngyán (方言) says,
“East of Guān (關),
it is called a flying fox (yì 犾翼).”
These three are all Yin insects,
thus they are all placed in Zǐ (子).
Chǒu (丑) is for the ox, crab, and turtle (biē 鼈);
Chǒu (丑) corresponds to Gèn (艮).
At the Jié (節) of Lìchūn (立春),
when agricultural work begins to thrive,
it is the strength of the ox.
Also, above it is the Niúxiù (牛宿) (Ox constellation).
The Shuōtící (說題辭) says,
“The ox performs Yin tasks,
pulling the plow to cultivate.”
Therefore, it is in Chǒu (丑).
The crab, at the time of Lìchūn (立春),
when mulberry trees put down roots,
is like its legs.
Gèn (艮) is a mountain;
Jùlíng (巨靈) and Bìxì (贔屓)
bear the spirit mountain on their heads,
and carry Mount Pénglái (蓬萊).
This is the giant crab.
The turtle (biē 鼈) is born from the essence of earth.
Soft inside and hard outside,
it symbolizes earth containing Yin and Yang.
Its yellow inner parts
are the color of earth.
The ox also has yellow,
and the crab's interior is also yellow,
all being the essence of earth.
Chǒu (丑) is in the northern water position,
thus it governs both water and earth.
Yín (寅) is for the tiger, leopard, and civet (lí 狸);
the shapes of these three beasts are all similar.
Yín (寅) is the wood position.
Wood rules thick forests.
Yín (寅) also belongs to Gèn (艮).
Gèn (艮) is a mountain,
where tigers reside.
The Jílíngjīng (集靈經) says,
“Yín (寅) is Lesser Yang,
its five colors are black and yellow.”
Yín (寅) also has generative fire,
and fire governs patterns and ornamentation (wénzhāng 文章).
The three beasts all have stripes,
all having patterns.
Above it is the Jīxiù (箕宿) (Sieve constellation).
Jī (箕) governs wind,
and the tiger's roar raises wind.
The Yì (易) says,
“Wind follows the tiger.”
The Jiāyǔ (家語) says,
“Three nines are twenty-seven,
seven rules the stars.”
“The stars rule the tiger.”
“Tigers are born in the seventh month.”
Shēn (申) clashes with Yín (寅).
Thus, the tiger is in Yín (寅).
The civet (lí 狸) and leopard follow as they are of the same kind.
