The Běnshēngjīng (本生經) says it governs wood,
because Yín (寅) has corresponding wood,
and it is the first month of growth.
Mǎo (卯) is for the rabbit, hedgehog (wèi 猬), and badger (hé 狢);
the rabbit is a Yang creature.
Residing in the moon,
it symbolizes Yin embracing Yang.
The Yuánmìngbāo (元命苞) says,
“The rabbit resides in the moon,
the qi (氣) of Kǎn (坎).”
Kǎn (坎) is in the Zǐ (子) position.
This is because Zǐ (子) punishes Mǎo (卯).
It belongs to Mǎo (卯).
An old rabbit becomes a hedgehog (wèi 猬),
and the badger (hé 狢) is also a rabbit-like creature,
thus they are all placed in Mǎo (卯).
Another says,
“The badger (hé 狢) is a fox.”
Foxes and badgers (hé 狢) are similar.
The Běnshēngjīng (本生經) mentions the crane (hè 鶴),
but this is a phonetic error for the character.
Chén (辰) is for the dragon, shark (jiāo 鮫), and fish;
Shēn (申) is the source of water,
Zǐ (子) is the middle stream,
Chén (辰) is the end of water,
like all rivers flowing east,
all returning to the sea.
The dragon can raise clouds and bring rain,
being the chief of aquatic creatures.
Without the sea, it cannot be contained,
thus it is divine and great.
Sharks (jiāo 鮫) and fish are also among the chief aquatic creatures,
thus they are all in Chén (辰).
Sì (巳) is for the snake, earthworm (shàn 蟮), and common earthworm (qiūyǐn 蚯蚓);
the Shìjīng (式經) says,
“Sì (巳) has the General of Tengshé (騰虵),”
and thus it is paired with it.
The snake is Yang.
Its original position is in the south.
The turtle is Yin.
Its original position is in the north.
Pairing the snake with the turtle
forms Xuánwǔ (玄武).
The two creatures together form one spirit,
paired as Yin.
Therefore, by number, it is in the north.
Earthworms (shàn 蟮) and common earthworms (qiūyǐn 蚯蚓) are all similar in shape.
The *Lǐjì* says,
“At the *Xiǎomǎn* season,
earthworms emerge and are seen.”
Shènzǐ says,
“Téngshé soars through the mist.”
This is similar to earthworms.
The Yellow Emperor had great borers (*dàmíng*),
like earthworms, to accord with the earth *dé*.
The *sì* terrestrial branch has the earth of parasitic growth.
Therefore, they are both assigned to it.
The *Běnshēngjīng* speaks of “earth”
as earth produced when combined with fire.
Upon examining various books,
the *shàn* (earthworm) is sometimes written as *tuó* (alligator).
The character *tuó* is again written as *chán* (cicada).
The *Běnshēngjīng* explains *chán* saying,
“Always hiding in water, fearing Luónà,
moaning sadly without speaking,
yet wishing to sing.”
Its sad moaning
is similar to that of a cicada.
Regarding its water dwelling,
it is similar to an alligator.
Examining its shape and connection to earth,
the *sì* terrestrial branch is associated with snakes, earthworms, and common earthworms,
which resemble alligators and cicadas.
This is all incorrect.
Also, the *Shèfùjīng* says,
“One who encounters a cicada is a water insect.”
It should be known that this refers to a maggot.
As for *wǔ* representing deer, horses, and musk deer:
*wǔ* represents great *yáng*,
and horses have round hooves,
symbolizing *yáng*.
*wǔ* is the heavenly path,
horses have swift feet,
and they travel long distances,
with males and females having specific times.
Therefore, the *Jiāyǔ* says,
“Eight times nine is seventy-two,
an even number supporting an odd one.”
The odd number rules the *chén* branch.
The *chén* branch is the moon.
The moon governs the horse,
and horses are born in the twelfth month.
*Chǒu* opposes *wèi*.
*Wèi* combines with *wǔ*.
Therefore, the deer’s cloven hooves in *wǔ*
symbolize *yīn*.
And its dwelling in a *yáng* position
symbolizes conceiving *yīn*.
The *Lǐjì*’s “Yuèlìng” chapter says,
“In the midsummer month,
deer shed their antlers.”
The *Yìwěi Tōngguàyàn* says,
“Deer are the *yáng* among beasts.”
They shed their antlers at the summer solstice.
The *Jiāyǔ* says,
“Four times nine is thirty-six,
six governs the *lǜ* (pitch-pipe),
and the *lǜ* governs the deer.”
Therefore, deer are born in the sixth month.
*Wèi* combines with *wǔ*.
Therefore, it is also in *wǔ*.
Musk deer and deer are of the same kind.
Hence, they are assigned to it.
Question:
In the assignment of animals to the Eight Trigrams,
*Lí* does not mention the horse.
Why, then, do animal transformations use *wǔ* for the horse?
Answer:
*Kūn* is the steadfastness of the mare.
Since *Kūn* is in *wèi*,
and *wèi* combines with *wǔ*,
the horse is therefore placed in *wǔ*.
Question:
*Qián* is also called horse,
and *Zhèn* is also called horse.
Why aren’t their combinations taken as well?
Answer:
Nothing travels over the earth more than the horse.
Since *Kūn* is earth,
its primary function is taken.
*Qián* is heaven and *Zhèn* is wood;
they are not earth bodies,
hence their combinations are not taken.
Question:
If this explanation is correct,
the six lines of *Qián*
are all called dragons.
Nothing travels through the heavens more than the dragon.
The dragon’s *dé* corresponds to *Qián*.
Why then is it suddenly placed in *chén*?
Answer:
If *wèi* were the horse,
your objection would indeed be valid.
But since the horse is in *wǔ*,
we directly take its combination.
The position of *Qián* is in *xū*.
*Xū* opposes *chén*.
Therefore, the dragon is assigned to *chén*.
Question:
*Kūn* takes a combination,
but *Qián* suddenly uses opposition.
This meaning is difficult to understand.
Answer:
*Kūn* is *yīn*.
It takes the meaning of being gentle, submissive, and following *yáng*,
hence it uses combination.
*Qián* is *yáng*.
The *yáng* body is strong and firm,
hence it uses opposition.
As for *wèi* representing sheep, hawks, and wild geese:
The *Shìjīng* says,
“*Wèi* is *Xiǎojí* (Small Auspiciousness).”
It governs marriage rituals and betrothal gifts.
Betrothal gifts include the use of sheep and geese.
Zhèng Xuán, in his commentary on the wedding etiquette, says,
“Wild geese observe *yīn* and *yáng*,
only flying when the time is right.”
The *Yì* considers *Kūn* to be sheep.
*Kūn* is in *wèi*.
The *Lǐjì*’s “Yuèlìng” chapter says,
“In the last month of summer,
hawks begin to practice.”
This is assigned based on observations.
The **Běnshēng Jīng** (本生經) says that a withered tree
refers to a tree that has not yet become a wooden tomb.
A tree withers and ages by the sixth month.
**Shēn** (申) representing monkeys, apes, and **yuán** (㹨),
because autumn signifies the killing **qì** (氣).
All things age and wither,
resembling the appearance of monkeys and apes.
All of them resemble old people.
In the seventh month, all mountain fruits ripen.
Monkeys and apes take advantage of this time to store food, thus becoming king.
The **Shì Jīng** (式經) says,
when the Metal **Qì** (氣) is flourishing,
it can age all things.
This is the appearance of monkeys and apes.
The **Jiāyǔ** (家語) says,
five nines are forty-five,
five represents sound,
and sound governs apes.
Apes are born in the fifth month.
In **Wǔ** (午) there is the Bathing Metal,
the killing **qì** (氣) is not yet strong;
by **Shēn** (申), Metal is king,
and the killing **qì** (氣) begins to strengthen.
It also says,
in fire there is no sound,
but once out of fire, its sound is formed,
hence it is associated with **Shēn** (申).
The **Běnshēng Jīng** (本生經) says that dawn represents jade,
because jade has a warm, lustrous, and resonant sound.
Therefore, it takes its dawn.
Dusk represents dead stone,
stone is a type of jade,
and also has a sound.
It refers to its **qì** (氣) waning,
hence it is called dead at dusk.
Both jade and stone are the essence of Metal,
thus both are assigned to the Metal position.
The **yuán** (㹨) is also of the same kind.
Therefore, it is assigned to it.
**Yǒu** (酉) represents chickens, pheasants, and crows,
because **Yǒu** (酉) is Metal,
used for martial might.
The chicken has five virtues,
with bravery as the first;
it will fight when it sees an enemy.
This is its inherent nature.
The **Shuōtící** (說題辭) says,
the chicken represents accumulated Yang,
an image of the South.
The fiery Yang essence ascends.
Thus, when Yang emerges, chickens crow,
responding by category.
The **Kǎoyìyóu** (考異郵) says,
the chicken is a fire animal,
**Chǒu** (丑) is near **Yín** (寅).
**Yín** (寅) Yang generates fire.
It crows out of joy.
Martial affairs must have commands,
hence it is in the West.
**Xùn** (巽) represents the chicken,
and also commands.
**Chén** (辰) and **Sì** (巳) combine with **Yǒu** (酉),
hence it is in **Yǒu** (酉).
The pheasant is a fire bird.
It embodies martial prowess.
The **Fāngjì Chuán** (方伎傳) says,
when **Tàibái** (太白) (Venus) shines brightly,
chickens crow;
when **Yínghuò** (熒惑) (Mars) glitters,
pheasants are startled.
The **Yìtōng Guàyàn** (易通卦驗) says,
the pheasant is Yang.
When the male crows, the female responds.
This signifies Yang initiating and Yin harmonizing.
When it crows, it is also a sign of command.
The crow is a Yin bird,
yet resides in the sun.
The **Yuánmìng Bāo** (元命苞) says,
the crow in the sun
symbolizes Yang embracing Yin.
Because it gains Yang **qì** (氣) in the sun,
it is benevolent and capable of filial regurgitation.
It is in **Yǒu** (酉) because
in spring, the sun approaches **Duì** (兌);
**Yǒu** (酉) is the gate of two and eight,
the place where the sun enters,
taking its end.
Therefore, all are assigned to **Yǒu** (酉).
It also says that dusk represents a dead right,
because its Metal **qì** (氣) wanes.
The **Qínbiàn** (禽變) says that dusk represents dead earth,
because Earth reaches the end of Metal,
and its **qì** (氣) declines and perishes.
The **Běnshēng Jīng** (本生經) says that dusk represents the owl,
because the owl also strikes swiftly and has martial uses.
It lacks the five virtues, hence it is at dusk.
**Xū** (戌) represents dogs, wolves, and jackals,
because **Xū** (戌) is twilight.
**Qián** (乾) is the Gate of Heaven.
As **Xū** (戌) belongs to **Qián** (乾),
at the time of dusk and darkness,
it is for vigilance.
**Jīng Shì Biéduì** (京氏別對) says,
dogs are for guarding,
to prevent evil.
The **Yì** (易) says,
**Gèn** (艮) is the dog.
As **Gèn** (艮) is a gate,
the dog is for guarding.
The **Jiāyǔ** (家語) says,
seven nines are sixty-three,
three governs the **Dǒu** (斗),
and the **Dǒu** (斗) governs dogs.
Dogs are born in the third month.
**Chén** (辰) clashes with **Xū** (戌),
and **Yín** (寅) combines with **Xū** (戌),
hence it is in **Xū** (戌).
The **Lǐjì Yuèlìng** (禮記月令) says,
in the ninth month,
the jackal sacrifices animals.
It is assigned based on this season.
Wolves are similar in form.
The **Shuōwén** (說文) says,
jackals belong to the wolf family.
Therefore, all reside in **Xū** (戌).
One theory says that dusk is dead Metal,
because Metal declines and perishes at **Xū** (戌).
The **Qínbiàn** (禽變) says that dusk is dead fire,
because **Xū** (戌) is the tomb of fire.
**Hài** (亥) represents pigs, boars, and wild boars,
The **Shì Jīng** (式經) says,
**Hài** (亥) represents mixed water,
an image of filth, turbidity, and a privy,
where pigs reside.
Pigs are black,
symbolizing the color of water.
Their cloven hooves
are an image of Yin.
They always rise at the fifth watch,
not deviating from their routine,
just as water has tides that do not miss their schedule.
The Jiāyǔ says:
"Six nines are fifty-four."
Four governs the hours (shí),
the hours govern the pig (shǐ).
Pigs are born in the fourth month.
As Sǐ is Chong, it is therefore in Hài.
Shǐ is the small kind of pig (zhū).
The yà also takes after its kind,
and is fond of nocturnal activity.
This is because of its yin nature.
Therefore, both are in Hài.
One explanation says that dān (旦) refers to "that which generates wood,"
as wood is generated in Hài.
Mù (暮) refers to the snail (qīyú),
but [犭＋俞] should be huì (𤠾).
Perhaps the character is mistaken.
Another explanation says that dān refers to tún (㹠),
and tún is the same as shǐ.
One explanation says that mù refers to "rotting wood,"
because wood initially grows soft,
and being submerged in water,
it thus rots.
Question:
The examples of birds and insects are numerous.
Why not choose the qílín (麟) and fènghuáng (鳳) for the属 (shǔ),
but instead choose earthworms, snakes, rats, and small insects?
Answer:
The reason for choosing the twelve shǔ
is that they all perceive the seasonal qi (qì) and timing,
either by color or form,
and all correspond to yin and yang.
The qílín and fènghuáng have already been matched with the Wǔlíng (五靈).
It is not that they are empty and unused.
Another question:
If the qílín and fènghuáng have already been matched with the Wǔlíng
and are therefore not chosen,
the lóng (龍) and hǔ (虎) are also matched;
why are they used again?
Answer:
When the lóng moves, clouds arise;
when the hǔ roars, wind stirs.
These respond to the qi of yin and yang.
This is why they must be chosen.
Although the qílín and fènghuáng are spiritual,
they do not cause any movement or activity,
and therefore are not used again.
The twelve shǔ
are all the qi of the Dǒuxīng (斗星).
They disperse to become human fate,
connected to the Běidǒu (北斗),
which is why they are used as the shǔ.
The Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū (春秋運斗樞) says:
"The Zhūxīng (樞星) disperses to become the lóng and mǎ (馬);
the Xuánxīng (旋星) disperses to become the hǔ;
the Jīxīng (機星) disperses to become the gǒu (狗);
the Quánxīng (權星) disperses to become the shé (虵);
the Yùhéng (玉衡) disperses to become the jī (雞), tù (兔), and shǔ (鼠);
the Héyáng (闔陽) disperses to become the yáng (羊) and niú (牛);
the Yáoguāng (搖光) disperses to become the hóu (猴) and yuán (猿)."
These all correspond to the celestial stars above,
and are linked to the annual destiny below.
The thirty-six birds and animals (qín)
each establish a direction,
acting as the chiefs of birds and insects,
leading three hundred and sixty,
which when multiplied by ten,
becomes three thousand six hundred.
All are matched with the Wǔxíng (五行),
and all are interconnected and lead each other.
Since they are not used for divination,
they will not be explained in detail here.
